{
  "timestamp":"2026-05-21T17:25:03.055Z",
  "message":{
    "content":[{
        "type":"tool_result",
        "content":"1\t# 306 — Lua language spec implementation (reference spec)\n2\t\n3\t## Status\n4\topen\n5\t\n6\t## Current behavior\n7\tLua boxes today run via `drivers/lua.sh`, which spawns a fresh `luajit`\n8\tprocess per box invocation, feeds it stdin, and reads stdout. Process\n9\tspawn cost dominates; each call is its own fresh interpreter. There is\n10\tno persistent Lua state between calls.\n11\t\n12\t## Concept\n13\tThe Lua language spec implements `lang_spec_t` (issue 303) for Lua. It\n14\tis the first reference implementation of the spec interface and the\n15\tproof that the in-process FFI model works. It is also the simplest\n16\tcase — no compile step, no out-of-process server.\n17\t\n18\tEach worker thread gets its own `lua_State`. States are not shared.\n19\tPer-thread states need no locking on the call path; the state's\n20\tinternals are only ever touched by the worker that owns it.\n21\t\n22\t`langs/lua/spec.c` is built into `langs/lua/spec.so` and loaded by\n23\tthe pool runner via `dlopen` at startup, like any other spec.\n24\t\n25\t## Per-worker state\n26\t\n27\tInit creates a fresh `lua_State` and configures it:\n28\t\n29\t```c\n30\tvoid *lua_init(int worker_idx) {\n31\t    lua_State *L = luaL_newstate();\n32\t    luaL_openlibs(L);\n33\t    set_package_path(L);   // libs/, map src/, meta.json src_dirs\n34\t    return L;\n35\t}\n36\t\n37\tvoid lua_teardown(void *handle) {\n38\t    lua_close((lua_State *)handle);\n39\t}\n40\t```\n41\t\n42\t`set_package_path` writes `package.path` and `package.cpath` to\n43\tinclude exactly one directory: the map's own `src/`. Everything the\n44\tmap needs — vendored libs, helper modules, anything — is copied into\n45\t`src/` by the compile step (issue 222). The compiled map is then a\n46\tself-contained directory: ship the directory to someone else and it\n47\truns without further setup.\n48\t\n49\tThis is a tightening of the phase 2 path, which also included\n50\tSoraMech's central `libs/` and any `meta.json src_dirs`. The new rule\n51\tis: one place to look for functions, the map's own `src/`, full stop.\n52\tCompile is the step that resolves dependencies into that location.\n53\t\n54\t## File-and-function caching\n55\t\n56\tA naive `invoke` would `luaL_loadfile` and look up the function on\n57\tevery call. Both are unnecessary work — the file's chunk does not\n58\tchange during a run, and the function reference is stable.\n59\t\n60\tThe Lua spec keeps a per-handle cache: for each box source file\n61\tloaded, store the table returned by the file's chunk as a Lua\n62\tregistry key (`LUA_REGISTRYINDEX`). On first invocation:\n63\t1. `luaL_loadfile(L, file_path)` — loads the chunk.\n64\t2. `lua_pcall(L, 0, 1, 0)` — runs the chunk, expecting a returned\n65\t   table.\n66\t3. Store the table in the registry under a key derived from `file_path`.\n67\t\n68\tOn subsequent invocations:\n69\t1. Look up the registry entry by `file_path`.\n70\t2. Index it by `fn_name` to get the function reference.\n71\t3. Skip `luaL_loadfile` entirely.\n72\t\n73\tThe cache is per-`lua_State` and therefore per-worker; no\n74\tsynchronization is needed.\n75\t\n76\t## Box file convention\n77\t\n78\tA Lua box file returns a table whose keys are the box's exported\n79\tfunction names:\n80\t\n81\t```lua\n82\t-- maps/<name>/src/classify.lua\n83\tlocal M = {}\n84\t\n85\tfunction M.classify(text)\n86\t    if text:match(\"^%d+$\") then return \"numeric\"\n87\t    elseif text:match(\"[a-z]\") then return \"alpha\"\n88\t    else return \"other\"\n89\t    end\n90\tend\n91\t\n92\treturn M\n93\t```\n94\t\n95\tThe box JSON references it by `ref = \"classify.lua\"`, `fn = \"classify\"`.\n96\tThe spec loads `classify.lua`, stores its returned table, and indexes\n97\tinto it with `\"classify\"` to get the function.\n98\t\n99\tThis is the existing phase 2 convention — kept as-is.\n100\t\n101\t## Input marshalling\n102\t\n103\tInputs arrive at `invoke` as `(void *bytes, int size)` pairs. The\n104\tspec is responsible for converting each input's bytes into the Lua\n105\tvalue type the user's function expects. The user's function sees\n106\targuments as native Lua values — never a raw byte buffer that the\n107\tfunction has to parse itself.\n108\t\n109\tEach input has a declared type in the box JSON\n110\t(`{\"name\": \"count\", \"type\": \"number\"}`). The graph loader (issue 305)\n111\trecords this type on the `input_decl_t` and passes the type alongside\n112\tthe bytes when calling `invoke`. The Lua spec dispatches on type:\n113\t\n114\t| Declared type | Lua spec action                                             |\n115\t|---------------|-------------------------------------------------------------|\n116\t| `string`      | `lua_pushlstring(L, bytes, size)`                           |\n117\t| `number`      | parse with `strtod`, `lua_pushnumber`                       |\n118\t| `integer`     | parse with `strtoll`, `lua_pushinteger`                     |\n119\t| `boolean`     | strcmp against `\"true\"` / `\"false\"`, `lua_pushboolean`      |\n120\t| `json`        | call `dkjson.decode` on the bytes, push the resulting table |\n121\t| `bytes`       | `lua_pushlstring` (raw, may contain nulls)                  |\n122\t| `any`         | treat as `string` for now                                   |\n123\t\n124\tThe Lua function then takes typed arguments:\n125\t\n126\t```lua\n127\tfunction M.add(a, b)            -- both already numbers\n128\t    return a + b\n129\tend\n130\t\n131\tfunction M.classify(payload)    -- payload is already a table\n132\t    return payload.kind\n133\tend\n134\t```\n135\t\n136\tThe user does not write `tonumber` or `dkjson.decode` calls inside\n137\ttheir box function. The spec did that work before the function was\n138\tcalled.\n139\t\n140\tIf a parse fails (`json` input that isn't valid JSON, `number` input\n141\tthat isn't a number), the spec returns nonzero and the dispatch layer\n142\taborts (per issue 303).\n143\t\n144\t## Return marshalling\n145\t\n146\tThe Lua function returns one or more values. The spec converts the\n147\treturn into bytes for the output slot:\n148\t\n149\t| Return shape           | Spec action                                                   |\n150\t|------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------|\n151\t| Single string          | `lua_tolstring` → copy into `out_buf`                         |\n152\t| Single number          | `snprintf(\"%.17g\", ...)` into `out_buf`                       |\n153\t| Single boolean         | write `\"true\"` or `\"false\"`                                   |\n154\t| Single table           | `dkjson.encode` into `out_buf`                                |\n155\t| Single nil             | `*out_size = 0` (zero-byte output)                            |\n156\t| Multiple values        | wrap into a table `{v1, v2, ...}` and `dkjson.encode`         |\n157\t\n158\t`nil` is a valid return. The spec writes zero bytes and sets\n159\t`*out_size = 0`. Downstream consumers receive a zero-byte slot value;\n160\thow they interpret it depends on their declared input type (typed\n161\t`number` consumer fails to parse; typed `string` consumer gets an\n162\tempty string; typed `json` consumer parses zero bytes as `null` via\n163\tdkjson). We cannot demand that user functions never return nil, so we\n164\thandle it.\n165\t\n166\tMultiple return values are wrapped into a table and JSON-encoded.\n167\tPhase 2 silently dropped extra returns; phase 3 keeps them — the\n168\tserialized form is `[v1, v2, ...]`.\n169\t\n170\tOutput buffer is sized to the box's declared `output_capacity`\n171\t(issue 305's `box_t`). If the serialized value exceeds that, abort\n172\t(per the hard-crash policy in issue 303). For variable-size outputs\n173\tthe box declares `output_capacity = 0` and uses the large-value heap\n174\t(issue 302); the spec writes into that heap and stores the handle in\n175\t`out_buf`.\n176\t\n177\tdkjson is the table serializer in both directions (input parsing\n178\tabove and output serialization here). It is already vendored.\n179\t\n180\t## Error handling\n181\t\n182\tEvery `lua_pcall` is wrapped:\n183\t```c\n184\tint rc = lua_pcall(L, n_args, 1, 0);\n185\tif (rc != LUA_OK) {\n186\t    fprintf(stderr, \"[lua spec] %s:%s — %s\\n\",\n187\t            file_path, fn_name, lua_tostring(L, -1));\n188\t    lua_pop(L, 1);\n189\t    return 1;  // dispatch layer aborts the program\n190\t}\n191\t```\n192\t\n193\tLua errors (`error(...)`, runtime errors, syntax errors during file\n194\tload) all surface here as nonzero `pcall` returns. The spec prints\n195\tthe box context and the Lua error message to stderr, then returns\n196\tnonzero. The dispatch layer aborts.\n197\t\n198\tThere is no try-and-recover. Per issue 303, errors crash the program.\n199\t\n200\t## Build\n201\t\n202\t```\n203\tlangs/lua/\n204\t    spec.c          ← lang_spec_t implementation\n205\t    Makefile        ← builds spec.so\n206\t    spec.so         ← built artifact (gitignored)\n207\t```\n208\t\n209\tThe Makefile target:\n210\t```make\n211\tspec.so: spec.c\n212\t\t$(CC) -shared -fPIC -O2 -Wall \\\n213\t\t    -I$(LUA_INCLUDE) \\\n214\t\t    -o $@ $< \\\n215\t\t    -L$(LUA_LIB) -lluajit-5.1\n216\t```\n217\t\n218\tLuaJIT is the assumed runtime — it matches the phase 2 driver and the\n219\tproject preference (LuaJIT-compatible Lua, no 5.4 syntax).       "content":"# 306 — Lua language spec implementation (reference spec)\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nLua boxes today run via `drivers/lua.sh`, which spawns a fresh `luajit`\nprocess per box invocation, feeds it stdin, and reads stdout. Process\nspawn cost dominates; each call is its own fresh interpreter. There is\nno persistent Lua state between calls.\n\n## Concept\nThe Lua language spec implements `lang_spec_t` (issue 303) for Lua. It\nis the first reference implementation of the spec interface and the\nproof that the in-process FFI model works. It is also the simplest\ncase — no compile step, no out-of-process server.\n\nEach worker thread gets its own `lua_State`. States are not shared.\nPer-thread states need no locking on the call path; the state's\ninternals are only ever touched by the worker that owns it.\n\n`langs/lua/spec.c` is built into `langs/lua/spec.so` and loaded by\nthe pool runner via `dlopen` at startup, like any other spec.\n\n## Per-worker state\n\nInit creates a fresh `lua_State` and configures it:\n\n```c\nvoid *lua_init(int worker_idx) {\n    lua_State *L = luaL_newstate();\n    luaL_openlibs(L);\n    set_package_path(L);   // libs/, map src/, meta.json src_dirs\n    return L;\n}\n\nvoid lua_teardown(void *handle) {\n    lua_close((lua_State *)handle);\n}\n```\n\n`set_package_path` writes `package.path` and `package.cpath` to\ninclude exactly one directory: the map's own `src/`. Everything the\nmap needs — vendored libs, helper modules, anything — is copied into\n`src/` by the compile step (issue 222). The compiled map is then a\nself-contained directory: ship the directory to someone else and it\nruns without further setup.\n\nThis is a tightening of the phase 2 path, which also included\nSoraMech's central `libs/` and any `meta.json src_dirs`. The new rule\nis: one place to look for functions, the map's own `src/`, full stop.\nCompile is the step that resolves dependencies into that location.\n\n## File-and-function caching\n\nA naive `invoke` would `luaL_loadfile` and look up the function on\nevery call. Both are unnecessary work — the file's chunk does not\nchange during a run, and the function reference is stable.\n\nThe Lua spec keeps a per-handle cache: for each box source file\nloaded, store the table returned by the file's chunk as a Lua\nregistry key (`LUA_REGISTRYINDEX`). On first invocation:\n1. `luaL_loadfile(L, file_path)` — loads the chunk.\n2. `lua_pcall(L, 0, 1, 0)` — runs the chunk, expecting a returned\n   table.\n3. Store the table in the registry under a key derived from `file_path`.\n\nOn subsequent invocations:\n1. Look up the registry entry by `file_path`.\n2. Index it by `fn_name` to get the function reference.\n3. Skip `luaL_loadfile` entirely.\n\nThe cache is per-`lua_State` and therefore per-worker; no\nsynchronization is needed.\n\n## Box file convention\n\nA Lua box file returns a table whose keys are the box's exported\nfunction names:\n\n```lua\n-- maps/<name>/src/classify.lua\nlocal M = {}\n\nfunction M.classify(text)\n    if text:match(\"^%d+$\") then return \"numeric\"\n    elseif text:match(\"[a-z]\") then return \"alpha\"\n    else return \"other\"\n    end\nend\n\nreturn M\n```\n\nThe box JSON references it by `ref = \"classify.lua\"`, `fn = \"classify\"`.\nThe spec loads `classify.lua`, stores its returned table, and indexes\ninto it with `\"classify\"` to get the function.\n\nThis is the existing phase 2 convention — kept as-is.\n\n## Input marshalling\n\nInputs arrive at `invoke` as `(void *bytes, int size)` pairs. The\nspec is responsible for converting each input's bytes into the Lua\nvalue type the user's function expects. The user's function sees\narguments as native Lua values — never a raw byte buffer that the\nfunction has to parse itself.\n\nEach input has a declared type in the box JSON\n(`{\"name\": \"count\", \"type\": \"number\"}`). The graph loader (issue 305)\nrecords this type on the `input_decl_t` and passes the type alongside\nthe bytes when calling `invoke`. The Lua spec dispatches on type:\n\n| Declared type | Lua spec action                                             |\n|---------------|-------------------------------------------------------------|\n| `string`      | `lua_pushlstring(L, bytes, size)`                           |\n| `number`      | parse with `strtod`, `lua_pushnumber`                       |\n| `integer`     | parse with `strtoll`, `lua_pushinteger`                     |\n| `boolean`     | strcmp against `\"true\"` / `\"false\"`, `lua_pushboolean`      |\n| `json`        | call `dkjson.decode` on the bytes, push the resulting table |\n| `bytes`       | `lua_pushlstring` (raw, may contain nulls)                  |\n| `any`         | treat as `string` for now                                   |\n\nThe Lua function then takes typed arguments:\n\n```lua\nfunction M.add(a, b)            -- both already numbers\n    return a + b\nend\n\nfunction M.classify(payload)    -- payload is already a table\n    return payload.kind\nend\n```\n\nThe user does not write `tonumber` or `dkjson.decode` calls inside\ntheir box function. The spec did that work before the function was\ncalled.\n\nIf a parse fails (`json` input that isn't valid JSON, `number` input\nthat isn't a number), the spec returns nonzero and the dispatch layer\naborts (per issue 303).\n\n## Return marshalling\n\nThe Lua function returns one or more values. The spec converts the\nreturn into bytes for the output slot:\n\n| Return shape           | Spec action                                                   |\n|------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------|\n| Single string          | `lua_tolstring` → copy into `out_buf`                         |\n| Single number          | `snprintf(\"%.17g\", ...)` into `out_buf`                       |\n| Single boolean         | write `\"true\"` or `\"false\"`                                   |\n| Single table           | `dkjson.encode` into `out_buf`                                |\n| Single nil             | `*out_size = 0` (zero-byte output)                            |\n| Multiple values        | wrap into a table `{v1, v2, ...}` and `dkjson.encode`         |\n\n`nil` is a valid return. The spec writes zero bytes and sets\n`*out_size = 0`. Downstream consumers receive a zero-byte slot value;\nhow they interpret it depends on their declared input type (typed\n`number` consumer fails to parse; typed `string` consumer gets an\nempty string; typed `json` consumer parses zero bytes as `null` via\ndkjson). We cannot demand that user functions never return nil, so we\nhandle it.\n\nMultiple return values are wrapped into a table and JSON-encoded.\nPhase 2 silently dropped extra returns; phase 3 keeps them — the\nserialized form is `[v1, v2, ...]`.\n\nOutput buffer is sized to the box's declared `output_capacity`\n(issue 305's `box_t`). If the serialized value exceeds that, abort\n(per the hard-crash policy in issue 303). For variable-size outputs\nthe box declares `output_capacity = 0` and uses the large-value heap\n(issue 302); the spec writes into that heap and stores the handle in\n`out_buf`.\n\ndkjson is the table serializer in both directions (input parsing\nabove and output serialization here). It is already vendored.\n\n## Error handling\n\nEvery `lua_pcall` is wrapped:\n```c\nint rc = lua_pcall(L, n_args, 1, 0);\nif (rc != LUA_OK) {\n    fprintf(stderr, \"[lua spec] %s:%s — %s\\n\",\n            file_path, fn_name, lua_tostring(L, -1));\n    lua_pop(L, 1);\n    return 1;  // dispatch layer aborts the program\n}\n```\n\nLua errors (`error(...)`, runtime errors, syntax errors during file\nload) all surface here as nonzero `pcall` returns. The spec prints\nthe box context and the Lua error message to stderr, then returns\nnonzero. The dispatch layer aborts.\n\nThere is no try-and-recover. Per issue 303, errors crash the program.\n\n## Build\n\n```\nlangs/lua/\n    spec.c          ← lang_spec_t implementation\n    Makefile        ← builds spec.so\n    spec.so         ← built artifact (gitignored)\n```\n\nThe Makefile target:\n```make\nspec.so: spec.c\n\t$(CC) -shared -fPIC -O2 -Wall \\\n\t    -I$(LUA_INCLUDE) \\\n\t    -o $@ $< \\\n\t    -L$(LUA_LIB) -lluajit-5.1\n```\n\nLuaJIT is the assumed runtime — it matches the phase 2 driver and the\nproject preference (LuaJIT-compatible Lua, no 5.4 syntax). The build\nlinks against the system LuaJIT shared library.\n\n## Open questions\n\n(none currently — earlier questions resolved as follows:)\n\n- nil return: valid. Zero-byte output, downstream consumers\n  interpret per their declared input type.\n- Multiple return values: wrapped into a table and JSON-encoded via\n  dkjson. No values dropped.\n- Table serializer: dkjson, already vendored. Used in both\n  directions (input parsing and output serialization).\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. Set up `langs/lua/` directory with a Makefile that builds an empty\n   `spec.so` exporting a stub `soramech_lang_spec`.\n2. Implement `init` and `teardown`. Verify the pool runner can\n   `dlopen` the spec and call `init` per worker without errors.\n3. Implement file-and-function caching — load a file, store its\n   returned table in the registry, look it up later.\n4. Implement input marshalling: push bytes as strings, count args.\n5. Implement `lua_pcall` invocation with error wrapping.\n6. Implement string return marshalling. Smoke test: `maps/hello`\n   end-to-end through the pool.\n7. Implement number return marshalling.\n8. Implement table-via-JSON return marshalling.\n9. Add `package.path` resolution for libs/, src/, and `meta.src_dirs`.\n10. Test against `maps/classify-demo` and `maps/driver-test` (Lua\n    portions).\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `drivers/lua.sh` — phase 2 Lua driver, retired by this spec\n- `langs/lang-spec.h` — interface header (issue 303)\n- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — spec contract this implements\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — dispatch layer that calls\n  `invoke`\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — large-value heap for\n  variable-size returns\n- `libs/dkjson` (vendored) — table-to-JSON serialization\n- `maps/hello`, `maps/classify-demo` — Lua-only smoke test maps\n\n## Implementation log\n\n### Init + invoke + teardown — 2026-05-12\n\n`langs/lua/spec.c` now exports a real `lang_spec_t`:\n\n- `init(worker_idx)` creates a `lua_State` and opens the standard\n  libraries via `luaL_openlibs`. Returns the state as the per-\n  worker handle.\n- `teardown(handle)` calls `lua_close`.\n- `invoke(handle, file_path, fn_name, inputs, sizes, n, out_buf,\n  out_cap, out_size)` loads the file with `luaL_loadfile`,\n  executes the chunk (which is expected to return a module\n  table), pulls the named function out of that table, pushes each\n  input as a Lua string, calls via `lua_pcall`, and copies the\n  return as a string into the caller's buffer. The state's stack\n  is rewound to its baseline depth at every entry/exit so\n  cross-call leaks don't accumulate. Errors at every step\n  surface as nonzero return and a stderr message.\n\nFive end-to-end tests in `tests/306-lua-spec-test.c` exercise the\ninit/teardown round-trip, a `greet(name, salutation)` call with\nboth args, the same call with one arg (the Lua side defaults\nsalutation to \"Hello\"), and the two failure modes (missing\nfunction, missing file). The test loads the spec through the\nreal spec registry via dlopen, so this is the actual artifact\nthe pool runner will consume.\n\nDeferred:\n- **Rich return types.** The current invoke serializes the return\n  with `lua_tolstring`, which handles strings/numbers/booleans/\n  nil via tostring semantics. Tables, closures, and other\n  structured values land with the fast-path work in issue 312.\n\n### Per-worker module cache — 2026-05-12\n\n`lua_init` now seeds an empty Lua table at\n`LUA_REGISTRYINDEX[LUA_CACHE_KEY]`. `lua_invoke` looks up the\nbox's `file_path` in that table; on a hit it skips the\n`luaL_loadfile + lua_pcall` round-trip and uses the cached\nmodule table directly; on a miss it loads, runs the chunk,\nverifies the module table shape, and stashes the result in the\ncache before proceeding.\n\nThe cache is per-worker (each worker has its own `lua_State`),\nwhich means no locking. It's also per-file-path string, so two\nboxes that share a source file share a module table on each\nworker — calling `M.greet` from one box doesn't reload the\nchunk when another box later calls `M.farewell` on the same\nfile.\n\nCache invalidation is intentionally absent for now: once a file\nis loaded, its module table sticks for the run. If the box\nsource changes mid-run, the worker won't notice. Fine for the\nread-once-then-execute usage; revisit when there's a use case\nfor hot-reload.\n"

        "content":"1\t# 307 — C language spec implementation\n2\t\n3\t## Status\n4\topen\n5\t\n6\t## Current behavior\n7\tC boxes today run via `drivers/c.sh`, which compiles the source on\n8\tdemand (mtime-based recompile to a binary), then spawns the binary as\n9\ta subprocess and reads stdout. Process spawn cost dominates; each call\n10\tis its own freshly-launched executable. The phase 2 driver compiles\n11\tto a standalone binary, not a `.so`.\n12\t\n13\t## Concept\n14\tThe C language spec implements `lang_spec_t` (issue 303) for C. It is\n15\tthe second reference implementation, and the first one that exercises\n16\tthe `compile` callback. After compile, invocation is in-process via\n17\t`dlopen` / `dlsym` — the user's compiled function is called directly\n18\tthrough a function pointer, with no subprocess and no IPC.\n19\t\n20\tThis is the \"Option 1 — LuaJIT FFI\" model from\n21\t`docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md`, applied to C: same-process call,\n22\tnanosecond-overhead invocation, native-typed access. The only thing\n23\tthe C spec adds over the Lua spec is the compile step.\n24\t\n25\t## Per-worker state\n26\t\n27\t`init` returns a small struct holding the dlopen-handle cache:\n28\t\n29\t```c\n30\ttypedef struct {\n31\t    void  *so_handles[MAX_BOXES];   // per-file .so handle, indexed by file id\n32\t    void  *fn_ptrs   [MAX_BOXES];   // per-(file, fn) cached function pointer\n33\t    int    n_cached;\n34\t    // (a hash table could replace these arrays if MAX_BOXES grows large)\n35\t} c_handle_t;\n36\t\n37\tvoid *c_init(int worker_idx);\n38\tvoid  c_teardown(void *handle);    // dlclose every cached handle\n39\t```\n40\t\n41\tEach worker thread has its own cache. The same `.so` will end up\n42\tloaded once per worker, since `dlopen` with the same path on the same\n43\tprocess returns a refcounted handle (the underlying code segment is\n44\tshared across all callers — the per-worker `dlopen` is just a\n45\trefcount bump after the first).\n46\t\n47\t## Compile callback\n48\t\n49\tThe C spec's `compile` callback receives the box's metadata in\n50\taddition to the source and output paths, so it knows the function's\n51\tsignature and can generate the wrapper:\n52\t\n53\t```c\n54\tint c_compile(const char *src_path, const char *out_path, const box_t *box);\n55\t```\n56\t\n57\t(This is a small extension to `lang_spec_t` in issue 303 — `compile`\n58\tgains a `box_t` pointer. Lua's compile is NULL, so unaffected.)\n59\t\n60\tThe callback:\n61\t1. Reads `box->inputs`, `box->returns`, `box->headers`, `box->link_libs`,\n62\t   `box->cflags` from the box metadata.\n63\t2. Generates a wrapper `.c` file (see \"Wrapper generation\" below) in\n64\t   the map's `compiled/bin/` directory next to where the `.so` will\n65\t   land.\n66\t3. Forks and execs the system `cc` with:\n67\t   - `-shared -fPIC -O2 -Wall` (defaults)\n68\t   - The user's `cflags`, if any\n69\t   - The wrapper `.c` and the user's `src_path` (if `ref` is set)\n70\t   - `-o out_path`\n71\t   - `-l<lib>` for each entry in `box->link_libs`\n72\t4. Waits for the compiler, returns 0 on success, 1 on failure.\n73\t\n74\tIf the resulting `.so` is newer than the user's source and the\n75\twrapper, compile is skipped (mtime check, same as phase 2).\n76\t\n77\tThe compiler is `cc` — the system default. `gcc` on most Linux,\n78\t`clang` on macOS. No SoraMech-specific compiler dependency.\n79\t\n80\t### cflags in box JSON\n81\tThe `cflags` field on the box JSON is a string of additional compiler\n82\tflags (`-O0 -g`, `-mavx2`, etc.). It is set by the user in the\n83\tinspector — a \"Compile flags\" text input shown when a C-language box\n84\tis selected. The editor saves it as part of the box's JSON; reads\n85\tpreserve the field; saves write it back. Nothing overwrites it.\n86\t\n87\t## Box file convention: any C function, no boilerplate\n88\t\n89\t**The rule, stated as a rule:** a box author writes code as if\n90\tSoraMech does not exist. The function they write must be a\n91\tfunction their non-SoraMech compiler can compile, their\n92\tnon-SoraMech editor can lint, their non-SoraMech test harness\n93\tcan call. No SoraMech-prefixed macros. No SoraMech-shaped\n94\treturn types. No `#include \"soramech.h\"`. Nothing in the\n95\tauthor's source betrays that the function will ever cross\n96\tSoraMech's wire.\n97\t\n98\tSoraMech bends to the language. The language never bends to\n99\tSoraMech. This is non-negotiable across every spec; it's the\n100\treason for the spec interface in the first place.\n101\t\n102\tUsers do not write a SoraMech-specific C signature. They reference\n103\tany C function — whether one they wrote themselves, or one from a\n104\tlibrary (zlib, OpenCV, libcurl, anything they have headers for) —\n105\tand the C spec generates a thin wrapper that bridges SoraMech's\n106\tbytes-in / bytes-out ABI to the function's natural typed C\n107\tsignature.\n108\t\n109\t### What the user provides\n110\tEither:\n111\t- A `.c` file containing the function, referenced by `ref` in the\n112\t  box JSON; or\n113\t- A library function from a header, no `.c` file of their own — the\n114\t  `ref` field is omitted, the function name and headers are\n115\t  declared in the box JSON, and the library is named in\n116\t  `link_libs`.\n117\t\n118\t### Box JSON for a user-written function\n119\t\n120\t```json\n121\t{\n122\t  \"id\": \"classify\",\n123\t  \"kind\": \"call\",\n124\t  \"lang\": \"c\",\n125\t  \"ref\": \"classify.c\",\n126\t  \"fn\": \"classify\",\n127\t  \"inputs\": [\n128\t    {\"name\": \"text\",   \"type\": \"string\"},\n129\t    {\"name\": \"weight\", \"type\": \"int\"}\n130\t  ],\n131\t  \"returns\": \"int\"\n132\t}\n133\t```\n134\t\n135\tThe user's `.c` file is naturally written:\n136\t\n137\t```c\n138\t// maps/<name>/src/classify.c\n139\tint classify(const char *text, int weight) {\n140\t    if (text[0] >= '0' && text[0] <= '9') return weight * 1;\n141\t    return weight * 2;\n142\t}\n143\t```\n144\t\n145\tNo header to include, no macro, no `int classify(SM_BOX_ARGS)`.\n146\tJust a function with a typed signature.\n147\t\n148\t### Box JSON for a library function (no user source)\n149\t\n150\t```json\n151\t{\n152\t  \"id\": \"compress\",\n153\t  \"kind\": \"call\",\n154\t  \"lang\": \"c\",\n155\t  \"fn\": \"compress2\",\n156\t  \"headers\": [\"<zlib.h>\"],\n157\t  \"link_libs\": [\"z\"],\n158\t  \"inputs\": [\n159\t    {\"name\": \"src\",   \"type\": \"bytes\"},\n160\t    {\"name\": \"level\", \"type\": \"int\"}\n161\t  ],\n162\t  \"returns\": \"bytes\"\n163\t}\n164\t```\n165\t\n166\tThe wrapper includes `<zlib.h>`, calls `compress2`, and the linker\n167\tpulls in `libz` via `-lz`. No user-written `.c` file.\n168\t\n169\t### Wrapper generation\n170\t\n171\tThe compile callback emits a wrapper `.c` for each C box. The\n172\twrapper has a fixed entry-point name (`sm_box_entry`) that the spec\n173\talways `dlsym`s. It declares the user's function (extern), unpacks\n174\tSoraMech's input bytes into typed C arguments per the box's `inputs`\n175\tdeclaration, calls the user's function, and writes the return value\n176\tinto `sm_out_buf` per the box's `returns` declaration.\n177\t\n178\tFor `classify` above, the generated wrapper is roughly:\n179\t\n180\t```c\n181\t// generated: classify_wrap.c\n182\textern int classify(const char *, int);\n183\t\n184\tint sm_box_entry(const void **inputs, const int *sizes, int n,\n185\t                 void *out_buf, int out_cap, int *out_size) {\n186\t    const char *text   = (const char *)inputs[0];\n187\t    int         weight = atoi((const char *)inputs[1]);\n188\t    int         result = classify(text, weight);\n189\t    *out_size = snprintf(out_buf, out_cap, \"%d\", result);\n190\t    return 0;\n191\t}\n192\t```\n193\t\n194\tThe wrapper is mechanical — same template for every box, varying\n195\tonly in the input-marshalling lines and the return-encoding line.\n196\tThe compile step writes it to `compiled/bin/<box-id>_wrap.c` and\n197\tcompiles `<box-id>_wrap.c` plus the user's source (if any) into a\n198\tsingle `.so`.\n199\t\n200\tThis means the C spec implements typed function calls without\n201\tlibffi (which would do the marshalling at runtime via the C ABI\n202\tmetadata). The same effect is achieved at compile time with\n203\tstraightforward generated code, no runtime dependency.\n204\t\n205\t## Input marshalling (in the generated wrapper)\n206\t\n207\tThe wrapper converts SoraMech's `(bytes, size)` input pairs into the\n208\ttyped C arguments the user's function expects, based on the\n209\tdeclared input types in the box JSON:\n210\t\n211\t| Declared type | Wrapper action                                                  |\n212\t|---------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------|\n213\t| `string`      | `(const char *)inputs[i]`                                       |\n214\t| `int`         | `atoi((const char *)inputs[i])`                                 |\n215\t| `long`        | `strtoll(...)`                                                  |\n216\t| `double`      | `strtod(...)`                                                   |\n217\t| `bool`        | `strcmp(\"true\", inputs[i]) == 0`                                |\n218\t| `bytes`       | `(const void *)inputs[i]`, paired with `sizes[i]` for the size  |\n219\t| `json`        | `cJSON_ParseWithLength(inputs[i], sizes[i])` → `cJSON *`        |\n220\t\n221\tThe `json` case uses the same vendored cJSON the graph loader uses\n222\t(issue 305) — one JSON library shared across the runner. When a box\n223\tinput is declared `\"type\": \"json\"`, the wrapper passes a `cJSON *`\n224\tto the user's function. The user navigates the tree with cJSON's\n225\tAPI (`cJSON_GetObjectItem`, `cJSON_GetArrayItem`, etc.) and the\n226\twrapper frees the parsed tree after the function returns.\n227\t\n228\tIf a parse fails (a `json` input that is not valid JSON, an `int`\n229\tinput that does not parse as an integer), the wrapper aborts the\n230\tprogram with the box id and the input position (per issue 303).\n231\t\n232\t## Output encoding (in the generated wrapper)\n233\t\n234\tThe wrapper takes the user function's return value and serializes\n235\tit into `sm_out_buf`, based on the declared `returns` type:\n236\t\n237\t| Declared `returns` | Wrapper action                                              |\n238\t|--------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------|\n239\t| `string`           | the user returns `const char *`; `strcpy` + set `out_size` |\n240\t| `int`              | `snprintf(\"%d\", ret)`                                       |\n241\t| `long`             | `snprintf(\"%lld\", ret)`                                     |\n242\t| `double`           | `snprintf(\"%.17g\", ret)`                                    |\n243\t| `bool`             | write `\"true\"` or `\"false\"`                                 |\n244\t| `bytes`            | the user returns `(void *, int)` via an out-parameter pair (see below) |\n245\t| `json`             | the user returns `cJSON *`; `cJSON_PrintUnformatted` → bytes |\n246\t| `void`             | `*out_size = 0` (zero-byte output)                          |\n247\t\n248\tFor `bytes` returns, the user function's signature has the form\n249\t`int my_fn(... const char *out_buf, int out_cap, int *out_size)` —\n250\textra parameters that the wrapper passes through from\n251\t`sm_out_buf` / `sm_out_capacity` / `sm_out_size`. This handles\n252\tlibrary functions like `compress` that write their output via an\n253\tout-pointer rather than a return value. The box JSON declares\n254\t`\"returns\": \"bytes\"` and the wrapper threads the buffer through.\n255\t\n256\tIf the encoded value exceeds `sm_out_capacity`, the wrapper aborts\n257\t(per issue 303). For boxes whose output capacity is not known at\n258\tcompile time, see \"Variable-size outputs\" below — the wrapper\n259\troutes through the large-value heap.\n260\t\n261\t## Variable-size outputs\n262\t\n263\tFor boxes whose output capacity is not known at compile time (issue\n264\t302's large-value heap): the box JSON declares `output_capacity = 0`\n265\tand the wrapper allocates from the large-value heap on each call.\n266\tFor `bytes` and `json` returns, the wrapper transparently picks the\n267\theap path when the box is variable-size — the user's function is\n268\tunchanged either way. The handle (pointer + size into the\n269\tlarge-value heap) is what ends up in `sm_out_buf`.\n270\t\n271\tFor string returns, similarly: if the returned string exceeds the\n272\tdeclared fixed `output_capacity`, the wrapper falls back to the\n273\tlarge-value heap. This decision is made at compile time based on the\n274\tbox JSON, not at runtime.\n275\t\n276\t## Thread safety of user code\n277\t\n278\tThe same `.so` is loaded by every worker thread that may call into\n279\tit. **Static variables and globals declared in the user's C source\n280\tare shared mutable state across all workers** unless explicitly\n281\tmade `const`.\n282\t\n283\tA note on `static` in C: it does not mean immutable. `static` at\n284\tfile scope means \"this symbol has internal linkage, only visible\n285\tinside this `.c` file.\" `static` inside a function means \"this\n286\tvariable persists across calls.\" Either way, the variable itself is\n287\tmutable — `static int counter = 0; counter++;` is perfectly legal\n288\tand does what it says, just with internal linkage. Immutable in C\n289\tis `const`.\n290\t\n291\tSo:\n292\t- `static int counter = 0;` at file scope — racy, shared across workers.\n293\t- `static int x = 0;` inside a function body — racy, shared across workers calling that function.\n294\t- `const int max = 100;` — safe, immutable.\n295\t- `static const int max = 100;` — safe, immutable.\n296\t\n297\tBox functions must be reentrant — no mutable shared state without\n298\texplicit locking. The C spec does not enforce this; the rule lives\n299\tin `docs/005-language-specs.md` (to be written) for box authors to\n300\tread.\n301\t\n302\t### Library functions that need global init\n303\t\n304\tMany real C libraries require a one-time setup call before any of\n305\ttheir functions work — `curl_global_init` for libcurl,\n306\t`OPENSSL_init_crypto` for OpenSSL, etc. A SoraMech box that calls\n307\tinto such a library cannot just be wired in cold; the library's\n308\tstate has to exist before the call.\n309\t\n310\tTwo patterns handle this without changing the spec interface:\n311\t\n312\t1. **Init box wired as an entry point.** The user creates a small C\n313\t   box whose function is the library's init call (e.g.\n314\t   `curl_global_init`). They mark it as an entry box and wire it\n315\t   such that any box using libcurl is downstream of it. The init\n316\t   runs once at startup before any consumer fires. Process-global\n317\t   library state — which is what most C libraries actually use — is\n318\t   set up by the time anyone needs it. Pairs with a teardown box\n319\t   wired as a terminal node if needed.\n320\t\n321\t2. **Per-worker init via spec extension** (future). For libraries\n322\t   that need per-worker setup (each thread gets its own handle),\n323\t   the C spec gains an optional per-box `worker_init_fn` field in\n324\t   the box JSON. The spec calls that function once per worker\n325\t   thread during pool startup, before any box invoke. Not in scope\n326\t   yet — pattern (1) covers the common case.\n327\t\n328\tThe init-box approach is the recommended starting point. The\n329\tspec-extension path is the escape hatch when (1) does not fit.\n330\t\n331\tA future fallback exists: `dlmopen`, a Linux variant of `dlopen`\n332\tthat loads each library into its own isolated \"namespace,\" giving\n333\teach worker its own copy of the library's symbols (statics\n334\tincluded). Two threads using two different namespaces would not\n335\tshare static state. Less portable than `dlopen` (Linux-only), so\n336\tnot the default — flagged here as the escape hatch if static-\n337\tvariable races become a real problem.\n338\t\n339\t## Build\n340\t\n341\t```\n342\tlangs/c/\n343\t    spec.c              ← lang_spec_t implementation\n344\t    soramech-c.h        ← user-facing header (shipped to maps via compile step)\n345\t    Makefile            ← builds spec.so\n346\t    spec.so             ← built artifact (gitignored)\n347\t```\n348\t\n349\tSpec Makefile target:\n350\t```make\n351\tspec.so: spec.c\n352\t\t$(CC) -shared -fPIC -O2 -Wall -o $@ $< -ldl\n353\t```\n354\t\n355\tLinking against `libdl` for `dlopen` / `dlsym` is the only\n356\tdependency. No interpreter, no helper library beyond libc.\n357\t\n358\t### What `dlopen` and `dlsym` do\n359\t- `dlopen(\"path/to/file.so\", flags)` loads a shared library at\n360\t  runtime. The OS loader maps the library's code into the process's\n361\t  memory and returns a handle. Same idea as Windows'\n362\t  `LoadLibrary`.\n363\t- `dlsym(handle, \"name\")` looks up a symbol — a function or a\n364\t  variable — by name inside an already-loaded library, and returns\n365\t  a pointer to it. Same idea as Windows' `GetProcAddress`.\n366\t\n367\tTogether they are how a program loads and calls code that wasn't\n368\tlinked at compile time. Plugin systems are the classic use case.\n369\tHere, every C box compiles to its own `.so`; the spec `dlopen`s the\n370\t`.so` once per worker, `dlsym`s `sm_box_entry` once per file, and\n371\tcalls the resulting function pointer per invocation.\n372\t\n373\tThe user's C box files are compiled by the `compile` callback at map\n374\tload time, not by this Makefile. The Makefile here builds only the\n375\tspec itself.\n376\t\n377\t## Error handling\n378\t\n379\t- `dlopen` failure (missing `.so`, link errors): print path + `dlerror()`\n380\t  to stderr, return 1, dispatch layer aborts.\n381\t- `dlsym` failure (missing function): print file/fn + `dlerror()`,\n382\t  return 1, abort.\n383\t- Compile failure: `cc` exit nonzero, print compiler stderr (already\n384\t  routed there by `cc`), return 1, abort.\n385\t- User function returns nonzero: propagate that as the spec's return,\n386\t  abort.\n387\t\n388\tNo retry, no fallback. Per issue 303.\n389\t\n390\t## Open questions\n391\t\n392\t(none currently — earlier questions resolved as follows:)\n393\t\n394\t- Per-box `cflags`: yes, add the field to the box JSON. The\n395\t  inspector shows a \"Compile flags\" text input when a C-language\n396\t  box is selected (phase 2 inspector work).\n397\t- Typed signatures: handled via compile-time wrapper generation\n398\t  (see \"Box file convention\" above). No libffi runtime dependency.\n399\t- Static-variable isolation via `dlmopen`: deferred. Current rule\n400\t  is \"C box authors write reentrant code\"; if that breaks down in\n401\t  practice, fall back to per-worker `dlmopen` namespaces (Linux-only).\n402\t\n403\t## Suggested implementation sequence\n404\t\n405\t1. Set up `langs/c/` directory with a Makefile that builds an empty\n406\t   `spec.so` exporting a stub `soramech_lang_spec`.\n407\t2. Implement `init` and `teardown` with the dlopen-handle cache.\n408\t3. Implement `compile` — fork/exec `cc` with the standard flags.\n409\t   Smoke test: compile a single hello-world `.c` file.\n410\t4. Implement `invoke` — dlsym, direct call, propagate return.\n411\t5. Write `soramech-c.h` with the `SM_BOX_ARGS` macro and the basic\n412\t   input/output helpers.\n413\t6. Smoke test: a C box that takes one string input, writes a string\n414\t   output, runs end-to-end through the pool.\n415\t7. Add the typed input helpers (`sm_in_int`, `sm_in_double`, etc.).\n416\t8. Add the typed output helpers.\n417\t9. Test against `maps/driver-test` (C portions).\n418\t10. Add variable-size output support (`sm_out_alloc`, `sm_out_handle`).\n419\t11. Document in `docs/005-language-specs.md` once it exists, with a\n420\t    note on thread safety.\n421\t\n422\t## Relevant files\n423\t\n424\t- `drivers/c.sh` — phase 2 C driver, retired by this spec\n425\t- `langs/lang-spec.h` — interface header (issue 303)\n426\t- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — spec contract this implements\n427\t- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — dispatch layer that calls\n428\t  `invoke`\n429\t- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — large-value heap\n430\t- `issues/222-compile-button-and-assets-directory.md` — where compiled\n431\t  `.so`s live (`compiled/bin/`)\n432\t- `issues/306-lua-language-spec.md` — sister spec; same shape, no\n433\t  compile step\n434\t- `maps/driver-test` — multi-language test map including C boxes\n435\t\n436\t## Implementation log\n437\t\n438\t### Compile + invoke — 2026-05-12\n439\t\n440\t`langs/c/spec.c`:\n441\t- `compile(src, out)` forks gcc with `-shared -fPIC -O2 -Wall`.\n442\t- `init` allocates a 32-entry dlopen cache; `teardown` walks it.\n443\t- `invoke` looks up the .so in the cache or dlopens it, dlsyms\n444\t  the named function, and calls it through a fixed signature:\n445\t  `int fn(const void **inputs, const int *sizes, int n,\n446\t  void *out_buf, int out_capacity, int *out_size)`.\n447\t\n448\tConvention: C box functions all match that signature. The\n449\toptional typed-wrapper mode (per-box signature parsing +\n450\tgenerated marshaller) is deferred until a box wants types that\n451\tdiverge from the byte-array shape.\n452\t\n453\t`tests/maps/hello/src/echo.c` ships two fixture functions; five\n454\ttests in `tests/307-c-spec-test.c` compile and invoke them, plus\n455\tthe missing-symbol and bad-source failure modes.\n456\t",

      }],

      "content":"# 307 — C language spec implementation\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nC boxes today run via `drivers/c.sh`, which compiles the source on\ndemand (mtime-based recompile to a binary), then spawns the binary as\na subprocess and reads stdout. Process spawn cost dominates; each call\nis its own freshly-launched executable. The phase 2 driver compiles\nto a standalone binary, not a `.so`.\n\n## Concept\nThe C language spec implements `lang_spec_t` (issue 303) for C. It is\nthe second reference implementation, and the first one that exercises\nthe `compile` callback. After compile, invocation is in-process via\n`dlopen` / `dlsym` — the user's compiled function is called directly\nthrough a function pointer, with no subprocess and no IPC.\n\nThis is the \"Option 1 — LuaJIT FFI\" model from\n`docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md`, applied to C: same-process call,\nnanosecond-overhead invocation, native-typed access. The only thing\nthe C spec adds over the Lua spec is the compile step.\n\n## Per-worker state\n\n`init` returns a small struct holding the dlopen-handle cache:\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    void  *so_handles[MAX_BOXES];   // per-file .so handle, indexed by file id\n    void  *fn_ptrs   [MAX_BOXES];   // per-(file, fn) cached function pointer\n    int    n_cached;\n    // (a hash table could replace these arrays if MAX_BOXES grows large)\n} c_handle_t;\n\nvoid *c_init(int worker_idx);\nvoid  c_teardown(void *handle);    // dlclose every cached handle\n```\n\nEach worker thread has its own cache. The same `.so` will end up\nloaded once per worker, since `dlopen` with the same path on the same\nprocess returns a refcounted handle (the underlying code segment is\nshared across all callers — the per-worker `dlopen` is just a\nrefcount bump after the first).\n\n## Compile callback\n\nThe C spec's `compile` callback receives the box's metadata in\naddition to the source and output paths, so it knows the function's\nsignature and can generate the wrapper:\n\n```c\nint c_compile(const char *src_path, const char *out_path, const box_t *box);\n```\n\n(This is a small extension to `lang_spec_t` in issue 303 — `compile`\ngains a `box_t` pointer. Lua's compile is NULL, so unaffected.)\n\nThe callback:\n1. Reads `box->inputs`, `box->returns`, `box->headers`, `box->link_libs`,\n   `box->cflags` from the box metadata.\n2. Generates a wrapper `.c` file (see \"Wrapper generation\" below) in\n   the map's `compiled/bin/` directory next to where the `.so` will\n   land.\n3. Forks and execs the system `cc` with:\n   - `-shared -fPIC -O2 -Wall` (defaults)\n   - The user's `cflags`, if any\n   - The wrapper `.c` and the user's `src_path` (if `ref` is set)\n   - `-o out_path`\n   - `-l<lib>` for each entry in `box->link_libs`\n4. Waits for the compiler, returns 0 on success, 1 on failure.\n\nIf the resulting `.so` is newer than the user's source and the\nwrapper, compile is skipped (mtime check, same as phase 2).\n\nThe compiler is `cc` — the system default. `gcc` on most Linux,\n`clang` on macOS. No SoraMech-specific compiler dependency.\n\n### cflags in box JSON\nThe `cflags` field on the box JSON is a string of additional compiler\nflags (`-O0 -g`, `-mavx2`, etc.). It is set by the user in the\ninspector — a \"Compile flags\" text input shown when a C-language box\nis selected. The editor saves it as part of the box's JSON; reads\npreserve the field; saves write it back. Nothing overwrites it.\n\n## Box file convention: any C function, no boilerplate\n\n**The rule, stated as a rule:** a box author writes code as if\nSoraMech does not exist. The function they write must be a\nfunction their non-SoraMech compiler can compile, their\nnon-SoraMech editor can lint, their non-SoraMech test harness\ncan call. No SoraMech-prefixed macros. No SoraMech-shaped\nreturn types. No `#include \"soramech.h\"`. Nothing in the\nauthor's source betrays that the function will ever cross\nSoraMech's wire.\n\nSoraMech bends to the language. The language never bends to\nSoraMech. This is non-negotiable across every spec; it's the\nreason for the spec interface in the first place.\n\nUsers do not write a SoraMech-specific C signature. They reference\nany C function — whether one they wrote themselves, or one from a\nlibrary (zlib, OpenCV, libcurl, anything they have headers for) —\nand the C spec generates a thin wrapper that bridges SoraMech's\nbytes-in / bytes-out ABI to the function's natural typed C\nsignature.\n\n### What the user provides\nEither:\n- A `.c` file containing the function, referenced by `ref` in the\n  box JSON; or\n- A library function from a header, no `.c` file of their own — the\n  `ref` field is omitted, the function name and headers are\n  declared in the box JSON, and the library is named in\n  `link_libs`.\n\n### Box JSON for a user-written function\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\": \"classify\",\n  \"kind\": \"call\",\n  \"lang\": \"c\",\n  \"ref\": \"classify.c\",\n  \"fn\": \"classify\",\n  \"inputs\": [\n    {\"name\": \"text\",   \"type\": \"string\"},\n    {\"name\": \"weight\", \"type\": \"int\"}\n  ],\n  \"returns\": \"int\"\n}\n```\n\nThe user's `.c` file is naturally written:\n\n```c\n// maps/<name>/src/classify.c\nint classify(const char *text, int weight) {\n    if (text[0] >= '0' && text[0] <= '9') return weight * 1;\n    return weight * 2;\n}\n```\n\nNo header to include, no macro, no `int classify(SM_BOX_ARGS)`.\nJust a function with a typed signature.\n\n### Box JSON for a library function (no user source)\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\": \"compress\",\n  \"kind\": \"call\",\n  \"lang\": \"c\",\n  \"fn\": \"compress2\",\n  \"headers\": [\"<zlib.h>\"],\n  \"link_libs\": [\"z\"],\n  \"inputs\": [\n    {\"name\": \"src\",   \"type\": \"bytes\"},\n    {\"name\": \"level\", \"type\": \"int\"}\n  ],\n  \"returns\": \"bytes\"\n}\n```\n\nThe wrapper includes `<zlib.h>`, calls `compress2`, and the linker\npulls in `libz` via `-lz`. No user-written `.c` file.\n\n### Wrapper generation\n\nThe compile callback emits a wrapper `.c` for each C box. The\nwrapper has a fixed entry-point name (`sm_box_entry`) that the spec\nalways `dlsym`s. It declares the user's function (extern), unpacks\nSoraMech's input bytes into typed C arguments per the box's `inputs`\ndeclaration, calls the user's function, and writes the return value\ninto `sm_out_buf` per the box's `returns` declaration.\n\nFor `classify` above, the generated wrapper is roughly:\n\n```c\n// generated: classify_wrap.c\nextern int classify(const char *, int);\n\nint sm_box_entry(const void **inputs, const int *sizes, int n,\n                 void *out_buf, int out_cap, int *out_size) {\n    const char *text   = (const char *)inputs[0];\n    int         weight = atoi((const char *)inputs[1]);\n    int         result = classify(text, weight);\n    *out_size = snprintf(out_buf, out_cap, \"%d\", result);\n    return 0;\n}\n```\n\nThe wrapper is mechanical — same template for every box, varying\nonly in the input-marshalling lines and the return-encoding line.\nThe compile step writes it to `compiled/bin/<box-id>_wrap.c` and\ncompiles `<box-id>_wrap.c` plus the user's source (if any) into a\nsingle `.so`.\n\nThis means the C spec implements typed function calls without\nlibffi (which would do the marshalling at runtime via the C ABI\nmetadata). The same effect is achieved at compile time with\nstraightforward generated code, no runtime dependency.\n\n## Input marshalling (in the generated wrapper)\n\nThe wrapper converts SoraMech's `(bytes, size)` input pairs into the\ntyped C arguments the user's function expects, based on the\ndeclared input types in the box JSON:\n\n| Declared type | Wrapper action                                                  |\n|---------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------|\n| `string`      | `(const char *)inputs[i]`                                       |\n| `int`         | `atoi((const char *)inputs[i])`                                 |\n| `long`        | `strtoll(...)`                                                  |\n| `double`      | `strtod(...)`                                                   |\n| `bool`        | `strcmp(\"true\", inputs[i]) == 0`                                |\n| `bytes`       | `(const void *)inputs[i]`, paired with `sizes[i]` for the size  |\n| `json`        | `cJSON_ParseWithLength(inputs[i], sizes[i])` → `cJSON *`        |\n\nThe `json` case uses the same vendored cJSON the graph loader uses\n(issue 305) — one JSON library shared across the runner. When a box\ninput is declared `\"type\": \"json\"`, the wrapper passes a `cJSON *`\nto the user's function. The user navigates the tree with cJSON's\nAPI (`cJSON_GetObjectItem`, `cJSON_GetArrayItem`, etc.) and the\nwrapper frees the parsed tree after the function returns.\n\nIf a parse fails (a `json` input that is not valid JSON, an `int`\ninput that does not parse as an integer), the wrapper aborts the\nprogram with the box id and the input position (per issue 303).\n\n## Output encoding (in the generated wrapper)\n\nThe wrapper takes the user function's return value and serializes\nit into `sm_out_buf`, based on the declared `returns` type:\n\n| Declared `returns` | Wrapper action                                              |\n|--------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------|\n| `string`           | the user returns `const char *`; `strcpy` + set `out_size` |\n| `int`              | `snprintf(\"%d\", ret)`                                       |\n| `long`             | `snprintf(\"%lld\", ret)`                                     |\n| `double`           | `snprintf(\"%.17g\", ret)`                                    |\n| `bool`             | write `\"true\"` or `\"false\"`                                 |\n| `bytes`            | the user returns `(void *, int)` via an out-parameter pair (see below) |\n| `json`             | the user returns `cJSON *`; `cJSON_PrintUnformatted` → bytes |\n| `void`             | `*out_size = 0` (zero-byte output)                          |\n\nFor `bytes` returns, the user function's signature has the form\n`int my_fn(... const char *out_buf, int out_cap, int *out_size)` —\nextra parameters that the wrapper passes through from\n`sm_out_buf` / `sm_out_capacity` / `sm_out_size`. This handles\nlibrary functions like `compress` that write their output via an\nout-pointer rather than a return value. The box JSON declares\n`\"returns\": \"bytes\"` and the wrapper threads the buffer through.\n\nIf the encoded value exceeds `sm_out_capacity`, the wrapper aborts\n(per issue 303). For boxes whose output capacity is not known at\ncompile time, see \"Variable-size outputs\" below — the wrapper\nroutes through the large-value heap.\n\n## Variable-size outputs\n\nFor boxes whose output capacity is not known at compile time (issue\n302's large-value heap): the box JSON declares `output_capacity = 0`\nand the wrapper allocates from the large-value heap on each call.\nFor `bytes` and `json` returns, the wrapper transparently picks the\nheap path when the box is variable-size — the user's function is\nunchanged either way. The handle (pointer + size into the\nlarge-value heap) is what ends up in `sm_out_buf`.\n\nFor string returns, similarly: if the returned string exceeds the\ndeclared fixed `output_capacity`, the wrapper falls back to the\nlarge-value heap. This decision is made at compile time based on the\nbox JSON, not at runtime.\n\n## Thread safety of user code\n\nThe same `.so` is loaded by every worker thread that may call into\nit. **Static variables and globals declared in the user's C source\nare shared mutable state across all workers** unless explicitly\nmade `const`.\n\nA note on `static` in C: it does not mean immutable. `static` at\nfile scope means \"this symbol has internal linkage, only visible\ninside this `.c` file.\" `static` inside a function means \"this\nvariable persists across calls.\" Either way, the variable itself is\nmutable — `static int counter = 0; counter++;` is perfectly legal\nand does what it says, just with internal linkage. Immutable in C\nis `const`.\n\nSo:\n- `static int counter = 0;` at file scope — racy, shared across workers.\n- `static int x = 0;` inside a function body — racy, shared across workers calling that function.\n- `const int max = 100;` — safe, immutable.\n- `static const int max = 100;` — safe, immutable.\n\nBox functions must be reentrant — no mutable shared state without\nexplicit locking. The C spec does not enforce this; the rule lives\nin `docs/005-language-specs.md` (to be written) for box authors to\nread.\n\n### Library functions that need global init\n\nMany real C libraries require a one-time setup call before any of\ntheir functions work — `curl_global_init` for libcurl,\n`OPENSSL_init_crypto` for OpenSSL, etc. A SoraMech box that calls\ninto such a library cannot just be wired in cold; the library's\nstate has to exist before the call.\n\nTwo patterns handle this without changing the spec interface:\n\n1. **Init box wired as an entry point.** The user creates a small C\n   box whose function is the library's init call (e.g.\n   `curl_global_init`). They mark it as an entry box and wire it\n   such that any box using libcurl is downstream of it. The init\n   runs once at startup before any consumer fires. Process-global\n   library state — which is what most C libraries actually use — is\n   set up by the time anyone needs it. Pairs with a teardown box\n   wired as a terminal node if needed.\n\n2. **Per-worker init via spec extension** (future). For libraries\n   that need per-worker setup (each thread gets its own handle),\n   the C spec gains an optional per-box `worker_init_fn` field in\n   the box JSON. The spec calls that function once per worker\n   thread during pool startup, before any box invoke. Not in scope\n   yet — pattern (1) covers the common case.\n\nThe init-box approach is the recommended starting point. The\nspec-extension path is the escape hatch when (1) does not fit.\n\nA future fallback exists: `dlmopen`, a Linux variant of `dlopen`\nthat loads each library into its own isolated \"namespace,\" giving\neach worker its own copy of the library's symbols (statics\nincluded). Two threads using two different namespaces would not\nshare static state. Less portable than `dlopen` (Linux-only), so\nnot the default — flagged here as the escape hatch if static-\nvariable races become a real problem.\n\n## Build\n\n```\nlangs/c/\n    spec.c              ← lang_spec_t implementation\n    soramech-c.h        ← user-facing header (shipped to maps via compile step)\n    Makefile            ← builds spec.so\n    spec.so             ← built artifact (gitignored)\n```\n\nSpec Makefile target:\n```make\nspec.so: spec.c\n\t$(CC) -shared -fPIC -O2 -Wall -o $@ $< -ldl\n```\n\nLinking against `libdl` for `dlopen` / `dlsym` is the only\ndependency. No interpreter, no helper library beyond libc.\n\n### What `dlopen` and `dlsym` do\n- `dlopen(\"path/to/file.so\", flags)` loads a shared library at\n  runtime. The OS loader maps the library's code into the process's\n  memory and returns a handle. Same idea as Windows'\n  `LoadLibrary`.\n- `dlsym(handle, \"name\")` looks up a symbol — a function or a\n  variable — by name inside an already-loaded library, and returns\n  a pointer to it. Same idea as Windows' `GetProcAddress`.\n\nTogether they are how a program loads and calls code that wasn't\nlinked at compile time. Plugin systems are the classic use case.\nHere, every C box compiles to its own `.so`; the spec `dlopen`s the\n`.so` once per worker, `dlsym`s `sm_box_entry` once per file, and\ncalls the resulting function pointer per invocation.\n\nThe user's C box files are compiled by the `compile` callback at map\nload time, not by this Makefile. The Makefile here builds only the\nspec itself.\n\n## Error handling\n\n- `dlopen` failure (missing `.so`, link errors): print path + `dlerror()`\n  to stderr, return 1, dispatch layer aborts.\n- `dlsym` failure (missing function): print file/fn + `dlerror()`,\n  return 1, abort.\n- Compile failure: `cc` exit nonzero, print compiler stderr (already\n  routed there by `cc`), return 1, abort.\n- User function returns nonzero: propagate that as the spec's return,\n  abort.\n\nNo retry, no fallback. Per issue 303.\n\n## Open questions\n\n(none currently — earlier questions resolved as follows:)\n\n- Per-box `cflags`: yes, add the field to the box JSON. The\n  inspector shows a \"Compile flags\" text input when a C-language\n  box is selected (phase 2 inspector work).\n- Typed signatures: handled via compile-time wrapper generation\n  (see \"Box file convention\" above). No libffi runtime dependency.\n- Static-variable isolation via `dlmopen`: deferred. Current rule\n  is \"C box authors write reentrant code\"; if that breaks down in\n  practice, fall back to per-worker `dlmopen` namespaces (Linux-only).\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. Set up `langs/c/` directory with a Makefile that builds an empty\n   `spec.so` exporting a stub `soramech_lang_spec`.\n2. Implement `init` and `teardown` with the dlopen-handle cache.\n3. Implement `compile` — fork/exec `cc` with the standard flags.\n   Smoke test: compile a single hello-world `.c` file.\n4. Implement `invoke` — dlsym, direct call, propagate return.\n5. Write `soramech-c.h` with the `SM_BOX_ARGS` macro and the basic\n   input/output helpers.\n6. Smoke test: a C box that takes one string input, writes a string\n   output, runs end-to-end through the pool.\n7. Add the typed input helpers (`sm_in_int`, `sm_in_double`, etc.).\n8. Add the typed output helpers.\n9. Test against `maps/driver-test` (C portions).\n10. Add variable-size output support (`sm_out_alloc`, `sm_out_handle`).\n11. Document in `docs/005-language-specs.md` once it exists, with a\n    note on thread safety.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `drivers/c.sh` — phase 2 C driver, retired by this spec\n- `langs/lang-spec.h` — interface header (issue 303)\n- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — spec contract this implements\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — dispatch layer that calls\n  `invoke`\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — large-value heap\n- `issues/222-compile-button-and-assets-directory.md` — where compiled\n  `.so`s live (`compiled/bin/`)\n- `issues/306-lua-language-spec.md` — sister spec; same shape, no\n  compile step\n- `maps/driver-test` — multi-language test map including C boxes\n\n## Implementation log\n\n### Compile + invoke — 2026-05-12\n\n`langs/c/spec.c`:\n- `compile(src, out)` forks gcc with `-shared -fPIC -O2 -Wall`.\n- `init` allocates a 32-entry dlopen cache; `teardown` walks it.\n- `invoke` looks up the .so in the cache or dlopens it, dlsyms\n  the named function, and calls it through a fixed signature:\n  `int fn(const void **inputs, const int *sizes, int n,\n  void *out_buf, int out_capacity, int *out_size)`.\n\nConvention: C box functions all match that signature. The\noptional typed-wrapper mode (per-box signature parsing +\ngenerated marshaller) is deferred until a box wants types that\ndiverge from the byte-array shape.\n\n`tests/maps/hello/src/echo.c` ships two fixture functions; five\ntests in `tests/307-c-spec-test.c` compile and invoke them, plus\nthe missing-symbol and bad-source failure modes.\n"
    }

pool_current_worker->handles[b->spec_idx]\n        : NULL;\n    if (!handle) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"dispatch: '%s' worker handle for spec[%d] is NULL\\n\",\n                b->id, b->spec_idx);\n        return -1;\n    }\n\n    /* Read inputs. */\n    int n = b->n_inputs;\n    char        *bufs[16]       = {0};\n    ua_chunk_t  *buf_chunks[16] = {0};\n    const void  *datas[16]      = {0};\n    int          sizes[16]      = {0};\n    if (n > (int)(sizeof bufs / sizeof bufs[0])) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"dispatch: '%s' has %d inputs (cap = %d)\\n\",\n                b->id, n, (int)(sizeof bufs / sizeof bufs[0]));\n        return -1;\n    }\n    int failed = 0;\n    int n_present = read_inputs(ctx, b, bufs, buf_chunks, datas, sizes,\n                                ctx->default_out_capacity, &failed);\n    if (failed) {\n        release_inputs(ctx, n, bufs, buf_chunks);\n        return -1;\n    }\n\n    /* Verbose: emit the input payloads now, before the spec runs. */\n    emit_input_events(ctx, task_id, bufs, sizes, n_present);\n\n    /* Resolve the box's source file relative to map_dir. */\n    char *ref_path = b->ref ?
