Stack after this\n87\t     * block: ..., cache, module. */\n88\t    lua_getfield(L, LUA_REGISTRYINDEX, LUA_CACHE_KEY);\n89\t    lua_getfield(L, -1, file_path);\n90\t    if (lua_isnil(L, -1)) {\n91\t        lua_pop(L, 1);   /* discard nil */\n92\t        /* Stack: ..., cache */\n93\t\n94\t        if (luaL_loadfile(L, file_path) != 0) {\n95\t            fprintf(stderr, \"lua spec: loadfile('%s'): %s\\n\",\n96\t                    file_path, lua_tostring(L, -1));\n97\t            lua_settop(L, baseline);\n98\t            return -1;\n99\t        }\n100\t        if (lua_pcall(L, 0, 1, 0) != 0) {\n101\t            fprintf(stderr, \"lua spec: chunk exec '%s': %s\\n\",\n102\t                    file_path, lua_tostring(L, -1));\n103\t            lua_settop(L, baseline);\n104\t            return -1;\n105\t        }\n106\t        if (!lua_istable(L, -1)) {\n107\t            fprintf(stderr, \"lua spec: '%s' did not return a table\\n\", file_path);\n108\t            lua_settop(L, baseline);\n109\t            return -1;\n110\t        }\n111\t        /* Stack: ..., cache, module. Cache the module under\n112\t         * file_path. */\n113\t        lua_pushvalue(L, -1);\n114\t        lua_setfield(L, -3, file_path);\n115\t    }\n116\t    /* Stack at this point: ..., cache, module. */\n117\t\n118\t    /* Pull the function out of the module table. */\n119\t    lua_getfield(L, -1, fn_name);\n120\t    if (!lua_isfunction(L, -1)) {\n121\t        fprintf(stderr, \"lua spec: '%s' is not a function in %s\\n\",\n122\t                fn_name, file_path);\n123\t        lua_settop(L, baseline);\n124\t        return -1;\n125\t    }\n126\t    /* Stack: ..., cache, module, function. Drop module + cache. */\n127\t    lua_remove(L, -2);   /* drop module */\n128\t    lua_remove(L, -2);   /* drop cache  */\n129\t\n130\t    /* Push each input as a Lua string. */\n131\t    for (int i = 0; i < n_inputs; i++) {\n132\t        if (input_data[i] == NULL && input_sizes[i] > 0) {\n133\t            fprintf(stderr, \"lua spec: input %d is NULL with size %d\\n\",\n134\t                    i, input_sizes[i]);\n135\t            lua_settop(L, baseline);\n136\t            return -1;\n137\t        }\n138\t        lua_pushlstring(L, (const char *)input_data[i], (size_t)input_sizes[i]);\n139\t    }\n140\t\n141\t    /* Call. One return value expected. */\n142\t    if (lua_pcall(L, n_inputs, 1, 0) != 0) {\n143\t        fprintf(stderr, \"lua spec: %s.%s: %s\\n\",\n144\t                file_path, fn_name, lua_tostring(L, -1));\n145\t        lua_settop(L, baseline);\n146\t        return -1;\n147\t    }\n148\t\n149\t    /* Convert the return to a string. tostring handles numbers /\n150\t     * booleans / nil; if the spec needs richer marshaling later\n151\t     * (tables, structs), that's an issue-312-shaped change. */\n152\t    size_t len = 0;\n153\t    const char *result = lua_tolstring(L, -1, &len);\n154\t    if (!result) {\n155\t        /* Non-coercible value. For now, surface as zero-length\n156\t         * output rather than an error — the box returned something\n157\t         * we can't serialize, but the call itself succeeded. */\n158\t        if (out_size) *out_size = 0;\n159\t        lua_settop(L, baseline);\n160\t        return 0;\n161\t    }\n162\t    if ((int)len > out_buf_capacity) {\n163\t        fprintf(stderr, \"lua spec: %s.%s returned %zu bytes; \"\n164\t                        \"buffer is %d\\n\",\n165\t                file_path, fn_name, len, out_buf_capacity);\n166\t        lua_settop(L, baseline);\n167\t        return -1;\n168\t    }\n169\t    if (out_buf && len > 0) memcpy(out_buf, result, len);\n170\t    if (out_size) *out_size = (int)len;\n171\t\n172\t    lua_settop(L, baseline);\n173\t    return 0;\n174\t}\n175\t/* }}} */\n176\t\n177\t/* {{{ encode_value() — write one Lua value at `abs_idx` as JSON */\n178\t/* Walk the value at absolute stack index `abs_idx` and emit JSON\n179\t * via the streaming writer `w`. Recurses into tables. Stack-neutral:\n180\t * the value at abs_idx stays put (we only push/pop scratch keys\n181\t * during table traversal). Returns 0 ok, -1 on unsupported type or\n182\t * writer truncation. The \"unsupported type\" path is loud — function,\n183\t * userdata, thread, lightuserdata produce a stderr error rather\n184\t * than a silent fallback (project convention forbids those). The\n185\t * richer primitives — $ref, $function_pointer, $lang_opaque — land\n186\t * later; this first cut only handles the JSON-clean scalars and\n187\t * containers. */\n188\tstatic int encode_value(lua_State *L, int abs_idx, json_writer_t *w)\n189\t{\n190\t    int t = lua_type(L, abs_idx);\n191\t    switch (t) {\n192\t    case LUA_TNIL:\n193\t        json_writer_null(w);\n194\t        return 0;\n195\t    case LUA_TBOOLEAN:\n196\t        json_writer_bool(w, lua_toboolean(L, abs_idx));\n197\t        return 0;\n198\t    case LUA_TNUMBER: {\n199\t        /* Integer-shaped numbers go via writer_int so JSON doesn't\n200\t         * show \"3.0\" where \"3\" reads better. The float path uses\n201\t         * %g internally inside the writer. */\n202\t        lua_Number n = lua_tonumber(L, abs_idx);\n203\t        long long  i = (long long)n;\n204\t        if ((lua_Number)i == n) json_writer_int(w, i);\n205\t        else                    json_writer_number(w, (double)n);\n206\t        return 0;\n207\t    }\n208\t    case LUA_TSTRING:\n209\t        json_writer_string(w, lua_tostring(L, abs_idx));\n210\t        return 0;\n211\t    case LUA_TTABLE: {\n212\t        /* n-field convention (issue 317, fidelity directive):\n213\t         *\n214\t         * If the table carries `n` as a non-negative integer, that\n215\t         * field declares \"this is a JSON array of length n; every\n216\t         * missing integer key in 1..n is an explicit null on the\n217\t         * wire.\" That's how the decoder records arrays it pushed\n218\t         * onto the stack — a full round-trip of [true,false,null]\n219\t         * leaves `{n=3, [1]=true, [2]=false}` here, and we have to\n220\t         * emit `[true,false,null]` from it. Idiomatic Lua tables\n221\t         * (no n field) still take the existing heuristic path.\n222\t         *\n223\t         * The intrusion of an explicit `n` field on values pushed\n224\t         * by the decoder is the price of preserving JSON fidelity\n225\t         * through Lua's nil-as-absence storage model. Documented\n226\t         * in issue 317. */\n227\t        lua_getfield(L, abs_idx, \"n\");\n228\t        int  has_declared_len = 0;\n229\t        long declared_len     = 0;\n230\t        if (lua_type(L, -1) == LUA_TNUMBER) {\n231\t            lua_Number nn = lua_tonumber(L, -1);\n232\t            long       ni = (long)nn;\n233\t            if ((lua_Number)ni == nn && ni >= 0) {\n234\t                has_declared_len = 1;\n235\t                declared_len     = ni;\n236\t            }\n237\t        }\n238\t        lua_pop(L, 1);\n239\t\n240\t        if (has_declared_len) {\n241\t            json_writer_array(w);\n242\t            for (long i = 1; i <= declared_len; i++) {\n243\t                lua_rawgeti(L, abs_idx, (int)i);\n244\t                int top = lua_gettop(L);\n245\t                /* Missing keys land here as nil and encode_value\n246\t                 * emits json null for them — exactly the round-trip\n247\t                 * behavior the n-field convention promises. */\n248\t                int r = encode_value(L, top, w);\n249\t                lua_pop(L, 1);\n250\t                if (r != 0) return -1;\n251\t            }\n252\t            json_writer_end(w);\n253\t            return 0;\n254\t        }\n255\t\n256\t        /* No n field — fall back to the existing heuristic: every\n257\t         * key in 1..N and no others → array; anything else → object.\n258\t         * Empty tables go through the object path because JSON `[]`\n259\t         * vs `{}` is a distinction Lua can't natively express, and\n260\t         * the n-field convention is the way to ask for `[]`. */\n261\t        int n = (int)lua_objlen(L, abs_idx);\n262\t        int total = 0;\n263\t        lua_pushnil(L);\n264\t        while (lua_next(L, abs_idx) != 0) {\n265\t            total++;\n266\t            lua_pop(L, 1);\n267\t        }\n268\t        int is_array = (n > 0 && total == n);\n269\t\n270\t        if (is_array) {\n271\t            json_writer_array(w);\n272\t            for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {\n273\t                lua_rawgeti(L, abs_idx, i);\n274\t                int top = lua_gettop(L);\n275\t                int r = encode_value(L, top, w);\n276\t                lua_pop(L, 1);\n277\t                if (r != 0) return -1;\n278\t            }\n279\t            json_writer_end(w);\n280\t        } else {\n281\t            json_writer_object(w);\n282\t            lua_pushnil(L);\n283\t            while (lua_next(L, abs_idx) != 0) {\n284\t                /* Key at -2, value at -1. We must NOT call\n285\t                 * lua_tostring on the key in-place because that\n286\t                 * would coerce numbers to strings and corrupt\n287\t                 * lua_next's iteration state — render numeric keys\n288\t                 * into a local buffer instead. */\n289\t                int kt = lua_type(L, -2);\n290\t                if (kt == LUA_TSTRING) {\n291\t                    json_writer_key(w, lua_tostring(L, -2));\n292\t                } else if (kt == LUA_TNUMBER) {\n293\t                    char keybuf[32];\n294\t                    lua_Number kn = lua_tonumber(L, -2);\n295\t                    long long  ki = (long long)kn;\n296\t                    if ((lua_Number)ki == kn) snprintf(keybuf, sizeof(keybuf), \"%lld\", ki);\n297\t                    else                      snprintf(keybuf, sizeof(keybuf), \"%g\", (double)kn);\n298\t                    json_writer_key(w, keybuf);\n299\t                } else {\n300\t                    fprintf(stderr, \"lua spec: table key of type %s is not JSON-encodable\\n\",\n301\t                            lua_typename(L, kt));\n302\t                    lua_pop(L, 2);\n303\t                    return -1;\n304\t                }\n305\t                int top = lua_gettop(L);   /* points at the value */\n306\t                int r = encode_value(L, top, w);\n307\t                lua_pop(L, 1);             /* drop value, keep key for lua_next */\n308\t                if (r != 0) {\n309\t                    lua_pop(L, 1);          /* drop the key too */\n310\t                    return -1;\n311\t                }\n312\t            }\n313\t            json_writer_end(w);\n314\t        }\n315\t        return 0;\n316\t    }\n317\t    default:\n318\t        /* Function / userdata / thread / lightuserdata. The richer\n319\t         * wire primitives ($function_pointer, $lang_opaque) decompose\n320\t         * these into data the destination can rebuild, but that\n321\t         * decomposition lands as a follow-on. Today: hard error. */\n322\t        fprintf(stderr, \"lua spec: cannot JSON-encode value of type %s\\n\",\n323\t                lua_typename(L, t));\n324\t        return -1;\n325\t    }\n326\t}\n327\t/* }}} */\n328\t\n329\t/* {{{ lua_native_to_json() — top-of-stack Lua value → JSON bytes */\n330\t/* Per the bridge stack-protocol convention (lang-spec.h): the\n331\t * producer leaves its native value at the top of its working store.\n332\t * For Lua, that's the top of `lua_State`. The bridge consumes it —\n333\t * one pop on success, on failure the stack is left untouched so the\n334\t * caller can inspect / log before tearing down. */\n335\tstatic int lua_native_to_json(void *handle,\n336\t                              const void *src, int src_size,\n337\t                              void *dst, int dst_capacity, int *dst_size)\n338\t{\n339\t    (void)src;\n340\t    (void)src_size;\n341\t    lua_State *L = (lua_State *)handle;\n342\t    if (!L || !dst || dst_capacity <= 0) return -1;\n343\t    if (lua_gettop(L) < 1) {\n344\t        fprintf(stderr, \"lua spec: native_to_json called with empty stack\\n\");\n345\t        return -1;\n346\t    }\n347\t\n348\t    json_writer_t w;\n349\t    json_writer_init(&w, (char *)dst, dst_capacity);\n350\t\n351\t    int top = lua_gettop(L);\n352\t    if (encode_value(L, top, &w) != 0) return -1;\n353\t\n354\t    int n = json_writer_finish(&w);\n355\t    if (n < 0) {\n356\t        fprintf(stderr, \"lua spec: native_to_json: output buffer (%d bytes) too small\\n\",\n357\t                dst_capacity);\n358\t        return -1;\n359\t    }\n360\t    if (dst_size) *dst_size = n;\n361\t    lua_pop(L, 1);\n362\t    return 0;\n363\t}\n364\t/* }}} */\n365\t\n366\t/* {{{ decode_node() — push one JSON node onto the Lua stack */\n367\t/* Recursive walk over the parsed DOM. Each call adds exactly one\n368\t * value to the stack on success; on failure the stack is wound back\n369\t * to where this call started so partial decodes don't pollute it. */\n370\tstatic int decode_node(lua_State *L, const json_node_t *node)\n371\t{\n372\t    int baseline = lua_gettop(L);\n373\t    switch (json_kind(node)) {\n374\t    case JSON_NULL:\n375\t        lua_pushnil(L);\n376\t        return 0;\n377\t    case JSON_BOOL:\n378\t        lua_pushboolean(L, json_bool_value(node));\n379\t        return 0;\n380\t    case JSON_NUMBER:\n381\t        lua_pushnumber(L, json_number_value(node));\n382\t        return 0;\n383\t    case JSON_STRING:\n384\t        lua_pushstring(L, json_string_value(node));\n385\t        return 0;\n386\t    case JSON_ARRAY: {\n387\t        /* Push as `{n = N, [1] = ..., [2] = ..., ...}` so the\n388\t         * encoder's n-field path can reconstruct the array\n389\t         * faithfully on the way out, including any embedded or\n390\t         * trailing nulls. `lua_rawseti` on a JSON `null` (which\n391\t         * decode_node pushed as Lua nil) is effectively a key\n392\t         * deletion — which is precisely the right representation\n393\t         * for \"missing slot, fill with null at encode time.\" */\n394\t        int n = json_array_size(node);\n395\t        lua_createtable(L, n, 1);\n396\t        lua_pushinteger(L, n);\n397\t        lua_setfield(L, -2, \"n\");\n398\t        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {\n399\t            if (decode_node(L, json_array_at(node, i)) != 0) {\n400\t                lua_settop(L, baseline);\n401\t                return -1;\n402\t            }\n403\t            lua_rawseti(L, -2, i + 1);\n404\t        }\n405\t        return 0;\n406\t    }\n407\t    case JSON_OBJECT: {\n408\t        int n = json_object_size(node);\n409\t        lua_createtable(L, 0, n);\n410\t        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {\n411\t            if (decode_node(L, json_object_value(node, i)) != 0) {\n412\t                lua_settop(L, baseline);\n413\t                return -1;\n414\t            }\n415\t            lua_setfield(L, -2, json_object_key(node, i));\n416\t        }\n417\t        return 0;\n418\t    }\n419\t    }\n420\t    fprintf(stderr, \"lua spec: decode_node: unknown JSON kind\\n\");\n421\t    lua_settop(L, baseline);\n422\t    return -1;\n423\t}\n424\t/* }}} */\n425\t\n426\t/* {{{ lua_json_to_native() — JSON bytes → push value onto Lua stack */\n427\t/* The bridge parses `src` into a transient arena, walks the DOM\n428\t * onto the lua_State stack, then frees the arena. The arena is\n429\t * created and destroyed inside the call — no per-bridge cache yet.\n430\t * If parse-time perf shows up in profiles, we can stash an arena\n431\t * inside the worker handle later.\n432\t *\n433\t * `src` may not be NUL-terminated (the caller passes us a slice\n434\t * out of a wire buffer), so we copy into a local NUL-terminated\n435\t * scratch before parsing — json_parse requires NUL termination\n436\t * (see libs/json/json.h). */\n437\tstatic int lua_json_to_native(void *handle,\n438\t                              const void *src, int src_size,\n439\t                              void *dst, int dst_capacity, int *dst_size)\n440\t{\n441\t    (void)dst;\n442\t    (void)dst_capacity;\n443\t    (void)dst_size;\n444\t    lua_State *L = (lua_State *)handle;\n445\t    if (!L || !src || src_size <= 0) return -1;\n446\t\n447\t    char *scratch = (char *)malloc((size_t)src_size + 1);\n448\t    if (!scratch) {\n449\t        fprintf(stderr, \"lua spec: json_to_native: out of memory\\n\");\n450\t        return -1;\n451\t    }\n452\t    memcpy(scratch, src, (size_t)src_size);\n453\t    scratch[src_size] = '\\0';\n454\t\n455\t    json_arena_t *arena = json_arena_create();\n456\t    if (!arena) {\n457\t        free(scratch);\n458\t        fprintf(stderr, \"lua spec: json_to_native: arena allocation failed\\n\");\n459\t        return -1;\n460\t    }\n461\t\n462\t    int err_offset = 0;\n463\t    const char *err_msg = NULL;\n464\t    json_node_t *node = json_parse(arena, scratch, &err_offset, &err_msg);\n465\t    free(scratch);\n466\t    if (!node) {\n467\t        fprintf(stderr, \"lua spec: json_to_native: parse error at byte %d: %s\\n\",\n468\t                err_offset, err_msg ? err_msg : \"(no message)\");\n469\t        json_arena_destroy(arena);\n470\t        return -1;\n471\t    }\n472\t\n473\t    int r = decode_node(L, node);\n474\t    json_arena_destroy(arena);\n475\t    return r;\n476\t}\n477\t/* }}} */\n478\t\n479\t/* {{{ soramech_lang_spec */\n480\tlang_spec_t soramech_lang_spec = {\n481\t    .name           = \"lua\",\n482\t    .file_ext       = \".lua\",\n483\t    .init           = lua_init,\n484\t    .teardown       = lua_teardown,\n485\t    .compile        = 0,\n486\t    .invoke         = lua_invoke,\n487\t    .native_to_json = lua_native_to_json,\n488\t    .json_to_native = lua_json_to_native,\n489\t};\n490\t/* }}} */\n491\t",

      "content":"/* langs/lua/spec.c — Lua language spec for SoraMech.\n *\n * Per-worker handle is a `lua_State` with the standard libraries\n * opened. Invocation convention: the box's source file is expected\n * to return a Lua table (`return M` at the bottom), and the\n * fn_name is a key into that table. Inputs arrive as byte arrays;\n * each one is pushed as a Lua string. The function's single return\n * value is converted to a string (via tostring semantics) and\n * memcpy'd into the caller's output buffer.\n *\n * Designed in issue 306. Implementation choices that matter:\n *\n *  - One lua_State per worker thread. lua_State is not\n *    thread-safe, but per-thread requires no locking.\n *  - The state's stack is rewound to its baseline depth at every\n *    invoke entry/exit so cross-call leaks don't accumulate.\n *  - File caching (luaL_loadfile once, replayed via lua_call) is\n *    deferred — this iteration loads the chunk on every invoke.\n *    Lands as a follow-on once profiling justifies it.\n *  - The chunk's side effects run on every invoke too (since\n *    we re-load and re-execute). Box source files should be pure\n *    \"return M\" modules for now.\n */\n\n#include \"lang-spec.h\"\n#include \"json.h\"\n\n#include <lua.h>\n#include <lauxlib.h>\n#include <lualib.h>\n\n#include <stdio.h>\n#include <stdlib.h>\n#include <string.h>\n\n/* Registry key for the per-worker file → module-table cache. The\n * key is a string in the Lua registry; the value is a Lua table\n * keyed by file path. Each entry's value is the module table the\n * file's chunk returned.\n *\n * Caching is per-`lua_State` (i.e. per-worker), which matches the\n * thread model: each worker has its own state, never shared. No\n * locking needed because only the worker that owns the state ever\n * touches the cache. */\n#define LUA_CACHE_KEY \"soramech.module_cache\"\n\n/* {{{ lua_init() — create a state, open standard libs, seed cache */\nstatic void *lua_init(int worker_idx)\n{\n    (void)worker_idx;\n    lua_State *L = luaL_newstate();\n    if (!L) return NULL;\n    luaL_openlibs(L);\n    /* Seed the empty cache table. */\n    lua_newtable(L);\n    lua_setfield(L, LUA_REGISTRYINDEX, LUA_CACHE_KEY);\n    return L;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ lua_teardown() */\nstatic void lua_teardown(void *handle)\n{\n    if (handle) lua_close((lua_State *)handle);\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ lua_invoke() */\nstatic int lua_invoke(void *handle,\n                      const char  *file_path,\n                      const char  *fn_name,\n                      const void **input_data,\n                      const int   *input_sizes,\n                      int          n_inputs,\n                      void        *out_buf,\n                      int          out_buf_capacity,\n                      int         *out_size)\n{\n    lua_State *L = (lua_State *)handle;\n    if (!L || !file_path || !fn_name) return -1;\n\n    int baseline = lua_gettop(L);\n\n    /* Module cache lookup. The cache table lives in the registry\n     * under LUA_CACHE_KEY; each key is a file path, each value is\n     * the module table the file's chunk returned. Stack after this\n     * block: ..., cache, module. */\n    lua_getfield(L, LUA_REGISTRYINDEX, LUA_CACHE_KEY);\n    lua_getfield(L, -1, file_path);\n    if (lua_isnil(L, -1)) {\n        lua_pop(L, 1);   /* discard nil */\n        /* Stack: ..., cache */\n\n        if (luaL_loadfile(L, file_path) != 0) {\n            fprintf(stderr, \"lua spec: loadfile('%s'): %s\\n\",\n                    file_path, lua_tostring(L, -1));\n            lua_settop(L, baseline);\n            return -1;\n        }\n        if (lua_pcall(L, 0, 1, 0) != 0) {\n            fprintf(stderr, \"lua spec: chunk exec '%s': %s\\n\",\n                    file_path, lua_tostring(L, -1));\n            lua_settop(L, baseline);\n            return -1;\n        }\n        if (!lua_istable(L, -1)) {\n            fprintf(stderr, \"lua spec: '%s' did not return a table\\n\", file_path);\n            lua_settop(L, baseline);\n            return -1;\n        }\n        /* Stack: ..., cache, module. Cache the module under\n         * file_path. */\n        lua_pushvalue(L, -1);\n        lua_setfield(L, -3, file_path);\n    }\n    /* Stack at this point: ..., cache, module. */\n\n    /* Pull the function out of the module table. */\n    lua_getfield(L, -1, fn_name);\n    if (!lua_isfunction(L, -1)) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"lua spec: '%s' is not a function in %s\\n\",\n                fn_name, file_path);\n        lua_settop(L, baseline);\n        return -1;\n    }\n    /* Stack: ..., cache, module, function.       "content":"/* langs/c/spec.c — C language spec for SoraMech.\n *\n * Per-worker handle is a small dlopen cache. `compile` runs gcc\n * to turn a box source file into a .so; `invoke` dlopens the .so\n * (caching the handle), dlsyms the named function, and calls it\n * through a fixed signature.\n *\n * Designed in issue 307. C box functions follow a single\n * convention that matches the spec's `invoke` shape minus the\n * per-worker handle:\n *\n *     int box_fn(const void **inputs, const int *sizes, int n,\n *                void *out_buf, int out_capacity, int *out_size);\n *\n * Return 0 on success, nonzero (fatal) on failure. True iff the\n  producer feeding that port has the same language as this box.\n- `output_edge_native[j]` — one bit per outgoing connection\n  (not per output port — a single output port can fan to\n  multiple consumers, each of which is classified independently\n  because the language pair may differ across consumers).\n\nBoth arrays are computed during `graph_attach_runtime` and live\non the box record. No runtime re-evaluation.\n\n## Runtime dispatch\n\nThe dispatch action calls `invoke_native` always (when the spec\nprovides one). The boundary work is per-edge in two places:\ninput-read and output-push.\n\n### Input-read: per-input-port\n\n```c\nfor (int i = 0; i < n_inputs; i++) {\n    slot_pop(input_slots[i], wire_buf, wire_buf_cap);\n    if (b->input_edge_native[i]) {\n        // wire bytes are native form already; hand to invoke_native as-is\n        native_inputs[i] = wire_buf;\n    } else {\n        // wire bytes are JSON; lift into native form\n        spec->json_to_native(ctx, wire_buf, wire_size,\n                             native_buf, native_cap, &native_size);\n        native_inputs[i] = native_buf;\n    }\n}\nspec->invoke_native(ctx, fn, native_inputs, n_inputs,\n                    native_out, native_out_cap, &native_out_size);\n```\n\n### Output-push: per-outgoing-connection\n\n```c\nfor (int j = 0; j < b->n_connections; j++) {\n    if (b->output_edge_native[j]) {\n        // consumer is same-lang; push native bytes directly\n        slot_push(consumer_slot, native_out, native_out_size, tag);\n    } else {\n        // consumer is cross-lang; serialize to JSON once per such edge\n        spec->native_to_json(ctx, native_out, native_out_size,\n                             json_buf, json_buf_cap, &json_size);\n        slot_push(consumer_slot, json_buf, json_size, tag);\n    }\n}\n```\n\nIf multiple cross-lang consumers share the producer's language,\nthe dispatch can cache the JSON encoding from the first such\nedge and reuse it for the rest (optimization, not required for\ncorrectness).\n\nIf the spec's `invoke_native` is NULL (e.g., bash), the dispatch\nfalls back to the universal `invoke` (JSON-in, JSON-out) and\ntreats every edge as JSON. This is the slow path; it's always\ncorrect.\n\n## Edge cases\n\n- **All-same-language graph**: every wire is fast-path; `invoke_json`\n  never runs. Spec writers can stub it out.\n- **All-different-language graph**: every wire is JSON;\n  `invoke_native` handles bytes that came back from `json_to_native`.\n- **One same-language wire, several cross-language wires from the same\n  producer**: the producer writes JSON. Same-language consumer\n  decodes via `json_to_native` (still cheaper than full encode +\n  decode round-trip — only one direction of conversion is paid,\n  not two).\n- **Type changes mid-development**: a wire that was Lua→Lua becomes\n  Lua→C as the user changes a downstream box's language. Compile\n  flips the flag; the producer now writes JSON. No runtime\n  surprises, no migration.\n\n## Implementation cost\n\nThe two-invoke spec interface adds maybe 30 lines per language\nspec. The compile-time wire classification is one pass over the\ngraph. The dispatch action's input-read branch is one `if` on the\nwire flag. None of this is hot-path complex; the gain is one less\nJSON encode/decode per same-language hop, which is the whole point.\n\n## Future: whole-program same-language compilation\n\nA bigger optimization beyond this issue: at compile time, merge\nall same-language boxes into one translation unit. The C spec\nbecomes whole-program; the Lua spec produces one bytecode chunk\ncovering every Lua function. Box-boundary crossings become regular\nfunction calls — no slot store, no dispatch layer, no spec\ninvocation. Only cross-language wires retain the slot machinery.\n\nThis is a phase-3.5+ optimization and a much bigger lift —\nrequires the spec's `compile` callback to coordinate across all\nboxes of its language, plus a runtime mode that bypasses the\ndispatch layer for fully-merged regions of the graph. The\nwire-level fast path in this issue is the immediate, smaller win.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. **Spec interface** (issue 303): add `invoke_native`,\n   `invoke_json`, `native_to_json`, `json_to_native` callbacks.\n   Update the contract doc.\n2. **Compile step** (issue 309): walk wires, set `fast_path` flag,\n   set `output_format` per box.\n3. **Dispatch action** (issue 304): branch on `fast_path` /\n   `output_format` when reading inputs and when writing the\n   output.\n4. **Per-language specs** (306, 307, 308): implement both invoke\n   paths. Bash's fast path is a thin alias around the JSON path.\n   C's fast path is `memcpy`. Lua's fast path picks a native\n   encoding (cjson for tables; raw bytes for primitives).\n5. **Tests**: smoke tests confirming a 100k-iteration Lua→Lua\n   pipeline with the fast path runs measurably faster than the\n   same pipeline with the JSON path, and that mixed-language\n   pipelines still work.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — adds the new callbacks\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — branch on fast_path\n- `issues/309-build-system.md` — wire-flag enrichment\n- `issues/306-lua-language-spec.md`, `307-c-language-spec.md`,\n  `308-bash-language-spec.md` — per-spec native implementations\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — slot still stores opaque\n  bytes; the format negotiation is at the spec layer, not the\n  store\n\n## Implementation note: ask the user about type-annotated cross-language encodings\n\nBefore implementing this issue, the implementer must ask the user\nto decide on **type-annotated wire encodings** for cross-language\nhops — primitives go raw bytes (4-byte int as 4 bytes, not as the\nJSON string `\"42\"`), strings go length-prefixed UTF-8, structured\ntypes go JSON. That decision affects the spec interface (whether\n`json_to_native` is enough or whether we need a `decode_wire(type,\nbytes)` shape) and the wire-format byte layout. Don't proceed with\nthe implementation without explicit user direction on this; the\ntwo designs aren't trivially interchangeable later.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Whether a spec must implement `invoke_json`**: leaning yes, so\n  any spec can talk to any other spec. A spec that wants to\n  shortcut can declare cross-language wires unsupported via\n  compile-time error, but that's an opt-out, not the default.\n- **How to share the bridge functions across consumers**: native_to_json\n  on the producer side runs once per output (not per consumer), and\n  the JSON bytes go in the slot. Each cross-language consumer pays\n  json_to_native independently. Same-language consumers pay nothing.\n  Symmetrically: if the producer chose native and there's one\n  cross-language consumer, that consumer pays native_to_json then\n  json_to_native_their_lang. Two conversions for one cross-language\n  hop in this case. Probably fine; it's a corner case.\n\n## Implementation status\n\nWhat's in place (per the round summaries on 2026-05-12 to\n2026-05-19):\n\n- `lang_spec_t` extended with `invoke_native`, `invoke_json`,\n  `native_to_json`, `json_to_native` callback slots (issue 303\n  spec interface).\n- Each of the three specs declares all four callbacks. Today\n  they all alias to the single existing `invoke` implementation;\n  the actual specialization (real native_to_json / json_to_native\n  bodies, real per-language binary native form) is not yet\n  implemented.\n- `graph_attach_runtime` computes a per-box `use_native_invoke`\n  bit (true iff all input producers and all output consumers\n  share this box's language). The dispatch picks\n  `invoke_native > invoke_json > invoke` based on that single\n  bit.\n\nWhat's still ahead:\n\n- **Replace per-box `use_native_invoke` with per-edge\n  classification.** The current bit is the simpler approximation\n  of the per-edge design above. It needs to be split into\n  `b->input_edge_native[i]` and `b->output_edge_native[j]` arrays\n  computed at graph load, with the dispatch's input-read and\n  output-push paths each consulting the relevant array.\n- **Per-language native binary serializations.** Each spec\n  needs a real `native_to_json` and `json_to_native` (also\n  required by issue 317 for data boxes), plus a real\n  `invoke_native` that operates on whatever the spec considers\n  its native handoff format.\n- The type-annotated cross-language encoding decision flagged\n  above is still pending user direction.\n"

Box-to-box transitions within a language region become\n12\tordinary function calls — the optimizer can inline across them, the\n13\tlanguage runtime stays warm, and the slot store and dispatch layer\n14\tdon't run for those transitions at all. Only cross-language wires\n15\tretain the slot machinery.\n16\t\n17\tFor C: every C box becomes a function in one big `.c` file, with\n18\tthe build emitting one `.so`. Wire endpoints become direct calls;\n19\tthe optimizer inlines based on its usual heuristics.\n20\t\n21\tFor Lua: every Lua function gets pre-compiled into one bytecode\n22\tchunk loaded into one shared `lua_State` per worker. Wire\n23\tendpoints become direct `lua_pcall`s into that chunk — no JSON\n24\tencode/decode, no slot push/pop, no spec re-entry per call.\n25\t\n26\tFor Bash: probably no benefit — Bash is already process-per-call;\n27\tfusing scripts doesn't help much. Skip.\n28\t\n29\t## Why this is research, not a feature\n30\t\n31\tThree open questions that need code-level investigation before\n32\tthe design is concrete:\n33\t\n34\t1. **Loop and iterator boundaries**: a same-language region with an\n35\t   iterator inside it has dynamic re-spawning. Is the iterator\n36\t   merged in (a loop in the generated code) or does it remain a\n37\t   spec-mediated boundary? If the latter, the merge buys less.\n38\t2. **Compile time**: whole-program optimization is slow. Does the\n39\t   incremental-compile model (issue 309's mtime check) still apply,\n40\t   or do edits require a full rebuild of the merged region?\n41\t3. **Debug story**: a stack trace inside the merged region needs to\n42\t   point back to a specific box. Either source-map-style mapping or\n43\t   per-function preserved names — both have costs.\n44\t\n45\tThe right way to answer these is to prototype: take a small all-Lua\n46\tgraph (like the hello map) and see what a merged version looks\n47\tlike, both for runtime cost and for build-system complexity. The\n48\tprototype should be able to fall back to the per-box path if the\n49\tmerge fails for any reason.\n50\t\n51\t## Why blocked until rest of phase 3 completes\n52\t\n53\tThe merge optimization piggybacks on the per-box model — same\n54\tspecs, same compile callback, same dispatch layer for cross-language\n55\twires. Building it before the per-box model is settled risks\n56\tdesigning against a target that's still moving. After phase 3 ships\n57\tand the per-box path is stable, the merge becomes a clean\n58\t\"everything except spec invocation gets shorter for this region.\"\n59\t\n60\tIt's also genuinely lower priority than getting the runtime working\n61\tat all. The same-language fast path (issue 312) captures the\n62\t~2x JSON-skip win without any of this complexity. The merge wins a\n63\tfurther factor only if profile data shows function-call overhead\n64\tmatters at all after 312 ships.\n65\t\n66\t## Scope of the research output\n67\t\n68\tThe deliverable is a written design (not code) with:\n69\t- Concrete answers to the three questions above.\n70\t- A worked example: the merged C generated from a 5-box C-only\n71\t  graph, showing what the build artifact looks like.\n72\t- Estimated runtime cost of the per-box path vs the merged path\n73\t  on that example.\n74\t- A recommendation: ship as a feature, ship as an opt-in flag, or\n75\t  shelve indefinitely.\n76\t\n77\tAfter the design is reviewed, a separate implementation issue\n78\topens (or doesn't, depending on the recommendation).\n79\t\n80\t## Relevant files\n81\t\n82\t- `issues/312-same-language-wire-fast-path.md` — the immediate JSON-\n83\t  skip win this builds on\n84\t- `issues/307-c-language-spec.md` — `compile` callback that would\n85\t  grow whole-program-aware semantics\n86\t- `issues/306-lua-language-spec.md` — Lua-side bytecode pre-compile\n87\t- `issues/309-build-system.md` — how the merge integrates with the\n88\t  compile/package step\n89\t\n90\t## Open questions (for the research, not for now)\n91\t\n92\t- Cross-language wires inside the merged region: the merged region\n93\t  still has cross-language outputs that exit to other regions. The\n94\t  spec interface still applies at those boundaries, so the merge is\n95\t  region-internal optimization, not a global rearchitecture.\n96\t- C ABI for inlined wrappers: with whole-program optimization the\n97\t  wrapper-per-box generation might collapse to nothing. If the\n98\t  optimizer can prove a wire endpoint is always called from the\n99\t  merged region with known types, it can skip the wrapper.\n100\t- Iterators-with-side-effects: an iterator self-rescheduling its\n101\t  own task is normally dispatch-layer machinery. Inside a merged\n102\t  region, it could become a `while` loop. Is the iterator\n   merged in (a loop in the generated code) or does it remain a\n   spec-mediated boundary? If the latter, the merge buys less.\n2. **Compile time**: whole-program optimization is slow. Does the\n   incremental-compile model (issue 309's mtime check) still apply,\n   or do edits require a full rebuild of the merged region?\n3. **Debug story**: a stack trace inside the merged region needs to\n   point back to a specific box. Either source-map-style mapping or\n   per-function preserved names — both have costs.\n\nThe right way to answer these is to prototype: take a small all-Lua\ngraph (like the hello map) and see what a merged version looks\nlike, both for runtime cost and for build-system complexity. The\nprototype should be able to fall back to the per-box path if the\nmerge fails for any reason.\n\n## Why blocked until rest of phase 3 completes\n\nThe merge optimization piggybacks on the per-box model — same\nspecs, same compile callback, same dispatch layer for cross-language\nwires. Building it before the per-box model is settled risks\ndesigning against a target that's still moving. After phase 3 ships\nand the per-box path is stable, the merge becomes a clean\n\"everything except spec invocation gets shorter for this region.\"\n\nIt's also genuinely lower priority than getting the runtime working\nat all. The same-language fast path (issue 312) captures the\n~2x JSON-skip win without any of this complexity. The merge wins a\nfurther factor only if profile data shows function-call overhead\nmatters at all after 312 ships.\n\n## Scope of the research output\n\nThe deliverable is a written design (not code) with:\n- Concrete answers to the three questions above.\n- A worked example: the merged C generated from a 5-box C-only\n  graph, showing what the build artifact looks like.\n- Estimated runtime cost of the per-box path vs the merged path\n  on that example.\n- A recommendation: ship as a feature, ship as an opt-in flag, or\n  shelve indefinitely.\n\nAfter the design is reviewed, a separate implementation issue\nopens (or doesn't, depending on the recommendation).\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `issues/312-same-language-wire-fast-path.md` — the immediate JSON-\n  skip win this builds on\n- `issues/307-c-language-spec.md` — `compile` callback that would\n  grow whole-program-aware semantics\n- `issues/306-lua-language-spec.md` — Lua-side bytecode pre-compile\n- `issues/309-build-system.md` — how the merge integrates with the\n  compile/package step\n\n## Open questions (for the research, not for now)\n\n- Cross-language wires inside the merged region: the merged region\n  still has cross-language outputs that exit to other regions. The\n  spec interface still applies at those boundaries, so the merge is\n  region-internal optimization, not a global rearchitecture.\n- C ABI for inlined wrappers: with whole-program optimization the\n  wrapper-per-box generation might collapse to nothing. If the\n  optimizer can prove a wire endpoint is always called from the\n  merged region with known types, it can skip the wrapper.\n- Iterators-with-side-effects: an iterator self-rescheduling its\n  own task is normally dispatch-layer machinery. Inside a merged\n  region, it could become a `while` loop. Whether that's safe\n  depends on whether other tasks are blocked on the iterator's\n  output slots — which they shouldn't be in a same-language region,\n  but the analysis has to confirm.\n"
    }

Each box invocation shells out to\n6\ta driver script, which starts a new process, runs the function, and exits. The\n7\treturn value passes through stdout. This works but has two structural problems:\n8\t\n9\t1. **Process-per-call cost.** Spawning a process takes roughly 1–10 ms depending\n10\t   on the runtime. For a map with ten boxes, that's dominated by spawn overhead,\n11\t   not by the actual work.\n12\t\n13\t2. **stdout is the wrong channel.** A box function that prints debug output\n14\t   corrupts the wire value. Values are transient — they vanish once the pipe is\n15\t   drained. The channel has no addressing, no framing, and no backpressure.\n16\t\n17\tThe goal is a design where cross-language calls are fast, values are addressable,\n18\tand the execution model is ready to parallelize without redesign.\n19\t\n20\t---\n21\t\n22\t## The threading roadmap\n23\t\n24\tThree stages, each building on the last:\n25\t\n26\t**Stage 1 — Synchronous (current).** A single-threaded ready-queue walks the\n27\tgraph in dependency order. `run_task(box, inputs)` in `src/004-executor.lua` is\n28\tthe task boundary. It blocks until the driver responds.\n29\t\n30\t**Stage 2 — Coroutine-based non-blocking.** The ready-queue becomes a coroutine\n31\tscheduler. Boxes yield when waiting on upstream results or cross-language calls.\n32\tLuaSocket non-blocking I/O lets the scheduler run other boxes while one is\n33\twaiting for a response. No true parallelism yet, but the graph's natural\n34\tconcurrency is exploited without blocking the whole process.\n35\t\n36\t**Stage 3 — SoraMech-owned thread pool.** A pool implementation\n37\twritten for SoraMech, with the 3d-rts pool design as a reference.\n38\tThe `task_fn` boundary swaps in the thread pool. Worker threads pull\n39\ttasks from the pool; OS-level scheduling replaces any single-threaded\n40\tordering. Cross-language calls block a worker thread while other\n41\tthreads continue. True parallelism across cores.\n42\t\n43\tEffil-jit is not used. Coroutines are not used. The path goes\n44\tstraight from synchronous (phase 2) to the C pool (phase 3) — no\n45\tintermediate coroutine stage.\n46\t\n47\t---\n48\t\n49\t## Stage 3 detail: pthreads task model\n50\t\n51\tEach box execution in the thread pool is a **task struct** containing:\n52\t\n53\t- **Function pointer** — the language-specific invocation wrapper (a C\n54\t  function, since pthreads requires a C entry point)\n55\t- **Shared memory pointer** — the region holding the input arguments and\n56\t  return value for this invocation\n57\t- **Dependency list** — pointers to the tasks this task is waiting on\n58\t- **Waiting list** — pointers to tasks that are waiting on this task\n59\t- **Counter** (iterator boxes only) — current iteration index, updated\n60\t  in-place when the iterator re-queues itself\n61\t\n62\tTask structs are allocated once at run start, one per box (not one per\n63\tinvocation). They live for the entire run.\n64\t\n65\t### Blocking and unblocking — pointer-only transitions\n66\t\n67\tWhen a task cannot run (upstream output not yet available), it is placed\n68\tin its upstream task's waiting list. This is a pointer move — no\n69\tallocation, no struct copy. The task struct stays exactly where it is.\n70\t\n71\tWhen an upstream task completes and writes its return value to shared\n72\tmemory, it walks its waiting list and re-adds each entry to the main task\n73\tqueue. Again, a pointer move only. The unblocked task's struct is\n74\tunchanged; only its position in the queue changes.\n75\t\n76\tThis means \"blocked\", \"queued\", and \"running\" are states defined by which\n77\tlist a task's pointer currently lives in — not by any field in the struct.\n78\t\n79\t### Per-thread language runtimes\n80\t\n81\tEach worker thread initializes its own language runtimes at startup:\n82\t- **Lua:** one `lua_State` per thread. Lua states are not thread-safe, but\n83\t  one per thread requires no locking. The task wrapper calls the box\n84\t  function via `lua_pcall`.\n85\t- **C:** the compiled box function is called directly through the function\n86\t  pointer. No interpreter, no overhead beyond the call itself.\n87\t- **Bash/other:** a persistent subprocess per thread (Unix domain socket\n88\t  server model — see Option 3 above). The task wrapper sends a request and\n89\t  blocks the thread waiting for the response.\n90\t\n91\t### Iterator self-re-queue\n92\t\n93\tAn iterator task does not terminate after one invocation. When it\n94\tcompletes:\n95\t1. It increments its `counter` field in-place (or wraps to 0).\n96\t2. It checks its input queue for the next pending value.\n97\t3. If a value is waiting: it updates its input pointer and re-adds itself\n98\t   to the main task queue. No allocation — the same task struct re-enters\n99\t   the queue with updated state.\n100\t4. If no value is waiting: it adds itself to the upstream task's waiting\n101\t   list, to be re-added when the next input arrives.\n102\t\n103\tInput values are processed one-at-a-time in arrival order. Ten queued\n104\tinputs means the iterator task visits the queue ten times, advancing the\n105\tcounter and firing a different output path each time.\n106\t\n107\t### Blocking semantics for long-running operations\n108\t\n109\tThe pool's parallelism comes from running N worker threads concurrently\n110\ton N cores. Each worker is sitting inside a single dispatch task at any\n111\tgiven moment. If a box function does something that takes a long time —\n112\t`sleep`, blocking I/O, a synchronous network request, waiting on a long-\n113\trunning subprocess — **the worker thread is occupied for the full\n114\tduration**. It cannot pick up other tasks while it waits.\n115\t\n116\tConcretely:\n117\t- 16-worker pool, 1 box sleeping 10 seconds → the other 15 workers\n118\t  continue normally.\n119\t- 16-worker pool, 16 boxes all sleeping → all workers parked, no other\n120\t  task runs until a sleep finishes.\n121\t- The pool size is also the budget for \"blocking activities\". Heavy\n122\t  use of `sleep`-style boxes means raising `SORAMECH_WORKERS`.\n123\t\n124\tWhy the runtime does not have a scheduler: SoraMech is deliberately not\n125\tin the business of \"park this task and wake it at time T.\" There is no\n126\tdelayed-spawn primitive, no timer thread, no polling loop. Adding one\n127\twould mean a second concurrency model alongside the pool, with its own\n128\tsynchronization story. Instead, we lean on the pool's existing\n129\tmechanism: a task either runs (occupying a worker) or is blocked on a\n130\tslot waiting for a value (parked, no worker held). Long sleeps are an\n131\t\"occupying a worker\" case.\n132\t\n133\tFor users who need many concurrent waits without burning workers, the\n134\tgraph-level pattern is cooperative: split the operation into \"kick off\n135\tthe thing\" (returns immediately) and \"check whether the thing is done\"\n136\t(returns immediately, returns a status), and wire them through an\n137\titerator with a queued input. The iterator polls. No individual box\n138\tblocks for long. Each box completes quickly, freeing its worker.\n139\t\n140\tThis is a documented constraint, not a bug. Box authors should know\n141\tthat an unbounded `sleep` inside a function is the equivalent of\n142\tholding a worker hostage. The cooperative pattern is the way around\n143\tit.\n144\t\n145\t---\n146\t\n147\t## The three IPC options\n148\t\n149\t### Option 1 — LuaJIT FFI (Lua ↔ C, in-process)\n150\t\n151\tThe Foreign Function Interface lets Lua call C functions that live in a shared\n152\tlibrary (`.so`) directly, in the same process, with no subprocess and no channel.\n153\tYou provide a C declaration (`ffi.cdef[[ int add(int a, int b); ]]`), load the\n154\tcompiled library (`ffi.load(\"./mybox.so\")`), and call `lib.add(3, 4)` — the CPU\n155\tjumps into native code and returns. Overhead is nanoseconds.\n156\t\n157\tSince the executor already does mtime-based dynamic compilation (see `drivers/c.sh`),\n158\tcompiling to a `.so` instead of a binary is just a flag change (`-shared -fPIC`).\n159\tThe box function signature changes from `main(argc, argv)` to a named function\n160\twith typed arguments — which is strictly cleaner.\n161\t\n162\t**Limitation:** FFI only works for languages that compile to a C-compatible ABI.\n163\tBash cannot. Python can (via `ctypes` on the other side), but it's awkward.\n164\tFFI is the right answer for Lua ↔ C only.\n165\t\n166\t**Cross-platform:** LuaJIT FFI works on Linux, macOS, and Windows. `.so` becomes\n167\t`.dylib` on macOS and `.dll` on Windows — the `ffi.load()` call is portable if\n168\tyou handle the extension.\n169\t\n170\t---\n171\t\n172\t### Option 2 — Shared memory (`shm_open` + `mmap`)\n173\t\n174\t`shm_open(\"/soramech-wire-0\", ...)` creates a named memory segment managed by\n175\tthe kernel — not a file on disk, but a named object in RAM. `mmap()` maps it\n176\tinto the calling process's address space. Any other process that opens the same\n177\tname gets access to the *same physical memory*. A write in one process is\n178\timmediately visible in another — no copy, no syscall per access after setup.\n179\t\n180\tFor SoraMech, each wire between two boxes would correspond to a named shared\n181\tmemory slot. The compiler (issue 219) generates the slot names and the read/write\n182\tcalls. Any language that can call POSIX can participate:\n183\t\n184\t- Lua: via LuaJIT FFI calling `shm_open` + `mmap` from libc\n185\t- C: natively\n186\t- Bash: via `/dev/shm/<name>` — on Linux, the tmpfs backing shared memory is\n187\t  exposed as a filesystem path, so bash can `cat /dev/shm/soramech-wire-0`\n188\t\n189\t**Performance:** After the initial `mmap()` setup, reads and writes are pointer\n190\tdereferences — no syscalls, no copies. For small values (strings, numbers) this\n191\tis essentially free.\n192\t\n193\t**Complication:** Shared memory is untyped raw bytes. You need a size header\n194\t(how many bytes is this value?), a type tag (string? number? JSON object?), and\n195\ta synchronization mechanism (how does the reader know the writer is done?). None\n196\tof these are hard — a small fixed header in the segment handles all three — but\n197\tthe compiler must generate all of it correctly for every wire.\n198\t\n199\t**Cross-platform:**\n200\t- Linux: full support. `/dev/shm/` filesystem exposure is Linux-specific.\n201\t- macOS: `shm_open()` works, but the objects are NOT exposed as files. No\n202\t  `/dev/shm/` path. Bash access via file path doesn't work.\n203\t- Windows: completely different API (`CreateFileMapping` / `MapViewOfFile`).\n204\t  No POSIX `shm_open` without WSL or Cygwin.\n205\t\n206\tShared memory is powerful but not the most portable option. The bash filesystem\n207\tshortcut that makes it cross-language is Linux-only.\n208\t\n209\t---\n210\t\n211\t### Option 3 — Unix domain socket servers (chosen direction)\n212\t\n213\tA Unix domain socket is a socket addressed by a filesystem path instead of an\n214\tIP address and port. `/tmp/soramech-bash.sock` is a special file; any process\n215\ton the same machine connects to it with the standard socket API. The kernel\n216\troutes data directly between processes in memory — no network stack, no loopback,\n217\tno protocol headers. Performance is bounded by memory bandwidth.\n218\t\n219\tUnlike anonymous pipes, a socket has a name that unrelated processes can find\n220\twithout inheriting file descriptors. Multiple clients connect simultaneously;\n221\teach gets its own channel. The server handles them with `accept()` in a loop.\n222\t\n223\t**The model for SoraMech:**\n224\t\n225\tEach language runtime runs as a persistent socket server. One server instance\n226\tper language per worker thread:\n227\t\n228\t```\n229\t/tmp/soramech-bash-0.sock   ← worker thread 0's bash runtime\n230\t/tmp/soramech-bash-1.sock   ← worker thread 1's bash runtime\n231\t/tmp/soramech-c-0.sock      ← worker thread 0's C runtime\n232\t```\n233\t\n234\tThe server starts when the program starts, stays alive for the whole run, and\n235\taccepts sequential requests — one box call at a time per instance. A Lua worker\n236\tconnects to its designated socket, sends a framed request (function name +\n237\targuments), and reads back a framed response (return value). The server is a\n238\tsmall script (~50 lines) that sources or compiles the box file, calls the\n239\tfunction, and writes the result.\n240\t\n241\t**Wire protocol:** Length-prefix framing. The sender writes a 4-byte big-endian\n242\tinteger (the message length in bytes), then that many bytes of content. The\n243\treceiver reads 4 bytes, then reads exactly that many bytes. This handles values\n244\tcontaining newlines or null bytes without ambiguity.\n245\t\n246\t**Cost of idle servers:** An idle server process is blocked on `accept()` — zero\n247\tCPU, approximately 3–5 MB RSS for a bash process. For 10 languages × 4 threads\n248\t= 40 processes ≈ 150–200 MB. Acceptable.\n249\t\n250\t**Integration with the coroutine scheduler (Stage 2):**\n251\t\n252\tWith LuaSocket non-blocking sockets, the coroutine that makes a cross-language\n253\tcall does this:\n254\t1. Connect to the language server socket (non-blocking)\n255\t2. Send the request\n256\t3. `coroutine.yield()` — registers the socket fd with the scheduler\n257\t4. Scheduler polls all pending fds with `select()`\n258\t5. When the fd is readable, scheduler resumes the coroutine\n259\t6. Coroutine reads the response and continues\n260\t\n261\tThe cross-language call never blocks the main Lua thread. Other boxes run in\n262\tother coroutines while the bash/C server is processing.\n263\t\n264\t**Integration with the SoraMech thread pool (Stage 3):**\n265\t\n266\tEach worker thread owns its set of language server sockets. When `run_task` calls\n267\ta cross-language box, it sends to the socket and blocks on the read — the thread\n268\tblocks, not the whole program. Other workers continue processing other boxes on\n269\tother cores. The server processes run concurrently on whatever cores the OS\n270\tschedules them to. This gives real parallelism: a bash box and a C box assigned\n271\tto different workers can run simultaneously.\n272\t\n273\t**Cross-platform:**\n274\t- Linux: full support.\n275\t- macOS: full support. Unix domain sockets are POSIX.\n276\t- Windows: supported since Windows 10 1803 (2018). `AF_UNIX` sockets work\n277\t  natively. Most languages abstract this through their socket libraries.\n278\t\n279\tUnix domain sockets are the most portable cross-language IPC mechanism that also\n280\tsupports concurrent connections. They are the chosen direction for the compiler\n281\toutput and the coroutine/thread-pool executor.\n282\t\n283\t---\n284\t\n285\t## Summary comparison\n286\t\n287\t| Property              | FFI (.so)       | Shared memory       | Unix domain socket  |\n288\t|-----------------------|-----------------|---------------------|---------------------|\n289\t| Speed (per call)      | nanoseconds     | nanoseconds*        | microseconds        |\n290\t| Languages supported   | C-ABI only      | any (with caveats)  | any                 |\n291\t| Parallel connections  | N/A (in-process)| yes (with sync)     | yes (natural)       |\n292\t| Linux                 | yes             | yes                 | yes                 |\n293\t| macOS                 | yes             | partial†            | yes                 |\n294\t| Windows               | yes (.dll)      | no (different API)  | yes (Win10+)        |\n295\t| Complexity            | low             | medium              | low-medium          |\n296\t\n297\t*After initial mmap setup. †shm_open works; /dev/shm filesystem path does not.\n298\t\n299\tThe compiler (issue 219) uses FFI for Lua ↔ C wires where the C source is\n300\tcompiled to a `.so`, and Unix domain sockets for all other cross-language wires.\n301\tSame-language Lua wires are direct function calls — no IPC at all.\n302\t\n303\t---\n304\t\n305\t## Relevant files\n306\t\n307\t- `src/004-executor.lua` — `run_task` boundary, ready-queue\n308\t- `src/007-runner-main.lua` — entry point for the interpreter path\n309\t- `issues/219-map-compiler.md` — compiler that generates the IPC calls\n310\t- `issues/104-runner-synchronous-executor.md` — task boundary design\n311\t- `issues/213-queued-inputs-and-task-model.md` — queue-per-port, thread pool notes\n312\t- `docs/002-roadmap.md` — phase plan for threading stages\n313\t",
        "tool_use_id":"toolu_01EaWYU9TAXfHMxfwp6yD5ov"

Each box invocation shells out to\na driver script, which starts a new process, runs the function, and exits. The\nreturn value passes through stdout. This works but has two structural problems:\n\n1. **Process-per-call cost.** Spawning a process takes roughly 1–10 ms depending\n   on the runtime. For a map with ten boxes, that's dominated by spawn overhead,\n   not by the actual work.\n\n2. **stdout is the wrong channel.** A box function that prints debug output\n   corrupts the wire value. Values are transient — they vanish once the pipe is\n   drained. The channel has no addressing, no framing, and no backpressure.\n\nThe goal is a design where cross-language calls are fast, values are addressable,\nand the execution model is ready to parallelize without redesign.\n\n---\n\n## The threading roadmap\n\nThree stages, each building on the last:\n\n**Stage 1 — Synchronous (current).** A single-threaded ready-queue walks the\ngraph in dependency order. `run_task(box, inputs)` in `src/004-executor.lua` is\nthe task boundary. It blocks until the driver responds.\n\n**Stage 2 — Coroutine-based non-blocking.** The ready-queue becomes a coroutine\nscheduler. Boxes yield when waiting on upstream results or cross-language calls.\nLuaSocket non-blocking I/O lets the scheduler run other boxes while one is\nwaiting for a response. No true parallelism yet, but the graph's natural\nconcurrency is exploited without blocking the whole process.\n\n**Stage 3 — SoraMech-owned thread pool.** A pool implementation\nwritten for SoraMech, with the 3d-rts pool design as a reference.\nThe `task_fn` boundary swaps in the thread pool. Worker threads pull\ntasks from the pool; OS-level scheduling replaces any single-threaded\nordering. Cross-language calls block a worker thread while other\nthreads continue. True parallelism across cores.\n\nEffil-jit is not used. Coroutines are not used. The path goes\nstraight from synchronous (phase 2) to the C pool (phase 3) — no\nintermediate coroutine stage.\n\n---\n\n## Stage 3 detail: pthreads task model\n\nEach box execution in the thread pool is a **task struct** containing:\n\n- **Function pointer** — the language-specific invocation wrapper (a C\n  function, since pthreads requires a C entry point)\n- **Shared memory pointer** — the region holding the input arguments and\n  return value for this invocation\n- **Dependency list** — pointers to the tasks this task is waiting on\n- **Waiting list** — pointers to tasks that are waiting on this task\n- **Counter** (iterator boxes only) — current iteration index, updated\n  in-place when the iterator re-queues itself\n\nTask structs are allocated once at run start, one per box (not one per\ninvocation). They live for the entire run.\n\n### Blocking and unblocking — pointer-only transitions\n\nWhen a task cannot run (upstream output not yet available), it is placed\nin its upstream task's waiting list. This is a pointer move — no\nallocation, no struct copy. The task struct stays exactly where it is.\n\nWhen an upstream task completes and writes its return value to shared\nmemory, it walks its waiting list and re-adds each entry to the main task\nqueue. Again, a pointer move only. The unblocked task's struct is\nunchanged; only its position in the queue changes.\n\nThis means \"blocked\", \"queued\", and \"running\" are states defined by which\nlist a task's pointer currently lives in — not by any field in the struct.\n\n### Per-thread language runtimes\n\nEach worker thread initializes its own language runtimes at startup:\n- **Lua:** one `lua_State` per thread. Lua states are not thread-safe, but\n  one per thread requires no locking. The task wrapper calls the box\n  function via `lua_pcall`.\n- **C:** the compiled box function is called directly through the function\n  pointer. No interpreter, no overhead beyond the call itself.\n- **Bash/other:** a persistent subprocess per thread (Unix domain socket\n  server model — see Option 3 above). The task wrapper sends a request and\n  blocks the thread waiting for the response.\n\n### Iterator self-re-queue\n\nAn iterator task does not terminate after one invocation. When it\ncompletes:\n1. It increments its `counter` field in-place (or wraps to 0).\n2. It checks its input queue for the next pending value.\n3. If a value is waiting: it updates its input pointer and re-adds itself\n   to the main task queue. No allocation — the same task struct re-enters\n   the queue with updated state.\n4. If no value is waiting: it adds itself to the upstream task's waiting\n   list, to be re-added when the next input arrives.\n\nInput values are processed one-at-a-time in arrival order. Ten queued\ninputs means the iterator task visits the queue ten times, advancing the\ncounter and firing a different output path each time.\n\n### Blocking semantics for long-running operations\n\nThe pool's parallelism comes from running N worker threads concurrently\non N cores. Each worker is sitting inside a single dispatch task at any\ngiven moment. If a box function does something that takes a long time —\n`sleep`, blocking I/O, a synchronous network request, waiting on a long-\nrunning subprocess — **the worker thread is occupied for the full\nduration**. It cannot pick up other tasks while it waits.\n\nConcretely:\n- 16-worker pool, 1 box sleeping 10 seconds → the other 15 workers\n  continue normally.\n- 16-worker pool, 16 boxes all sleeping → all workers parked, no other\n  task runs until a sleep finishes.\n- The pool size is also the budget for \"blocking activities\". Heavy\n  use of `sleep`-style boxes means raising `SORAMECH_WORKERS`.\n\nWhy the runtime does not have a scheduler: SoraMech is deliberately not\nin the business of \"park this task and wake it at time T.\" There is no\ndelayed-spawn primitive, no timer thread, no polling loop. Adding one\nwould mean a second concurrency model alongside the pool, with its own\nsynchronization story. Instead, we lean on the pool's existing\nmechanism: a task either runs (occupying a worker) or is blocked on a\nslot waiting for a value (parked, no worker held). Long sleeps are an\n\"occupying a worker\" case.\n\nFor users who need many concurrent waits without burning workers, the\ngraph-level pattern is cooperative: split the operation into \"kick off\nthe thing\" (returns immediately) and \"check whether the thing is done\"\n(returns immediately, returns a status), and wire them through an\niterator with a queued input. The iterator polls. No individual box\nblocks for long. Each box completes quickly, freeing its worker.\n\nThis is a documented constraint, not a bug. Box authors should know\nthat an unbounded `sleep` inside a function is the equivalent of\nholding a worker hostage. The cooperative pattern is the way around\nit.\n\n---\n\n## The three IPC options\n\n### Option 1 — LuaJIT FFI (Lua ↔ C, in-process)\n\nThe Foreign Function Interface lets Lua call C functions that live in a shared\nlibrary (`.so`) directly, in the same process, with no subprocess and no channel.\nYou provide a C declaration (`ffi.cdef[[ int add(int a, int b); ]]`), load the\ncompiled library (`ffi.load(\"./mybox.so\")`), and call `lib.add(3, 4)` — the CPU\njumps into native code and returns. Overhead is nanoseconds.\n\nSince the executor already does mtime-based dynamic compilation (see `drivers/c.sh`),\ncompiling to a `.so` instead of a binary is just a flag change (`-shared -fPIC`).\nThe box function signature changes from `main(argc, argv)` to a named function\nwith typed arguments — which is strictly cleaner.\n\n**Limitation:** FFI only works for languages that compile to a C-compatible ABI.\nBash cannot. Python can (via `ctypes` on the other side), but it's awkward.\nFFI is the right answer for Lua ↔ C only.\n\n**Cross-platform:** LuaJIT FFI works on Linux, macOS, and Windows. `.so` becomes\n`.dylib` on macOS and `.dll` on Windows — the `ffi.load()` call is portable if\nyou handle the extension.\n\n---\n\n### Option 2 — Shared memory (`shm_open` + `mmap`)\n\n`shm_open(\"/soramech-wire-0\", ...)` creates a named memory segment managed by\nthe kernel — not a file on disk, but a named object in RAM. `mmap()` maps it\ninto the calling process's address space. Any other process that opens the same\nname gets access to the *same physical memory*. A write in one process is\nimmediately visible in another — no copy, no syscall per access after setup.\n\nFor SoraMech, each wire between two boxes would correspond to a named shared\nmemory slot. The compiler (issue 219) generates the slot names and the read/write\ncalls. Any language that can call POSIX can participate:\n\n- Lua: via LuaJIT FFI calling `shm_open` + `mmap` from libc\n- C: natively\n- Bash: via `/dev/shm/<name>` — on Linux, the tmpfs backing shared memory is\n  exposed as a filesystem path, so bash can `cat /dev/shm/soramech-wire-0`\n\n**Performance:** After the initial `mmap()` setup, reads and writes are pointer\ndereferences — no syscalls, no copies. For small values (strings, numbers) this\nis essentially free.\n\n**Complication:** Shared memory is untyped raw bytes. You need a size header\n(how many bytes is this value?), a type tag (string? number? JSON object?), and\na synchronization mechanism (how does the reader know the writer is done?). None\nof these are hard — a small fixed header in the segment handles all three — but\nthe compiler must generate all of it correctly for every wire.\n\n**Cross-platform:**\n- Linux: full support. `/dev/shm/` filesystem exposure is Linux-specific.\n- macOS: `shm_open()` works, but the objects are NOT exposed as files. No\n  `/dev/shm/` path. Bash access via file path doesn't work.\n- Windows: completely different API (`CreateFileMapping` / `MapViewOfFile`).\n  No POSIX `shm_open` without WSL or Cygwin.\n\nShared memory is powerful but not the most portable option. The bash filesystem\nshortcut that makes it cross-language is Linux-only.\n\n---\n\n### Option 3 — Unix domain socket servers (chosen direction)\n\nA Unix domain socket is a socket addressed by a filesystem path instead of an\nIP address and port. `/tmp/soramech-bash.sock` is a special file; any process\non the same machine connects to it with the standard socket API. The kernel\nroutes data directly between processes in memory — no network stack, no loopback,\nno protocol headers. Performance is bounded by memory bandwidth.\n\nUnlike anonymous pipes, a socket has a name that unrelated processes can find\nwithout inheriting file descriptors. Multiple clients connect simultaneously;\neach gets its own channel. The server handles them with `accept()` in a loop.\n\n**The model for SoraMech:**\n\nEach language runtime runs as a persistent socket server. One server instance\nper language per worker thread:\n\n```\n/tmp/soramech-bash-0.sock   ← worker thread 0's bash runtime\n/tmp/soramech-bash-1.sock   ← worker thread 1's bash runtime\n/tmp/soramech-c-0.sock      ← worker thread 0's C runtime\n```\n\nThe server starts when the program starts, stays alive for the whole run, and\naccepts sequential requests — one box call at a time per instance. A Lua worker\nconnects to its designated socket, sends a framed request (function name +\narguments), and reads back a framed response (return value). The server is a\nsmall script (~50 lines) that sources or compiles the box file, calls the\nfunction, and writes the result.\n\n**Wire protocol:** Length-prefix framing. The sender writes a 4-byte big-endian\ninteger (the message length in bytes), then that many bytes of content. The\nreceiver reads 4 bytes, then reads exactly that many bytes. This handles values\ncontaining newlines or null bytes without ambiguity.\n\n**Cost of idle servers:** An idle server process is blocked on `accept()` — zero\nCPU, approximately 3–5 MB RSS for a bash process. For 10 languages × 4 threads\n= 40 processes ≈ 150–200 MB. Acceptable.\n\n**Integration with the coroutine scheduler (Stage 2):**\n\nWith LuaSocket non-blocking sockets, the coroutine that makes a cross-language\ncall does this:\n1. Connect to the language server socket (non-blocking)\n2. Send the request\n3. `coroutine.yield()` — registers the socket fd with the scheduler\n4. Scheduler polls all pending fds with `select()`\n5. When the fd is readable, scheduler resumes the coroutine\n6. Coroutine reads the response and continues\n\nThe cross-language call never blocks the main Lua thread. Other boxes run in\nother coroutines while the bash/C server is processing.\n\n**Integration with the SoraMech thread pool (Stage 3):**\n\nEach worker thread owns its set of language server sockets. When `run_task` calls\na cross-language box, it sends to the socket and blocks on the read — the thread\nblocks, not the whole program. Other workers continue processing other boxes on\nother cores. The server processes run concurrently on whatever cores the OS\nschedules them to. This gives real parallelism: a bash box and a C box assigned\nto different workers can run simultaneously.\n\n**Cross-platform:**\n- Linux: full support.\n- macOS: full support. Unix domain sockets are POSIX.\n- Windows: supported since Windows 10 1803 (2018). `AF_UNIX` sockets work\n  natively. Most languages abstract this through their socket libraries.\n\nUnix domain sockets are the most portable cross-language IPC mechanism that also\nsupports concurrent connections. They are the chosen direction for the compiler\noutput and the coroutine/thread-pool executor.\n\n---\n\n## Summary comparison\n\n| Property              | FFI (.so)       | Shared memory       | Unix domain socket  |\n|-----------------------|-----------------|---------------------|---------------------|\n| Speed (per call)      | nanoseconds     | nanoseconds*        | microseconds        |\n| Languages supported   | C-ABI only      | any (with caveats)  | any                 |\n| Parallel connections  | N/A (in-process)| yes (with sync)     | yes (natural)       |\n| Linux                 | yes             | yes                 | yes                 |\n| macOS                 | yes             | partial†            | yes                 |\n| Windows               | yes (.dll)      | no (different API)  | yes (Win10+)        |\n| Complexity            | low             | medium              | low-medium          |\n\n*After initial mmap setup. †shm_open works; /dev/shm filesystem path does not.\n\nThe compiler (issue 219) uses FFI for Lua ↔ C wires where the C source is\ncompiled to a `.so`, and Unix domain sockets for all other cross-language wires.\nSame-language Lua wires are direct function calls — no IPC at all.\n\n---\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `src/004-executor.lua` — `run_task` boundary, ready-queue\n- `src/007-runner-main.lua` — entry point for the interpreter path\n- `issues/219-map-compiler.md` — compiler that generates the IPC calls\n- `issues/104-runner-synchronous-executor.md` — task boundary design\n- `issues/213-queued-inputs-and-task-model.md` — queue-per-port, thread pool notes\n- `docs/002-roadmap.md` — phase plan for threading stages\n"
    }
