The runner has no embedded Lua state at the\n132\t  top level; Lua only appears inside a Lua language spec's per-worker\n133\t  handle.\n134\t- A **per-input-port slot store** (`src/slot-store.c`) — ring-buffer\n135\t  cells in process heap, durable for the run, plus a large-value heap\n136\t  for variable-size payloads.\n137\t- A **dispatch layer** (`src/dispatch.c`) — the single worker-side\n138\t  action: read inputs → invoke spec → pick branch → push outputs.\n139\t- A **language spec registry** (`src/spec-registry.c`) — `dlopen`s\n140\t  every `langs/<name>/spec.so` at startup and registers it by name\n141\t  and file extension.\n142\t- A **run-output writer** — a dedicated thread that drains a\n143\t  multi-producer-single-consumer ring of events and appends one JSON\n144\t  line per event to `tmp/last-run.jsonl`.\n145\t\n146\tOne pool per map run. Created after the graph loads and validates;\n147\tdestroyed after the active-task counter reaches zero. Worker count\n148\tdefaults to logical CPUs (capped at `MAX_WORKERS=16`), overridable\n149\tvia `SORAMECH_WORKERS=N`.\n150\t\n151\tSee \"Execution model — phase 3\" below for the action loop and slot\n152\tmechanics.\n153\t\n154\t### assets/index.html (the editor)\n155\t\n156\tStatic HTML + vanilla JS. Infinite-scroll canvas. Box diagram editor.\n157\tTalks to `src/006-server-main.lua` for all file operations. No run\n158\tbutton. The Compile button (added in phase 2 as UI only) wires into\n159\tthe phase 3 build/package pipeline once it lands.\n160\t\n161\t## Map directory format\n162\t\n163\t```\n164\tmaps/<name>/\n165\t  meta.json          — { name, description, src_dirs?, lang? }\n166\t  boxes/\n167\t    <id>.json        — one file per box (see Box file format below)\n168\t  data/\n169\t    <name>.json      — soramech-data tables; section-level \"constant\" flag\n170\t  src/\n171\t    *.lua, *.c, *.sh — box function source files\n172\t  compiled/          — produced by the compile pipeline (issue 309)\n173\t    pool-runner      — copy or symlink of soramech-pool\n174\t    src/             — every source file the map uses\n175\t    bin/             — compiled .so files (C boxes via the C spec's compile callback)\n176\t    langs/<name>/    — copy of each language spec .so the map uses\n177\t    manifest.json    — every box, its language, its artifact path, build version\n178\t  tmp/               — symlink to /tmp/<name>/\n179\t    last-run.jsonl   — phase 3 run log (JSON Lines)\n180\t    logs/            — additional run logs\n181\t```\n182\t\n183\tA compiled map runs standalone: `./compiled/pool-runner` looks up its\n184\tspecs in `compiled/langs/`, reads `manifest.json`, and executes\n185\twithout any reference to the live editor source tree.\n186\t\n187\tPhase 2's `drivers.json` file is gone. Phase 2 resolves drivers by\n188\tfile extension via the `drivers/` directory; phase 3 resolves\n189\tlanguages by file extension via the spec registry (each spec declares\n190\tits `file_ext`). No map-local driver config file is needed in either\n191\tphase.\n192\t\n193\tThe `data/` directory is for `soramech-data` storage (see \"Data\n194\tfiles\" below). It is **not** where file-source boxes read from — those\n195\tread arbitrary paths, see Box kinds.\n196\t\n197\t## Box file format\n198\t\n199\tEvery box is a single JSON file under `boxes/<id>.json`. Every box\n200\thas exactly **one output wire** (issue 218). There is no `outputs`\n201\tarray. Whatever the function returns travels down the single output\n202\twire as one value; multi-value returns are encoded as JSON (or a\n203\tlanguage-native struct on a same-language wire — see \"Language spec\n204\tsystem\" below) and decoded downstream.\n205\t\n206\t### Box kinds\n207\t\n208\t| `kind`  | Runs a function? | Notes                                                                |\n209\t|---------|------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------|\n210\t| `call`  | yes              | Plain call, comparator, iterator, etc. — see `routing` below.        |\n211\t| `read`  | no               | Value source. Inline literal `value` OR file at `path`.              |\n212\t| `write` | no               | File sink. Writes the `value` input; emits boolean `\"true\"` downstream. |\n213\t\n214\t`read` and `write` are dispatch-layer primitives — the runtime\n215\treads/writes the file directly, no language spec is invoked. A\n216\t`read` box with an inline `value` literal skips file IO entirely\n217\tand emits the literal bytes. A `write` box atomically commits\n218\tits `value` input to disk and pushes `\"true\"` to any downstream\n219\twires; if no wire reads its output, the boolean is discarded per\n220\tthe unwired-output rule.\n221\t\n222\t```json\n223\t{ \"id\": \"from_file\", \"kind\": \"read\", \"path\": \"config.json\",\n224\t  \"ui\": { \"x\": 100, \"y\": 100 } }\n225\t\n226\t{ \"id\": \"from_literal\", \"kind\": \"read\",\n227\t  \"value\": \"hello, world!\",\n228\t  \"ui\": { \"x\": 100, \"y\": 200 } }\n229\t\n230\t{ \"id\": \"save\", \"kind\": \"write\",\n231\t  \"inputs\": [\n232\t    { \"name\": \"path\",  \"type\": \"string\" },\n233\t    { \"name\": \"value\", \"type\": \"string\" }\n234\t  ],\n235\t  \"ui\": { \"x\": 400, \"y\": 100 } }\n236\t```\n237\t\n238\t**Unwired-output discard rule.** If an output value is produced\n239\tbut no wire carries it downstream, the value is discarded. A\n240\t`write` box with no wire on its done-boolean output still\n241\tcommits the file — the boolean just goes nowhere. The rule\n242\tapplies to every kind; `write` is the most visible case.\n243\t\n244\t`data` has `path` (not `ref`), no `fn`, no inputs; emits the file's\n245\tbytes-as-UTF-8 string on its one output wire. `file_write` takes\n246\t`path` and `text` as inputs; the `path` input can be wired (dynamic)\n247\tor filled by a literal (static). Binary files are out of scope for\n248\tboth — non-UTF-8 reads fail with a clear error.\n249\t\n250\t### Call boxes and the `routing` field\n251\t\n252\tA `call` box runs a function (`ref` + `fn`) and produces one output\n253\tvalue. The `routing` field decides where that value goes. Every\n254\tcall box carries `routing` explicitly — there is no implicit default:\n255\t\n256\t```json\n257\t{ \"id\": \"plain-call\", \"kind\": \"call\",\n258\t  \"ref\": \"src/strings.lua\", \"fn\": \"trim\",\n259\t  \"inputs\": [{ \"name\": \"text\", \"type\": \"string\" }],\n260\t  \"routing\": { \"kind\": \"plain\" },\n261\t  \"connections\": [\n262\t    { \"from_box\": \"plain-call\", \"from_branch\": null,\n263\t      \"to_box\": \"next\", \"to_input\": \"text\" }\n264\t  ],\n265\t  \"ui\": { \"x\": 120, \"y\": 340 } }\n266\t```\n267\t\n268\tThe function **always runs**, regardless of routing kind. Routing\n269\tdecides which downstream branch receives the function's output; the\n270\tfunction itself doesn't know.\n271\t\n272\t#### Routing kinds\n273\t\n274\t| `routing.kind`  | Output ports          | Branch picker                                                | Status     |\n275\t|-----------------|-----------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------|------------|\n276\t| `plain`         | single port           | fan to all outgoing wires                                    | shipped    |\n277\t| `comparator`    | `lt` / `eq` / `gt`    | `compare(output, comparand)` → lt/eq/gt                      | shipped    |\n278\t| `iterator`      | `out_0` … `out_N-1`   | `slot_read_inc(counter_slot, N)`                             | shipped    |\n279\t| `randomizer`    | `out_0` … `out_N-1`   | `hash(slot_read_inc(counter_slot, MAX)) % N`                 | follow-on  |\n280\t| `weighted`      | `out_0` … `out_N-1`   | cumulative-band lookup against a counter scaled to PRECISION | follow-on  |\n281\t| `distributor`   | `out_0` … `out_N-1`   | argmin over downstream slot fill levels                      | follow-on  |\n282\t\n283\t```json\n284\t\"routing\": { \"kind\": \"plain\" }\n285\t\"routing\": { \"kind\": \"comparator\", \"comparand\": \"0\" }\n286\t\"routing\": { \"kind\": \"iterator\",   \"n_outputs\": 3 }\n287\t\"routing\": { \"kind\": \"weighted\",   \"weights\": [0.8, 0.2] }\n288\t\"routing\": { \"kind\": \"distributor\", \"n_outputs\": 3 }\n289\t```\n290\t\n291\t**Branch-level fan-out**: for `comparator` / `iterator` / etc., each\n292\tbranch port acts like a small plain output of its own. If the\n293\tcomparator's `lt` port has three wires going to three consumers, then\n294\ton every invocation where the routing decision picks `lt`, all three\n295\tof those wires fire. The routing decision picks which branch;\n296\tfan-out picks which consumers on that branch receive the value.\n297\t\n298\tPlain output port can fan freely too — multiple connections from\n299\t`from_branch: null` send copies to every wired consumer. Pulling\n300\tmultiple wires from a single output is not a routing decision.\n301\t\n302\t### Input ports\n303\t\n304\t```json\n305\t\"inputs\": [\n306\t  { \"name\": \"text\",        \"type\": \"string\" },\n307\t  { \"name\": \"config_path\", \"type\": \"string\", \"optional\": true,\n308\t    \"value\": \"config.json\" }\n309\t]\n310\t```\n311\t\n312\tEvery input port is in one of three states at compile time:\n313\t\n314\t1. A wire is connected to it.\n315\t2. A literal `value` is set on it.\n316\t3. It carries `optional: true`.\n317\t\n318\t**Compile fails** when any port is in none of those states. The\n319\terror is precise: which box, which port. Enforced at the Compile\n320\tbutton (phase 2 UI / phase 3 build) and again in the C graph loader\n321\tat runtime — belt and suspenders against hand-edited maps.\n322\t\n323\t`optional: true` does **not** mean \"pass null\" — it means the\n324\targument doesn't have to be passed. The dispatch layer assembles\n325\t`input_data[]` / `input_sizes[]` from the slots that actually have\n326\tvalues; an absent optional port shortens `n_inputs` by one and the\n327\tlanguage's native short-arg convention handles the rest. Each\n328\tlanguage picks up the convention natively (Lua: missing args are\n329\t`nil`; Bash: positional unset; C: wrapper reads `n_inputs` and\n330\tforwards what's present).\n331\t\n332\tNull as an **explicit** value (typed `null` into the literal field)\n333\tis a different thing: it arrives through the function call as a real\n334\targument, mapped to the language's native null (Lua `nil`, Bash empty\n335\tstring `\"\"`, C `NULL`).\n336\t\n337\tVariadic inputs (`variadic_inputs`) carry base names whose ports\n338\texpand to `<base>_0`, `<base>_1`, … in the editor (issue 217).\n339\t\n340\t### Connections\n341\t\n342\tConnections are written to **both** endpoint box files. The loader\n343\tvalidates at load time that both ends agree — disagreement is a\n344\thard error.\n345\t\n346\t```json\n347\t{ \"from_box\": \"...\",\n348\t  \"from_branch\": null | \"lt\" | \"eq\" | \"gt\" | \"out_0\" | ...,\n349\t  \"to_box\":   \"...\",\n350\t  \"to_input\": \"...\" }\n351\t```\n352\t\n353\t`from_branch` is `null` for `routing: plain` and for boxes without a\n354\trouting field; otherwise it names the branch port the wire leaves\n355\tfrom.\n356\t\n357\t## Language spec system (phase 3)\n358\t\n359\tEach language is a **spec** — a `.so` library at\n360\t`langs/<name>/spec.so` that exports a `lang_spec_t` symbol. The pool\n361\trunner loads every `langs/*/spec.so` at startup via `dlopen` and\n362\tregisters it by `name` (for box lookup) and `file_ext` (for source\n363\tresolution). The spec contract is uniform across languages; no\n364\tlanguage is privileged. The runner itself does not link to liblua,\n365\tlibc++, or any language-specific runtime — only specs do.\n366\t\n367\t### `lang_spec_t`\n368\t\n369\t```c\n370\ttypedef struct {\n371\t    const char *name;       // \"lua\", \"bash\", \"c\", \"python\", ...\n372\t    const char *file_ext;   // \".lua\", \".sh\", \".c\", \".py\"\n373\t\n374\t    // Once-per-worker. Pool startup calls init() for every spec on\n375\t    // every worker before unblocking the init barrier; teardown()\n376\t    // runs at shutdown.\n377\t    void *(*init)    (int worker_idx);\n378\t    void  (*teardown)(void *handle);\n379\t\n380\t    // Optional: at map-compile time. C uses this to gcc -shared -fPIC.\n381\t    // Lua and Bash leave this NULL.\n382\t    int   (*compile) (const char *src_path, const char *out_path);\n383\t\n384\t    // Universal invoke path: JSON bytes in, JSON bytes out.\n385\t    // Used across every cross-language wire.\n386\t    int   (*invoke_json)  (void *handle,\n387\t                           const char *file_path, const char *fn_name,\n388\t                           const void **input_data, const int *input_sizes, int n_inputs,\n389\t                           void *out_buf, int out_buf_capacity, int *out_size);\n390\t\n391\t    // Fast invoke path: language-native bytes in, language-native bytes out.\n392\t    // Used when producer and consumer share a language (see \"Same-language\n393\t    // wire fast path\" below).\n394\t    int   (*invoke_native)(void *handle, /* same signature */);\n395\t\n396\t    // Bridges used when a value crosses a language boundary.\n397\t    int   (*native_to_json)(const void *src, int src_size,\n398\t                            void *dst, int dst_capacity, int *dst_size);\n399\t    int   (*json_to_native)(const void *src, int src_size,\n400\t                            void *dst, int dst_capacity, int *dst_size);\n401\t} lang_spec_t;\n402\t\n403\textern lang_spec_t soramech_lang_spec;\n404\t```\n405\t\n406\tA nonzero return from `invoke_*` is a fatal error. The dispatch\n407\tlayer prints the context (box id, function name, language) and\n408\taborts. There is no recovery, no retry, no per-task \"failed\" state.\n409\tBugs do not belong in production.\n410\t\n411\t### Init barrier\n412\t\n413\tWorkers are not safe to dispatch to until every worker has completed\n414\t`init` for every spec the map uses. Pool startup runs each worker's\n415\t`init` calls, increments a shared `workers_ready` atomic, and blocks\n416\ton a condition variable. The main thread waits for\n417\t`workers_ready == n_workers`, then broadcasts — all workers release\n418\ttogether and begin pulling tasks. One-shot; doesn't re-engage.\n419\t\n420\t### Same-language wire fast path\n421\t\n422\tWire format defaults to JSON. At compile time, every wire is\n423\tclassified `fast_path: true` (same language at both ends) or `false`\n424\t(crosses a language boundary). The compile step also records the\n425\tproducer's `output_format` per box — `native` if **all** consumers\n426\tof its output share its language, `json` if any consumer is\n427\tdifferent.\n428\t\n429\tAt runtime:\n430\t\n431\t- `fast_path && output_format=native`: producer writes native bytes;\n432\t  same-language consumers read native bytes directly.\n433\t- `output_format=json`: producer writes JSON bytes; cross-language\n434\t  consumers read directly; same-language consumers call\n435\t  `json_to_native` on the way in.\n436\t\n437\tPer-language native forms:\n438\t- **Lua** — `lua_dump` for closures, `cjson` or msgpack for tables,\n439\t  raw bytes for strings/numbers.\n440\t- **C** — `memcpy` of the typed struct (the C spec's `compile`\n441\t  callback knows the types).\n442\t- **Bash** — strings only; the fast path is an alias of the JSON\n443\t  path.\n444\t\n445\tA spec that only ever talks to itself can stub out `invoke_json`\n446\t(compile error if a cross-language wire ever points at it). A spec\n447\tthat participates in cross-language wires must implement all four\n448\tcallbacks.\n449\t\n450\t### Shipped specs\n451\t\n452\t`langs/lua/spec.so`, `langs/c/spec.so`, `langs/bash/spec.so` ship as\n453\treference implementations:\n454\t\n455\t- **Lua** — `init` constructs a `lua_State`; `invoke_*` does\n456\t  `luaL_loadfile` (cached) + `lua_pcall`.\n457\t- **C** — `compile` runs `gcc -shared -fPIC -o <out> <src>` (caching\n458\t  by mtime); `invoke_*` does `dlsym` + direct call through a wrapper\n459\t  the compile step generates from the box signature.\n460\t- **Bash** — `init` spawns a persistent bash subprocess and connects\n461\t  to it over a Unix domain socket. `invoke_*` sends a framed request,\n462\t  reads a framed response. The same shape every future\n463\t  non-embeddable-runtime language uses (Python optional, Node\n464\t  optional, etc.).\n465\t\n466\tA user adds a new language by writing a `langs/<name>/spec.c` and a\n467\tsmall Makefile. SoraMech itself does not transpile box source between\n468\tlanguages.\n469\t\n470\t## Execution model — phase 2 (synchronous)\n471\t\n472\tThe runner walks the graph depth-first from the boxes that have all\n473\ttheir inputs satisfied. Each box call:\n474\t\n475\t1. Read wired output values from predecessor boxes.\n476\t2. Shell out to the appropriate driver script (`drivers/<lang>.sh`).\n477\t3. Decode the single JSON value from driver stdout.\n478\t4. Hold the output in runner memory, keyed by box id.\n479\t5. Fire connections — enqueue boxes whose inputs are now met.\n480\t\n481\tSingle-threaded; one process per box call. The `task_fn` boundary\n482\tmatches the phase 3 dispatch action signature, so the executor can\n483\tbe swapped without changing the box execution model.\n484\t\n485\t## Execution model — phase 3 (thread pool)\n486\t\n487\tTasks are ephemeral; box state is durable. Each box owns one slot\n488\tper input port plus optional state (iterator counter, language\n489\thandle). A **task** is one stack frame on a worker — `box_id` is\n490\tall it carries. Tasks come and go; boxes persist for the run.\n491\t\n492\t### Slots\n493\t\n494\tEvery input port has exactly one slot, allocated at graph load and\n495\tfreed at run end. A wire is a routing declaration; the producer\n496\tdoesn't own a slot — its output is a push event into every\n497\tdownstream input slot it's wired to. Fan-out is N pushes; fan-in is\n498\tN producers pushing into one slot.\n499\t\n500\tSlot modes:\n501\t\n502\t| Mode                    | Cells   | Reads via         | Used for                                    |\n503\t|-------------------------|---------|-------------------|---------------------------------------------|\n504\t| 1-cell peek             | 1       | `slot_peek`       | Literals; wires from runs-once producers    |\n505\t| N-cell pop              | N       | `slot_pop`        | Wires whose producer runs many times        |\n506\t| `SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER`   | 1 atom  | `slot_read_inc`   | Iterator / randomizer / weighted counters   |\n507\t\n508\tCompile-time analysis decides per wire: a producer is \"runs-once\" if\n509\tno transitive ancestor is an iterator, else \"runs-N-times.\" The\n510\tformer gets a 1-cell peek slot (subsequent consumer tasks re-read the\n511\tsame value); the latter gets an N-cell ring (FIFO drain, one cell\n512\tper consumer task).\n513\t\n514\tVariable-size payloads (long LLM outputs, dynamically-sized arrays)\n515\tlive in a separate **large-value heap**. The slot then holds a small\n516\tfixed-size handle `{ uint32_t size; uint32_t offset; }`. The slot\n517\tallocator only ever sees fixed-size slots; the two-tier scheme keeps\n518\tthe hot path simple while supporting unbounded values.\n519\t\n520\t### Cell tagging for parallel iterators\n521\t\n522\tEach cell optionally carries a 4-byte ordering tag alongside its\n523\tdata. Iterator pushes carry their counter value as the tag; slots\n524\tdownstream of an iterator are allocated with `SLOT_TAGGED`, and\n525\t`slot_pop` on a tagged slot returns the **lowest-tag** cell — not\n526\tthe head. This preserves iteration order across parallel iterator\n527\tworkers (task K of iterator A may push before task K-1 if it landed\n528\ton a faster worker; the tag makes the consumer see the values in\n529\titeration order regardless).\n530\t\n531\tWhen a consumer has two tagged inputs from two iterators, each port\n532\tpops in tag order independently — pairing falls out as `(A_K, B_K)`\n533\tfor every K.\n534\t\n535\t### The dispatch action — the attempt loop\n536\t\n537\tEvery task in the pool is an **attempt task**. The pool's queue\n538\tholds attempt tasks; workers pick them up; each attempt either\n539\tadvances the graph by one box invocation or returns without doing\n540\tanything. There is no separate \"readiness check\" task kind. An\n541\tattempt that finds its inputs ready *is* the work invocation; an\n542\tattempt that doesn't, returns and disappears.\n543\t\n544\t```\n545\tproducer task:\n546\t   compute output\n547\t   for each downstream consumer box C this producer just touched:\n548\t      write all values to C's input slots\n549\t         (snapshotted into the attempt's cell at the END)\n550\t   for each distinct C:\n551\t      slab_alloc() → attempt_task for C\n552\t      pool_spawn(attempt_task)\n553\t   slab_free(this cell)\n554\t\n555\tattempt task:\n556\t   if every required input on C is satisfiable\n557\t      (slot value or data-box pull):\n558\t      snapshot values into local vars\n559\t      invoke spec, get output\n560\t      push output to downstream consumer slots\n561\t      submit one attempt per distinct downstream consumer\n562\t      decrement input $ref counts\n563\t      decrement upstream boxes' live_predecessor_count if applicable\n564\t   slab_free(this cell)\n565\t```\n566\t\n567\tThe producer task and the attempt task are the same shape of\n568\tallocation, same call site, same return path. One cell per\n569\tinvocation in the steady-state hot path; no double-allocation\n570\tbetween \"check that I'm ready\" and \"do my work.\"\n571\t\n572\tThree properties fall out:\n573\t\n574\t- **Targeted attempts.** A producer knows which consumer boxes it\n575\t  just pushed to; the attempts it submits are for those specific\n576\t  consumers, not a generic re-evaluation of every consumer in the\n577\t  graph.\n578\t- **One readiness check per producer task.** Even if a producer\n579\t  writes to multiple slots on the same consumer, only one attempt\n580\t  is submitted for that consumer. The submission happens at the\n581\t  END of the producer, after every output value has been placed —\n582\t  the attempt is guaranteed to find a coherent input set, not a\n583\t  half-written one.\n584\t- **No parking.** An attempt that finds its inputs unsatisfied\n585\t  returns. The shell does not hold tasks in waiting states. The\n586\t  next producer push to any of the consumer's input slots triggers\n587\t  another attempt with the same shape. Eventually one of those\n588\t  attempts finds the input set complete and runs the work.\n589\t\n590\t> \"the most recent change that would enable the box to run —\n591\t> essentially, our logic is such that the fewest amount of steps\n592\t> between each function call must be made, while enabling the\n593\t> long-tail async threads to do non-blocking tasks on their own\n594\t> time. As soon as they can, they knit themselves with their\n595\t> fellow threads, co-creating a weaving texture of computer\n596\t> programming. proving without a doubt that intelligence can have\n597\t> a dynamical host.\" — 2026-05-20\n598\t\n599\tRouting kinds (per 233) dispatch the output-side push: `plain` fans\n600\tto every wire, `comparator` picks one of `lt`/`eq`/`gt` by numeric\n601\tcomparison, `iterator` reads-and-increments a per-box atomic\n602\tcounter slot mod `n_outputs` and fires only the picked branch. The\n603\tfollow-on kinds (randomizer / weighted / distributor) live in\n604\tissues 240–242.\n605\t\n606\tCross-language pushes carry a `$ref` handle when the output value\n607\tis variable-size (per 312/317): the producer writes the bytes to\n608\tthe large-value heap once, refcount = number of consuming slots,\n609\tand writes the `(ptr, length)` handle into each consumer slot. The\n610\tbytes themselves are never copied; the consumer's spec follows the\n611\tpointer to read.\n612\t\n613\t### Startup, quiescence, and termination\n614\t\n615\tStartup: the pool runner pushes literal-input values into the\n616\tcorresponding slots, then spawns first tasks for boxes whose input\n617\tsets are now satisfied. Iterator counter slots start at 0.\n618\t\n619\tQuiescence: the main thread waits on a condition variable that\n620\tsignals when the pool's active-task counter reaches zero with no\n621\tpending spawns. That's the run-over signal. The graph validator at\n622\tload time rejects non-iterator cycles, so the run cannot deadlock —\n623\tan iterator with no upstream pushes simply contributes nothing\n624\tfurther, and once the counter drains, termination fires.\n625\t\n626\tHard-crash error policy: a nonzero `invoke_*` return aborts the\n627\tprocess. No retry, no per-task failed state, no fallback executor.\n628\t\n629\t### Blocking-aware iterator pattern\n630\t\n631\tLong-running operations (network calls, LLM inference) hold their\n632\tworker for the duration. Pool size is the budget. The cooperative\n633\tpattern for not holding a worker for minutes: split the call into a\n634\t\"kickoff\" box and a \"check-done\" iterator that polls. Each pass\n635\tthrough the iterator releases the worker between checks. Documented\n636\tfully in `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md`.\n637\t\n638\t## Run output — `tmp/last-run.jsonl`\n639\t\n640\tPhase 3 writes one JSON object per event, one event per line, to\n641\t`tmp/last-run.jsonl`. The format decouples the runner from the\n642\teditor — the editor never displays run results; the file is for LLM\n643\tconsumption, CLI viewers, and the integration test harness.\n644\t\n645\tEvent types:\n646\t\n647\t```jsonl\n648\t{\"event\":\"run_start\", \"ts\":..., \"map\":\"maps/<name>\", \"n_workers\":16}\n649\t{\"event\":\"task_submit\", \"ts\":..., \"task_id\":42, \"box_id\":\"classify\"}\n650\t{\"event\":\"task_start\",  \"ts\":..., \"task_id\":42, \"worker_idx\":3}\n651\t{\"event\":\"task_end\",    \"ts\":..., \"task_id\":42, \"duration_us\":127, \"output_size\":12}\n652\t{\"event\":\"slot_alloc\",  \"ts\":..., \"slot_id\":5, \"size\":256, \"n_cells\":1}   // SORAMECH_LOG_SLOTS=1\n653\t{\"event\":\"slot_free\",   \"ts\":..., \"slot_id\":5}                              // SORAMECH_LOG_SLOTS=1\n654\t{\"event\":\"run_end\",     \"ts\":..., \"duration_us\":1850, \"n_tasks\":7}\n655\t```\n656\t\n657\tMechanism: a dedicated writer thread drains a multi-producer\n658\tsingle-consumer ring buffer of fixed-size event records, serializes\n659\teach to JSON, and appends to the file. Workers push records into the\n660\tring without contending on a file mutex. The writer joins before\n661\t`pool_destroy`, including a final `run_end` summary.\n662\t\n663\tInputs/outputs per task are off by default (`SORAMECH_LOG_VALUES=1`\n664\tto enable; truncated past 4 KB). Slot allocator events are off by\n665\tdefault (`SORAMECH_LOG_SLOTS=1` to enable). Timestamps are Unix\n666\tepoch floats.\n667\t\n668\tThe file is overwritten on every run. Rotation is out of scope —\n669\tusers who want history copy the file.\n670\t\n671\t## Build & compile pipeline\n672\t\n673\tA top-level `Makefile` builds:\n674\t\n675\t1. `soramech-pool` — statically links the pool, JSON parser, slot\n676\t   store, graph loader, dispatch layer, spec registry.\n677\t2. `langs/<name>/spec.so` — per-spec, via the per-language Makefile\n678\t   (Lua links LuaJIT; C links `-ldl`; Bash links nothing extra).\n679\t\n680\tModes: `make` (release, `-O2 -Wall`), `make DEBUG=1` (`-O0 -g`),\n681\t`make STRICT=1` (release + `-Werror -Wextra -Wpedantic`).\n682\t\n683\tVendored dependencies (the task pool, the JSON parser) live under\n684\t`libs/` as plain source — no submodules, no fetches at build time.\n685\t\n686\tSpec discovery at runtime: the runner reads `/proc/self/exe`,\n687\tfollows the symlink, and scans for `langs/` next to its own binary.\n688\t`SORAMECH_LANGS_DIR=/path/to/langs` overrides for development.\n689\t\n690\t### Compile a map for standalone execution\n691\t\n692\t`./compiled/pool-runner` runs a map independently of the editor and\n693\tthe surrounding source tree. The compile step (Compile button in the\n694\teditor, or `soramech-compile <map-dir>` from the CLI) produces:\n695\t\n696\t```\n697\tmaps/<name>/compiled/\n698\t  pool-runner          ← copy or symlink of soramech-pool\n699\t  src/                 ← every source file the map uses\n700\t  bin/                 ← per-box compiled .so files (C boxes)\n701\t  langs/<name>/spec.so ← one per language the map uses\n702\t  manifest.json        ← every box, its language, artifact path, build version\n703\t```\n704\t\n705\tSteps: walk the graph (reusing the C loader's validation); copy\n706\tsource files and transitive `require` / `#include` dependencies;\n707\tinvoke each spec's `compile` callback for boxes whose language needs\n708\tit; copy the spec `.so` files used by the map; copy or symlink the\n709\trunner binary; write the manifest. Per-box artifacts mtime-compare\n710\tso a re-compile recompiles only what changed. Any failure aborts\n711\tthe step and leaves the partial output for inspection but does not\n712\twrite the manifest, so the deployment is recognizably broken until\n713\ta clean compile succeeds.\n714\t\n715\t## Data files\n716\t\n717\tPersistent data lives in `data/<name>.json` and is accessed via\n718\t`libs/soramech-data.lua` (`data.get` / `data.set` / `data.load`).\n719\tFormat:\n720\t\n721\t```json\n722\t{\n723\t  \"constant\": false,\n724\t  \"fields\": {\n725\t    \"history\": [],\n726\t    \"config\": { \"constant\": true, \"value\": { \"model\": \"soramind-default\" } }\n727\t  }\n728\t}\n729\t```\n730\t\n731\tTop-level `constant: true` makes the whole file read-only;\n732\tfield-level `constant` flags individual fields within an otherwise\n733\tmutable file. This is **separate** from the `data` box kind (which\n734\treads arbitrary files at the dispatch layer) — `soramech-data` is\n735\tthe per-map structured-table store; `data` boxes are unstructured\n736\tfile sources.\n737\t\n738\tEphemeral state (scratch tables, run logs, `last-run.jsonl`) goes to\n739\t`tmp/`, a symlink to `/tmp/<map-name>/`. Survives the run but not a\n740\treboot — intentionally.\n741\t",

      "content":"# SoraMech — Architecture\n\n## The structural shell\n\nSoraMech is a structural shell. The thread pool, the slot store, the\ndispatch layer, the allocator — these are the steel and concrete of\nan apartment building. They hold the roof up. They do not decorate\nthe rooms.\n\nBox authors design the rooms. Library authors furnish them. The\nshell provides the framing, the load-bearing walls, the structural\nguarantees of what can hang where. The shell does not know what\ncolour the curtains are.\n\n> \"We are creating a structural shell, like an apartment building\n> that is just steel and concrete at first, and the user can build\n> the walls and windows and design the doors and movement paths as\n> they please. The library authors are doing the actual decorating,\n> with tables and chairs and pictures of the beach. We are\n> structural, we keep the roof from caving in. To that end, we must\n> be rigid. We must be firm. We must be flexible.\" — 2026-05-20\n\nTwo consequences shape every design decision below.\n\n### One allocator function per kind of operation\n\nFor each distinct kind of allocation the runtime needs, exactly one\nfunction performs it. The same function is called from every box's\nhot path; only its parameters vary. The user's code, the spec's\ncode, the dispatch layer's code — all reach the same entry point.\n\nThis is the rigidity. The shell does not present \"convenient\nshortcuts\" for special cases. Every value lifecycle goes through\nthe same allocator. Every task struct comes from the same slab.\nEvery wire push goes through the same `slot_push`. No alternatives,\nno escape hatches.\n\nThe exceptions are setup and teardown: the graph loader allocates\nevery box's slot table once at startup before the pool launches;\n`pool_destroy` releases everything in one shot at the end. Outside\nthose two moments, the shell is uniform.\n\n### No single-threaded process outside the pool\n\nEvery piece of runtime work — every allocation, every reference\ncount update, every dispatch action, every cleanup — happens\ninside a pool task. There is no background garbage collector, no\nmaintenance daemon, no separate scheduler. The pool is the\nuniversal scheduler; the pool task is the universal unit of work.\n\nConsequences:\n\n- The allocator's deep sweep, when it runs, runs inside the\n  failing-to-allocate task. There is no \"sweep thread\" polling for\n  free memory. There is no quiescence-triggered sweep either — we\n  cannot assume there will ever be a quiescent moment in a graph\n  with self-feeding iterators.\n- Reference count decrements happen at the end of the task that\n  was holding the reference. Cleanup is the task's last act, not\n  a separate worker's job.\n- Box-level retirement (when all of a box's possible inputs are\n  exhausted) is checked inside the task whose completion may have\n  triggered the retirement condition.\n\nThe pool's parallelism is the only parallelism the runtime\nprovides. A side thread would be a different shape — a violation\nof the uniform \"one allocator, one scheduler\" rule.\n\n## Three programs, one data format\n\nSoraMech is three independent programs that share a common on-disk\nformat: the map directory. None of the three knows about the others\nat runtime.\n\n```\n  Browser (assets/index.html)\n       |  HTTP (file CRUD)\n       v\n  src/006-server-main.lua       [map directory]\n                                maps/<name>/\n                                  meta.json\n                                  boxes/\n                                  data/\n                                  src/\n                                  compiled/   (after compile button)\n                                  tmp/ -> /tmp/<name>/\n       ^\n       | reads & writes\n  Runner (one of):\n    src/007-runner-main.lua     ← phase 2, synchronous Lua interpreter\n    soramech-pool (binary)      ← phase 3, C thread pool runner\n```\n\n### src/006-server-main.lua (the editor's HTTP backend)\n\nThin file CRUD proxy. Receives JSON requests from the browser and\ntranslates them into reads and writes on the map directory. No logic\nbeyond path validation and basic consistency checks (e.g. reject a\ndelete if the box is still referenced by another box's connection\nlist).\n\nStarted with: `luajit src/006-server-main.lua [port]` (default 7700).\nThe `run` script at the project root starts the server and opens the\neditor.\n\nThe editor is editor-only — no run button, no run results display.\nThe runner is invoked separately, by command line. `last-run.jsonl`\nis the runner's output, consumed by external tooling, not by the\neditor.\n\n### Phase 2 runner — `src/007-runner-main.lua`\n\nSynchronous Lua interpreter. Loads a map directory, validates the\ngraph, walks boxes in dependency order, invokes language drivers per\nbox (`drivers/lua.sh`, `drivers/c.sh`, `drivers/bash.sh`). Each box\ninvocation is wrapped in a `task_fn(inputs) -> outputs` boundary that\nmatches the phase 3 thread pool's action signature.\n\nThis is the development target while the editor is being built out.\nPhase 2 retires wholesale when phase 3 lands; the editor and the\nmap-directory format are unchanged across the cutover.\n\n### Phase 3 runner — `soramech-pool` (`src/008-pool-runner.c`)\n\nThe phase 3 runner is a single C binary. It owns:\n\n- A **SoraMech-built thread pool** under `libs/task-pool/` (3d-rts at\n  `/home/ritz/programming/ai-stuff/games/3d-rts/libs/900-task-pool.h`\n  is the design reference, not vendored).\n- A **C graph loader** (`src/graph-loader.c`) — replaces\n  `src/003-loader.lua`. The runner has no embedded Lua state at the\n  top level; Lua only appears inside a Lua language spec's per-worker\n  handle.\n- A **per-input-port slot store** (`src/slot-store.c`) — ring-buffer\n  cells in process heap, durable for the run, plus a large-value heap\n  for variable-size payloads.\n- A **dispatch layer** (`src/dispatch.c`) — the single worker-side\n  action: read inputs → invoke spec → pick branch → push outputs.\n- A **language spec registry** (`src/spec-registry.c`) — `dlopen`s\n  every `langs/<name>/spec.so` at startup and registers it by name\n  and file extension.\n- A **run-output writer** — a dedicated thread that drains a\n  multi-producer-single-consumer ring of events and appends one JSON\n  line per event to `tmp/last-run.jsonl`.\n\nOne pool per map run. Created after the graph loads and validates;\ndestroyed after the active-task counter reaches zero. Worker count\ndefaults to logical CPUs (capped at `MAX_WORKERS=16`), overridable\nvia `SORAMECH_WORKERS=N`.\n\nSee \"Execution model — phase 3\" below for the action loop and slot\nmechanics.\n\n### assets/index.html (the editor)\n\nStatic HTML + vanilla JS. Infinite-scroll canvas. Box diagram editor.\nTalks to `src/006-server-main.lua` for all file operations. No run\nbutton. The Compile button (added in phase 2 as UI only) wires into\nthe phase 3 build/package pipeline once it lands.\n\n## Map directory format\n\n```\nmaps/<name>/\n  meta.json          — { name, description, src_dirs?, lang? }\n  boxes/\n    <id>.json        — one file per box (see Box file format below)\n  data/\n    <name>.json      — soramech-data tables; section-level \"constant\" flag\n  src/\n    *.lua, *.c, *.sh — box function source files\n  compiled/          — produced by the compile pipeline (issue 309)\n    pool-runner      — copy or symlink of soramech-pool\n    src/             — every source file the map uses\n    bin/             — compiled .so files (C boxes via the C spec's compile callback)\n    langs/<name>/    — copy of each language spec .so the map uses\n    manifest.json    — every box, its language, its artifact path, build version\n  tmp/               — symlink to /tmp/<name>/\n    last-run.jsonl   — phase 3 run log (JSON Lines)\n    logs/            — additional run logs\n```\n\nA compiled map runs standalone: `./compiled/pool-runner` looks up its\nspecs in `compiled/langs/`, reads `manifest.json`, and executes\nwithout any reference to the live editor source tree.\n\nPhase 2's `drivers.json` file is gone. Phase 2 resolves drivers by\nfile extension via the `drivers/` directory; phase 3 resolves\nlanguages by file extension via the spec registry (each spec declares\nits `file_ext`). No map-local driver config file is needed in either\nphase.\n\nThe `data/` directory is for `soramech-data` storage (see \"Data\nfiles\" below). It is **not** where file-source boxes read from — those\nread arbitrary paths, see Box kinds.\n\n## Box file format\n\nEvery box is a single JSON file under `boxes/<id>.json`. Every box\nhas exactly **one output wire** (issue 218). There is no `outputs`\narray. Whatever the function returns travels down the single output\nwire as one value; multi-value returns are encoded as JSON (or a\nlanguage-native struct on a same-language wire — see \"Language spec\nsystem\" below) and decoded downstream.\n\n### Box kinds\n\n| `kind`  | Runs a function? | Notes                                                                |\n|---------|------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------|\n| `call`  | yes              | Plain call, comparator, iterator, etc. — see `routing` below.        |\n| `read`  | no               | Value source. Inline literal `value` OR file at `path`.              |\n| `write` | no               | File sink. Writes the `value` input; emits boolean `\"true\"` downstream. |\n\n`read` and `write` are dispatch-layer primitives — the runtime\nreads/writes the file directly, no language spec is invoked. A\n`read` box with an inline `value` literal skips file IO entirely\nand emits the literal bytes. A `write` box atomically commits\nits `value` input to disk and pushes `\"true\"` to any downstream\nwires; if no wire reads its output, the boolean is discarded per\nthe unwired-output rule.\n\n```json\n{ \"id\": \"from_file\", \"kind\": \"read\", \"path\": \"config.json\",\n  \"ui\": { \"x\": 100, \"y\": 100 } }\n\n{ \"id\": \"from_literal\", \"kind\": \"read\",\n  \"value\": \"hello, world!\",\n  \"ui\": { \"x\": 100, \"y\": 200 } }\n\n{ \"id\": \"save\", \"kind\": \"write\",\n  \"inputs\": [\n    { \"name\": \"path\",  \"type\": \"string\" },\n    { \"name\": \"value\", \"type\": \"string\" }\n  ],\n  \"ui\": { \"x\": 400, \"y\": 100 } }\n```\n\n**Unwired-output discard rule.** If an output value is produced\nbut no wire carries it downstream, the value is discarded. A\n`write` box with no wire on its done-boolean output still\ncommits the file — the boolean just goes nowhere. The rule\napplies to every kind; `write` is the most visible case.\n\n`data` has `path` (not `ref`), no `fn`, no inputs; emits the file's\nbytes-as-UTF-8 string on its one output wire. `file_write` takes\n`path` and `text` as inputs; the `path` input can be wired (dynamic)\nor filled by a literal (static). Binary files are out of scope for\nboth — non-UTF-8 reads fail with a clear error.\n\n### Call boxes and the `routing` field\n\nA `call` box runs a function (`ref` + `fn`) and produces one output\nvalue. The `routing` field decides where that value goes. Every\ncall box carries `routing` explicitly — there is no implicit default:\n\n```json\n{ \"id\": \"plain-call\", \"kind\": \"call\",\n  \"ref\": \"src/strings.lua\", \"fn\": \"trim\",\n  \"inputs\": [{ \"name\": \"text\", \"type\": \"string\" }],\n  \"routing\": { \"kind\": \"plain\" },\n  \"connections\": [\n    { \"from_box\": \"plain-call\", \"from_branch\": null,\n      \"to_box\": \"next\", \"to_input\": \"text\" }\n  ],\n  \"ui\": { \"x\": 120, \"y\": 340 } }\n```\n\nThe function **always runs**, regardless of routing kind. Routing\ndecides which downstream branch receives the function's output; the\nfunction itself doesn't know.\n\n#### Routing kinds\n\n| `routing.kind`  | Output ports          | Branch picker                                                | Status     |\n|-----------------|-----------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------|------------|\n| `plain`         | single port           | fan to all outgoing wires                                    | shipped    |\n| `comparator`    | `lt` / `eq` / `gt`    | `compare(output, comparand)` → lt/eq/gt                      | shipped    |\n| `iterator`      | `out_0` … `out_N-1`   | `slot_read_inc(counter_slot, N)`                             | shipped    |\n| `randomizer`    | `out_0` … `out_N-1`   | `hash(slot_read_inc(counter_slot, MAX)) % N`                 | follow-on  |\n| `weighted`      | `out_0` … `out_N-1`   | cumulative-band lookup against a counter scaled to PRECISION | follow-on  |\n| `distributor`   | `out_0` … `out_N-1`   | argmin over downstream slot fill levels                      | follow-on  |\n\n```json\n\"routing\": { \"kind\": \"plain\" }\n\"routing\": { \"kind\": \"comparator\", \"comparand\": \"0\" }\n\"routing\": { \"kind\": \"iterator\",   \"n_outputs\": 3 }\n\"routing\": { \"kind\": \"weighted\",   \"weights\": [0.8, 0.2] }\n\"routing\": { \"kind\": \"distributor\", \"n_outputs\": 3 }\n```\n\n**Branch-level fan-out**: for `comparator` / `iterator` / etc., each\nbranch port acts like a small plain output of its own. If the\ncomparator's `lt` port has three wires going to three consumers, then\non every invocation where the routing decision picks `lt`, all three\nof those wires fire. The routing decision picks which branch;\nfan-out picks which consumers on that branch receive the value.\n\nPlain output port can fan freely too — multiple connections from\n`from_branch: null` send copies to every wired consumer. Pulling\nmultiple wires from a single output is not a routing decision.\n\n### Input ports\n\n```json\n\"inputs\": [\n  { \"name\": \"text\",        \"type\": \"string\" },\n  { \"name\": \"config_path\", \"type\": \"string\", \"optional\": true,\n    \"value\": \"config.json\" }\n]\n```\n\nEvery input port is in one of three states at compile time:\n\n1. A wire is connected to it.\n2. A literal `value` is set on it.\n3. It carries `optional: true`.\n\n**Compile fails** when any port is in none of those states. The\nerror is precise: which box, which port. Enforced at the Compile\nbutton (phase 2 UI / phase 3 build) and again in the C graph loader\nat runtime — belt and suspenders against hand-edited maps.\n\n`optional: true` does **not** mean \"pass null\" — it means the\nargument doesn't have to be passed. The dispatch layer assembles\n`input_data[]` / `input_sizes[]` from the slots that actually have\nvalues; an absent optional port shortens `n_inputs` by one and the\nlanguage's native short-arg convention handles the rest. Each\nlanguage picks up the convention natively (Lua: missing args are\n`nil`; Bash: positional unset; C: wrapper reads `n_inputs` and\nforwards what's present).\n\nNull as an **explicit** value (typed `null` into the literal field)\nis a different thing: it arrives through the function call as a real\nargument, mapped to the language's native null (Lua `nil`, Bash empty\nstring `\"\"`, C `NULL`).\n\nVariadic inputs (`variadic_inputs`) carry base names whose ports\nexpand to `<base>_0`, `<base>_1`, … in the editor (issue 217).\n\n### Connections\n\nConnections are written to **both** endpoint box files. The loader\nvalidates at load time that both ends agree — disagreement is a\nhard error.\n\n```json\n{ \"from_box\": \"...\",\n  \"from_branch\": null | \"lt\" | \"eq\" | \"gt\" | \"out_0\" | ...,\n  \"to_box\":   \"...\",\n  \"to_input\": \"...\" }\n```\n\n`from_branch` is `null` for `routing: plain` and for boxes without a\nrouting field; otherwise it names the branch port the wire leaves\nfrom.\n\n## Language spec system (phase 3)\n\nEach language is a **spec** — a `.so` library at\n`langs/<name>/spec.so` that exports a `lang_spec_t` symbol. The pool\nrunner loads every `langs/*/spec.so` at startup via `dlopen` and\nregisters it by `name` (for box lookup) and `file_ext` (for source\nresolution). The spec contract is uniform across languages; no\nlanguage is privileged. The runner itself does not link to liblua,\nlibc++, or any language-specific runtime — only specs do.\n\n### `lang_spec_t`\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    const char *name;       // \"lua\", \"bash\", \"c\", \"python\", ...\n    const char *file_ext;   // \".lua\", \".sh\", \".c\", \".py\"\n\n    // Once-per-worker. Pool startup calls init() for every spec on\n    // every worker before unblocking the init barrier; teardown()\n    // runs at shutdown.\n    void *(*init)    (int worker_idx);\n    void  (*teardown)(void *handle);\n\n    // Optional: at map-compile time. C uses this to gcc -shared -fPIC.\n    // Lua and Bash leave this NULL.\n    int   (*compile) (const char *src_path, const char *out_path);\n\n    // Universal invoke path: JSON bytes in, JSON bytes out.\n    // Used across every cross-language wire.\n    int   (*invoke_json)  (void *handle,\n                           const char *file_path, const char *fn_name,\n                           const void **input_data, const int *input_sizes, int n_inputs,\n                           void *out_buf, int out_buf_capacity, int *out_size);\n\n    // Fast invoke path: language-native bytes in, language-native bytes out.\n    // Used when producer and consumer share a language (see \"Same-language\n    // wire fast path\" below).\n    int   (*invoke_native)(void *handle, /* same signature */);\n\n    // Bridges used when a value crosses a language boundary.\n    int   (*native_to_json)(const void *src, int src_size,\n                            void *dst, int dst_capacity, int *dst_size);\n    int   (*json_to_native)(const void *src, int src_size,\n                            void *dst, int dst_capacity, int *dst_size);\n} lang_spec_t;\n\nextern lang_spec_t soramech_lang_spec;\n```\n\nA nonzero return from `invoke_*` is a fatal error. The dispatch\nlayer prints the context (box id, function name, language) and\naborts. There is no recovery, no retry, no per-task \"failed\" state.\nBugs do not belong in production.\n\n### Init barrier\n\nWorkers are not safe to dispatch to until every worker has completed\n`init` for every spec the map uses. Pool startup runs each worker's\n`init` calls, increments a shared `workers_ready` atomic, and blocks\non a condition variable. The main thread waits for\n`workers_ready == n_workers`, then broadcasts — all workers release\ntogether and begin pulling tasks. One-shot; doesn't re-engage.\n\n### Same-language wire fast path\n\nWire format defaults to JSON. At compile time, every wire is\nclassified `fast_path: true` (same language at both ends) or `false`\n(crosses a language boundary). The compile step also records the\nproducer's `output_format` per box — `native` if **all** consumers\nof its output share its language, `json` if any consumer is\ndifferent.\n\nAt runtime:\n\n- `fast_path && output_format=native`: producer writes native bytes;\n  same-language consumers read native bytes directly.\n- `output_format=json`: producer writes JSON bytes; cross-language\n  consumers read directly; same-language consumers call\n  `json_to_native` on the way in.\n\nPer-language native forms:\n- **Lua** — `lua_dump` for closures, `cjson` or msgpack for tables,\n  raw bytes for strings/numbers.\n- **C** — `memcpy` of the typed struct (the C spec's `compile`\n  callback knows the types).\n- **Bash** — strings only; the fast path is an alias of the JSON\n  path.\n\nA spec that only ever talks to itself can stub out `invoke_json`\n(compile error if a cross-language wire ever points at it). A spec\nthat participates in cross-language wires must implement all four\ncallbacks.\n\n### Shipped specs\n\n`langs/lua/spec.so`, `langs/c/spec.so`, `langs/bash/spec.so` ship as\nreference implementations:\n\n- **Lua** — `init` constructs a `lua_State`; `invoke_*` does\n  `luaL_loadfile` (cached) + `lua_pcall`.\n- **C** — `compile` runs `gcc -shared -fPIC -o <out> <src>` (caching\n  by mtime); `invoke_*` does `dlsym` + direct call through a wrapper\n  the compile step generates from the box signature.\n- **Bash** — `init` spawns a persistent bash subprocess and connects\n  to it over a Unix domain socket. `invoke_*` sends a framed request,\n  reads a framed response. The same shape every future\n  non-embeddable-runtime language uses (Python optional, Node\n  optional, etc.).\n\nA user adds a new language by writing a `langs/<name>/spec.c` and a\nsmall Makefile. SoraMech itself does not transpile box source between\nlanguages.\n\n## Execution model — phase 2 (synchronous)\n\nThe runner walks the graph depth-first from the boxes that have all\ntheir inputs satisfied. Each box call:\n\n1. Read wired output values from predecessor boxes.\n2. Shell out to the appropriate driver script (`drivers/<lang>.sh`).\n3. Decode the single JSON value from driver stdout.\n4. Hold the output in runner memory, keyed by box id.\n5. Fire connections — enqueue boxes whose inputs are now met.\n\nSingle-threaded; one process per box call. The `task_fn` boundary\nmatches the phase 3 dispatch action signature, so the executor can\nbe swapped without changing the box execution model.\n\n## Execution model — phase 3 (thread pool)\n\nTasks are ephemeral; box state is durable. Each box owns one slot\nper input port plus optional state (iterator counter, language\nhandle). A **task** is one stack frame on a worker — `box_id` is\nall it carries. Tasks come and go; boxes persist for the run.\n\n### Slots\n\nEvery input port has exactly one slot, allocated at graph load and\nfreed at run end. A wire is a routing declaration; the producer\ndoesn't own a slot — its output is a push event into every\ndownstream input slot it's wired to. Fan-out is N pushes; fan-in is\nN producers pushing into one slot.\n\nSlot modes:\n\n| Mode                    | Cells   | Reads via         | Used for                                    |\n|-------------------------|---------|-------------------|---------------------------------------------|\n| 1-cell peek             | 1       | `slot_peek`       | Literals; wires from runs-once producers    |\n| N-cell pop              | N       | `slot_pop`        | Wires whose producer runs many times        |\n| `SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER`   | 1 atom  | `slot_read_inc`   | Iterator / randomizer / weighted counters   |\n\nCompile-time analysis decides per wire: a producer is \"runs-once\" if\nno transitive ancestor is an iterator, else \"runs-N-times.\" The\nformer gets a 1-cell peek slot (subsequent consumer tasks re-read the\nsame value); the latter gets an N-cell ring (FIFO drain, one cell\nper consumer task).\n\nVariable-size payloads (long LLM outputs, dynamically-sized arrays)\nlive in a separate **large-value heap**. The slot then holds a small\nfixed-size handle `{ uint32_t size; uint32_t offset; }`. The slot\nallocator only ever sees fixed-size slots; the two-tier scheme keeps\nthe hot path simple while supporting unbounded values.\n\n### Cell tagging for parallel iterators\n\nEach cell optionally carries a 4-byte ordering tag alongside its\ndata. Iterator pushes carry their counter value as the tag; slots\ndownstream of an iterator are allocated with `SLOT_TAGGED`, and\n`slot_pop` on a tagged slot returns the **lowest-tag** cell — not\nthe head. This preserves iteration order across parallel iterator\nworkers (task K of iterator A may push before task K-1 if it landed\non a faster worker; the tag makes the consumer see the values in\niteration order regardless).\n\nWhen a consumer has two tagged inputs from two iterators, each port\npops in tag order independently — pairing falls out as `(A_K, B_K)`\nfor every K.\n\n### The dispatch action — the attempt loop\n\nEvery task in the pool is an **attempt task**. The pool's queue\nholds attempt tasks; workers pick them up; each attempt either\nadvances the graph by one box invocation or returns without doing\nanything. There is no separate \"readiness check\" task kind. An\nattempt that finds its inputs ready *is* the work invocation; an\nattempt that doesn't, returns and disappears.\n\n```\nproducer task:\n   compute output\n   for each downstream consumer box C this producer just touched:\n      write all values to C's input slots\n         (snapshotted into the attempt's cell at the END)\n   for each distinct C:\n      slab_alloc() → attempt_task for C\n      pool_spawn(attempt_task)\n   slab_free(this cell)\n\nattempt task:\n   if every required input on C is satisfiable\n      (slot value or data-box pull):\n      snapshot values into local vars\n      invoke spec, get output\n      push output to downstream consumer slots\n      submit one attempt per distinct downstream consumer\n      decrement input $ref counts\n      decrement upstream boxes' live_predecessor_count if applicable\n   slab_free(this cell)\n```\n\nThe producer task and the attempt task are the same shape of\nallocation, same call site, same return path. One cell per\ninvocation in the steady-state hot path; no double-allocation\nbetween \"check that I'm ready\" and \"do my work.\"\n\nThree properties fall out:\n\n- **Targeted attempts.** A producer knows which consumer boxes it\n  just pushed to; the attempts it submits are for those specific\n  consumers, not a generic re-evaluation of every consumer in the\n  graph.\n- **One readiness check per producer task.** Even if a producer\n  writes to multiple slots on the same consumer, only one attempt\n  is submitted for that consumer. The submission happens at the\n  END of the producer, after every output value has been placed —\n  the attempt is guaranteed to find a coherent input set, not a\n  half-written one.\n- **No parking.** An attempt that finds its inputs unsatisfied\n  returns. The shell does not hold tasks in waiting states. The\n  next producer push to any of the consumer's input slots triggers\n  another attempt with the same shape. Eventually one of those\n  attempts finds the input set complete and runs the work.\n\n> \"the most recent change that would enable the box to run —\n> essentially, our logic is such that the fewest amount of steps\n> between each function call must be made, while enabling the\n> long-tail async threads to do non-blocking tasks on their own\n> time. As soon as they can, they knit themselves with their\n> fellow threads, co-creating a weaving texture of computer\n> programming. proving without a doubt that intelligence can have\n> a dynamical host.\" — 2026-05-20\n\nRouting kinds (per 233) dispatch the output-side push: `plain` fans\nto every wire, `comparator` picks one of `lt`/`eq`/`gt` by numeric\ncomparison, `iterator` reads-and-increments a per-box atomic\ncounter slot mod `n_outputs` and fires only the picked branch. The\nfollow-on kinds (randomizer / weighted / distributor) live in\nissues 240–242.\n\nCross-language pushes carry a `$ref` handle when the output value\nis variable-size (per 312/317): the producer writes the bytes to\nthe large-value heap once, refcount = number of consuming slots,\nand writes the `(ptr, length)` handle into each consumer slot. The\nbytes themselves are never copied; the consumer's spec follows the\npointer to read.\n\n### Startup, quiescence, and termination\n\nStartup: the pool runner pushes literal-input values into the\ncorresponding slots, then spawns first tasks for boxes whose input\nsets are now satisfied. Iterator counter slots start at 0.\n\nQuiescence: the main thread waits on a condition variable that\nsignals when the pool's active-task counter reaches zero with no\npending spawns. That's the run-over signal. The graph validator at\nload time rejects non-iterator cycles, so the run cannot deadlock —\nan iterator with no upstream pushes simply contributes nothing\nfurther, and once the counter drains, termination fires.\n\nHard-crash error policy: a nonzero `invoke_*` return aborts the\nprocess. No retry, no per-task failed state, no fallback executor.\n\n### Blocking-aware iterator pattern\n\nLong-running operations (network calls, LLM inference) hold their\nworker for the duration. Pool size is the budget. The cooperative\npattern for not holding a worker for minutes: split the call into a\n\"kickoff\" box and a \"check-done\" iterator that polls. Each pass\nthrough the iterator releases the worker between checks. Documented\nfully in `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md`.\n\n## Run output — `tmp/last-run.jsonl`\n\nPhase 3 writes one JSON object per event, one event per line, to\n`tmp/last-run.jsonl`. The format decouples the runner from the\neditor — the editor never displays run results; the file is for LLM\nconsumption, CLI viewers, and the integration test harness.\n\nEvent types:\n\n```jsonl\n{\"event\":\"run_start\", \"ts\":..., \"map\":\"maps/<name>\", \"n_workers\":16}\n{\"event\":\"task_submit\", \"ts\":..., \"task_id\":42, \"box_id\":\"classify\"}\n{\"event\":\"task_start\",  \"ts\":..., \"task_id\":42, \"worker_idx\":3}\n{\"event\":\"task_end\",    \"ts\":..., \"task_id\":42, \"duration_us\":127, \"output_size\":12}\n{\"event\":\"slot_alloc\",  \"ts\":..., \"slot_id\":5, \"size\":256, \"n_cells\":1}   // SORAMECH_LOG_SLOTS=1\n{\"event\":\"slot_free\",   \"ts\":..., \"slot_id\":5}                              // SORAMECH_LOG_SLOTS=1\n{\"event\":\"run_end\",     \"ts\":..., \"duration_us\":1850, \"n_tasks\":7}\n```\n\nMechanism: a dedicated writer thread drains a multi-producer\nsingle-consumer ring buffer of fixed-size event records, serializes\neach to JSON, and appends to the file. Workers push records into the\nring without contending on a file mutex. The writer joins before\n`pool_destroy`, including a final `run_end` summary.\n\nInputs/outputs per task are off by default (`SORAMECH_LOG_VALUES=1`\nto enable; truncated past 4 KB). Slot allocator events are off by\ndefault (`SORAMECH_LOG_SLOTS=1` to enable). Timestamps are Unix\nepoch floats.\n\nThe file is overwritten on every run. Rotation is out of scope —\nusers who want history copy the file.\n\n## Build & compile pipeline\n\nA top-level `Makefile` builds:\n\n1. `soramech-pool` — statically links the pool, JSON parser, slot\n   store, graph loader, dispatch layer, spec registry.\n2. `langs/<name>/spec.so` — per-spec, via the per-language Makefile\n   (Lua links LuaJIT; C links `-ldl`; Bash links nothing extra).\n\nModes: `make` (release, `-O2 -Wall`), `make DEBUG=1` (`-O0 -g`),\n`make STRICT=1` (release + `-Werror -Wextra -Wpedantic`).\n\nVendored dependencies (the task pool, the JSON parser) live under\n`libs/` as plain source — no submodules, no fetches at build time.\n\nSpec discovery at runtime: the runner reads `/proc/self/exe`,\nfollows the symlink, and scans for `langs/` next to its own binary.\n`SORAMECH_LANGS_DIR=/path/to/langs` overrides for development.\n\n### Compile a map for standalone execution\n\n`./compiled/pool-runner` runs a map independently of the editor and\nthe surrounding source tree. The compile step (Compile button in the\neditor, or `soramech-compile <map-dir>` from the CLI) produces:\n\n```\nmaps/<name>/compiled/\n  pool-runner          ← copy or symlink of soramech-pool\n  src/                 ← every source file the map uses\n  bin/                 ← per-box compiled .so files (C boxes)\n  langs/<name>/spec.so ← one per language the map uses\n  manifest.json        ← every box, its language, artifact path, build version\n```\n\nSteps: walk the graph (reusing the C loader's validation); copy\nsource files and transitive `require` / `#include` dependencies;\ninvoke each spec's `compile` callback for boxes whose language needs\nit; copy the spec `.so` files used by the map; copy or symlink the\nrunner binary; write the manifest. Per-box artifacts mtime-compare\nso a re-compile recompiles only what changed. Any failure aborts\nthe step and leaves the partial output for inspection but does not\nwrite the manifest, so the deployment is recognizably broken until\na clean compile succeeds.\n\n## Data files\n\nPersistent data lives in `data/<name>.json` and is accessed via\n`libs/soramech-data.lua` (`data.get` / `data.set` / `data.load`).\nFormat:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"constant\": false,\n  \"fields\": {\n    \"history\": [],\n    \"config\": { \"constant\": true, \"value\": { \"model\": \"soramind-default\" } }\n  }\n}\n```\n\nTop-level `constant: true` makes the whole file read-only;\nfield-level `constant` flags individual fields within an otherwise\nmutable file. This is **separate** from the `data` box kind (which\nreads arbitrary files at the dispatch layer) — `soramech-data` is\nthe per-map structured-table store; `data` boxes are unstructured\nfile sources.\n\nEphemeral state (scratch tables, run logs, `last-run.jsonl`) goes to\n`tmp/`, a symlink to `/tmp/<map-name>/`. Survives the run but not a\nreboot — intentionally.\n"
    }
  },

}

In-process specs (Lua, C) deref directly or copy per their language's needs (`lua_pushlstring` copies into Lua's heap; C reads at the pointer).           "content":"---\nname: Cross-language wire format\ndescription: Wire is native within same-language regions; JSON only at cross-language borders. Compile-time per-language concatenation merges same-language source into one file per language.\ntype: project\n---\nThe cross-language data passing design, corrected 2026-05-21.\n\n**Wire is native within same-language regions; JSON appears only when a wire crosses a language boundary.** An earlier memory note (\"JSON always\") was wrong. Within a same-language region the value passes in whatever shape the language wants. The language spec acts as a getter/setter that bridges between SoraMech's wire and the language runtime's in-memory representation.\n\n**Two compile-time products work together:**\n\n1. **Per-edge runtime classification (issue 312).** The graph loader — the only single-threaded phase — walks every wire and records `input_edge_native[i]` per input port and `output_edge_native[j]` per outgoing connection on each box. True iff producer and consumer share a language across that edge. The dispatch layer consults these per box invocation: native bytes for native edges, JSON for crossings. The classification is also useful for memory-clearing (knowing when a box's outputs are exhausted) and potentially as a single source of truth for the dispatch's per-box function lookup.\n\n2. **Per-language source concatenation (issue 313).** At compile time, all the C source for the map gets merged into one `.c` file; all the Lua source into one `.lua` file; etc. Same-language hops become direct function calls inside the concatenated module — the slot store and dispatch layer don't run for those transitions at all. Only cross-language wires go through the slot machinery.\n\n**They are not redundant.** 312's per-edge bits classify the wires that *do* go through the slot store (i.e. the cross-language ones, plus any same-language wires that 313's merge couldn't eliminate — e.g. iterator boundaries inside a same-language region). 313 eliminates as many wires as possible; 312 makes the surviving wires take the right format.\n\n**Spec callbacks (current shape in `langs/lang-spec.h`):**\n- `init(worker_idx)` / `teardown(handle)` — once per worker.\n- `compile(src_path, out_path)` — optional, used by C. May grow a `box_t *` arg for typed wrappers (deferred contract change).\n- `invoke` — universal bytes-in/bytes-out fallback (still required for languages that don't specialize).\n- `invoke_native` — fast path for same-language hops. Bytes on the wire are this language's native serialization.\n- `invoke_json` — cross-language path. Bytes on the wire are JSON.\n- `native_to_json(handle, src, ..., dst, ...)` / `json_to_native(handle, src, ..., dst, ...)` — bridges used at language borders. Lua's are real; C and Bash are still stubs.\n\n**Richer JSON sentinels for cross-language payloads** (deferred to a later slice):\n- `$ref` — pointer + length + type tag for shared-heap bytes; in-process only, inline at cross-process boundary.\n- `$function_pointer` — address + signature for callables; in-process only, wire compile fails into a language that can't reconstruct.\n- `$lang_opaque` — \"these bytes are language-X-internal\"; destination either knows what to do or wire compile fails.\n\n**How to apply:** When discussing wire format, dispatch routing, or compile-time merging: native within a language region, JSON at borders, slot store only mediates the wires that 313's merge didn't collapse. The earlier \"JSON always\" framing was a misread.\n",
          "file_path":"/home/ritz/.claude/projects/-mnt-mtwo-programs-sora-soramech/memory/project_cross_language_wire.md"
        },

Only cross-language wires go through the slot machinery.\n\n**They are not redundant.** 312's per-edge bits classify the wires that *do* go through the slot store (i.e. the cross-language ones, plus any same-language wires that 313's merge couldn't eliminate — e.g. iterator boundaries inside a same-language region). 313 eliminates as many wires as possible; 312 makes the surviving wires take the right format.\n\n**Spec callbacks (current shape in `langs/lang-spec.h`):**\n- `init(worker_idx)` / `teardown(handle)` — once per worker.\n- `compile(src_path, out_path)` — optional, used by C. May grow a `box_t *` arg for typed wrappers (deferred contract change).\n- `invoke` — universal bytes-in/bytes-out fallback (still required for languages that don't specialize).\n- `invoke_native` — fast path for same-language hops. Bytes on the wire are this language's native serialization.\n- `invoke_json` — cross-language path. Bytes on the wire are JSON.\n- `native_to_json(handle, src, ..., dst, ...)` / `json_to_native(handle, src, ..., dst, ...)` — bridges used at language borders. Lua's are real; C and Bash are still stubs.\n\n**Richer JSON sentinels for cross-language payloads** (deferred to a later slice):\n- `$ref` — pointer + length + type tag for shared-heap bytes; in-process only, inline at cross-process boundary.\n- `$function_pointer` — address + signature for callables; in-process only, wire compile fails into a language that can't reconstruct.\n- `$lang_opaque` — \"these bytes are language-X-internal\"; destination either knows what to do or wire compile fails.\n\n**How to apply:** When discussing wire format, dispatch routing, or compile-time merging: native within a language region, JSON at borders, slot store only mediates the wires that 313's merge didn't collapse. The arrays `input_edge_native[]` and `output_edge_native[]` are populated correctly. What's left is the dispatch migration, which is where I'm hitting a design gap that wasn't obvious from outside the code.\n\nThe current dispatch passes bytes-in / bytes-out to `invoke` and that's all. To actually use the per-edge bits, the spec needs to know — *per input* — whether the bytes in `input_data[i]` are native (this spec's language) or JSON (from a cross-language producer). Same on the output side. But the `lang_spec_t` invoke signature is uniform — it doesn't carry per-input/per-output format flags.\n\nThree ways to thread the format through, picking one is a design choice:\n\n1. **Spec sees mixed-format inputs.** Extend the invoke signature with `const int *input_native_flags`, `int output_native_flag` (or similar). Dispatch reads bytes verbatim from each slot. Spec dispatches internally per input — parses JSON or native depending on the flag. Output is written in one format the spec chooses (native if any consumer is same-lang, else JSON), and dispatch fans out + converts at cross-lang consumers on push.\n\n2. **Dispatch normalizes inputs first.** For each cross-lang input, dispatch calls `json_to_native` which pushes onto the spec's runtime store (Lua stack, etc.). For native inputs, bytes pass through. Now invoke_native receives \"some inputs are bytes, some are runtime-resident\" — requires per-input flag too, plus the spec must read from two different places.\n\n3. **Slot stores JSON when there's any cross-lang consumer of that wire** (the per-box `output_format` rule the architecture doc currently describes — the per-box approximation). Simpler dispatch, but loses the per-edge benefit when same-lang and cross-lang consumers share a producer.\n\nOption 1 is the cleanest match to the per-edge model and doesn't compromise on the speedup. It does require a one-time change to `lang_spec_t` (adding the flag arrays/parameters to invoke), which means touching every spec — but right now C/Bash specs don't implement invoke_native at all, so they're unaffected, and Lua's invoke can grow the parameter trivially.\n\nWant me to go with Option 1, or did you have a different shape in mind?"

    "content":"So, the way I see it working is there's a spec function that's run on each input. There's two, one for json and one for native. The native one will receive values as arguments and then pass them along to the invoke function. The json will handle parsing the values from the json into native datastructures, and then passing it along to invoke. Invoke only ever sees native values, never json. The json is purely a translation layer.\n\nSo. A box writes it's outputs to an input. Let's say this crosses an input boundary. The wire these boxes pass along is always going to be a cross-language wire, while the input slot itself might receive inputs from both json and native - many wires from many boxes can go into the same input slot.\n\na box writes it's outputs to an input slot. The wire knows about the receiving slot, it knows if it needs to use the native or json style wire. In-fact, can we write an issue file to color the json wires green, and the native wires gray? a dark green, forest green.\n\na box writes it's outputs to an input slot. the wire-type corresponds to which function it runs - in the native case, \n\n-- stack overflow --\n\nhmmmm what if instead of using json we just asked each spec to explain how they're planning on writing their values into a C struct that can be passed across language boundaries by the thread pool runner?         "type":"text",
        "text":"Sure, I'll duck. Two questions to get you started:\n\n**What's in the struct's fields?** Specifically — is the struct's shape *per-box* (one field per input port, types pulled from the box JSON's input declarations), or is it *universal* (one shape carries any value, with tag bits or a discriminator per field)? Because that's the fork. Per-box gives you zero-copy and types-known-at-compile-time, but it means producer and consumer have to share a schema derived from the box JSON, and a wire fanning from one producer to two different-shaped consumers gets awkward. Universal lets any spec write any value into any wire, but you're paying for self-description — which is what JSON was already doing.\n\n**If the struct replaces JSON, where does JSON live?** Your original framing was \"JSON is the translation layer at language boundaries.\" But if there's now a universal C struct that every spec reads and writes, and same-language hops also go through it… JSON has no remaining job. Did you mean to displace JSON entirely, or is the struct an *additional* layer that sits between same-language specs (faster than JSON), with JSON still showing up for cross-language hops? Because those are different designs — and the architecture's already promising both green and gray wires, which assumes there's still a distinction.\n\n(For the wire-coloring issue — happy to draft it once the design settles, since the colors only mean something if there's still a native-vs-JSON distinction in the wire. If the struct subsumes both, every wire is the same color and the issue dissolves.)"
      }]
  },

        "type":"text",
        "text":"okay duck, eat this bread. *thinks out loud*\n\nThe multi-ring idea is real. Two paths it could go though.\n\n**Trap version:** read literally, \"spec the translation from one language to another\" means every spec knows how to translate Lua→C, Lua→Bash, C→Lua, C→Bash, etc. Add a new language and every existing spec needs new code. That's the pair-wise paths shape — and your own memory file already said no to that for exactly this reason. So if the multi-ring slot stores N different language-native byte streams, and the consumer reads (lang_tag, bytes) pairs and has to decode each one… the consumer's spec needs N-1 decoders. N² problem, sneaking back in through the cellar door.\n\n**Refined version:** the slot has only *two* rings. One native ring for \"bytes in the consumer's language\" and one JSON ring for \"bytes from anyone else.\" Plus the ordering ring of (which_ring, idx) tuples. Now same-lang producers write native to the native ring (zero translation), cross-lang producers translate-to-JSON on the way in and write to the JSON ring (one translation, exactly as today), and the consumer pops the ordering ring to know which ring to read from next. Two rings regardless of how many languages exist in the project. Each spec still just implements `to_json` / `from_json` plus its own native read/write. No pairwise matrix.\n\nThat refined version is actually strictly better than the per-port-classification thing I was about to code. The per-port version is pessimistic: if any one producer feeding a port is cross-lang, the *whole port* goes JSON, and the same-lang fan-in producers eat translation cost they didn't need to. The two-ring version keeps the same-lang producers native even when a cross-lang sibling is feeding the same port. Precision goes from per-port to per-cell.\n\nCost is a constant factor — one extra pointer indirection on pop, one extra `which_ring?` decision on push, two ring buffers' worth of memory per slot instead of one. Cheap.\n\nThe interesting question is when this actually matters. For a port with no cross-lang producers, both designs are identical (everything stays native). For a port with only cross-lang producers, both are identical (everything's JSON). The win is on **mixed fan-in** — a port that some same-language box and some cross-language box both feed. Probably uncommon in the grand scheme, but free correctness is free correctness.\n\nOne thing the multi-ring shape gives us that the per-port one doesn't: it lets 313's compile-time concatenation collapse the *same-lang ring entirely* for the regions it merges. If every producer to a port is in the merged Lua module, the native ring is unused (those wires became direct function calls). The slot then only carries cross-lang JSON values, if any. The two designs hand off cleanly between compile-time and runtime.\n\nSo I think the design is:\n- **Per-slot two-ring architecture**, ordering ring + (native-ring | json-ring) cells.\n- **Per-edge tag at push time** decides which ring receives — based on producer-lang vs slot-owner-lang, computed at graph load.\n- **Consumer reads via the ordering ring**, branches on tag, decodes accordingly.\n- **JSON stays the universal interop format** — the cross-lang ring is JSON, that role doesn't go away.\n- **The C-struct pivot dissolves.** You don't need it; binary-vs-text on the wire was a separate question (JSON encode cost), and msgpack-vs-JSON is a follow-on optimization, not a structural one.\n\nThat mean we're back to JSON-at-boundaries, native-otherwise, just with more precise fan-in semantics than what's in the code today. And the wire-coloring issue *does* survive — green for the JSON ring, forest-gray for the native ring, ordering ring stays invisible since it's plumbing.\n\nquack? 🦆"
      }]
  },
  "version":"2.1.121",
  "gitBranch":"master",

        "type":"text",
        "text":"Right — good catch, I had 313 wrong. The merge doesn't replace \"wire\" with \"function call\" — it replaces \"spec.invoke goes through dlsym + bytes-marshal + lua_pcall\" with \"the worker that picked up this box's task calls the merged function directly on its lua_State.\" The wire still exists in the slot, the dispatch still queues the task, the thread pool still picks which worker runs it. What 313 thins out is the per-invocation translation overhead, not the slot machinery.\n\nSo the native ring stays alive after 313 merges — the slot still buffers values waiting for sibling inputs, the thread pool still distributes invocations across workers. 313 makes the cells *cheaper to write and read*; the dual-ring shape is what controls how values flow between boxes in the first place. The two layers stack, they don't cancel.\n\n(Want me to draft the wire-coloring issue file now, or wait until the dual-ring design has more concrete edges?)"
      }]

    "content":[{
