        "input":{
          "content":"# 245 — Wire color by cross-language classification\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\n\nEvery wire on the canvas is drawn the same dim slate-blue (`#4a6080`)\nwhen its `from_branch` is null, or one of the comparator branch\ncolors (orange / blue / green) when it's a branch wire. Wire color\nencodes routing kind, not language pairing. Two wires leaving the\nsame producer — one to a Lua consumer, one to a C consumer — look\nidentical.\n\nThe runtime treats those wires very differently: the same-language\nhop carries native bytes, the cross-language hop carries JSON\n(issue 312). The editor gives the box author no visual signal that\nthe JSON translation step exists. It's invisible until someone\nreads the dispatch code.\n\n## Concept\n\nWires are colored by **language pairing across the edge**:\n\n- **Forest green** (`#228b22` or similar) — cross-language wire.\n  Producer and consumer are different languages; the runtime\n  translates via JSON at the wire. A reminder that this hop costs\n  encode + decode.\n- **Dark gray** (`#666` or similar; \"forest-gray\" is the verbal\n  cue) — same-language wire. Producer and consumer share a\n  language; native bytes pass without translation.\n- **Existing branch colors** (`lt` / `eq` / `gt` / iterator\n  branches) remain — they encode routing semantics, which is\n  orthogonal to language classification.\n\nWhen a wire is both branch-colored AND language-classified, the\ntwo signals compose. One workable composition: branch color drives\nthe wire's stroke, language classification drives a small marker\n(a colored dot at the midpoint, or a dashed-vs-solid line style).\nThe implementation picks the form; the rule is that both signals\nare visible on the same wire.\n\n## How the editor computes the classification\n\nFor each connection `{from_box, to_box, ...}`:\n\n1. Look up `from_box`'s box JSON; read its `lang` field.\n2. Look up `to_box`'s box JSON; read its `lang` field.\n3. If either box is a `read` / `write` / `data` kind (no `lang`\n   field), treat the wire as cross-language — those boxes deal in\n   language-agnostic bytes and any consumer's spec reads them\n   through its JSON bridge.\n4. Otherwise: same-language iff `from_box.lang === to_box.lang`.\n\nThe editor already has every box's JSON in memory (state populated\nby the HTTP backend). The classification is one comparison per\nconnection at draw time — no separate index needed.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `assets/js/006-wires.js` — wire rendering. Line 121–122 is the\n  current color-picking site. Add the language classification\n  there.\n- `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — box state, source of the `lang` field\n  for each box.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. Add a `wire_classification(from_box, to_box)` helper returning\n   `\"native\"` or `\"json\"`, in `assets/js/006-wires.js` or wherever\n   it composes with the rest of the draw loop.\n2. Update the color-picking branch in `006-wires.js` to use the\n   classification when `from_branch` is null. Pick the two\n   concrete hex values for forest-green and forest-gray.\n3. For branch wires (`from_branch` set), pick a composition: keep\n   the branch color as the stroke, add a midpoint dot in the\n   classification color. Or pick the dashed-vs-solid route. The\n   issue's only requirement is both signals visible.\n4. Add a legend somewhere unobtrusive — bottom-left corner of the\n   canvas, behind the existing zoom indicator — so the color\n   meaning isn't tribal knowledge.\n5. Verify on `maps/driver-test` (multi-language map) and on a\n   single-language map (everything one color).\n\n## Open questions\n\n- Exact hex values for forest-green and forest-gray. Pick something\n  that reads well against the dark canvas background and doesn't\n  collide with the branch palette.\n- Branch + classification composition: stroke vs. dot vs. dash.\n  Whichever is more legible.\n- Whether `read` / `write` / `data` boxes should also visually\n  carry a \"language-agnostic\" badge somewhere on the box itself,\n  so users can see at a glance which boxes will trigger JSON\n  translation when wired to typed call boxes. Out of scope for\n  this issue; a separate UX ticket if it comes up.\n\n## Relevant documents\n\n- `issues/312-same-language-wire-fast-path.md` — runtime\n  classification this mirrors visually\n- `docs/001-architecture.md` — wire format section\n",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/245-wire-color-by-cross-language-classification.md"
        },

Line 121–122 is the\n  current color-picking site. Add the language classification\n  there.\n- `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — box state, source of the `lang` field\n  for each box.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. Add a `wire_classification(from_box, to_box)` helper returning\n   `\"native\"` or `\"json\"`, in `assets/js/006-wires.js` or wherever\n   it composes with the rest of the draw loop.\n2. Update the color-picking branch in `006-wires.js` to use the\n   classification when `from_branch` is null. Pick the two\n   concrete hex values for forest-green and forest-gray.\n3. For branch wires (`from_branch` set), pick a composition: keep\n   the branch color as the stroke, add a midpoint dot in the\n   classification color. Or pick the dashed-vs-solid route. The\n   issue's only requirement is both signals visible.\n4. Add a legend somewhere unobtrusive — bottom-left corner of the\n   canvas, behind the existing zoom indicator — so the color\n   meaning isn't tribal knowledge.\n5. Verify on `maps/driver-test` (multi-language map) and on a\n   single-language map (everything one color).\n\n## Open questions\n\n- Exact hex values for forest-green and forest-gray. Pick something\n  that reads well against the dark canvas background and doesn't\n  collide with the branch palette.\n- Branch + classification composition: stroke vs. dot vs. dash.\n  Whichever is more legible.\n- Whether `read` / `write` / `data` boxes should also visually\n  carry a \"language-agnostic\" badge somewhere on the box itself,\n  so users can see at a glance which boxes will trigger JSON\n  translation when wired to typed call boxes.         "input":{
          "content":"# 312 — Same-language wire fast path: dual-ring slot, JSON at language borders\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\n\nToday every wire's bytes are whatever the producing spec wrote, and\nthe consuming spec reads them verbatim. The Lua spec emits JSON via\n`lua_native_to_json` (`langs/lua/spec.c:335`); the C and Bash specs\nhave no bridge implementations yet and only carry whatever bytes\ntheir bytes-in-bytes-out `invoke` produced.\n\nThe dispatch layer picks the spec callback (`invoke_native` /\n`invoke_json` / fallback `invoke`) based on a single per-box\n`use_native_invoke` bit computed at graph load — true only when\n**every** input edge and **every** output edge of the box stays\nwithin one language. That's the pessimistic per-box approximation:\na box whose output fans to one same-language consumer and one\ncross-language consumer is classified as cross-language for the\nwhole box, so the same-language neighbor eats the JSON cost too.\n\nThe wire-format design question — what shape the slot has when\nsame-language hops should stay native and JSON should only show up\nat language borders — has not been settled in code. This issue\nsettles it.\n\n## Intended behavior — dual-ring slot\n\n**Each input slot is two ring buffers plus an ordering ring.**\n\n```\nslot {\n    ring_native  : ring of cells holding consumer-lang's native bytes\n    ring_json    : ring of cells holding JSON bytes (cross-language values)\n    ring_order   : ring of (which_ring, idx) tuples in arrival order\n    ... existing peek / pop modes apply to ring_order ...\n}\n```\n\n**Producer push** (per outgoing connection):\n\n- If the connection's per-edge bit `output_edge_native[j]` is true,\n  the producer's spec writes its native bytes to the consumer\n  slot's `ring_native`.\n- Otherwise the spec converts to JSON via `native_to_json` and\n  writes to `ring_json`.\n- Either way, push a `(which_ring, idx)` tuple to `ring_order`.\n\n**Consumer pop**:\n\n- Pop `ring_order` to learn which ring the next value lives in.\n- Pop the cell at the indicated index in the indicated ring.\n- The consumer's spec receives a `(native | json, bytes)` pair per\n  input and picks the matching decoder.\n\nThis shape is precise on **mixed fan-in ports**: a port fed by one\nLua producer and one C producer keeps the Lua values native in\n`ring_native` and the C-translated-to-JSON values in `ring_json`.\nThe consumer pays JSON-decode cost only on cross-language cells,\nnot on the entire port. The per-port-classification alternative\n(slot is all-JSON if any fan-in is cross-lang) is the simpler\nfallback — strictly correct, but forces native producers to eat\nJSON on mixed-fan-in ports. Dual-ring keeps each cell at the\nright cost.\n\n### Per-language native bytes\n\nEach spec picks its own native byte format. The only contract is\ninternal symmetry: the spec's own native-write and native-read have\nto round-trip its own runtime values.\n\n- **Lua** — bytes the spec can deserialize back to a Lua value\n  quickly. Candidates: msgpack, `lua_dump` for closures, a custom\n  binary form. `cjson.encode` is a valid starting point (a JSON\n  string the Lua spec parses with `cjson.decode`); refine later if\n  profiling shows the encode/decode is hot.\n- **C** — `memcpy` of the typed struct. The C spec's generated\n  wrapper (issue 307) knows the layout, so the ring cell holds the\n  struct's bytes verbatim.\n- **Bash** — strings. Bash has no other native form; its native\n  ring stores string bytes directly.\n\n### Why JSON for the cross-language ring\n\nJSON's structure is self-describing — six kinds (object, array,\nnumber, string, bool, null), each with an obvious mapping into\nevery language's runtime. Adding a new language K means K's spec\nimplements one pair of bridges: `native_to_json` and\n`json_to_native`. No spec ever needs code that knows another\nlanguage's types. The N-language matrix collapses to N spec-pair\nimplementations, not N² pair-wise paths.\n\nThe harder cases — closures, opaque language values, function\npointers — don't fit JSON's structure. JSON carries them via\nsentinel primitives:\n\n- `$ref` — pointer + length + type tag for bytes in the large-value\n  heap. In-process specs deref directly; cross-process boundaries\n  inline the bytes at the UDS marshaller.\n- `$function_pointer` — in-process address + signature for\n  callables. Wire compile fails if the consumer's language can't\n  reconstruct.\n- `$lang_opaque` — \"these bytes are language-X-internal.\" The\n  destination spec either knows what to do or wire compile fails.\n\nFirst-cut behavior: `encode_value` in the Lua spec hard-errors on\nfunction / userdata / thread (`langs/lua/spec.c:317`). Sentinels\nland in a later slice.\n\n## Per-edge classification at graph load\n\nThe graph loader's single-threaded phase walks every connection\nand computes per-box arrays:\n\n- `input_edge_native[i]` — one bit per input port. True iff every\n  producer feeding that port shares the consumer's language.\n- `output_edge_native[j]` — one bit per outgoing connection. True\n  iff the consumer on the other end shares this box's language.\n\nBoth arrays are already declared and populated — see\n`src/010-graph-loader.h:145` and `src/010-graph-loader.c:689-754`.\n\nUnder dual-ring, only `output_edge_native[j]` is consulted on the\npush path (it picks the ring at write time). The consumer-side bit\n`input_edge_native[i]` is now informational — the actual per-cell\nring tag lives in `ring_order` and is precise per cell.\n\nThe per-box `use_native_invoke` summary is **removed**. The\ndispatch reads `ring_order` per pop and consults the cell's tag\ndirectly.\n\n### Why per-edge, not per-box\n\nThe earlier per-box approximation collapsed on the first\ncross-language edge it found — a Lua box with one C neighbor went\nJSON across all its other edges. Per-edge keeps the cost local to\nthe actual cross-language boundary. The interior of any\nsame-language island skips JSON; only the boundary edges pay. The\nimplementation cost is identical: same number of bits per box,\nstored per-port / per-connection instead of per-box.\n\nDual-ring takes precision one step further: even on a single port\nwith mixed fan-in, each individual cell is in the right ring. The\nboundary tightens from \"edges that cross languages\" to \"cells\nthat crossed languages.\"\n\n## Runtime dispatch\n\n### Input-read\n\nFor each input port:\n```c\n(which_ring, idx) = ring_order_pop(slot->ring_order)\ncell_bytes        = ring_at(which_ring == NATIVE ? slot->ring_native\n                                                  : slot->ring_json,\n                            idx)\ninput_data[i]   = cell_bytes\ninput_native[i] = (which_ring == NATIVE)\n```\n\n`input_native[i]` is a per-input flag the spec consults to know\nwhether `input_data[i]` is its native form or JSON.\n\n### Spec invoke\n\nThe spec's `invoke` signature gains per-input and per-output flags:\n\n```c\nint invoke(handle, file_path, fn_name,\n           const void **input_data, const int *input_sizes,\n           const int *input_native, int n_inputs,\n           int output_native,\n           void *out_buf, int out_buf_capacity, int *out_size);\n```\n\nThe spec dispatches per input: if `input_native[i]`, decode as\nnative; else decode as JSON. The output is written in whatever\nform `output_native` indicates — one form, one write. The previously\nseparate `invoke_native` and `invoke_json` callbacks collapse into\nthis single dispatching `invoke`; the per-input dispatch is what\nthe design actually needs.\n\nFor boxes whose output fans to multiple consumers in different\nlanguages, the dispatch picks one form for `output_native` based\non whichever ring is dominant (typically native if any\nsame-language consumer exists; the cross-language consumers eat a\n`native_to_json` conversion at push time). The detail is a runtime\noptimization, not a correctness concern.\n\n### Output-push\n\n```c\nfor each outgoing connection j:\n    if output_edge_native[j]:\n        push native_bytes      to consumer->ring_native\n        push (NATIVE, idx)     to consumer->ring_order\n    else:\n        if output_was_native: json_bytes = spec->native_to_json(native_bytes)\n        push json_bytes        to consumer->ring_json\n        push (JSON, idx)       to consumer->ring_order\n```\n\nIf the spec produced native and multiple cross-language consumers\nexist, the dispatch calls `native_to_json` once and reuses the\nJSON bytes across every cross-language push (optimization, not\nrequired for correctness).\n\n## Edge cases\n\n- **All-same-language graph**: every connection's\n  `output_edge_native[j]` is true; `ring_json` stays unallocated\n  across every slot; activity is on `ring_native` and `ring_order`\n  only.\n- **All-different-language graph**: every connection routes to\n  `ring_json`; `ring_native` stays unallocated.\n- **Mixed fan-in**: both rings active on the same slot. Consumer\n  sees a mix of native and JSON cells, picked apart by\n  `ring_order`.\n- **Type changes mid-development**: a wire that was Lua→Lua\n  becomes Lua→C when the user changes a downstream box's language.\n  The graph loader recomputes the per-edge bits on the next load;\n  no data conversion at runtime, no migration.\n\n## Implementation cost\n\n- **Slot store**: two rings per slot instead of one, plus the\n  ordering ring. Allocate `ring_json` and `ring_order` lazily —\n  same-language-only slots pay nothing for them. Per-cell cost:\n  one extra ordering-ring write on push, one extra read on pop.\n- **Spec interface**: one signature change to the `invoke`\n  callback adding `input_native[]` and `output_native`. Every\n  spec's `invoke` gains a per-input branch. Lua's branch is\n  almost free — both decoders (`json_to_native` and the future\n  native one) already exist as bridges. C and Bash need their\n  JSON bridges written, which is shared with the broader\n  cross-language work in 307/308.\n- **Dispatch**: one extra step on read (consult ordering ring),\n  one extra branch on push (which ring to write).\n\nThe win is exactness: same-language values stay native even when\ntheir port has a cross-language sibling producer.\n\n## Future: whole-program same-language compilation (issue 313)\n\n313 describes merging all same-language source into one\ntranslation unit per language at compile time. The merge does\n**not** eliminate the slot store for same-language wires — boxes\nstill run as separate tasks in the thread pool, possibly on\ndifferent workers, so values still need a place to wait for\nsibling inputs to arrive. The thread pool's parallelism depends\non tasks being scheduled independently; collapsing same-language\nhops to direct function calls would serialize execution and defeat\nthe pool.\n\nWhat 313 thins is the **spec invocation overhead**: for boxes in\nthe merged region, the dispatch can call the function directly on\nthe worker's `lua_State` (or compiled C code) without going\nthrough dlsym + bytes-marshal + bridge. The dual-ring slot shape\nremains; 313 makes the native-ring's read/write cheaper. The two\nlayers stack, they don't cancel.\n\n## Resolved design choice: JSON, not type-annotated raw bytes\n\nAn earlier note asked whether cross-language wires should use\ntype-annotated raw byte encodings (length-prefixed ints, raw\nfloats, etc.) instead of JSON. **Decided: JSON across the board\nfor the cross-language ring.** Rationale:\n\n- JSON's self-describing structure makes a new language one\n  spec-pair of `native_to_json` / `json_to_native` — no per-pair\n  language paths.\n- The native ring's format is each spec's private choice, so the\n  per-language performance flexibility is there without universal\n  type-tag complexity.\n- Sentinel primitives in JSON (`$ref`, `$function_pointer`,\n  `$lang_opaque`) carry the structurally awkward cases without\n  forcing the wire format to grow new top-level shapes.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. **Extend the slot data structure**. Add `ring_native`,\n   `ring_json`, `ring_order` to the slot type in\n   `src/009-slot-store.{c,h}`. Allocate `ring_json` and\n   `ring_order` lazily.\n2. **Extend the spec `invoke` signature**. Update `lang_invoke_fn`\n   in `langs/lang-spec.h` to add `const int *input_native`,\n   `int output_native`. Touch every spec's `invoke` stub to accept\n   (and initially ignore) the new parameters.\n3. **Update dispatch input-read** (`src/012-dispatch.c`). Pop\n   `ring_order` first, then the named ring. Populate\n   `input_native[]` per input port.\n4. **Update dispatch output-push** (`src/012-dispatch.c`). Select\n   the consumer's ring based on `output_edge_native[j]`. Write\n   the ordering-ring tuple. Reuse JSON across cross-language\n   consumers when the producer fanned to multiple.\n5. **Lua spec** (`langs/lua/spec.c`). Branch per `input_native[i]`\n   — decode native or JSON accordingly. Pick the native byte\n   format (start with `cjson.encode`; refine later).\n6. **C and Bash spec bridges**. Implement `native_to_json` and\n   `json_to_native` for C and Bash so cross-language pushes work.\n   C's native form is `memcpy` of the wrapper's declared struct;\n   Bash's native form is plain strings.\n7. **Remove `use_native_invoke`**. Drop the per-box field from\n   `box_t` and its computation from `graph_load`. The dispatch\n   consults the ordering ring's per-cell tag, not a per-box\n   summary.\n8. **Tests**. A 100k-iteration Lua→Lua pipeline uses `ring_native`\n   exclusively. A mixed-lang pipeline exercises both rings. A\n   mixed-fan-in port shows both rings active on one slot.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `src/009-slot-store.{c,h}` — slot data structure; the\n  dual-ring extension lands here.\n- `src/010-graph-loader.{c,h}` — per-edge classification (already\n  done at `010-graph-loader.c:689-754`).\n- `src/012-dispatch.{c,h}` — input-read, output-push.\n- `langs/lang-spec.h` — `invoke` signature extension.\n- `langs/lua/spec.c`, `langs/c/spec.c`, `langs/bash/spec.c` — per-spec\n  implementations.\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — original single-ring\n  slot design (completed); the dual-ring extension is the structural\n  amendment captured here.\n- `issues/306-lua-language-spec.md`, `307-c-language-spec.md`,\n  `308-bash-language-spec.md` — per-spec typed marshalling lands on\n  top of this issue.\n- `issues/313-research-whole-program-same-language-merge.md` —\n  follow-on that thins spec invocation for merged regions.\n- `issues/245-wire-color-by-cross-language-classification.md` —\n  editor-side visual reflection of the per-edge classification\n  (green for JSON, gray for native).\n\n## Implementation status\n\nWhat's in place:\n\n- `lang_spec_t` carries `invoke_native`, `invoke_json`,\n  `native_to_json`, `json_to_native` slots (current shape — to be\n  collapsed to a single `invoke` with per-input/per-output flags\n  per this issue).\n- Lua's `native_to_json` and `json_to_native` are real\n  (`langs/lua/spec.c:335` and `:437`).\n- `input_edge_native[]` and `output_edge_native[]` are computed at\n  graph load (`src/010-graph-loader.c:689-754`).\n- Per-box `use_native_invoke` summary is computed and consulted by\n  dispatch — to be removed.\n- Single-ring slot store (`src/009-slot-store.c`).\n\nWhat's still ahead:\n\n- Dual-ring slot shape (this issue's core).\n- Spec `invoke` signature extension (`input_native[]`,\n  `output_native`).\n- Dispatch reads from the ordering ring; push selects ring based\n  on `output_edge_native[j]`.\n- C and Bash bridges, plus native byte formats per language.\n- Removal of `use_native_invoke`.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Lua's native byte format**: start with `cjson.encode` (still a\n  win over the json-ring path because the consumer's spec\n  recognises its own format and skips a parse), or jump straight\n  to msgpack? Defer the decision; the dual-ring shape doesn't\n  depend on the choice.\n- **Sharing JSON across multiple cross-language consumers**: the\n  dispatch can call `native_to_json` once and push the same bytes\n  to N cross-language consumer slots. Worthwhile when N > 1; the\n  push path needs a small buffer to hold the JSON across the fan\n  loop. Implement after the basic path works.\n- **Bash native = JSON?**: Bash has no native form distinct from\n  strings, and JSON is already a string. Bash's native ring may\n  hold JSON-shaped strings (effectively aliasing the JSON ring's\n  content). Resolve by inspection once the bash spec writeup\n  starts.\n",

    "content":"# 312 — Same-language wire fast path: dual-ring slot, JSON at language borders\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\n\nToday every wire's bytes are whatever the producing spec wrote, and\nthe consuming spec reads them verbatim. The Lua spec emits JSON via\n`lua_native_to_json` (`langs/lua/spec.c:335`); the C and Bash specs\nhave no bridge implementations yet and only carry whatever bytes\ntheir bytes-in-bytes-out `invoke` produced.\n\nThe dispatch layer picks the spec callback (`invoke_native` /\n`invoke_json` / fallback `invoke`) based on a single per-box\n`use_native_invoke` bit computed at graph load — true only when\n**every** input edge and **every** output edge of the box stays\nwithin one language. That's the pessimistic per-box approximation:\na box whose output fans to one same-language consumer and one\ncross-language consumer is classified as cross-language for the\nwhole box, so the same-language neighbor eats the JSON cost too.\n\nThe wire-format design question — what shape the slot has when\nsame-language hops should stay native and JSON should only show up\nat language borders — has not been settled in code. This issue\nsettles it.\n\n## Intended behavior — dual-ring slot\n\n**Each input slot is two ring buffers plus an ordering ring.**\n\n```\nslot {\n    ring_native  : ring of cells holding consumer-lang's native bytes\n    ring_json    : ring of cells holding JSON bytes (cross-language values)\n    ring_order   : ring of (which_ring, idx) tuples in arrival order\n    ... existing peek / pop modes apply to ring_order ...\n}\n```\n\n**Producer push** (per outgoing connection):\n\n- If the connection's per-edge bit `output_edge_native[j]` is true,\n  the producer's spec writes its native bytes to the consumer\n  slot's `ring_native`.\n- Otherwise the spec converts to JSON via `native_to_json` and\n  writes to `ring_json`.\n- Either way, push a `(which_ring, idx)` tuple to `ring_order`.\n\n**Consumer pop**:\n\n- Pop `ring_order` to learn which ring the next value lives in.\n- Pop the cell at the indicated index in the indicated ring.\n- The consumer's spec receives a `(native | json, bytes)` pair per\n  input and picks the matching decoder.\n\nThis shape is precise on **mixed fan-in ports**: a port fed by one\nLua producer and one C producer keeps the Lua values native in\n`ring_native` and the C-translated-to-JSON values in `ring_json`.\nThe consumer pays JSON-decode cost only on cross-language cells,\nnot on the entire port. The per-port-classification alternative\n(slot is all-JSON if any fan-in is cross-lang) is the simpler\nfallback — strictly correct, but forces native producers to eat\nJSON on mixed-fan-in ports. Dual-ring keeps each cell at the\nright cost.\n\n### Per-language native bytes\n\nEach spec picks its own native byte format. The only contract is\ninternal symmetry: the spec's own native-write and native-read have\nto round-trip its own runtime values.\n\n- **Lua** — bytes the spec can deserialize back to a Lua value\n  quickly. Candidates: msgpack, `lua_dump` for closures, a custom\n  binary form. `cjson.encode` is a valid starting point (a JSON\n  string the Lua spec parses with `cjson.decode`); refine later if\n  profiling shows the encode/decode is hot.\n- **C** — `memcpy` of the typed struct. The C spec's generated\n  wrapper (issue 307) knows the layout, so the ring cell holds the\n  struct's bytes verbatim.\n- **Bash** — strings. Bash has no other native form; its native\n  ring stores string bytes directly.\n\n### Why JSON for the cross-language ring\n\nJSON's structure is self-describing — six kinds (object, array,\nnumber, string, bool, null), each with an obvious mapping into\nevery language's runtime. Adding a new language K means K's spec\nimplements one pair of bridges: `native_to_json` and\n`json_to_native`. No spec ever needs code that knows another\nlanguage's types. The N-language matrix collapses to N spec-pair\nimplementations, not N² pair-wise paths.\n\nThe harder cases — closures, opaque language values, function\npointers — don't fit JSON's structure. JSON carries them via\nsentinel primitives:\n\n- `$ref` — pointer + length + type tag for bytes in the large-value\n  heap. In-process specs deref directly; cross-process boundaries\n  inline the bytes at the UDS marshaller.\n- `$function_pointer` — in-process address + signature for\n  callables. Wire compile fails if the consumer's language can't\n  reconstruct.\n- `$lang_opaque` — \"these bytes are language-X-internal.\" The\n  destination spec either knows what to do or wire compile fails.\n\nFirst-cut behavior: `encode_value` in the Lua spec hard-errors on\nfunction / userdata / thread (`langs/lua/spec.c:317`). Sentinels\nland in a later slice.\n\n## Per-edge classification at graph load\n\nThe graph loader's single-threaded phase walks every connection\nand computes per-box arrays:\n\n- `input_edge_native[i]` — one bit per input port. True iff every\n  producer feeding that port shares the consumer's language.\n- `output_edge_native[j]` — one bit per outgoing connection. True\n  iff the consumer on the other end shares this box's language.\n\nBoth arrays are already declared and populated — see\n`src/010-graph-loader.h:145` and `src/010-graph-loader.c:689-754`.\n\nUnder dual-ring, only `output_edge_native[j]` is consulted on the\npush path (it picks the ring at write time). The consumer-side bit\n`input_edge_native[i]` is now informational — the actual per-cell\nring tag lives in `ring_order` and is precise per cell.\n\nThe per-box `use_native_invoke` summary is **removed**. The\ndispatch reads `ring_order` per pop and consults the cell's tag\ndirectly.\n\n### Why per-edge, not per-box\n\nThe earlier per-box approximation collapsed on the first\ncross-language edge it found — a Lua box with one C neighbor went\nJSON across all its other edges. Per-edge keeps the cost local to\nthe actual cross-language boundary. The interior of any\nsame-language island skips JSON; only the boundary edges pay. The\nimplementation cost is identical: same number of bits per box,\nstored per-port / per-connection instead of per-box.\n\nDual-ring takes precision one step further: even on a single port\nwith mixed fan-in, each individual cell is in the right ring. The\nboundary tightens from \"edges that cross languages\" to \"cells\nthat crossed languages.\"\n\n## Runtime dispatch\n\n### Input-read\n\nFor each input port:\n```c\n(which_ring, idx) = ring_order_pop(slot->ring_order)\ncell_bytes        = ring_at(which_ring == NATIVE ? slot->ring_native\n                                                  : slot->ring_json,\n                            idx)\ninput_data[i]   = cell_bytes\ninput_native[i] = (which_ring == NATIVE)\n```\n\n`input_native[i]` is a per-input flag the spec consults to know\nwhether `input_data[i]` is its native form or JSON.\n\n### Spec invoke\n\nThe spec's `invoke` signature gains per-input and per-output flags:\n\n```c\nint invoke(handle, file_path, fn_name,\n           const void **input_data, const int *input_sizes,\n           const int *input_native, int n_inputs,\n           int output_native,\n           void *out_buf, int out_buf_capacity, int *out_size);\n```\n\nThe spec dispatches per input: if `input_native[i]`, decode as\nnative; else decode as JSON. The output is written in whatever\nform `output_native` indicates — one form, one write. The previously\nseparate `invoke_native` and `invoke_json` callbacks collapse into\nthis single dispatching `invoke`; the per-input dispatch is what\nthe design actually needs.\n\nFor boxes whose output fans to multiple consumers in different\nlanguages, the dispatch picks one form for `output_native` based\non whichever ring is dominant (typically native if any\nsame-language consumer exists; the cross-language consumers eat a\n`native_to_json` conversion at push time). The detail is a runtime\noptimization, not a correctness concern.\n\n### Output-push\n\n```c\nfor each outgoing connection j:\n    if output_edge_native[j]:\n        push native_bytes      to consumer->ring_native\n        push (NATIVE, idx)     to consumer->ring_order\n    else:\n        if output_was_native: json_bytes = spec->native_to_json(native_bytes)\n        push json_bytes        to consumer->ring_json\n        push (JSON, idx)       to consumer->ring_order\n```\n\nIf the spec produced native and multiple cross-language consumers\nexist, the dispatch calls `native_to_json` once and reuses the\nJSON bytes across every cross-language push (optimization, not\nrequired for correctness).\n\n## Edge cases\n\n- **All-same-language graph**: every connection's\n  `output_edge_native[j]` is true; `ring_json` stays unallocated\n  across every slot; activity is on `ring_native` and `ring_order`\n  only.\n- **All-different-language graph**: every connection routes to\n  `ring_json`; `ring_native` stays unallocated.\n- **Mixed fan-in**: both rings active on the same slot. Consumer\n  sees a mix of native and JSON cells, picked apart by\n  `ring_order`.\n- **Type changes mid-development**: a wire that was Lua→Lua\n  becomes Lua→C when the user changes a downstream box's language.\n  The graph loader recomputes the per-edge bits on the next load;\n  no data conversion at runtime, no migration.\n\n## Implementation cost\n\n- **Slot store**: two rings per slot instead of one, plus the\n  ordering ring. Allocate `ring_json` and `ring_order` lazily —\n  same-language-only slots pay nothing for them. Per-cell cost:\n  one extra ordering-ring write on push, one extra read on pop.\n- **Spec interface**: one signature change to the `invoke`\n  callback adding `input_native[]` and `output_native`. Every\n  spec's `invoke` gains a per-input branch. Lua's branch is\n  almost free — both decoders (`json_to_native` and the future\n  native one) already exist as bridges. C and Bash need their\n  JSON bridges written, which is shared with the broader\n  cross-language work in 307/308.\n- **Dispatch**: one extra step on read (consult ordering ring),\n  one extra branch on push (which ring to write).\n\nThe win is exactness: same-language values stay native even when\ntheir port has a cross-language sibling producer.\n\n## Future: whole-program same-language compilation (issue 313)\n\n313 describes merging all same-language source into one\ntranslation unit per language at compile time. The merge does\n**not** eliminate the slot store for same-language wires — boxes\nstill run as separate tasks in the thread pool, possibly on\ndifferent workers, so values still need a place to wait for\nsibling inputs to arrive. The thread pool's parallelism depends\non tasks being scheduled independently; collapsing same-language\nhops to direct function calls would serialize execution and defeat\nthe pool.\n\nWhat 313 thins is the **spec invocation overhead**: for boxes in\nthe merged region, the dispatch can call the function directly on\nthe worker's `lua_State` (or compiled C code) without going\nthrough dlsym + bytes-marshal + bridge. The dual-ring slot shape\nremains; 313 makes the native-ring's read/write cheaper. The two\nlayers stack, they don't cancel.\n\n## Resolved design choice: JSON, not type-annotated raw bytes\n\nAn earlier note asked whether cross-language wires should use\ntype-annotated raw byte encodings (length-prefixed ints, raw\nfloats, etc.) instead of JSON. **Decided: JSON across the board\nfor the cross-language ring.** Rationale:\n\n- JSON's self-describing structure makes a new language one\n  spec-pair of `native_to_json` / `json_to_native` — no per-pair\n  language paths.\n- The native ring's format is each spec's private choice, so the\n  per-language performance flexibility is there without universal\n  type-tag complexity.\n- Sentinel primitives in JSON (`$ref`, `$function_pointer`,\n  `$lang_opaque`) carry the structurally awkward cases without\n  forcing the wire format to grow new top-level shapes.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. **Extend the slot data structure**. Add `ring_native`,\n   `ring_json`, `ring_order` to the slot type in\n   `src/009-slot-store.{c,h}`. Allocate `ring_json` and\n   `ring_order` lazily.\n2. **Extend the spec `invoke` signature**. Update `lang_invoke_fn`\n   in `langs/lang-spec.h` to add `const int *input_native`,\n   `int output_native`. Touch every spec's `invoke` stub to accept\n   (and initially ignore) the new parameters.\n3. **Update dispatch input-read** (`src/012-dispatch.c`). Pop\n   `ring_order` first, then the named ring. Populate\n   `input_native[]` per input port.\n4. **Update dispatch output-push** (`src/012-dispatch.c`). Select\n   the consumer's ring based on `output_edge_native[j]`. Write\n   the ordering-ring tuple. Reuse JSON across cross-language\n   consumers when the producer fanned to multiple.\n5. **Lua spec** (`langs/lua/spec.c`). Branch per `input_native[i]`\n   — decode native or JSON accordingly. Pick the native byte\n   format (start with `cjson.encode`; refine later).\n6. **C and Bash spec bridges**. Implement `native_to_json` and\n   `json_to_native` for C and Bash so cross-language pushes work.\n   C's native form is `memcpy` of the wrapper's declared struct;\n   Bash's native form is plain strings.\n7. **Remove `use_native_invoke`**. Drop the per-box field from\n   `box_t` and its computation from `graph_load`. The dispatch\n   consults the ordering ring's per-cell tag, not a per-box\n   summary.\n8. **Tests**. A 100k-iteration Lua→Lua pipeline uses `ring_native`\n   exclusively. A mixed-lang pipeline exercises both rings. A\n   mixed-fan-in port shows both rings active on one slot.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `src/009-slot-store.{c,h}` — slot data structure; the\n  dual-ring extension lands here.\n- `src/010-graph-loader.{c,h}` — per-edge classification (already\n  done at `010-graph-loader.c:689-754`).\n- `src/012-dispatch.{c,h}` — input-read, output-push.\n- `langs/lang-spec.h` — `invoke` signature extension.\n- `langs/lua/spec.c`, `langs/c/spec.c`, `langs/bash/spec.c` — per-spec\n  implementations.\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — original single-ring\n  slot design (completed); the dual-ring extension is the structural\n  amendment captured here.\n- `issues/306-lua-language-spec.md`, `307-c-language-spec.md`,\n  `308-bash-language-spec.md` — per-spec typed marshalling lands on\n  top of this issue.\n- `issues/313-research-whole-program-same-language-merge.md` —\n  follow-on that thins spec invocation for merged regions.\n- `issues/245-wire-color-by-cross-language-classification.md` —\n  editor-side visual reflection of the per-edge classification\n  (green for JSON, gray for native).\n\n## Implementation status\n\nWhat's in place:\n\n- `lang_spec_t` carries `invoke_native`, `invoke_json`,\n  `native_to_json`, `json_to_native` slots (current shape — to be\n  collapsed to a single `invoke` with per-input/per-output flags\n  per this issue).\n- Lua's `native_to_json` and `json_to_native` are real\n  (`langs/lua/spec.c:335` and `:437`).\n- `input_edge_native[]` and `output_edge_native[]` are computed at\n  graph load (`src/010-graph-loader.c:689-754`).\n- Per-box `use_native_invoke` summary is computed and consulted by\n  dispatch — to be removed.\n- Single-ring slot store (`src/009-slot-store.c`).\n\nWhat's still ahead:\n\n- Dual-ring slot shape (this issue's core).\n- Spec `invoke` signature extension (`input_native[]`,\n  `output_native`).\n- Dispatch reads from the ordering ring; push selects ring based\n  on `output_edge_native[j]`.\n- C and Bash bridges, plus native byte formats per language.\n- Removal of `use_native_invoke`.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Lua's native byte format**: start with `cjson.encode` (still a\n  win over the json-ring path because the consumer's spec\n  recognises its own format and skips a parse), or jump straight\n  to msgpack? Defer the decision; the dual-ring shape doesn't\n  depend on the choice.\n- **Sharing JSON across multiple cross-language consumers**: the\n  dispatch can call `native_to_json` once and push the same bytes\n  to N cross-language consumer slots. Worthwhile when N > 1; the\n  push path needs a small buffer to hold the JSON across the fan\n  loop. Implement after the basic path works.\n- **Bash native = JSON?**: Bash has no native form distinct from\n  strings, and JSON is already a string. Bash's native ring may\n  hold JSON-shaped strings (effectively aliasing the JSON ring's\n  content). Resolve by inspection once the bash spec writeup\n  starts.\n",

    "originalFile":"---\nname: Cross-language wire format\ndescription: Wire is native within same-language regions; JSON only at cross-language borders. Compile-time per-language concatenation merges same-language source into one file per language.\ntype: project\noriginSessionId: 5670858b-274f-49c4-89b8-a4b83ce33d7c\n---\nThe cross-language data passing design, corrected 2026-05-21.\n\n**Wire is native within same-language regions; JSON appears only when a wire crosses a language boundary.** An earlier memory note (\"JSON always\") was wrong. Within a same-language region the value passes in whatever shape the language wants. The language spec acts as a getter/setter that bridges between SoraMech's wire and the language runtime's in-memory representation.\n\n**Two compile-time products work together:**\n\n1. **Per-edge runtime classification (issue 312).** The graph loader — the only single-threaded phase — walks every wire and records `input_edge_native[i]` per input port and `output_edge_native[j]` per outgoing connection on each box. True iff producer and consumer share a language across that edge. The dispatch layer consults these per box invocation: native bytes for native edges, JSON for crossings. The classification is also useful for memory-clearing (knowing when a box's outputs are exhausted) and potentially as a single source of truth for the dispatch's per-box function lookup.\n\n2. **Per-language source concatenation (issue 313).** At compile time, all the C source for the map gets merged into one `.c` file; all the Lua source into one `.lua` file; etc. Same-language hops become direct function calls inside the concatenated module — the slot store and dispatch layer don't run for those transitions at all. Only cross-language wires go through the slot machinery.\n\n**They are not redundant.** 312's per-edge bits classify the wires that *do* go through the slot store (i.e. the cross-language ones, plus any same-language wires that 313's merge couldn't eliminate — e.g. iterator boundaries inside a same-language region). 313 eliminates as many wires as possible; 312 makes the surviving wires take the right format.\n\n**Spec callbacks (current shape in `langs/lang-spec.h`):**\n- `init(worker_idx)` / `teardown(handle)` — once per worker.\n- `compile(src_path, out_path)` — optional, used by C. May grow a `box_t *` arg for typed wrappers (deferred contract change).\n- `invoke` — universal bytes-in/bytes-out fallback (still required for languages that don't specialize).\n- `invoke_native` — fast path for same-language hops. Bytes on the wire are this language's native serialization.\n- `invoke_json` — cross-language path. Bytes on the wire are JSON.\n- `native_to_json(handle, src, ..., dst, ...)` / `json_to_native(handle, src, ..., dst, ...)` — bridges used at language borders.           "new_string":"### Same-language wire fast path — dual-ring slot\n\nEach input slot is a **dual-ring buffer plus an ordering ring**. One\nring holds bytes in the consumer's native language form; one ring\nholds JSON bytes from cross-language producers; the ordering ring\nrecords `(which_ring, idx)` tuples so consumers pop in arrival order.\n\nAt graph load (the single-threaded phase), per-edge classification\nfills two arrays on each box:\n\n- `input_edge_native[i]` — one bit per input port. True iff every\n  producer feeding that port shares the consumer's language.\n- `output_edge_native[j]` — one bit per outgoing connection. Passes the\n  bytes and a per-input `native | json` flag to the spec's invoke.\n- **Invoke**: the spec dispatches per input — decode native or\n  decode JSON — and writes its output in whichever form the\n  dispatch tells it (`output_native` per box).\n\nThe dual-ring shape is precise per cell. The pessimistic per-port\nalternative (slot is all-JSON if any fan-in is cross-lang) is\nstrictly correct but forces same-language producers to translate\non mixed-fan-in ports; dual-ring keeps each cell at the right cost.\n\nPer-language native forms (each spec's private choice; only the\nspec's own write/read need to be symmetric):\n- **Lua** — candidates include `cjson.encode`, msgpack, `lua_dump`\n  for closures, raw bytes for primitives.\n- **C** — `memcpy` of the typed struct (the C spec's `compile`\n  callback knows the layout).\n- **Bash** — strings; native ring stores string bytes directly.\n\nJSON's role: the universal cross-language ring format.     "content":[{
        "type":"text",
        "text":"Done with the issue file edits. To your concern about agnostic JSON parsing:\n\n**The \"agnostic\" part is JSON itself.** Six kinds — object, array, number, string, bool, null. Every language has an obvious mapping (Lua: object → table with string keys, array → table with `n` field for fidelity, number → Lua number, etc.). The Lua spec's `decode_node` at `langs/lua/spec.c:370` already does this in 60-ish lines. No type annotations on the wire are required because JSON's structure is self-describing — the parser sees `{` and knows it's an object; sees `42` and knows it's a number.\n\n**Type annotations live in box JSON, not on the wire.** The consumer box's `inputs` array declares `{\"name\": \"weight\", \"type\": \"int\"}`. The spec uses that declaration to coerce or validate after parsing — if the JSON tree at that input slot is a string `\"42\"` but the box declared `int`, the spec parses-as-int or errors. The spec never has to ask \"what type is this JSON value\" — JSON tells it directly — and never has to know about *other* languages' types, just JSON and its own.\n\n**Lua not having static annotations is fine.** Lua values are runtime-typed: every value carries its type tag (`LUA_TNUMBER`, `LUA_TSTRING`, etc.). The Lua spec inspects the value's type via `lua_type()` and writes the matching JSON kind. Symmetric on the way in. The spec's encoder at `langs/lua/spec.c:188` is the existing implementation.\n\n**The genuinely hard cases — closures, file handles, opaque values — don't fit JSON's structure period.** Those get sentinel primitives (`$function_pointer`, `$lang_opaque`) inside the JSON, and any cross-language consumer that can't reconstruct fails at wire compile. There's no honest way to pass a Lua closure to a Bash box, so the wire is wrong, not the format.\n\nSo adding a new language K is genuinely just: K's spec implements `native_to_json` (walk K's values, emit JSON) and `json_to_native` (walk JSON, build K's values). N spec-pairs, never N². That's the whole reason JSON gets to be the universal ring format.\n\n---\n\nRecap of what I touched:\n\n- **`issues/245-wire-color-by-cross-language-classification.md`** (new) — editor work, forest-green for cross-lang wires, gray for native, computed in `assets/js/006-wires.js`.\n- **`issues/312-same-language-wire-fast-path.md`** — rewrote to capture the dual-ring design (native ring + JSON ring + ordering ring per slot), per-edge push routing, the spec invoke signature change (collapsing `invoke_native` / `invoke_json` into one `invoke` with per-input/per-output flags), the resolved \"JSON not type-annotated\" question, and the corrected understanding of 313 (slot machinery stays; only spec invocation thins).\n- **`docs/001-architecture.md`** — replaced the per-box `output_format` description with the dual-ring per-edge model.\n- **Memory** — rewrote `project_cross_language_wire.md` to match.\n\n306 and 307 didn't need rewriting — 312 now explicitly names them in its implementation sequence steps 5 and 6 (per-spec typed input dispatch + bridge implementations), so the dependency is captured.\n\nReady to start coding on slice 1 — extending the slot data structure with the dual-ring shape — whenever you are. Or did you want to look the issue rewrites over first?"
      }]

## [219]

```json
{
  "timestamp":"2026-05-21T19:01:37.043Z",
  "message":{
    "content":"  The \"agnostic\" part is JSON itself. Six kinds — object, array, number, string, bool, null. Every language has an obvious mapping (Lua:\n  object → table with string keys, array → table with n field for fidelity, number → Lua number, etc.). The Lua spec's decode_node at\n  langs/lua/spec.c:370 already does this in 60-ish lines. No type annotations on the wire are required because JSON's structure is\n  self-describing — the parser sees { and knows it's an object; sees 42 and knows it's a number.\n\n\nokay so... C++ has a concept of methods on classes. What happens if we have a class that has some data fields and some method functions? if we're trying to interpret that into C, will we need to use like, function pointers and such? would it make sense to make a \"custom translation\" section for each box that can run instead of the language spec if the user needs to do something funky? If so, we'd want to make it run at the start of the box's lifecycle, instead of when the upstream producer is filling in the input values, just-in-case the user writes something that's blocking or which takes a long time.\n\nI'm thinking, similar to how we have \"view\" for the source-code, we could say \"custom spec\" which is another file browser to a small little shim file that the user writes in their own text editor. We can create a new file for the user if we want to keep them organized in the map file - there's no reason for them to need to use external libraries for this type of custom code. Basically just a \"new\" and \"delete\" functionality is all the management we need, plus the ability to \"view\" it just to confirm that yes, it will be baked into the map when you hit compile.\n\nthe idea is, they'd use the well-defined spec for most things, and make a custom translation spec (which initializes to the default spec btw, to make it easier to apply edits or insert extra translation steps) for each of the weird options. Like if we need to turn a function pointer into a class method, but the C++ spec doesn't necessarily know that because it's just been presented with, like, a pointer to a spot in memory, and it's like... okay, what is that? who can say. But the user can say, and if we force them to make these little translation specs (also when we delete a box we should say \"this box has a custom translation spec, are you sure you want to delete? the spec will be safe on disk if you want to re-use it later.\") if we force them to make these, then they'll be A. more empowered to do things that are impossible to do agnostically, and B. we can relinquish the final responsibility of managing this part of the dataflow to the user. We'll do our best, and the language spec authors will try very hard, but some things might just be impossible without the user adding their own bit of glue code. Mostly because of the ambiguity between different language constructs. That stuff can't be known at runtime, or even at compile time.           "content":"# 246 — Custom translation specs per box\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Concept\n\nThe default language specs (issues 306 / 307 / 308) handle most\ncross-language translations via the dual-ring shape in issue 312:\nproducer's spec serializes native or JSON per the per-edge bit;\nconsumer's spec dispatches per input flag and decodes accordingly.\nThe default contract is sufficient for the cases JSON's structure\ncovers cleanly — primitives, strings, arrays, objects.\n\nSome translations cannot be inferred by the spec alone. The\nambiguity is in the language constructs themselves:\n\n- A C++ class with both data fields and method functions arrives\n  at a C box. C has no notion of methods; the default spec only\n  sees raw bytes. Whether to expose the methods as function\n  pointers, drop them, or restructure the data into a tagged\n  union is a development-time decision the user has to make.\n- A `void *` arrives carrying a libcurl handle the receiving\n  language's spec has no general way to interpret.\n- A union type whose discriminator lives in a separate input\n  port — the spec doesn't know which port is the tag.\n\nThese are the cases where the system can't ever infer the\ntranslation. Only the user, at development time, knows what the\nvalue means.\n\n**A custom translation spec is a per-box shim** the user writes\nto handle the cases the default spec cannot. It runs at the start\nof the consumer box's task, replaces the default decode step for\nthat box, and otherwise leaves the dispatch path unchanged.\n\n## Lifecycle (editor)\n\nThe box inspector grows three buttons for the selected box:\n\n- **New** — creates a translation file in\n  `maps/<name>/translations/<some-name>.<lang_ext>` and sets the\n  box JSON's `custom_translation` field to that path. The file\n  is initialised to a copy of what the default spec would do for\n  that box's declared inputs — the user can run it without edits\n  and behaviour is identical to no custom spec. Edits add or\n  replace specific translation steps.\n- **View** — opens the translation file in the editor's read-only\n  source view, the same affordance as \"view source\" on the\n  box's main function. The user-facing message is \"this is what\n  gets baked into the map at compile time.\"\n- **Delete** — clears the `custom_translation` field on the box.\n  The translation file itself stays on disk. Box-delete (the\n  whole box) with a custom translation attached prompts: \"this\n  box has a custom translation spec; the file stays on disk for\n  re-use, but the box's reference will go.\" Confirm or cancel.\n\nThe \"file stays on disk if you delete the box\" rule means custom\ntranslations are identifiable by path, not by box. The user can\nattach the same file to a different box later if they want, or\ndelete the file explicitly through a file-browser pane.\n\n## Lifecycle (runtime)\n\nThe dispatch's input-read step gains a per-box branch:\n\n```\nfor each input port i:\n    (which_ring, idx) = ring_order_pop(slot)\n    raw_bytes         = ring_at(...)\n    if box->custom_translation:\n        translated[i] = custom_translation(box, raw_bytes,\n                                            which_ring, i)\n    else:\n        translated[i] = default_spec_decode(raw_bytes,\n                                             which_ring, i)\n```\n\nThe custom translation runs in the **consumer's language**, on\nthe **consumer's worker thread**, at the **start of the consumer\nbox's task**. Three consequences fall out:\n\n- A custom spec that does something slow or surprising holds the\n  consumer's worker, not the producer's. The producer is free as\n  soon as it's done writing raw bytes to the ring.\n- Each consumer eats its own translation cost; mixed fan-in\n  consumers translate cell-by-cell as they pop.\n- The custom translation is in the same language as the box's\n  main function, so it has full access to that language's\n  runtime (Lua tables, C structs, etc.) without crossing another\n  language boundary first.\n\n## Where it sits relative to the dual-ring (issue 312)\n\nThe dual-ring routing still applies. The producer chooses a ring\nper `output_edge_native[j]` as today. The consumer's custom\ntranslation sees the raw bytes plus the `which_ring` tag — so it\ncan distinguish \"these bytes are my own language's native format\"\nfrom \"these bytes are JSON from a cross-language producer\" and\nact accordingly.\n\nIn the easy cases (same-language same-shape), the bytes pass\nthrough native-ring-to-native-value and the custom spec is\ntypically just an identity. The custom spec earns its keep on\nthe cells where the default `json_to_native` would error or\nproduce something useless — that's where the user-written code\ntakes over.\n\n## File layout\n\n```\nmaps/<name>/\n    boxes/\n        <box_id>.json                ← references translations/\n    translations/\n        <shim_name>.<lang_ext>       ← per-shim file\n    src/\n        <box_id>.<lang_ext>          ← box's main function\n```\n\nBox JSON gains one optional field:\n\n```json\n{\n    \"id\": \"consume_class\",\n    \"lang\": \"c\",\n    \"ref\": \"consume.c\",\n    \"fn\": \"consume\",\n    \"custom_translation\": \"translations/cpp_class_to_c.c\",\n    \"inputs\": [...],\n    \"...\": \"...\"\n}\n```\n\nIf `custom_translation` is absent, the default-spec path runs as\ntoday. The translations directory may contain shims with no\nattached box (orphaned, kept on disk by the delete-doesn't-delete-\nfile rule).\n\n## Custom translation function signature (per language)\n\nWorking draft for C:\n\n```c\nint sm_translate(const void **inputs_raw, const int *input_sizes,\n                 const int *input_native, int n_inputs,\n                 void *outputs_native, int outputs_capacity,\n                 int *outputs_size);\n```\n\nThe shim reads each input's raw bytes (with the `input_native[i]`\nflag telling it whether the bytes are this language's native\nform or JSON), produces the translated values in whatever shape\nthe box's main function expects, and writes them to\n`outputs_native`. The dispatch then hands those translated values\nto the spec's `invoke`.\n\nLua's shape is analogous but in Lua-native form — the function\ntakes the raw byte strings, returns the translated values.\n\nOne signature per box (rather than per port) for simplicity. A\nshim that needs per-port granularity can dispatch on the input\nindex internally.\n\n## Default content of a freshly-created shim\n\nThe \"New\" button writes a file that's a copy of what the default\nspec would do for that box's declared inputs. For C, that's a\nsmall generated wrapper that walks `inputs_raw[]`, parses each\ninput per its declared type, and writes the result. For Lua, it's\na few lines that decode each input via the existing JSON / native\nhelpers.\n\nThis lets the user add a single line of translation logic\nwithout rewriting the entire decode. The alternative — an empty\nstub that errors until filled in — would force the user to write\nboilerplate for every shim. The \"starts as default, edits in\nplace\" shape matches the project's preference for upgrade paths\nover from-scratch authoring.\n\n## Compile pipeline (issue 309)\n\nThe custom translation file ships as part of the compiled map's\nartifacts. For C, it compiles to a `.so` alongside the box's main\nfunction. For Lua, it loads into the worker's `lua_State` like\nany other Lua source. The compile pipeline already walks every\nbox's `ref` to copy source into `compiled/src/`; the same walk\ncopies `custom_translation` files.\n\nWhen issue 313 (same-language source merge) lands, custom\ntranslation files get concatenated into the per-language bundle\nthe same way box main functions do — a translation file is just\nanother function in the merged module.\n\n## Why this is the right escape hatch\n\nThe default spec contract is \"JSON is the universal interop, each\nspec handles its own native form, sentinels carry the in-process\nexotic cases.\" That's enough for the overwhelming majority of\ndata flow. The cases where it fails are exactly the cases where\nthe user has knowledge the system can't ever infer — the meaning\nof a `void *`, the structure of a serialized object, the\ndiscriminator of a union.\n\nPushing those back to the user via a per-box shim is honest\nabout where the knowledge has to come from. It also lets the\ndefault spec contract stay narrow and predictable — the spec\nauthors don't have to chase every possible ambiguous type with\nnew special cases.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — box state; `custom_translation` field\n  read/write.\n- `assets/index.html` — inspector UI (New / View / Delete\n  buttons).\n- `src/006-server-main.lua` — HTTP backend for translation file\n  CRUD (path validation against `maps/<name>/translations/`).\n- `src/010-graph-loader.{c,h}` — load the `custom_translation`\n  field onto `box_t`.\n- `src/012-dispatch.c` — input-read branch on\n  `box->custom_translation`.\n- `scripts/soramech-compile.sh` — package translation files into\n  the compiled map (issue 309).\n- `issues/312-same-language-wire-fast-path.md` — dual-ring shape\n  the translation slots into.\n- `issues/313-research-whole-program-same-language-merge.md` —\n  custom translations get merged alongside box source.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. **Box JSON schema**: add the optional `custom_translation`\n   field. Graph loader reads it; absence means default path.\n2. **HTTP backend**: CRUD routes for translation files. Path\n   validation against `maps/<name>/translations/`.\n3. **Editor inspector**: New / View / Delete buttons. \"New\"\n   generates the file with default-spec-equivalent contents\n   parameterised on the box's declared inputs.\n4. **Box-delete confirmation**: detect attached translation;\n   prompt before deletion; preserve the file on disk regardless.\n5. **Dispatch**: input-read branch on `custom_translation`;\n   route bytes through the shim instead of the default decode.\n6. **Compile pipeline**: package translation files into\n   `compiled/translations/` and the per-language source bundle.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Output-side custom translation.** A symmetric case exists: a\n  box wanting to push a value the default spec can't serialize\n  (Lua closure, libcurl handle) needs a custom translator on its\n  output, not its input. The shape mirrors this issue —\n  per-box `custom_output_translation` field, runs at the end of\n  the producer's task, before push. Slated as a follow-on slice\n  once the input-side shape settles.\n- **Shared translations across multiple boxes.** Right now each\n  box references one translation file; ten boxes that need the\n  same translation duplicate the reference. Sharing the file\n  across boxes is supported (just point both boxes at the same\n  path); the editor's \"New\" button always creates a fresh file\n  for the box that asked. Library imports inside translation\n  files for shared helpers are out of scope here — the user can\n  do that via the language's normal import mechanism.\n- **Per-port vs. per-box signature.** Currently the shim has one\n  call for all inputs. Per-port would let each shim declare which\n  input it translates and pass the rest through to the default.\n  Probably useful eventually; defer until a real use case asks.\n- **Compile-time validation.** Should the compile button check\n  that every `custom_translation` path exists and parses? Easy\n  add to the existing compile validation; do it once translations\n  exist as a feature.\n\n## Quote\n\n> \"Mostly because of the ambiguity between different language\n> constructs. That stuff can't be known at runtime, or even at\n> compile time. Only at 'development time' is it possible.\" —\n> 2026-05-21\n",

The consumer's custom\ntranslation sees the raw bytes plus the `which_ring` tag — so it\ncan distinguish \"these bytes are my own language's native format\"\nfrom \"these bytes are JSON from a cross-language producer\" and\nact accordingly.\n\nIn the easy cases (same-language same-shape), the bytes pass\nthrough native-ring-to-native-value and the custom spec is\ntypically just an identity. The custom spec earns its keep on\nthe cells where the default `json_to_native` would error or\nproduce something useless — that's where the user-written code\ntakes over.\n\n## File layout\n\n```\nmaps/<name>/\n    boxes/\n        <box_id>.json                ← references translations/\n    translations/\n        <shim_name>.<lang_ext>       ← per-shim file\n    src/\n        <box_id>.<lang_ext>          ← box's main function\n```\n\nBox JSON gains one optional field:\n\n```json\n{\n    \"id\": \"consume_class\",\n    \"lang\": \"c\",\n    \"ref\": \"consume.c\",\n    \"fn\": \"consume\",\n    \"custom_translation\": \"translations/cpp_class_to_c.c\",\n    \"inputs\": [...],\n    \"...\": \"...\"\n}\n```\n\nIf `custom_translation` is absent, the default-spec path runs as\ntoday. The translations directory may contain shims with no\nattached box (orphaned, kept on disk by the delete-doesn't-delete-\nfile rule).\n\n## Custom translation function signature (per language)\n\nWorking draft for C:\n\n```c\nint sm_translate(const void **inputs_raw, const int *input_sizes,\n                 const int *input_native, int n_inputs,\n                 void *outputs_native, int outputs_capacity,\n                 int *outputs_size);\n```\n\nThe shim reads each input's raw bytes (with the `input_native[i]`\nflag telling it whether the bytes are this language's native\nform or JSON), produces the translated values in whatever shape\nthe box's main function expects, and writes them to\n`outputs_native`. The dispatch then hands those translated values\nto the spec's `invoke`.\n\nLua's shape is analogous but in Lua-native form — the function\ntakes the raw byte strings, returns the translated values.\n\nOne signature per box (rather than per port) for simplicity. A\nshim that needs per-port granularity can dispatch on the input\nindex internally.\n\n## Default content of a freshly-created shim\n\nThe \"New\" button writes a file that's a copy of what the default\nspec would do for that box's declared inputs. For C, that's a\nsmall generated wrapper that walks `inputs_raw[]`, parses each\ninput per its declared type, and writes the result. For Lua, it's\na few lines that decode each input via the existing JSON / native\nhelpers.\n\nThis lets the user add a single line of translation logic\nwithout rewriting the entire decode. The alternative — an empty\nstub that errors until filled in — would force the user to write\nboilerplate for every shim. The \"starts as default, edits in\nplace\" shape matches the project's preference for upgrade paths\nover from-scratch authoring.\n\n## Compile pipeline (issue 309)\n\nThe custom translation file ships as part of the compiled map's\nartifacts. For C, it compiles to a `.so` alongside the box's main\nfunction. For Lua, it loads into the worker's `lua_State` like\nany other Lua source. The compile pipeline already walks every\nbox's `ref` to copy source into `compiled/src/`; the same walk\ncopies `custom_translation` files.\n\nWhen issue 313 (same-language source merge) lands, custom\ntranslation files get concatenated into the per-language bundle\nthe same way box main functions do — a translation file is just\nanother function in the merged module.\n\n## Why this is the right escape hatch\n\nThe default spec contract is \"JSON is the universal interop, each\nspec handles its own native form, sentinels carry the in-process\nexotic cases.\" That's enough for the overwhelming majority of\ndata flow. The cases where it fails are exactly the cases where\nthe user has knowledge the system can't ever infer — the meaning\nof a `void *`, the structure of a serialized object, the\ndiscriminator of a union.\n\nPushing those back to the user via a per-box shim is honest\nabout where the knowledge has to come from. It also lets the\ndefault spec contract stay narrow and predictable — the spec\nauthors don't have to chase every possible ambiguous type with\nnew special cases.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — box state; `custom_translation` field\n  read/write.\n- `assets/index.html` — inspector UI (New / View / Delete\n  buttons).\n- `src/006-server-main.lua` — HTTP backend for translation file\n  CRUD (path validation against `maps/<name>/translations/`).\n- `src/010-graph-loader.{c,h}` — load the `custom_translation`\n  field onto `box_t`.\n- `src/012-dispatch.c` — input-read branch on\n  `box->custom_translation`.\n- `scripts/soramech-compile.sh` — package translation files into\n  the compiled map (issue 309).\n- `issues/312-same-language-wire-fast-path.md` — dual-ring shape\n  the translation slots into.\n- `issues/313-research-whole-program-same-language-merge.md` —\n  custom translations get merged alongside box source.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. **Box JSON schema**: add the optional `custom_translation`\n   field. Graph loader reads it; absence means default path.\n2. **HTTP backend**: CRUD routes for translation files. Path\n   validation against `maps/<name>/translations/`.\n3. **Editor inspector**: New / View / Delete buttons. \"New\"\n   generates the file with default-spec-equivalent contents\n   parameterised on the box's declared inputs.\n4. **Box-delete confirmation**: detect attached translation;\n   prompt before deletion; preserve the file on disk regardless.\n5. **Dispatch**: input-read branch on `custom_translation`;\n   route bytes through the shim instead of the default decode.\n6. **Compile pipeline**: package translation files into\n   `compiled/translations/` and the per-language source bundle.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Output-side custom translation.** A symmetric case exists: a\n  box wanting to push a value the default spec can't serialize\n  (Lua closure, libcurl handle) needs a custom translator on its\n  output, not its input. The shape mirrors this issue —\n  per-box `custom_output_translation` field, runs at the end of\n  the producer's task, before push. Slated as a follow-on slice\n  once the input-side shape settles.\n- **Shared translations across multiple boxes.** Right now each\n  box references one translation file; ten boxes that need the\n  same translation duplicate the reference. Sharing the file\n  across boxes is supported (just point both boxes at the same\n  path); the editor's \"New\" button always creates a fresh file\n  for the box that asked. Library imports inside translation\n  files for shared helpers are out of scope here — the user can\n  do that via the language's normal import mechanism.\n- **Per-port vs. per-box signature.** Currently the shim has one\n  call for all inputs. Per-port would let each shim declare which\n  input it translates and pass the rest through to the default.\n  Probably useful eventually; defer until a real use case asks.\n- **Compile-time validation.** Should the compile button check\n  that every `custom_translation` path exists and parses? Easy\n  add to the existing compile validation; do it once translations\n  exist as a feature.\n\n## Quote\n\n> \"Mostly because of the ambiguity between different language\n> constructs. That stuff can't be known at runtime, or even at\n> compile time. Only at 'development time' is it possible.\" —\n> 2026-05-21\n",
    "structuredPatch":[]
  },

}

    "content":"  1. What language is the custom spec written in? Consumer's language, I'm assuming — so a C box's custom translation is C code, a Lua box's\n  is Lua. Compiles / loads through the same spec machinery as the box's main function. The alternative is \"always C\" (universal) which would\n  force Lua users into a foreign language for their shim.\n\n\nI think it has to be in the consumer's language, if we want to interpret the values from text (json) and build them into the new language's datastructures... yeah it has to be the consumer's language.\n\n  2. Custom translation replaces the default (json|native)_to_native step, but the dual-ring routing still applies. Producer still picks a\n  ring per output_edge_native[j]; consumer's custom translation sees the raw bytes plus a which_ring tag. So same-language same-shape cases\n  bypass the custom spec entirely (default native pass-through still works). The custom spec only kicks in for the cases the default can't\n  handle.\n\n\n(json|native)_to_native still applies when no custom spec is defined. Mostly for primitive types and such. Other than that, this looks correct.\n\nThe custom spec should be defined on a per-slot basis, by the way. Each slot should (ideally) only need to handle one particular type of information. That's... why we have separate arguments at all, instead of just using void pointers for everything.\n\n  3. Input side only for the first cut, output side as a follow-on? Your description was about translation at the start of the consumer's\n  task. A symmetric case exists — a Lua box wanting to output a closure runs into the default spec's hard-error on functions. The\n  producer-side custom translation would serialize the closure (via lua_dump or whatever). Both sides exist; the user fills in either or\n  both. I'll mention output-side in the issue's open questions so it's captured but not in the first slice.\n\n\nso, my thinking is, a particular language will always know exactly how to serialize every single one of it's language features. Those are known beforehand. What isn't known is how to parse/interpret an... ambiguously defined value or function or something from a json file. That's where the custom spec comes in. the language spec should be able to describe, losslessly, everything about the particular data it's writing to json - what we can't do is know how to *read* that data, because reading depends on the receiving language and the sending language, while writing only depends on the sending language.\n\n  4. Default content of a freshly-created shim: a literal copy of what the default spec would do, so the user can edit individual steps in\n  place, vs. an empty stub that errors until filled in. I'm leaning the former — easier to add small tweaks than to write the whole decode\n  from scratch.\n\n\njust a copy of the default spec.\n\nhow about, with the wire coloring issue, if there's a custom shim then we turn the wires bright goldenrod cheddar cheese orange-yellow?",

    "originalFile":"# 245 — Wire color by cross-language classification\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\n\nEvery wire on the canvas is drawn the same dim slate-blue (`#4a6080`)\nwhen its `from_branch` is null, or one of the comparator branch\ncolors (orange / blue / green) when it's a branch wire. Wire color\nencodes routing kind, not language pairing. Two wires leaving the\nsame producer — one to a Lua consumer, one to a C consumer — look\nidentical.\n\nThe runtime treats those wires very differently: the same-language\nhop carries native bytes, the cross-language hop carries JSON\n(issue 312). The editor gives the box author no visual signal that\nthe JSON translation step exists. It's invisible until someone\nreads the dispatch code.\n\n## Concept\n\nWires are colored by **language pairing across the edge**:\n\n- **Forest green** (`#228b22` or similar) — cross-language wire.\n  Producer and consumer are different languages; the runtime\n  translates via JSON at the wire. A reminder that this hop costs\n  encode + decode.\n- **Dark gray** (`#666` or similar; \"forest-gray\" is the verbal\n  cue) — same-language wire. Producer and consumer share a\n  language; native bytes pass without translation.\n- **Existing branch colors** (`lt` / `eq` / `gt` / iterator\n  branches) remain — they encode routing semantics, which is\n  orthogonal to language classification.\n\nWhen a wire is both branch-colored AND language-classified, the\ntwo signals compose. One workable composition: branch color drives\nthe wire's stroke, language classification drives a small marker\n(a colored dot at the midpoint, or a dashed-vs-solid line style).\nThe implementation picks the form; the rule is that both signals\nare visible on the same wire.\n\n## How the editor computes the classification\n\nFor each connection `{from_box, to_box, ...}`:\n\n1. Look up `from_box`'s box JSON; read its `lang` field.\n2. Look up `to_box`'s box JSON; read its `lang` field.\n3.
