          "content":"# 246 — Custom translation specs per input port\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Concept\n\nThe default language specs (issues 306 / 307 / 308) handle most\ncross-language translations via the dual-ring shape in issue 312:\nproducer's spec serializes native or JSON per the per-edge bit;\nconsumer's spec dispatches per input flag and decodes accordingly.\nThe default contract is sufficient for the cases JSON's structure\ncovers cleanly — primitives, strings, arrays, objects.\n\nSome translations cannot be inferred by the spec alone. The\nambiguity is in the language constructs themselves:\n\n- A C++ class with both data fields and method functions arrives\n  at a C box. C has no notion of methods; the default spec only\n  sees raw bytes. Whether to expose the methods as function\n  pointers, drop them, or restructure the data into a tagged\n  union is a development-time decision the user has to make.\n- A `void *` arrives carrying a libcurl handle the receiving\n  language's spec has no general way to interpret.\n- A union type whose discriminator lives in a separate input\n  port — the spec doesn't know which port is the tag.\n\nThese are the cases where the system can't ever infer the\ntranslation. Only the user, at development time, knows what the\nvalue means.\n\n**A custom translation spec is a per-input-port shim** the user\nwrites to handle the cases the default spec cannot. It runs at the\nstart of the consumer box's task, replaces the default decode for\nthat one port, and otherwise leaves the dispatch path unchanged.\n\n### Why per-port, not per-box\n\n> \"the custom spec should be defined on a per-slot basis. Each\n> slot should (ideally) only need to handle one particular type\n> of information. That's why we have separate arguments at all,\n> instead of just using void pointers for everything.\" —\n> 2026-05-21\n\nPer-port matches the principled reason input ports exist in the\nfirst place: each port carries one kind of value, and the user\ndeclares the kind. If a box has three input ports — two of them\nordinary strings and one of them a C++ class instance — only the\nclass-instance port needs custom translation. The two string ports\nkeep the default decode. A per-box shim would force the user to\nwrite decode code for every port even when only one is weird.\n\n### Why no output-side custom translation\n\nA producer's spec always knows how to serialize every one of its\nown language's values losslessly — Lua's spec knows every Lua type,\nC's spec knows every typed struct field. Writing depends only on\nthe sending language, which has full reflective access to its own\ntype system. The Lua spec's `encode_value` is expected to grow\nsentinel primitives (`$function_pointer`, `$lang_opaque`) for the\nvalues JSON can't represent structurally; that's a spec-author\nresponsibility, not a user-shim responsibility.\n\nReading is the asymmetric direction. The receiver doesn't know\nwhat the sender meant by an opaque pointer or a sentinel-tagged\nvalue — that interpretation is the user's call. Hence the custom\nshim lives on the input side only.\n\n## Lifecycle (editor)\n\nThe box inspector's input-port rows each grow a small affordance\nfor managing the port's custom translation:\n\n- **New** — creates a translation file in\n  `maps/<name>/translations/<box_id>__<port_name>.<lang_ext>`\n  and sets the port's `custom_translation` field in the box JSON\n  to that path. The file is initialized to a copy of what the\n  default spec would do for that port's declared type — the user\n  can run it without edits and behaviour is identical to no\n  custom shim. Edits add or replace the decode logic.\n- **View** — opens the translation file in the editor's read-only\n  source view (same affordance as \"view source\" on the box's main\n  function). The user-facing message is \"this is what gets baked\n  into the map at compile time.\"\n- **Delete** — clears the port's `custom_translation` field. The\n  translation file itself stays on disk. Box-delete (the whole\n  box) with any custom translations attached prompts: \"this box\n  has N custom translation specs; the files stay on disk for\n  re-use, but the box's references will go.\" Confirm or cancel.\n\nThe \"file stays on disk if you delete the box\" rule means custom\ntranslations are identifiable by path, not by box. The user can\nattach the same file to a different box's port later, or delete\nthe file explicitly through a file-browser pane.\n\n## Lifecycle (runtime)\n\nThe dispatch's input-read step gains a per-port branch:\n\n```\nfor each input port i:\n    (which_ring, idx) = ring_order_pop(slot)\n    raw_bytes         = ring_at(...)\n    if box->inputs[i].custom_translation:\n        translated[i] = custom_translation[i](raw_bytes, which_ring)\n        input_native[i] = NATIVE   # custom shim output is always native\n    else:\n        translated[i] = raw_bytes\n        input_native[i] = (which_ring == NATIVE)\n```\n\nWhen the port has a custom shim, the shim does the decode and the\nspec's `invoke` sees native bytes (with `input_native[i] = NATIVE`).\nWhen the port has no custom shim, the default decode runs inside\nthe spec's invoke as today.\n\nThree consequences fall out from running on the consumer's worker:\n\n- A custom shim that does something slow or surprising holds the\n  consumer's worker, not the producer's. The producer is free as\n  soon as it's done writing raw bytes to the ring.\n- Each consumer eats its own translation cost; mixed fan-in\n  consumers translate cell-by-cell as they pop.\n- The custom shim is in the same language as the box's main\n  function, so it has full access to that language's runtime\n  (Lua tables, C structs, etc.) without crossing another\n  language boundary first.\n\n## Where it sits relative to the dual-ring (issue 312)\n\nThe dual-ring routing still applies. The producer chooses a ring\nper `output_edge_native[j]` as today. The consumer's per-port\ncustom shim sees the raw bytes plus the `which_ring` tag — so it\ncan distinguish \"these bytes are my own language's native format\"\nfrom \"these bytes are JSON from a cross-language producer\" and act\naccordingly.\n\nIn the easy cases (same-language same-shape), no custom shim is\nneeded; the default native pass-through still works. The custom\nshim earns its keep on the cells where the default\n`json_to_native` would error or produce something useless — that's\nwhere the user-written code takes over.\n\n## File layout\n\n```\nmaps/<name>/\n    boxes/\n        <box_id>.json                ← per-input port may reference translations/\n    translations/\n        <box_id>__<port_name>.<lang_ext>     ← per-port shim\n    src/\n        <box_id>.<lang_ext>                  ← box's main function\n```\n\nThe box JSON's `inputs` array grows an optional per-port field:\n\n```json\n{\n    \"id\": \"consume_class\",\n    \"lang\": \"c\",\n    \"ref\": \"consume.c\",\n    \"fn\": \"consume\",\n    \"inputs\": [\n        { \"name\": \"instance\", \"type\": \"bytes\",\n          \"custom_translation\": \"translations/consume_class__instance.c\" },\n        { \"name\": \"weight\",   \"type\": \"int\" }\n    ],\n    \"...\": \"...\"\n}\n```\n\nIf a port omits `custom_translation`, the default-spec decode runs\nfor that port as today. The `translations/` directory may contain\nshims with no attached port (orphaned, kept on disk by the\ndelete-doesn't-delete-file rule).\n\n## Custom translation function signature\n\nPer-port shims take one input's raw bytes and the `which_ring`\nflag, return one translated value in the consumer's native form.\nWorking draft for C:\n\n```c\nint sm_translate(const void *input_raw, int input_size,\n                 int input_native,\n                 void *output_native, int output_capacity,\n                 int *output_size);\n```\n\nLua's shape is analogous but in Lua-native terms — the function\ntakes a Lua string (the raw bytes) and a boolean (the native\nflag), returns the translated Lua value.\n\nOne signature per port keeps each shim's surface area exactly\nmatched to the port's job. A shim that needs to consult other\nports has a problem this design doesn't try to solve (per-port\nisolation is the principled choice); the user can fall back to\nplain decode-then-validate inside the box's main function for\ncross-port logic.\n\n## Default content of a freshly-created shim\n\nThe \"New\" button writes a file containing a literal copy of what\nthe default spec would do for that port's declared type. For C,\nthat's the small generated wrapper that parses `input_raw` per\nthe port's declared type and writes the result. For Lua, it's a\nfew lines that decode via the existing JSON / native helpers\nbased on `input_native`.\n\nThe user can run the shim without edits and behaviour matches the\nno-shim default. Edits typically replace one branch (the\nspecific weird case) and leave the rest alone. The \"starts as\ndefault, edits in place\" shape matches the project's preference\nfor upgrade paths over from-scratch authoring.\n\n## Compile pipeline (issue 309)\n\nThe compile pipeline already walks every box's `ref` to copy\nsource into `compiled/src/`. The same walk inspects each input\nport's `custom_translation` field and copies referenced files\ninto `compiled/translations/`. For C, each translation file\ncompiles to a `.so` alongside the box's main function. For Lua,\nfiles load into the worker's `lua_State` like any other Lua\nsource.\n\nWhen issue 313 (same-language source merge) lands, translation\nfiles get concatenated into the per-language bundle the same way\nbox main functions do — a translation file is just another\nfunction in the merged module.\n\n## Why this is the right escape hatch\n\nThe default spec contract is \"JSON is the universal interop, each\nspec handles its own native form, sentinels carry the in-process\nexotic cases on the producer side.\" That's enough for the\noverwhelming majority of data flow. The cases where it fails are\nexactly the cases where the user has knowledge the system can't\never infer — what a `void *` points to, how a serialized object\nis structured, which port is a discriminator for which other port.\n\nPushing those back to the user via a per-port shim is honest\nabout where the knowledge has to come from. It also lets the\ndefault spec contract stay narrow and predictable — the spec\nauthors don't have to chase every possible ambiguous receive-side\ntype with new special cases.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — box state; per-input\n  `custom_translation` field read/write.\n- `assets/index.html` — inspector UI (New / View / Delete buttons\n  on each input-port row).\n- `src/006-server-main.lua` — HTTP backend for translation file\n  CRUD (path validation against `maps/<name>/translations/`).\n- `src/010-graph-loader.{c,h}` — load each input port's\n  `custom_translation` onto `box_t->inputs[i]`.\n- `src/012-dispatch.c` — input-read branch on\n  `box->inputs[i].custom_translation`.\n- `scripts/soramech-compile.sh` — package translation files into\n  the compiled map (issue 309).\n- `issues/245-wire-color-by-cross-language-classification.md` —\n  goldenrod-cheddar wires for ports with custom translations.\n- `issues/312-same-language-wire-fast-path.md` — dual-ring shape\n  the translation slots into.\n- `issues/313-research-whole-program-same-language-merge.md` —\n  custom translations get merged alongside box source.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. **Box JSON schema**: add the optional per-input\n   `custom_translation` field. Graph loader reads it; absence\n   means default path for that port.\n2. **HTTP backend**: CRUD routes for translation files. Path\n   validation against `maps/<name>/translations/`.\n3. **Editor inspector**: New / View / Delete affordances on each\n   input-port row. \"New\" generates the file with\n   default-spec-equivalent contents parameterized on the port's\n   declared type. The 245 wire-coloring change activates\n   automatically once the field exists.\n4. **Box-delete confirmation**: detect any ports with attached\n   translations; prompt before deletion; preserve the files on\n   disk regardless.\n5. **Dispatch**: input-read per-port branch on\n   `custom_translation`; route bytes through the shim instead of\n   the default decode for that port.\n6. **Compile pipeline**: walk each input port's\n   `custom_translation`; package files into\n   `compiled/translations/` and the per-language source bundle.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Shared translations across multiple ports.** Two ports on\n  different boxes that need the same shim can both reference the\n  same file path — the system supports it implicitly. The\n  editor's \"New\" button always creates a fresh file with the\n  default naming so users don't accidentally share by default.\n  Library imports inside translation files (for shared helpers\n  inside a shim) are out of scope here — the user can do that via\n  the language's normal import mechanism.\n- **Compile-time validation.** Should the compile button check\n  that every `custom_translation` path exists and parses? Easy\n  add to the existing compile validation; do once translations\n  exist as a feature.\n- **Shim author seeing cross-port context.** Per-port isolation\n  means a shim only sees its own input. A union whose\n  discriminator is in another port has to validate inside the\n  box's main function rather than in the shim. If a real\n  cross-port case shows up, the workaround is a follow-on\n  ticket — not a reason to abandon per-port isolation.\n",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/246-custom-translation-specs-per-box.md"
        },

          "type":"direct"

The `translations/` directory may contain\nshims with no attached port (orphaned, kept on disk by the\ndelete-doesn't-delete-file rule).\n\n## Custom translation function signature\n\nPer-port shims take one input's raw bytes and the `which_ring`\nflag, return one translated value in the consumer's native form.\nWorking draft for C:\n\n```c\nint sm_translate(const void *input_raw, int input_size,\n                 int input_native,\n                 void *output_native, int output_capacity,\n                 int *output_size);\n```\n\nLua's shape is analogous but in Lua-native terms — the function\ntakes a Lua string (the raw bytes) and a boolean (the native\nflag), returns the translated Lua value.\n\nOne signature per port keeps each shim's surface area exactly\nmatched to the port's job. A shim that needs to consult other\nports has a problem this design doesn't try to solve (per-port\nisolation is the principled choice); the user can fall back to\nplain decode-then-validate inside the box's main function for\ncross-port logic.\n\n## Default content of a freshly-created shim\n\nThe \"New\" button writes a file containing a literal copy of what\nthe default spec would do for that port's declared type. For C,\nthat's the small generated wrapper that parses `input_raw` per\nthe port's declared type and writes the result. For Lua, it's a\nfew lines that decode via the existing JSON / native helpers\nbased on `input_native`.\n\nThe user can run the shim without edits and behaviour matches the\nno-shim default. Edits typically replace one branch (the\nspecific weird case) and leave the rest alone. The \"starts as\ndefault, edits in place\" shape matches the project's preference\nfor upgrade paths over from-scratch authoring.\n\n## Compile pipeline (issue 309)\n\nThe compile pipeline already walks every box's `ref` to copy\nsource into `compiled/src/`. The same walk inspects each input\nport's `custom_translation` field and copies referenced files\ninto `compiled/translations/`. For C, each translation file\ncompiles to a `.so` alongside the box's main function. For Lua,\nfiles load into the worker's `lua_State` like any other Lua\nsource.\n\nWhen issue 313 (same-language source merge) lands, translation\nfiles get concatenated into the per-language bundle the same way\nbox main functions do — a translation file is just another\nfunction in the merged module.\n\n## Why this is the right escape hatch\n\nThe default spec contract is \"JSON is the universal interop, each\nspec handles its own native form, sentinels carry the in-process\nexotic cases on the producer side.\" That's enough for the\noverwhelming majority of data flow. The cases where it fails are\nexactly the cases where the user has knowledge the system can't\never infer — what a `void *` points to, how a serialized object\nis structured, which port is a discriminator for which other port.\n\nPushing those back to the user via a per-port shim is honest\nabout where the knowledge has to come from. It also lets the\ndefault spec contract stay narrow and predictable — the spec\nauthors don't have to chase every possible ambiguous receive-side\ntype with new special cases.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — box state; per-input\n  `custom_translation` field read/write.\n- `assets/index.html` — inspector UI (New / View / Delete buttons\n  on each input-port row).\n- `src/006-server-main.lua` — HTTP backend for translation file\n  CRUD (path validation against `maps/<name>/translations/`).\n- `src/010-graph-loader.{c,h}` — load each input port's\n  `custom_translation` onto `box_t->inputs[i]`.\n- `src/012-dispatch.c` — input-read branch on\n  `box->inputs[i].custom_translation`.\n- `scripts/soramech-compile.sh` — package translation files into\n  the compiled map (issue 309).\n- `issues/245-wire-color-by-cross-language-classification.md` —\n  goldenrod-cheddar wires for ports with custom translations.\n- `issues/312-same-language-wire-fast-path.md` — dual-ring shape\n  the translation slots into.\n- `issues/313-research-whole-program-same-language-merge.md` —\n  custom translations get merged alongside box source.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. **Box JSON schema**: add the optional per-input\n   `custom_translation` field. Graph loader reads it; absence\n   means default path for that port.\n2. **HTTP backend**: CRUD routes for translation files. Path\n   validation against `maps/<name>/translations/`.\n3. **Editor inspector**: New / View / Delete affordances on each\n   input-port row. \"New\" generates the file with\n   default-spec-equivalent contents parameterized on the port's\n   declared type. The 245 wire-coloring change activates\n   automatically once the field exists.\n4. **Box-delete confirmation**: detect any ports with attached\n   translations; prompt before deletion; preserve the files on\n   disk regardless.\n5. **Dispatch**: input-read per-port branch on\n   `custom_translation`; route bytes through the shim instead of\n   the default decode for that port.\n6. **Compile pipeline**: walk each input port's\n   `custom_translation`; package files into\n   `compiled/translations/` and the per-language source bundle.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Shared translations across multiple ports.** Two ports on\n  different boxes that need the same shim can both reference the\n  same file path — the system supports it implicitly. The\n  editor's \"New\" button always creates a fresh file with the\n  default naming so users don't accidentally share by default.\n  Library imports inside translation files (for shared helpers\n  inside a shim) are out of scope here — the user can do that via\n  the language's normal import mechanism.\n- **Compile-time validation.** Should the compile button check\n  that every `custom_translation` path exists and parses? Easy\n  add to the existing compile validation; do once translations\n  exist as a feature.\n- **Shim author seeing cross-port context.** Per-port isolation\n  means a shim only sees its own input. A union whose\n  discriminator is in another port has to validate inside the\n  box's main function rather than in the shim. If a real\n  cross-port case shows up, the workaround is a follow-on\n  ticket — not a reason to abandon per-port isolation.\n",

{
  "timestamp":"2026-05-21T19:32:42.963Z",
  "message":{
    "content":"one neat benefit of the goldenrod cheddar cheese wire custom specs is that it's genuinely a third type of wire. It also can be useful for the native->native path - if we want to, for example, produce a float in one C function and pass it to another C function, we'd normally get a type error. But with the custom spec, we can say \"actually instead of doing the default native->native pass, instead here's a copy of that spec that the user edited to handle just specifically floats. They want you to truncate it and round up, and they show you how to do that in this little C code. Please run this computer, instead of the default language spec, so our program doesn't break!\"\n\n  - Output-side custom translation is decided no in the body — the producer's spec is fully responsible for lossless serialization of its own\n   language's values (including via $function_pointer / $lang_opaque sentinels, which become a follow-on extending 312, not a user-shim\n  concern).\n\n\ncan you tell me about these sentinel files? how do we handle like, a pointer to a large dataset? or a function pointer? if we need lua code to run a C function, and the C function passes a function pointer to json (then to lua), how does that function pointer's function get run? Do we auto-generate the glue code? Do we ask the language spec authors to design that? How would we? what's the goal here, to be able to have infinite flexibility at the cost of runtime performance, gained back with the multithreading-by-default system?",
    "role":"user"

    "content":[{
        "type":"text",
        "text":"No dedicated sentinel issue exists — they're mentioned descriptively in 312, 246, and the architecture doc, but the mechanics haven't been written down anywhere as a real design. They probably should be. Let me answer your questions first, then propose what to capture.\n\n**Sentinel mechanics, walked through your function-pointer example.**\n\nC box produces `int compare(void *, void *)`. The box JSON declares the output type as a function pointer with that signature. The C spec's `native_to_json` recognizes \"this isn't a JSON-shaped value, it's a callable\" and emits:\n\n```json\n{\"$function_pointer\": {\"addr\": \"0x7fffabcd1234\",\n                       \"signature\": \"int(void*,void*)\"}}\n```\n\nThe Lua consumer pops the JSON. Its `json_to_native` sees the `$function_pointer` sentinel and reconstructs the callable using **LuaJIT FFI** — code the Lua spec author wrote once:\n\n```c\n// Pseudocode inside lua_json_to_native when it sees $function_pointer\nlua_getglobal(L, \"ffi\");\nlua_getfield(L, -1, \"cast\");\nlua_pushstring(L, signature);   // \"int (*)(void*, void*)\"\nlua_pushinteger(L, addr);\nlua_call(L, 2, 1);\n// Stack top now holds an FFI callable Lua can call like a Lua function\n```\n\nThe Lua box's user code then calls it normally — `compare_fn(a, b)` — and LuaJIT FFI does the actual C call. **In-process only**, because the address is a raw memory pointer that's only meaningful in this process.\n\nNo auto-generation in the general case. The spec author writes the reconstruction once per sentinel kind per language. For Python (hypothetical): `ctypes.CFUNCTYPE(...)`. For Bash: no FFI capability, so a wire carrying a function pointer to a Bash box **fails at compile time**. That's the \"compile error if a cross-language wire ever points at a language that can't reconstruct\" half of the design.\n\n**`$ref` for large datasets** works the same shape, simpler:\n\n```json\n{\"$ref\": {\"ptr\": \"0x...\", \"len\": 1048576, \"type\": \"bytes\"}}\n```\n\nThe bytes live in the large-value heap (`src/015-large-value-heap.c`). Refcount = number of consumer slots. Lua reads with `lua_pushlstring(ptr, len)` (copies into Lua's heap). C uses the pointer directly. Bash via UDS — the marshaller inlines the bytes at the socket boundary, since cross-process can't share a raw pointer. The user never knows it's a reference unless they care; it just looks like a value.\n\n**`$lang_opaque`** — a tagged blob the producer's language wraps around a value it can't structurally describe (a Lua coroutine, a Python generator). The consumer either knows what to do (same language family) or wire compile fails. This is the catch-all when `$ref` and `$function_pointer` don't fit.\n\n**The flexibility-vs-performance question — honest answer:**\n\nIt's not \"huge flexibility cost recovered by threading.\" Threading is orthogonal parallelism, not a per-cell-cost reduction. The cost story is **paid per edge, where it actually occurs:**\n\n- Same-language native wires: bytes pass through, no translation. Native ring of the slot.\n- Cross-language wires: JSON encode + decode at the boundary. JSON ring of the slot. Bounded by value size.\n- Sentinels: tiny — a few dozen bytes of JSON wrapping a pointer. The reconstruction is `ffi.cast` or equivalent: nanoseconds.\n- Custom shims: whatever the user writes. Could be one line or could be a parser.\n\nThe \"flexibility\" doesn't impose a uniform tax. Primitives and structured data flow at JSON-parse cost across borders; same-language stays native; in-process references flow at pointer-copy cost via sentinels. Threading adds throughput on top by running boxes concurrently — but it doesn't make a JSON parse faster, it just lets two of them happen at once on different cores.\n\nThe real long-term optimization isn't threading-recovers-cost; it's **313's same-language merge** thinning the spec-invocation overhead inside same-language regions (no dlsym + marshal + bridge per call; the merged module is one big function pile and calls are direct). That's where the structural perf win lands, and it stacks cleanly on top of the dual-ring design.\n\n---\n\nTwo things to do, want me to:\n\n1. **Update 246** to broaden the framing from \"cross-language ambiguity\" to \"any user intervention at a port\" — with your float-rounding case as the second motivating example alongside the C++-class one? The shape doesn't change; the rationale section grows.\n\n2. **Open a new issue for sentinel primitives** — the canonical JSON shapes, the per-language reconstruction protocol, the compile-time validation that wires don't point sentinels at languages that can't handle them, the in-process-only constraint, the UDS-marshaller bytes-inlining for `$ref`. Probably 318 since it's phase-3 runtime work that spec authors implement, not editor work.\n\nBoth?"

          "old_string":"## Concept\n\nThe default language specs (issues 306 / 307 / 308) handle most\ncross-language translations via the dual-ring shape in issue 312:\nproducer's spec serializes native or JSON per the per-edge bit;\nconsumer's spec dispatches per input flag and decodes accordingly.\nThe default contract is sufficient for the cases JSON's structure\ncovers cleanly — primitives, strings, arrays, objects.\n\nSome translations cannot be inferred by the spec alone. The\nambiguity is in the language constructs themselves:\n\n- A C++ class with both data fields and method functions arrives\n  at a C box. C has no notion of methods; the default spec only\n  sees raw bytes. Whether to expose the methods as function\n  pointers, drop them, or restructure the data into a tagged\n  union is a development-time decision the user has to make.\n- A `void *` arrives carrying a libcurl handle the receiving\n  language's spec has no general way to interpret.\n- A union type whose discriminator lives in a separate input\n  port — the spec doesn't know which port is the tag.\n\nThese are the cases where the system can't ever infer the\ntranslation. Only the user, at development time, knows what the\nvalue means.\n\n**A custom translation spec is a per-input-port shim** the user\nwrites to handle the cases the default spec cannot. It runs at the\nstart of the consumer box's task, replaces the default decode for\nthat one port, and otherwise leaves the dispatch path unchanged.",
          "new_string":"## Concept\n\nThe default language specs (issues 306 / 307 / 308) handle most\ndata flow via the dual-ring shape in issue 312: producer's spec\nserializes native or JSON per the per-edge bit; consumer's spec\ndispatches per input flag and decodes accordingly. The default\ncontract is sufficient for primitives, strings, arrays, objects\n— the cases JSON's structure covers cleanly and the cases native\npass-through covers cleanly.\n\nA custom translation spec lets the user intervene at a specific\ninput port for **any reason** — not just cross-language\nambiguity. Two motivating cases:\n\n**Cross-language ambiguity.** Some translations cannot be\ninferred by the spec because the language constructs don't have\nuniversal mappings:\n\n- A C++ class with both data fields and method functions arrives\n  at a C box. C has no notion of methods; whether to expose them\n  as function pointers, drop them, or restructure into a tagged\n  union is a development-time decision the user has to make.\n- A `void *` arrives carrying a libcurl handle the receiving\n  language's spec has no general way to interpret.\n- A union type whose discriminator lives in a separate input\n  port — the spec doesn't know which port is the tag.\n\n**Same-language transformation the user wants.** Even when\nno language boundary is crossed, the default native pass-through\nmay not be what the user wants on a particular port:\n\n- A C box emits a float; a downstream C box wants it truncated\n  and rounded up before consumption. The default native-to-native\n  pass copies the bytes verbatim and the downstream code sees\n  the wrong precision. A custom shim on the destination port\n  applies the truncate-then-round transformation before invoke\n  sees the value. No language ambiguity — just user-specific\n  semantics at that wire.\n- A consumer wants units normalized (degrees → radians) on one\n  port but not on a sibling port; the custom shim handles it.\n- A consumer wants to enforce a value range, clamping or\n  erroring out of bounds; the shim does the check.\n\nIn both cases the principle is the same: **the user has\nknowledge about how this specific port should interpret its\ninput, and the default spec doesn't.** A per-port shim is where\nthat knowledge gets written down.\n\n**A custom translation spec is a per-input-port shim** the user\nwrites to handle these cases. It runs at the start of the\nconsumer box's task, replaces the default decode (or pass-through)\nfor that one port, and otherwise leaves the dispatch path\nunchanged."
        },

Whether to expose the methods as function\n  pointers, drop them, or restructure the data into a tagged\n  union is a development-time decision the user has to make.\n- A `void *` arrives carrying a libcurl handle the receiving\n  language's spec has no general way to interpret.\n- A union type whose discriminator lives in a separate input\n  port — the spec doesn't know which port is the tag.\n\nThese are the cases where the system can't ever infer the\ntranslation. Only the user, at development time, knows what the\nvalue means.\n\n**A custom translation spec is a per-input-port shim** the user\nwrites to handle the cases the default spec cannot. It runs at the\nstart of the consumer box's task, replaces the default decode for\nthat one port, and otherwise leaves the dispatch path unchanged.",
          "new_string":"## Concept\n\nThe default language specs (issues 306 / 307 / 308) handle most\ndata flow via the dual-ring shape in issue 312: producer's spec\nserializes native or JSON per the per-edge bit; consumer's spec\ndispatches per input flag and decodes accordingly. The default\ncontract is sufficient for primitives, strings, arrays, and\nobjects — the cases JSON's structure covers cleanly and the cases\nnative pass-through covers cleanly.\n\nA custom translation spec lets the user intervene at a specific\ninput port for **any reason** — not just cross-language\nambiguity. Two motivating cases:\n\n**Cross-language ambiguity.** Some translations cannot be\ninferred by the spec because the language constructs don't have\nuniversal mappings:\n\n- A C++ class with both data fields and method functions arrives\n  at a C box. C has no notion of methods; whether to expose them\n  as function pointers, drop them, or restructure into a tagged\n  union is a development-time decision the user has to make.\n- A `void *` arrives carrying a libcurl handle the receiving\n  language's spec has no general way to interpret.\n- A union type whose discriminator lives in a separate input\n  port — the spec doesn't know which port is the tag.\n\n**Same-language transformation the user wants.** Even when no\nlanguage boundary is crossed, the default native pass-through\nmay not be what the user wants on a particular port:\n\n- A C box emits a float; a downstream C box wants it truncated\n  and rounded up before consumption. The default native pass\n  copies the bytes verbatim and downstream code sees the wrong\n  precision. A custom shim on the destination port applies\n  truncate-then-round before invoke sees the value. No language\n  ambiguity — just user-specific semantics at that wire.\n- A consumer wants units normalized on one port but not on a\n  sibling port (degrees → radians on the angle input, leave the\n  magnitude input alone).\n- A consumer wants to clamp or range-check a value before its\n  function sees it.\n\nIn both cases the principle is the same: **the user has knowledge\nabout how this specific port should interpret its input, and the\ndefault spec doesn't.** A per-port shim is where that knowledge\ngets written down.\n\n**A custom translation spec is a per-input-port shim** the user\nwrites to handle these cases. It runs at the start of the\nconsumer box's task, replaces the default decode (or pass-through)\nfor that one port, and otherwise leaves the dispatch path\nunchanged."

  "uuid":"acf33016-9f43-4e6a-83e7-abba5e22141f",

  "sourceToolAssistantUUID":"146ab82f-ac47-4637-a3b9-0d179cfeb2a2",

    "filePath":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/247-debug-build-and-per-box-statistics-lens.md",
    "content":"# 247 — Debug build alternative and per-box statistics lens\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Concept\n\nThe Compile button currently produces one artifact: a release\nbuild of the map. Box authors who want to know which boxes are\nslow, which fire often, or which produce variably-sized outputs\nhave no editor-side way to see it — the run-output JSONL exists\n(`tmp/last-run.jsonl`) but reading it requires leaving the\neditor.\n\nThis issue adds two things that work together:\n\n1. **Compile-button alternatives.** A small dropdown (right-click\n   the button, or a tiny arrow next to it) opens a menu of build\n   modes. The default is the existing release build. The first\n   alternative is a **debug build** that turns on per-box\n   instrumentation. Other modes can land here later (strict\n   build, profile build, etc.) — the dropdown is the entry point.\n2. **Per-box statistics lens.** After a debug-build run, the\n   editor reads `tmp/last-run.jsonl`, aggregates per-box stats\n   (run count, mean / p50 / p95 duration, mean output size,\n   output-size variance), and colors each box on the canvas\n   according to a user-chosen filter. The filter is a small\n   panel in the editor — \"color by: run count / speed /\n   consistency / cumulative time\" — and the canvas re-tints as\n   the user picks.\n\n## What \"debug build\" turns on\n\nMost of the data already exists in `tmp/last-run.jsonl`. The\nrunner's event types include `task_end` with `duration_us` and\n`output_size` already (`docs/001-architecture.md:651`). What the\ndebug build does is **enable the optional event toggles**:\n\n- `SORAMECH_LOG_VALUES=1` — input/output payloads per task (truncated\n  at 4 KB). Useful for the consistency lens.\n- `SORAMECH_LOG_SLOTS=1` — slot allocator events. Useful for the\n  memory lens.\n\nIn the future the debug build can layer on actual instrumentation\n(per-spec-invoke timing, custom-shim timing, etc.). The first cut\njust toggles the env vars the existing runner already supports.\n\n## Lenses (color filters)\n\nEach lens maps `box_id → some_number → color`. The editor\nnormalizes the number across all boxes in the run, then maps to a\ngradient.\n\n| Lens | Per-box value | Gradient (low → high) |\n|------|---------------|------------------------|\n| **Run count** | how many times the box's task fired during the run | cool → warm |\n| **Mean duration** | mean `duration_us` over all firings | green → red |\n| **Cumulative time** | sum of `duration_us` over all firings | green → red |\n| **p95 duration** | 95th-percentile single-firing time | green → red |\n| **Output size variance** | stdev / mean of `output_size`; high variance = \"unpredictable size\" | calm → loud |\n| **Output size mean** | mean output bytes | small → large |\n\nThe lens panel is a dropdown of these options plus a small\nlegend (gradient strip + min/max values for the current run).\n\nSelecting \"(none)\" returns boxes to their default styling.\n\n## Where the data lives\n\n```\nmaps/<name>/tmp/\n    last-run.jsonl         ← runner's event stream (existing)\n    last-run-stats.json    ← editor-aggregated per-box stats (new)\n```\n\nThe editor reads `last-run.jsonl`, aggregates by `box_id`, and\ncaches the result in `last-run-stats.json` so subsequent lens\nswitches don't re-parse the JSONL. The cache file is\nregenerated each time the user clicks Compile-debug-and-run\n(or just Run, if a debug build is loaded).\n\nThe aggregation is dumb: walk events, accumulate per-box\ncounters and arrays of durations / sizes, compute the summary\nstatistics. Runs in the editor's HTTP backend (Lua), since the\nfile is already accessible there.\n\n## UI: Compile button dropdown\n\nThe Compile button grows a small right-arrow affordance (▾) on\nits right edge. Clicking the button proper still runs the\ndefault release build (unchanged behaviour). Clicking the arrow\nopens a small menu:\n\n- **Release build** (current default)\n- **Debug build** (this issue)\n- **Strict build** (`make STRICT=1` equivalent — added later)\n- **Profile build** (future, with detailed timing)\n\nThe chosen mode persists per-map (saved in the map's local UI\nstate) so re-clicking the button main face reruns the last mode.\nThe button's label / icon changes subtly to indicate which mode\nis active.\n\n## UI: Lens panel\n\nA small panel in the editor sidebar (or a popover near the\ncanvas-zoom indicator):\n\n```\n┌─ Box statistics ─────────────────┐\n│ Color by:                         │\n│   ( ) None                        │\n│   (•) Run count                   │\n│   ( ) Mean duration               │\n│   ( ) Cumulative time             │\n│   ( ) p95 duration                │\n│   ( ) Output size variance        │\n│   ( ) Output size mean            │\n│                                   │\n│ Legend: [▮▮▮▮▮▮]                  │\n│         1            18,300        │\n└───────────────────────────────────┘\n```\n\nThe legend's min/max reflect the current run's actual values.\nBoxes that didn't fire in the run get a \"no data\" styling\n(dimmed or outlined-only).\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `assets/index.html` — compile button + lens panel UI.\n- `assets/js/005-app.js` — compile-button click handlers; mode\n  state.\n- `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — box rendering; lens color override.\n- `src/006-server-main.lua` — aggregation route, reads\n  `last-run.jsonl`, produces `last-run-stats.json`.\n- `Makefile` / `scripts/soramech-compile.sh` — debug build mode\n  (sets the env vars; possibly compiles with `-O0 -g`).\n- `docs/001-architecture.md:638-666` — event format reference.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. **Compile-button dropdown UI.** Arrow affordance, menu, mode\n   state persisted per-map.\n2. **Debug build mode** in the compile script. Sets\n   `SORAMECH_LOG_VALUES=1` and `SORAMECH_LOG_SLOTS=1` for the\n   subsequent run. Optionally adds `-O0 -g` to per-box compiles\n   so stack traces are meaningful.\n3. **Aggregation route** in the HTTP backend. Reads\n   `last-run.jsonl`, computes per-box stats, writes\n   `last-run-stats.json`.\n4. **Lens panel** in the editor. Reads\n   `last-run-stats.json`, applies the selected color filter to\n   the boxes on the canvas.\n5. **Legend** with current-run min/max.\n6. **No-data styling** for boxes that didn't fire.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Where the lens panel docks**: sidebar vs. floating popover.\n  Whatever fits the existing editor layout.\n- **Color gradient choice**: a perceptually-uniform palette\n  (viridis, magma) reads better than a linear hue gradient.\n  Pick once; reuse across lenses.\n- **Live updates during a run**: the first cut reads stats after\n  the run finishes. A streaming version (tail the JSONL, update\n  the lens as boxes fire) is a follow-on if useful.\n- **Lens combination**: only one lens active at a time in the\n  first cut. Layered lenses (size of dot + color of dot from two\n  filters) are a follow-on.\n- **History / comparisons**: comparing two runs side by side (was\n  this box slower before my last edit?) is interesting but out\n  of scope here; would be a separate ticket.\n",
    "structuredPatch":[]
  },
  "cwd":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech"
}

        "text":"Done with 246 broadening and 247 draft. Now your questions.\n\n**Bash-via-compiled-binary as a `$function_pointer` alternative:** yes possible, and it's a real escape hatch worth knowing about — basically the CGI pattern, where the \"function pointer\" presented to Bash is a path to an executable Bash can spawn. The C spec would notice at compile time that a function-pointer output is wired to a cross-process consumer and emit a standalone binary instead of (or in addition to) the in-process address. Bash invokes it with `$(/path/to/binary arg1 arg2)` per call.\n\nThe cost: process spawn per call, 1–10 ms — exactly the phase-2 problem the spec system was built to eliminate. It's worth doing as an opt-in for the cases where you genuinely need C-from-Bash and you accept the cost. The mechanism slots into the broader sentinel-primitives design (issue I'm still pitching at 318): in the matrix of \"consumer language can reconstruct `$function_pointer` →,\" Bash's cell goes from \"compile error\" to \"spawn-via-binary, with the cost noted in the editor.\" Memory-allocation-into-shared-region is the further escape hatch and yes, that direction is operating-system shape — leave it for when there's a real demand.\n\n**How 312 and 313 relate.**\n\n**312 is the wire format.** Dual-ring slots, per-edge classification, JSON-only-at-borders. Defines how *values* move between boxes. Active every box invocation, every wire, every cell.\n\n**313 is the spec invocation thinner.** Defines how *the function gets called* once dispatch has the inputs ready and is about to invoke. Default (post-312): the dispatch calls `spec->invoke(handle, file_path, fn_name, input_data, ...)` which does dlsym + bridge + lua_pcall. 313 says: for boxes in the merged same-language region, skip all that — the function is already a callable in the merged module loaded on the worker's lua_State, so dispatch calls it directly.\n\nThe layering, made concrete in one box invocation under both 312 and 313:\n\n```\n1. Worker picks up the task.\n2. Dispatch reads inputs from the box's slots.        ← 312 (dual-ring slot)\n3. Dispatch decides which function to call.\n   - Default: look up spec by box->spec_idx, call its invoke\n   - 313 merged region: function is already a known callable\n     in the merged module; direct call.\n4. Function runs, returns a value.\n5. Dispatch writes output to consumer slots.          ← 312 (per-edge ring routing)\n```\n\nSteps 2 and 5 are 312's territory and are unchanged by 313. Step 3 is where they differ. The slot machinery stays alive in the merged region because tasks are still scheduled across worker threads — a producer on worker 0 and a consumer on worker 1 still need the slot to hand off the value. 313 doesn't collapse parallelism; it just makes the per-call overhead near-zero for in-region calls.\n\n**Order I'd propose for the parallel work:**\n\n1. **246 broadening** ✓ (just landed — the framing now covers same-language user-intervention, not just cross-language ambiguity).\n2. **247 debug-lens** ✓ (drafted, ready for review — can build independently in parallel with everything else).\n3. **312 slice 1** — extend the slot data structure with `ring_native`, `ring_json`, `ring_order`. Touches `src/009-slot-store.{c,h}`. Pure data-structure work, no dispatch or spec changes yet.\n4. **312 slice 2** — extend the `lang_invoke_fn` signature with `input_native[]` / `output_native`. Touches `langs/lang-spec.h` and every spec's stub.\n5. **313 written design** — the issue says the deliverable is a design doc, not code. Pick a small all-Lua graph (`maps/hello`), work out what the merged Lua file looks like, how dispatch identifies \"this is a merged-region call\" and gets the function pointer, how iterator boundaries are handled inside the merge. This is design-thinking work that can happen between 312 slices.\n6. **312 slice 3** — dispatch input-read consults `ring_order`; output-push routes per `output_edge_native[j]`.\n7. **312 slice 4** — Lua spec branches per `input_native[i]`. C / Bash bridges land here too (or in 307/308 — overlapping work).\n8. **313 prototype** — implement the merged-Lua-file path. Now that 312 is real, 313 has a stable foundation to bolt onto.\n\n312 slices 1, 2, 3, 4 are the unblocking core. 313 design can happen in parallel any time; 313 prototype waits for 312 to be in. 247 is fully independent.\n\nWant me to start on 312 slice 1 now? Or take a pass at 313's written design first while you look 246/247 over?"

    "filePath":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/318-sentinel-primitives-in-cross-language-json.md",
    "content":"# 318 — Sentinel primitives in the cross-language JSON wire\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Concept\n\nJSON's structure covers six kinds of value cleanly — object,\narray, number, string, bool, null — and the cross-language ring\nin the dual-ring slot (issue 312) carries JSON for any wire that\ncrosses a language boundary. The structural cases that don't fit\nthose six kinds — Lua closures, libcurl handles, C++ class\ninstances, file handles, function pointers, large byte buffers\nwhere serialization would be expensive — need somewhere to live\nin the JSON ring without forcing the wire format to grow new\ntop-level shapes.\n\n**Sentinel primitives** are JSON object shapes with reserved key\nnames that mean \"this isn't a structural value, it's a reference\nto something the consumer must reconstruct using language-specific\nmachinery.\"\n\nThree kinds, each solving a different structural gap:\n\n```json\n{\"$ref\":              {\"ptr\": \"0x...\",  \"len\": 1048576,\n                       \"type\": \"bytes\"}}\n{\"$function_pointer\": {\"addr\": \"0x...\", \"signature\": \"int(void*,void*)\"}}\n{\"$lang_opaque\":      {\"lang\": \"lua\",   \"tag\": 12345,\n                       \"shape\": \"coroutine\"}}\n```\n\nSentinels are **emitted by the producer's spec** when its language\nhas a value JSON can't represent structurally. They are\n**reconstructed by the consumer's spec** using whatever runtime\nmachinery that language provides (LuaJIT FFI, ctypes for Python,\ndirect cast for C, etc.). Wires whose consumer cannot reconstruct\na sentinel kind **fail at compile time** — the editor catches the\nmismatch when the user wires a function-pointer output into a\nBash input.\n\n## Why these three, not more\n\nThe three sentinels carve up the structural gap by ownership:\n\n- **`$ref`** — bytes in a shared heap. The producer wrote the\n  bytes to the large-value heap (issue 302 / `src/015-large-value-heap.c`)\n  and emits a pointer-and-length reference. The bytes are\n  immutable for the wire's lifetime; refcount tracks consumers.\n  Solves: \"I have a megabyte to share; copying it through the\n  slot would be wasteful.\"\n- **`$function_pointer`** — a callable, identified by a raw\n  address and a signature interpretable in C-function-pointer\n  syntax. The address is process-local. The signature is the\n  contract between producer and consumer. Solves: \"I have a\n  function I want my consumer to be able to call directly.\"\n- **`$lang_opaque`** — a language-private value. The producer\n  tags it with the language name and a worker-private reference\n  the producer's spec can resolve back. Already supported\n  by the large-value heap's refcount, but worth verifying the\n  test coverage when sentinels land.\n- **Sentinel inside sentinel.** A `$ref` whose bytes are\n  themselves JSON containing a `$function_pointer` is legal but\n  weird. Document the recursive case; probably falls out of the\n  walker for free.\n- **Versioning the sentinel format**. The reserved key names\n  (`$ref`, `$function_pointer`, `$lang_opaque`) and the\n  value-object schemas are part of the compile-time contract.\n  Changing them is breaking. Worth a one-line stability note\n  somewhere.\n- **Cross-process `$ref` semantics**. In-process `$ref` is a raw\n  pointer + length. Cross-process (Bash via UDS), the marshaller\n  stages the bytes at the socket boundary. Decide whether the\n  Bash-side `$ref` reconstruction reads from a file path or\n  inlines the bytes in the request. The latter is simpler; the\n  former scales to bigger values.\n",

          "new_string":"For Bash: probably no benefit — Bash is already process-per-call;\nfusing scripts doesn't help much. Skip.\n\n## Relationship to 312 — what stays, what thins\n\n312 defines the **wire format**: dual-ring slots (native ring,\nJSON ring, ordering ring) per input port, per-edge classification\nat graph load, JSON-only-at-borders, native-otherwise. Every\nvalue movement between boxes goes through this machinery.\n\nThis issue's merge thins the **spec invocation overhead** — the\ndlsym + bridge + lua_pcall (or equivalent) that happens once\nper box invocation. For boxes in the merged region, the dispatch\nholds a direct pointer to the function inside the merged module\nand calls it without going through the spec interface.\n\nThe slot machinery stays alive in the merged region. Why:\n**boxes still run as separate thread-pool tasks**. A producer\non worker 0 and a consumer on worker 1 still need slots to hand\noff the value across threads. The thread pool's parallelism\ndepends on tasks being scheduled independently; collapsing\nsame-language hops to synchronous function calls would defeat\nthe pool entirely. The merge wins on the per-call indirection\ncost, not on the wire format.\n\nSo a box invocation inside the merged region looks like:\n\n1. Worker picks up the task.\n2. Dispatch reads inputs from the box's slots (same as 312 —\n   dual-ring native side).\n3. Dispatch jumps to the merged function directly (this is\n   what 313 wins).\n4. Function runs, returns a value.\n5. Dispatch writes output to consumer slots (same as 312).\n\nSteps 2 and 5 are unchanged from 312. Step 3 is the savings.\n\n## Why this is research, not a feature"
        },

    "originalFile":"# 313 — Research: whole-program same-language compilation\n\n## Status\nresearch / low priority / blocked until rest of phase 3 is complete\n\n## Concept\n\nInstead of one box = one function call going through the dispatch\nlayer + slot store + spec invocation, **merge all same-language\nboxes at compile time into a single translation unit** for that\nlanguage. Box-to-box transitions within a language region become\nordinary function calls — the optimizer can inline across them, the\nlanguage runtime stays warm, and the slot store and dispatch layer\ndon't run for those transitions at all. Only cross-language wires\nretain the slot machinery.\n\nFor C: every C box becomes a function in one big `.c` file, with\nthe build emitting one `.so`. Wire endpoints become direct calls;\nthe optimizer inlines based on its usual heuristics.\n\nFor Lua: every Lua function gets pre-compiled into one bytecode\nchunk loaded into one shared `lua_State` per worker. Wire\nendpoints become direct `lua_pcall`s into that chunk — no JSON\nencode/decode, no slot push/pop, no spec re-entry per call.\n\nFor Bash: probably no benefit — Bash is already process-per-call;\nfusing scripts doesn't help much. Skip.\n\n## Why this is research, not a feature\n\nThree open questions that need code-level investigation before\nthe design is concrete:\n\n1. **Loop and iterator boundaries**: a same-language region with an\n   iterator inside it has dynamic re-spawning. Is the iterator\n   merged in (a loop in the generated code) or does it remain a\n   spec-mediated boundary? If the latter, the merge buys less.\n2. **Compile time**: whole-program optimization is slow. Does the\n   incremental-compile model (issue 309's mtime check) still apply,\n   or do edits require a full rebuild of the merged region?\n3. **Debug story**: a stack trace inside the merged region needs to\n   point back to a specific box. Either source-map-style mapping or\n   per-function preserved names — both have costs.\n\nThe right way to answer these is to prototype: take a small all-Lua\ngraph (like the hello map) and see what a merged version looks\nlike, both for runtime cost and for build-system complexity. The\nprototype should be able to fall back to the per-box path if the\nmerge fails for any reason.\n\n## Why blocked until rest of phase 3 completes\n\nThe merge optimization piggybacks on the per-box model — same\nspecs, same compile callback, same dispatch layer for cross-language\nwires. Building it before the per-box model is settled risks\ndesigning against a target that's still moving. After phase 3 ships\nand the per-box path is stable, the merge becomes a clean\n\"everything except spec invocation gets shorter for this region.\"\n\nIt's also genuinely lower priority than getting the runtime working\nat all. The same-language fast path (issue 312) captures the\n~2x JSON-skip win without any of this complexity. The merge wins a\nfurther factor only if profile data shows function-call overhead\nmatters at all after 312 ships.\n\n## Scope of the research output\n\nThe deliverable is a written design (not code) with:\n- Concrete answers to the three questions above.\n- A worked example: the merged C generated from a 5-box C-only\n  graph, showing what the build artifact looks like.\n- Estimated runtime cost of the per-box path vs the merged path\n  on that example.\n- A recommendation: ship as a feature, ship as an opt-in flag, or\n  shelve indefinitely.\n\nAfter the design is reviewed, a separate implementation issue\nopens (or doesn't, depending on the recommendation).\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `issues/312-same-language-wire-fast-path.md` — the immediate JSON-\n  skip win this builds on\n- `issues/307-c-language-spec.md` — `compile` callback that would\n  grow whole-program-aware semantics\n- `issues/306-lua-language-spec.md` — Lua-side bytecode pre-compile\n- `issues/309-build-system.md` — how the merge integrates with the\n  compile/package step\n\n## Open questions (for the research, not for now)\n\n- Cross-language wires inside the merged region: the merged region\n  still has cross-language outputs that exit to other regions. The\n  spec interface still applies at those boundaries, so the merge is\n  region-internal optimization, not a global rearchitecture.\n- C ABI for inlined wrappers: with whole-program optimization the\n  wrapper-per-box generation might collapse to nothing. If the\n  optimizer can prove a wire endpoint is always called from the\n  merged region with known types, it can skip the wrapper.\n- Iterators-with-side-effects: an iterator self-rescheduling its\n  own task is normally dispatch-layer machinery. Inside a merged\n  region, it could become a `while` loop. Whether that's safe\n  depends on whether other tasks are blocked on the iterator's\n  output slots — which they shouldn't be in a same-language region,\n  but the analysis has to confirm.\n",

Skip.\n\n## Relationship to 312 — what stays, what thins\n\n312 defines the **wire format**: dual-ring slots (native ring,\nJSON ring, ordering ring) per input port, per-edge classification\nat graph load, JSON-only-at-borders, native-otherwise. Every\nvalue movement between boxes goes through this machinery.\n\nThis issue's merge thins the **spec invocation overhead** — the\ndlsym + bridge + lua_pcall (or equivalent) that happens once\nper box invocation. For boxes in the merged region, the dispatch\nholds a direct pointer to the function inside the merged module\nand calls it without going through the spec interface.\n\nThe slot machinery stays alive in the merged region. Why:\n**boxes still run as separate thread-pool tasks**. A producer\non worker 0 and a consumer on worker 1 still need slots to hand\noff the value across threads. The thread pool's parallelism\ndepends on tasks being scheduled independently; collapsing\nsame-language hops to synchronous function calls would defeat\nthe pool entirely. The merge wins on the per-call indirection\ncost, not on the wire format.\n\nSo a box invocation inside the merged region looks like:\n\n1. Worker picks up the task.\n2. Dispatch reads inputs from the box's slots (same as 312 —\n   dual-ring native side).\n3. Dispatch jumps to the merged function directly (this is\n   what 313 wins).\n4. Function runs, returns a value.\n5. Dispatch writes output to consumer slots (same as 312).\n\nSteps 2 and 5 are unchanged from 312. Step 3 is the savings.\n\n## Why this is research, not a feature",

        "type":"text",
        "text":"Before I dive into the slot store code — quick API check, since this affects every spec and the dispatch layer downstream.\n\nProposed surface for slice 1:\n\n**New constants in `009-slot-store.h`:**\n```c\nSLOT_FLAG_DUAL_RING   = 1 << 3\nSLOT_RING_NATIVE      = 0\nSLOT_RING_JSON        = 1\n```\n\n**Slot allocation:** existing `slot_alloc(s, cell_capacity, n_cells, flags)` accepts the new flag. When set, the slot internally manages three rings (native, json, order) under one lock. The native ring uses the existing fields (no layout churn for non-dual slots); json and order rings are additional fields that are NULL on non-dual slots.\n\n**New push/pop API:**\n```c\nint     slot_push_native (s, id, data, size, tag);\nint     slot_push_json   (s, id, data, size, tag);\nint32_t slot_pop_ordered (s, id, buf, buf_size, int32_t *out_which_ring);\n```\n\nFor dual-ring slots: `slot_push_native` writes to native ring + ordering tuple under one lock; `slot_push_json` mirrors; `slot_pop_ordered` reads ordering ring first, then the indicated data ring.\n\nFor non-dual slots (backward compat): `slot_push_native` aliases to existing `slot_push`. `slot_push_json` returns -1 (not a dual-ring slot). `slot_pop_ordered` aliases to `slot_pop` and sets `*out_which_ring = SLOT_RING_NATIVE`.\n\nExisting `slot_push` / `slot_pop` continue to work on non-dual slots unchanged. On a dual-ring slot they return -1 (caller must use the dual-aware functions).\n\n**Internal: one lock per slot covers all three rings.** Atomic data + ordering write. No multi-slot races for the dispatch layer to worry about.\n\n**Tests** added for: alloc dual slot, mixed push order preserved on pop, error on calling single-ring API on dual slot, lazy json-ring allocation works.\n\nMatch what you had in mind, or do you want to change anything (naming, ring-ordering encoding, lazy vs. eager allocation)?"
      }]

          "new_string":"/* {{{ Internal slot record */\ntypedef struct slot_rec {\n    uint32_t    cell_capacity;   /* bytes per cell payload (ring slots) */\n    uint32_t    n_cells;         /* ring size (ring slots)              */\n    _Atomic uint32_t head;       /* read index, mod n_cells             */\n    _Atomic uint32_t tail;       /* write index, mod n_cells            */\n    atomic_flag lock;            /* per-slot spinlock for header+cells  */\n    uint32_t    flags;           /* SLOT_FLAG_*                         */\n    uint32_t    cell_record;     /* derived: 4 (+4 if tagged) + cap     */\n\n    /* For atomic-counter slots: a single atomic uint, used by\n     * slot_read_inc.           "new_string":"    /* Acquire the cell-array memory from the unified allocator. Ring\n     * slots take one chunk sized to n_cells * cell_record; atomic\n     * counter slots have no cells and skip this step. The chunk's\n     * refcount starts at 1 — the slot itself owns that reference for\n     * the duration of the run. */\n    if (bytes_cells > 0) {\n        r->cells_chunk = ua_alloc(s->heap, bytes_cells);\n        if (!r->cells_chunk) { free(r); return SLOT_INVALID; }\n        r->cells = ua_data(r->cells_chunk);\n        /* The allocator hands back uninitialized bytes. The cell\n         * header's filled_size must start at zero so empty cells\n         * look empty to peek and pop. */\n        memset(r->cells, 0, bytes_cells);\n    }\n\n    /* Dual-ring slots: allocate the JSON-ring cell array (same shape\n     * as the native cell array) and the ordering ring (8 bytes per\n     * cell). All three rings live in the same unified allocator so\n     * they recycle on slot destroy like every other slot byte. */\n    if (flags & SLOT_FLAG_DUAL_RING) {\n        size_t json_bytes  = (size_t)n_cells * cell_record;\n        size_t order_bytes = (size_t)n_cells * ORDER_CELL_RECORD;\n        r->json_cells_chunk  = ua_alloc(s->heap, json_bytes);\n        if (!r->json_cells_chunk) {\n            if (r->cells_chunk) ua_unref(s->heap, r->cells_chunk);\n            free(r);\n            return SLOT_INVALID;\n        }\n        r->json_cells = ua_data(r->json_cells_chunk);\n        memset(r->json_cells, 0, json_bytes);\n\n        r->order_cells_chunk = ua_alloc(s->heap, order_bytes);\n        if (!r->order_cells_chunk) {\n            ua_unref(s->heap, r->json_cells_chunk);\n            if (r->cells_chunk) ua_unref(s->heap, r->cells_chunk);\n            free(r);\n            return SLOT_INVALID;\n        }\n        r->order_cells = ua_data(r->order_cells_chunk);\n        memset(r->order_cells, 0, order_bytes);\n    }\n\n    if (grow_store_if_needed(s) != 0) {\n        if (r->cells_chunk)       ua_unref(s->heap, r->cells_chunk);\n        if (r->json_cells_chunk)  ua_unref(s->heap, r->json_cells_chunk);\n        if (r->order_cells_chunk) ua_unref(s->heap, r->order_cells_chunk);\n        free(r);\n        return SLOT_INVALID;\n    }\n    slot_id_t id = s->count++;\n    s->slots[id] = r;\n    return id;\n}"

          "new_string":"    if (released_chunk) ua_unref(s->heap, released_chunk);\n\n    return (int32_t)fs;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ Dual-ring helpers (issue 312)\n *\n * The three rings (native data, JSON data, ordering) all live on the\n * same slot_rec and share one lock. A push writes (data cell +\n * ordering entry) under the lock — readers either see both writes or\n * neither.\n *\n * Data-ring cell layout for dual-ring slots is the standard layout\n * minus the tag field (DUAL_RING doesn't combine with TAGGED in\n * slice 1): bytes 0..3 are filled_size, bytes 4.. are payload. The\n * ordering ring uses ORDER_CELL_RECORD (8 bytes — 4 for which_ring,\n * 4 for idx); empty-cell detection is via head/tail, not filled_size.\n *\n * Sizing: all three rings have n_cells cells. The order ring is the\n * binding constraint on total in-flight pushes (n_cells across both\n * data rings combined). Callers that need more pending pushes pass\n * a larger n_cells. */\n\n/* dual_push_locked() — write `data` into the indicated data ring at\n * its tail, write the (which_ring, idx) tuple into the ordering ring\n * at its tail, advance both tails. Caller holds the slot lock.\n * Returns 0 on success, -1 if either ring is full. */\nstatic int dual_push_locked(slot_rec_t *r, int32_t which_ring,\n                            const void *data, int32_t size)\n{\n    _Atomic uint32_t *data_head, *data_tail;\n    uint8_t          *data_cells;\n    if (which_ring == SLOT_RING_NATIVE) {\n        data_head  = &r->head;\n        data_tail  = &r->tail;\n        data_cells = r->cells;\n    } else {\n        data_head  = &r->json_head;\n        data_tail  = &r->json_tail;\n        data_cells = r->json_cells;\n    }\n\n    uint32_t dh = atomic_load_explicit(data_head,     memory_order_relaxed);\n    uint32_t dt = atomic_load_explicit(data_tail,     memory_order_relaxed);\n    uint32_t oh = atomic_load_explicit(&r->order_head, memory_order_relaxed);\n    uint32_t ot = atomic_load_explicit(&r->order_tail, memory_order_relaxed);\n    if (dt - dh >= r->n_cells) return -1;\n    if (ot - oh >= r->n_cells) return -1;\n\n    uint32_t di = dt % r->n_cells;\n    uint8_t *dp = data_cells + (size_t)di * r->cell_record;\n    uint32_t fs = (uint32_t)size;\n    memcpy(dp, &fs, sizeof fs);\n    if (size > 0) memcpy(dp + 4, data, (size_t)size);\n\n    uint32_t oi = ot % r->n_cells;\n    uint8_t *op = r->order_cells + (size_t)oi * ORDER_CELL_RECORD;\n    uint32_t which_u32 = (uint32_t)which_ring;\n    memcpy(op,     &which_u32, sizeof which_u32);\n    memcpy(op + 4, &di,        sizeof di);\n\n    atomic_store_explicit(data_tail,      dt + 1u, memory_order_release);\n    atomic_store_explicit(&r->order_tail, ot + 1u, memory_order_release);\n    return 0;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ slot_push_native() */\nint slot_push_native(slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id,\n                     const void *data, int32_t size, uint32_t tag)\n{\n    slot_rec_t *r = get_slot(s, id);\n    if (!r) return -1;\n\n    /* Non-dual: alias to slot_push.       "content":"static int test_pop_fifo_ncell(void)\n{\n    slot_store_t *s = slot_store_create();\n    slot_id_t id = slot_alloc(s, 8, 4, SLOT_FLAG_NONE);\n    ASSERT(id != SLOT_INVALID);\n\n    const char *vals[] = {\"a\", \"bb\", \"ccc\", \"dddd\"};\n    for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) {\n        ASSERT(slot_push(s, id, vals[i], (int)strlen(vals[i]), 0) == 0);\n    }\n    ASSERT(slot_fill_count(s, id) == 4);\n    /* Ring full — fifth push should fail. */\n    ASSERT(slot_push(s, id, \"eeeee\", 5, 0) == -1);\n\n    char buf[16];\n    for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) {\n        memset(buf, 0, sizeof buf);\n        int32_t got = slot_pop(s, id, buf, sizeof buf);\n        ASSERT(got == (int32_t)strlen(vals[i]));\n        ASSERT(memcmp(buf, vals[i], (size_t)got) == 0);\n    }\n    /* Empty — pop fails. */\n    ASSERT(slot_pop(s, id, buf, sizeof buf) == -1);\n    ASSERT(slot_has_value(s, id) == 0);\n\n    /* Push again after drain — wrap-around. */\n    ASSERT(slot_push(s, id, \"wrap\", 4, 0) == 0);\n    ASSERT(slot_pop(s, id, buf, sizeof buf) == 4);\n    ASSERT(memcmp(buf, \"wrap\", 4) == 0);\n\n    slot_store_destroy(s);\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ test_buf_too_small() */\nstatic int test_buf_too_small(void)\n{\n    slot_store_t *s = slot_store_create();\n    slot_id_t id = slot_alloc(s, 16, 1, SLOT_FLAG_NONE);"

          "old_string":"What's in place:\n\n- `lang_spec_t` carries `invoke_native`, `invoke_json`,\n  `native_to_json`, `json_to_native` slots (current shape — to be\n  collapsed to a single `invoke` with per-input/per-output flags\n  per this issue).\n- Lua's `native_to_json` and `json_to_native` are real\n  (`langs/lua/spec.c:335` and `:437`).\n- `input_edge_native[]` and `output_edge_native[]` are computed at\n  graph load (`src/010-graph-loader.c:689-754`).\n- Per-box `use_native_invoke` summary is computed and consulted by\n  dispatch — to be removed.\n- Single-ring slot store (`src/009-slot-store.c`).\n\nWhat's still ahead:\n\n- Dual-ring slot shape (this issue's core).\n- Spec `invoke` signature extension (`input_native[]`,\n  `output_native`).\n- Dispatch reads from the ordering ring; push selects ring based\n  on `output_edge_native[j]`.\n- C and Bash bridges, plus native byte formats per language.\n- Removal of `use_native_invoke`.",
          "new_string":"What's in place:\n\n- `lang_spec_t` carries `invoke_native`, `invoke_json`,\n  `native_to_json`, `json_to_native` slots (current shape — to be\n  collapsed to a single `invoke` with per-input/per-output flags\n  per this issue).\n- Lua's `native_to_json` and `json_to_native` are real\n  (`langs/lua/spec.c:335` and `:437`).\n- `input_edge_native[]` and `output_edge_native[]` are computed at\n  graph load (`src/010-graph-loader.c:689-754`).\n- Per-box `use_native_invoke` summary is computed and consulted by\n  dispatch — to be removed.\n- **Slice 1 complete (2026-05-21).** Dual-ring slot data structure\n  in `src/009-slot-store.{c,h}`: `SLOT_FLAG_DUAL_RING`,\n  `SLOT_RING_NATIVE` / `SLOT_RING_JSON` constants, three internal\n  rings per slot (native data, JSON data, ordering) under one\n  per-slot spinlock, new API `slot_push_native`, `slot_push_json`,\n  `slot_pop_ordered`. Single per-slot lock makes the data+ordering\n  write atomic so consumers see push pairs intact. On non-dual\n  slots `slot_push_native` and `slot_pop_ordered` alias to the\n  existing `slot_push` / `slot_pop`; `slot_push_json` returns -1.\n  On dual slots the old single-ring API returns -1 (caller must\n  pick a ring). `slot_has_value` and `slot_fill_count` consult\n  the ordering ring on dual slots so spawn-on-input-ready and\n  test introspection still work. Five new tests in\n  `tests/009-slot-store-test.c` cover the happy paths\n  (native-only, mixed arrival order, wraparound), the\n  order-ring-as-binding-capacity-constraint, and the back-compat\n  cases.\n\nWhat's still ahead:\n\n- **Slice 2** — Spec `invoke` signature extension\n  (`input_native[]`, `output_native`). Touches\n  `langs/lang-spec.h` and every spec stub.\n- **Slice 3** — Dispatch reads from the ordering ring; push\n  selects ring based on `output_edge_native[j]`. Touches\n  `src/012-dispatch.c`.\n- **Slice 4** — Lua spec branches per `input_native[i]`. C and\n  Bash bridges land in 307 / 308 alongside this.\n- **Slice 5** — Remove the per-box `use_native_invoke` field and\n  its computation now that the dispatch consults per-cell."
        },
        "caller":{
          "type":"direct"
        },
        "id":"toolu_014pPkv5yhNZDM2AFTeScxDS"
      }]
  },

    "originalFile":"/* langs/lang-spec.h — public interface for SoraMech language specs.\n *\n * What it is, in a sentence: the C contract that every language\n * spec (Lua, C, Bash, anything user-added) implements. The pool\n * runner discovers specs by dlopen()ing langs/<name>/spec.so at\n * startup and reading the exported soramech_lang_spec symbol.\n *\n * Designed in issue 303. The init barrier (issue 301) calls init()\n * for every spec on every worker before unblocking task dispatch;\n * the dispatch action (issue 304) calls invoke() per task; the\n * compile-button pipeline (issue 309) calls compile() per source\n * file for languages whose compile pointer is non-NULL.\n *\n * Errors: a nonzero return from any callback is fatal. The dispatch\n * layer prints the error context and aborts. There is no recovery,\n * no retry, no per-task failed state. This is intentional.\n *\n * Issue 312 extends this contract with optional fast-path\n * callbacks: `invoke_native` and `invoke_json` are specialised\n * variants the dispatch layer prefers when wire classification\n * says they apply; `native_to_json` and `json_to_native` are\n * bridges used at language boundaries. Specs that don't set them\n * fall back to `invoke` for every call.\n */\n\n#ifndef SORAMECH_LANG_SPEC_H\n#define SORAMECH_LANG_SPEC_H\n\n#include <stddef.h>\n\n#ifdef __cplusplus\nextern \"C\" {\n#endif\n\n/* {{{ Shared signatures */\n/* Invoke signature — shared by `invoke`, `invoke_native`, and\n * `invoke_json`. The dispatch layer picks which one to call based\n * on the wire-format classification in issue 312. */\ntypedef int (*lang_invoke_fn)(void *handle,\n                              const char *file_path,\n                              const char *fn_name,\n                              const void **input_data,\n                              const int   *input_sizes,\n                              int          n_inputs,\n                              void        *out_buf,\n                              int          out_buf_capacity,\n                              int         *out_size);\n\n/* Wire-format bridge: convert one direction of native ↔ JSON.\n * Used when a value crosses a language boundary. Spec sets one\n * or both; if NULL, the dispatch layer treats native and JSON as\n * identical byte streams (the current uniform-byte default).\n *\n * `handle` is the worker's per-language handle (the same one\n * `invoke` receives) — bridges may need it to reach a runtime-side\n * scratch area: Lua reads/writes via the lua_State stack, C may\n * keep a typed-pointer table, Bash may need its sub-process. Specs\n * that don't need it ignore the argument.\n *\n * Stack-protocol convention for `native_to_json`: the producer\n * leaves its native value on top of its runtime's working store\n * (Lua: top of stack); the bridge consumes it. For `json_to_native`:\n * the bridge pushes the reconstructed value onto the same store.\n * `src` / `dst` carry only the JSON side. */\ntypedef int (*lang_bridge_fn)(void *handle,\n                              const void *src, int src_size,\n                              void *dst, int dst_capacity, int *dst_size);\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ lang_spec_t */\ntypedef struct lang_spec {\n    const char *name;       /* \"lua\", \"bash\", \"c\", \"python\", ... */\n    const char *file_ext;   /* \".lua\", \".sh\", \".c\", \".py\"        */\n\n    /* init: once per worker thread at pool startup.     "originalFile":"/* langs/c/spec.c — C language spec for SoraMech.\n *\n * Per-worker handle is a small dlopen cache. `compile` runs gcc\n * to turn a box source file into a .so; `invoke` dlopens the .so\n * (caching the handle), dlsyms the named function, and calls it\n * through a fixed signature.\n *\n * Designed in issue 307. C box functions follow a single\n * convention that matches the spec's `invoke` shape minus the\n * per-worker handle:\n *\n *     int box_fn(const void **inputs, const int *sizes, int n,\n *                void *out_buf, int out_capacity, int *out_size);\n *\n * Return 0 on success, nonzero (fatal) on failure. This iteration\n * does not generate per-box wrappers from declared signatures\n * (issue 307's optional advanced mode) — every C box uses the\n * fixed signature above. Wrapper generation can land as a follow-on\n * once we have a box whose declared types diverge from the byte-\n * array shape.\n */\n\n#include \"lang-spec.h\"\n\n#include <dlfcn.h>\n#include <stdio.h>\n#include <stdlib.h>\n#include <string.h>\n#include <sys/wait.h>\n#include <unistd.h>\n\n#define C_CACHE_SIZE 32\n\n/* {{{ Per-worker dlopen cache */\ntypedef struct {\n    char *path;     /* strdup'd; identifies the cache entry         */\n    void *dl;       /* dlopen handle                                */\n} c_cache_entry_t;\n\ntypedef struct {\n    c_cache_entry_t entries[C_CACHE_SIZE];\n    int             count;\n} c_handle_t;\n\ntypedef int (*c_box_fn_t)(const void **inputs, const int *sizes, int n,\n                          void *out_buf, int out_capacity, int *out_size);\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ c_init() */\nstatic void *c_init(int worker_idx)\n{\n    (void)worker_idx;\n    c_handle_t *h = calloc(1, sizeof *h);\n    return h;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ c_teardown() */\nstatic void c_teardown(void *handle)\n{\n    if (!handle) return;\n    c_handle_t *h = (c_handle_t *)handle;\n    for (int i = 0; i < h->count; i++) {\n        if (h->entries[i].dl) dlclose(h->entries[i].dl);\n        free(h->entries[i].path);\n    }\n    free(h);\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ c_compile() — gcc -shared -fPIC */\nstatic int c_compile(const char *src_path, const char *out_path)\n{\n    if (!src_path || !out_path) return -1;\n    pid_t pid = fork();\n    if (pid < 0) return -1;\n    if (pid == 0) {\n        /* Child: replace ourselves with gcc. */\n        execlp(\"gcc\", \"gcc\",\n               \"-shared\", \"-fPIC\", \"-O2\", \"-Wall\",\n               \"-o\", out_path, src_path, (char *)NULL);\n        _exit(127);\n    }\n    int status = 0;\n    if (waitpid(pid, &status, 0) < 0) return -1;\n    if (!WIFEXITED(status) || WEXITSTATUS(status) != 0) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"c spec: gcc failed for '%s' → '%s' (status=%d)\\n\",\n                src_path, out_path, status);\n        return -1;\n    }\n    return 0;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ ends_in_dot_c() */\nstatic int ends_in_dot_c(const char *p)\n{\n    size_t n = strlen(p);\n    return n >= 2 && p[n - 2] == '.' && p[n - 1] == 'c';\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ hash_path() — small DJB2-like hash for deriving cache filenames */\nstatic unsigned long hash_path(const char *p)\n{\n    unsigned long h = 5381;\n    for (; *p; p++) h = h * 33u + (unsigned char)*p;\n    return h;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ maybe_lazy_compile() — if file_path is a .c source, compile it\n * to a /tmp .so and return that path; otherwise return file_path\n * unchanged. The output buffer is the caller-supplied so_buf. */\nstatic const char *maybe_lazy_compile(const char *file_path,\n                                      char *so_buf, size_t so_cap)\n{\n    if (!ends_in_dot_c(file_path)) return file_path;\n    /* Hash the source path so repeat opens of the same source file\n     * pick up the same .so. Concurrent invokes will race on gcc but\n     * the inputs are identical, so the output converges. */\n    unsigned long h = hash_path(file_path);\n    int n = snprintf(so_buf, so_cap, \"/tmp/soramech-c-%lx.so\", h);\n    if (n < 0 || (size_t)n >= so_cap) return NULL;\n    if (c_compile(file_path, so_buf) != 0) return NULL;\n    return so_buf;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ get_or_load() — find a cached .so or dlopen and add */\nstatic void *get_or_load(c_handle_t *h, const char *path)\n{\n    for (int i = 0; i < h->count; i++) {\n        if (strcmp(h->entries[i].path, path) == 0) return h->entries[i].dl;\n    }\n    if (h->count >= C_CACHE_SIZE) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"c spec: dlopen cache full (%d entries)\\n\", C_CACHE_SIZE);\n        return NULL;\n    }\n    void *dl = dlopen(path, RTLD_NOW | RTLD_LOCAL);\n    if (!dl) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"c spec: dlopen('%s'): %s\\n\", path, dlerror());\n        return NULL;\n    }\n    h->entries[h->count].path = strdup(path);\n    h->entries[h->count].dl   = dl;\n    h->count++;\n    return dl;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ c_invoke() */\nstatic int c_invoke(void *handle,\n                    const char  *file_path,    /* path to a .so */\n                    const char  *fn_name,\n                    const void **input_data,\n                    const int   *input_sizes,\n                    int          n_inputs,\n                    void        *out_buf,\n                    int          out_capacity,\n                    int         *out_size)\n{\n    c_handle_t *h = (c_handle_t *)handle;\n    if (!h || !file_path || !fn_name) return -1;\n\n    /* If a graph passed a .c source path, build a /tmp .so for it on\n     * the fly and proceed with that. */\n    char so_buf[4096];\n    const char *to_open = maybe_lazy_compile(file_path, so_buf, sizeof so_buf);\n    if (!to_open) return -1;\n    void *dl = get_or_load(h, to_open);\n    if (!dl) return -1;\n\n    /* dlsym returns void*, but the cast to a function pointer is\n     * formally implementation-defined;     "stop_reason":"tool_use",
