      "iterations":[{
          "type":"message",
          "output_tokens":9297,
          "cache_creation_input_tokens":893,
          "cache_read_input_tokens":348980,
          "input_tokens":6,
          "cache_creation":{
            "ephemeral_5m_input_tokens":0,
            "ephemeral_1h_input_tokens":893
          }
        }],
      "speed":"standard",
      "server_tool_use":{
        "web_search_requests":0,
        "web_fetch_requests":0
      },
      "cache_read_input_tokens":348980,
      "input_tokens":6,
      "output_tokens":9297
    },
    "content":[{
        "type":"tool_use",
        "name":"Write",
        "input":{
          "content":"# 248 — Encapsulated map as box\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Concept\n\nA map directory is normally opened via the map-select UI as the\ntop-level graph being edited. **This issue adds a second way to\nopen a map:** through the file browser, as an *encapsulated box*\non the currently-edited parent map. The opened map becomes a\nsingle box on the parent's canvas. Its inputs come from input\nports inside the sub-map that have been marked as\nexternally-supplied; its outputs come from the sub-map's\n`write` boxes, packed into a single byte-blob with a leading\nsize index.\n\nEncapsulation is a function-like abstraction over a sub-graph.\nThe parent doesn't see the sub-map's internals; it sees one box\nwith declared input ports, declared output ports, and known\nsemantics. The sub-map can be edited independently, reused across\nparent maps, and packaged once for distribution.\n\n## Marked input ports inside the sub-map\n\nA box inside the sub-map can be marked as **externally-supplied**\nvia a small toggle (a slider, in the same visual vocabulary as\nissue 239's literal-port nodule) on one of its input ports.\nToggling a port's slider declares: \"this port accepts its value\nfrom the encapsulating box's matching input, not from a wire\ninternal to this map.\"\n\nThe toggle records the port's binding kind on the box JSON:\n\n```json\n{\n    \"id\": \"sum_input\",\n    \"kind\": \"read\",\n    \"external\": {\n        \"kind\": \"named\",            // or \"positional\" / \"numbered\"\n        \"name\": \"count\",            // for named\n        \"index\": 0                  // for positional / numbered\n    },\n    \"...\": \"...\"\n}\n```\n\nThree binding kinds capture how the encapsulating box's input\nmaps to this internal port:\n\n- **`positional`** — bound by argument order. The encapsulating\n  box has N input ports; the *k*th port's value flows to the\n  internal box whose `external.index` is *k*. Conceptually\n  matches positional function arguments.\n- **`numbered`** — bound by an explicit integer index. Same shape\n  as positional but the user picks the number (so they can leave\n  gaps, reorder freely, etc.).\n- **`named`** — bound by a string name. The encapsulating box's\n  input port has a label; the matching internal box's\n  `external.name` is the same string.\n\nA single sub-map can mix kinds across its marked boxes — some\npositional, some named — and the parent map's encapsulated box\nexposes the union as its input ports.\n\n## Output collection from `write` boxes\n\nThe sub-map's `write` boxes (issue 229's file-write kind) become\nthe encapsulating box's output ports. Each `write` box's `value`\ninput feeds an output slot of the encapsulating box. The boxes\nkeep their normal disk-write behaviour (they write the file as a\nside effect) AND emit the value upward as the encapsulating\nbox's output.\n\nIf the sub-map has N write boxes, the encapsulating box has one\noutput wire carrying a packed byte-blob with all N values.\n\n### Packed output format\n\n```\n+-----------------------------------------------+\n| size[0] | size[1] | ... | size[N-1] | 0       |   ← size index\n+-----------------------------------------------+\n| data[0] (size[0] bytes)                       |\n+-----------------------------------------------+\n| data[1] (size[1] bytes)                       |\n+-----------------------------------------------+\n| ...                                           |\n+-----------------------------------------------+\n| data[N-1] (size[N-1] bytes)                   |\n+-----------------------------------------------+\n```\n\nEach `size[i]` is a 4-byte unsigned little-endian integer. The\nsize array is **NULL-terminated** with a trailing zero, so a\nreader can walk it without knowing N up front. Data sections\nimmediately follow the size index, packed end-to-end with no\npadding.\n\nTo read field *i*:\n\n```\nsize_array_bytes = (i_count + 1) * 4     // includes terminator\noffset = size_array_bytes + sum(size[0..i-1])\ndata_i = blob[offset .. offset + size[i]]\n```\n\nThis is a self-describing format. The parent map can pull out\nindividual fields with the offset arithmetic, or pass the whole\nblob downstream and let further consumers slice it. A small\nhelper library (probably `libs/encap-output.{lua,c}`) packages\nthe unpack logic so consumers don't have to write the\narithmetic themselves.\n\n## File layout in the parent map\n\nThe parent map's directory grows a reference to the sub-map. The\nsub-map itself lives wherever the user put it — somewhere on\ndisk reachable by a path. Options for the reference:\n\n```json\n{\n    \"id\": \"stats_pipeline\",\n    \"kind\": \"map\",\n    \"ref\": \"../shared-maps/stats-pipeline\",     // path to sub-map dir\n    \"...\": \"...\"\n}\n```\n\nA new box kind, `map`, parallels the existing `call` / `read` /\n`write` / `data` kinds. The graph loader resolves the `ref`\npath, loads the sub-map's graph, validates that the sub-map's\nmarked input ports match the parent's wiring expectations, and\nattaches it.\n\nThe sub-map's input ports (derived from its marked internal\nboxes) are exposed on the encapsulating box's JSON as a normal\n`inputs` array. The user doesn't write that array themselves —\nthe editor generates it from the sub-map on first encapsulation\nand re-syncs it when the sub-map changes.\n\n## Editor UI\n\n### File browser\n\nThe file browser (issue 207's source-file-browser, or its\ndescendant) shows map directories with a distinct icon — a\nfolder-like glyph annotated to suggest \"this is a runnable\ngraph, not a source file.\" Clicking opens a small menu:\n\n- **Edit this map** — switches the editor's active map (the\n  existing map-select behaviour).\n- **Encapsulate** — adds the map as a `kind: \"map\"` box to the\n  currently-edited parent map. The new box appears on the\n  canvas at the cursor position; the user wires it in like any\n  other box.\n\n### Input-port slider\n\nThe inspector for any input port (on read / data / write boxes)\ngrows a small toggle next to the port name:\n\n```\n  ┌─────────────────────────────┐\n  │ count   [● external]        │ ← toggle on, port is externally-bound\n  │   kind:    named            │\n  │   name:    \"count\"          │\n  └─────────────────────────────┘\n```\n\nWhen the toggle is on, the inspector reveals the kind selector\n(positional / numbered / named) and the name / index field.\nWhen off, the port behaves normally (wires-in or literal-value).\n\nA map with no marked inputs encapsulates to a no-input box (just\na source of write-box outputs). A map with no write boxes\nencapsulates to a box with no output (side-effecting only —\nunusual but legal).\n\n### Visual on the canvas\n\nThe encapsulating box renders distinctly — different border,\nmaybe a small \"sub-map\" badge — so the user sees at a glance\nthat this isn't a leaf call. Hovering shows the sub-map's name\nand a small thumbnail of its graph.\n\n## Runtime model\n\nTwo implementation paths exist; pick after prototyping.\n\n**A. Compile-time inlining.** At compile (issue 309), the\nencapsulating box is replaced by its sub-graph: every internal\nbox gets a prefixed id (`<encap_id>__<internal_id>`), every\ninternal wire stays internal, marked-input boxes get their\nexternal bindings hooked to the parent's incoming wires, and\nwrite boxes get their outputs hooked into the packing-into-blob\nmachinery. Runtime sub-graph dispatch.** The graph loader builds the\nsub-map as a child graph, and the encapsulating box's task\nspawns a sub-run that drives the child graph to quiescence,\ncollects its write-box outputs, packs them, and emits. The\nchild runs on the same thread pool — its tasks are just normal\npool tasks distinguished by their box-id namespace.\n\nCompile-time inlining is the cleaner design for performance and\ndebugging (one flat task pool, no recursion in the dispatch\nlayer). Runtime sub-graph dispatch is the more flexible design\nfor hot-reload and dynamic linking (the parent doesn't need to\nrecompile when the sub-map changes). The prototype picks one;\nthe alternative remains an open question until profile data\njustifies the choice.\n\nRecursion (a sub-map encapsulates another sub-map) falls out of\neither path naturally — inlining recurses through; runtime\ndispatch recurses through. Cycles between maps are a compile-time\nerror.\n\n## Relationship to existing issues\n\n- **Issue 207 (source-file-browser)** — the file browser is the\n  entry point for the \"encapsulate\" action.\n- **Issue 239 (literal port shrinks to nodule)** — the\n  external-input slider reuses the same visual idiom on the\n  input-port row.\n- **Issue 229 (data box as language-agnostic file IO)** — the\n  write boxes whose outputs become the encapsulating box's\n  output ports are already specified by that issue. No change\n  needed to the write box itself; the encapsulation observes\n  its emitted value.\n- **Issue 309 (build system / compile pipeline)** — the\n  compile-time inlining path (option A above) extends the\n  pipeline with an \"encapsulation expansion\" step.\n- **Issue 313 (whole-program same-language merge)** — composes\n  with compile-time inlining; the inlined sub-graph's same-\n  language regions merge into the parent's merge as if they\n  were always part of one map.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — box state, the `kind: \"map\"` box,\n  the per-input-port external-binding state.\n- `assets/js/005-app.js` — file browser; menu with Edit /\n  Encapsulate actions.\n- `assets/index.html` — inspector UI for the external-binding\n  toggle.\n- `src/006-server-main.lua` — HTTP backend; resolving sub-map\n  paths, validating bindings.\n- `src/010-graph-loader.{c,h}` — graph loader; recognise\n  `kind: \"map\"`, resolve the sub-map, build the encapsulated\n  shape.\n- `src/012-dispatch.c` — encapsulating-box dispatch (runtime\n  path) or compile-time expansion (compile path).\n- `scripts/soramech-compile.sh` — encapsulation expansion if the\n  compile-time path wins.\n- `libs/encap-output.{lua,c}` — packed-output unpacker library\n  for downstream consumers.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. **Box JSON schema**: add `kind: \"map\"`, the `ref` field, and\n   the per-input `external` block. Graph loader rejects with a\n   clear error if any field is missing where required.\n2. **External-input slider UI**: inspector toggle on input ports;\n   kind / name / index selectors when on.\n3. **File browser \"Encapsulate\" action**: adds a `kind: \"map\"`\n   box to the parent at the cursor position. Reads the sub-map's\n   marked inputs and write boxes to populate the new box's\n   `inputs` and `outputs` arrays.\n4. **Graph loader sub-map resolution**: load the sub-map's\n   `meta.json` and `boxes/`; record its marked-input and\n   write-box lists on the parent box record.\n5. **Packed-output format**: implement the size-index +\n   data-section serializer at the encapsulation boundary. Add a\n   small unpacker library for parent-side consumers.\n6. **Pick A or B**: compile-time inlining or runtime sub-graph\n   dispatch. Prototype the simpler of the two end-to-end on a\n   trivial sub-map (`maps/encap-trivial`).\n7. **Recursion**: nested encapsulation; cycle detection at\n   compile (or load) time.\n8. **Editor visualization**: distinct canvas rendering for\n   encapsulating boxes; tooltip / thumbnail.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Sub-map identity for the editor**: when the parent\n  encapsulates `maps/<sub>`, what happens if the user later\n  renames or moves `<sub>`? The reference path is brittle.\n  Options: store a stable id in the sub-map's `meta.json` and\n  reference that, plus a path hint; or require the sub-map to\n  live inside the parent's map directory tree.\n- **Re-sync behaviour when the sub-map changes**: if the user\n  edits the sub-map and changes its marked inputs, the parent's\n  encapsulating box's `inputs` array drifts out of date. The encapsulating\n  box has N input ports; the *k*th port's value flows to the\n  internal box whose `external.index` is *k*. Conceptually\n  matches positional function arguments.\n- **`numbered`** — bound by an explicit integer index. {
  "timestamp":"2026-05-22T00:05:57.536Z",
  "message":{
    "content":"let's continue on to slice 3 of 312.\n\nalso can we create an issue file to enable \"tap input mode\" which changes the method that you attach wires. First you have to click on the box (or tap), and then it shows a radial menu of break-out bubbles that are easier to tap on than a small port in the box view or inspector. If you tap one of the bubbles, it'll open the port menu for it - if you drag it to another port, it'll connect them with a wire.\n\nwe can also remove the titles of the boxes, and replace them with 4 emojis that the user can select and set. if they tap the box, then it'll show the actual name.\n\nif we wanted to be extra fancy, we could run a word embedding calculation on the title of the box (it's filename and function concatenated together) and then cosine similarity check that embedding value to each of the embeddings of each of the emojis in the game. Then we could auto-generate a 4 character name for each box that'd... sorta work, and the user can correct if they want.\n\n  1. New box kind map alongside the existing call / read / write / data. The encapsulating box's JSON references a sub-map by path and the\n  loader resolves it.\n\nno it's just a normal call box from the perspective of the editor. Behind the scenes, we're treating it a bit different, but only because it's a specialized type of file format that needs some processing in order to read.\n\n  2. The slider is per-input-port, not per-box, and lives on read (or any) boxes inside the sub-map. Three binding kinds — positional /\n  numbered / named — captured in an external block on the port.\n\nactually what if we made it an option on the data_read boxes? that way we don't clutter the menu for the rest of the functions. we can store each command line argument in shared memory and then treat it like a value to be pointed to as an example of excellence.\n\n  5. Compile-time inlining vs. runtime sub-graph dispatch is left as an open question with both paths sketched. Compile-time inlining\n  composes more cleanly with 313's same-language merge; runtime dispatch is more flexible for hot-reload. Prototype picks one.\n\nI'd need to see a more expansive explanation of this one before I could weigh in on it.",

Each `write` box's `value`\n70\tinput feeds an output slot of the encapsulating box. The boxes\n71\tkeep their normal disk-write behaviour (they write the file as a\n72\tside effect) AND emit the value upward as the encapsulating\n73\tbox's output.\n74\t\n75\tIf the sub-map has N write boxes, the encapsulating box has one\n76\toutput wire carrying a packed byte-blob with all N values.\n77\t\n78\t### Packed output format\n79\t\n80\t```\n81\t+-----------------------------------------------+\n82\t| size[0] | size[1] | ... | size[N-1] | 0       |   ← size index\n83\t+-----------------------------------------------+\n84\t| data[0] (size[0] bytes)                       |\n85\t+-----------------------------------------------+\n86\t| data[1] (size[1] bytes)                       |\n87\t+-----------------------------------------------+\n88\t| ...                                           |\n89\t+-----------------------------------------------+\n90\t| data[N-1] (size[N-1] bytes)                   |\n91\t+-----------------------------------------------+\n92\t```\n93\t\n94\tEach `size[i]` is a 4-byte unsigned little-endian integer. The\n95\tsize array is **NULL-terminated** with a trailing zero, so a\n96\treader can walk it without knowing N up front. Data sections\n97\timmediately follow the size index, packed end-to-end with no\n98\tpadding.\n99\t\n100\tTo read field *i*:\n101\t\n102\t```\n103\tsize_array_bytes = (i_count + 1) * 4     // includes terminator\n104\toffset = size_array_bytes + sum(size[0..i-1])\n105\tdata_i = blob[offset .. offset + size[i]]\n106\t```\n107\t\n108\tThis is a self-describing format. The parent map can pull out\n109\tindividual fields with the offset arithmetic, or pass the whole\n110\tblob downstream and let further consumers slice it. A small\n111\thelper library (probably `libs/encap-output.{lua,c}`) packages\n112\tthe unpack logic so consumers don't have to write the\n113\tarithmetic themselves.\n114\t\n115\t## File layout in the parent map\n116\t\n117\tThe parent map's directory grows a reference to the sub-map. The\n118\tsub-map itself lives wherever the user put it — somewhere on\n119\tdisk reachable by a path. Options for the reference:\n120\t\n121\t```json\n122\t{\n123\t    \"id\": \"stats_pipeline\",\n124\t    \"kind\": \"map\",\n125\t    \"ref\": \"../shared-maps/stats-pipeline\",     // path to sub-map dir\n126\t    \"...\": \"...\"\n127\t}\n128\t```\n129\t\n130\tA new box kind, `map`, parallels the existing `call` / `read` /\n131\t`write` / `data` kinds. The graph loader resolves the `ref`\n132\tpath, loads the sub-map's graph, validates that the sub-map's\n133\tmarked input ports match the parent's wiring expectations, and\n134\tattaches it.\n135\t\n136\tThe sub-map's input ports (derived from its marked internal\n137\tboxes) are exposed on the encapsulating box's JSON as a normal\n138\t`inputs` array. The user doesn't write that array themselves —\n139\tthe editor generates it from the sub-map on first encapsulation\n140\tand re-syncs it when the sub-map changes.\n141\t\n142\t## Editor UI\n143\t\n144\t### File browser\n145\t\n146\tThe file browser (issue 207's source-file-browser, or its\n147\tdescendant) shows map directories with a distinct icon — a\n148\tfolder-like glyph annotated to suggest \"this is a runnable\n149\tgraph, not a source file.\" Clicking opens a small menu:",

          "old_string":"## Marked input ports inside the sub-map\n\nA box inside the sub-map can be marked as **externally-supplied**\nvia a small toggle (a slider, in the same visual vocabulary as\nissue 239's literal-port nodule) on one of its input ports.\nToggling a port's slider declares: \"this port accepts its value\nfrom the encapsulating box's matching input, not from a wire\ninternal to this map.\"\n\nThe toggle records the port's binding kind on the box JSON:\n\n```json\n{\n    \"id\": \"sum_input\",\n    \"kind\": \"read\",\n    \"external\": {\n        \"kind\": \"named\",            // or \"positional\" / \"numbered\"\n        \"name\": \"count\",            // for named\n        \"index\": 0                  // for positional / numbered\n    },\n    \"...\": \"...\"\n}\n```",
          "new_string":"## Marked input ports inside the sub-map\n\nA **data** box inside the sub-map (kind: `data`, the existing\nlanguage-agnostic file-IO source) can be marked as\n**externally-supplied** via a small toggle on the box's\ninspector. Toggling declares: \"this data box's value comes from\nthe encapsulating context, not from its `path` or `value`\nfield.\"\n\nThe toggle is intentionally scoped to `data` boxes — those are\nthe natural entry points for external values into a map. Call\nboxes / read boxes / write boxes don't carry the toggle, which\nkeeps the inspector uncluttered for the common cases. Each\nexternal input becomes a small shared-memory chunk seeded by\nthe encapsulating call's invoke; the marked data box reads from\nthat chunk on each fire, treating it identically to a value\nloaded from disk.\n\nThe toggle records the port's binding kind on the box JSON:\n\n```json\n{\n    \"id\": \"sum_input\",\n    \"kind\": \"data\",\n    \"external\": {\n        \"kind\": \"named\",            // or \"positional\" / \"numbered\"\n        \"name\": \"count\",            // for named\n        \"index\": 0                  // for positional / numbered\n    },\n    \"...\": \"...\"\n}\n```"
        },

        },

          "old_string":"## File layout in the parent map\n\nThe parent map's directory grows a reference to the sub-map. The\nsub-map itself lives wherever the user put it — somewhere on\ndisk reachable by a path. Options for the reference:\n\n```json\n{\n    \"id\": \"stats_pipeline\",\n    \"kind\": \"map\",\n    \"ref\": \"../shared-maps/stats-pipeline\",     // path to sub-map dir\n    \"...\": \"...\"\n}\n```\n\nA new box kind, `map`, parallels the existing `call` / `read` /\n`write` / `data` kinds. The graph loader resolves the `ref`\npath, loads the sub-map's graph, validates that the sub-map's\nmarked input ports match the parent's wiring expectations, and\nattaches it.\n\nThe sub-map's input ports (derived from its marked internal\nboxes) are exposed on the encapsulating box's JSON as a normal\n`inputs` array. The user doesn't write that array themselves —\nthe editor generates it from the sub-map on first encapsulation\nand re-syncs it when the sub-map changes.",
          "new_string":"## File layout in the parent map\n\n**The encapsulating box is a normal `call` box.** From the\neditor's perspective it has the same JSON shape as any other\ncall box — `kind: \"call\"`, `lang`, `ref`, `fn`, `inputs`,\n`connections`, `routing`. What makes it an encapsulation is\nthat its `lang` is `map` and its `ref` points to a sub-map\ndirectory rather than a source file. The map-language spec\n(`langs/map/spec.so`) is responsible for the \"behind the\nscenes\" processing — running the sub-graph and packing the\noutputs.\n\n```json\n{\n    \"id\": \"stats_pipeline\",\n    \"kind\": \"call\",\n    \"lang\": \"map\",\n    \"ref\": \"../shared-maps/stats-pipeline\",\n    \"fn\": null,                                  // unused for map kind\n    \"inputs\": [\n        { \"name\": \"count\", \"type\": \"int\" },\n        { \"name\": \"label\", \"type\": \"string\" }\n    ],\n    \"...\": \"...\"\n}\n```\n\nThe map-language spec is registered in the spec registry the\nsame way `lua` / `c` / `bash` are. Its `file_ext` is `.map`\n(or no extension if the ref points to a directory). The graph\nloader resolves the `ref`, the map spec's `init` (per worker)\nloads the sub-graph, and its `invoke` runs the sub-graph and\npacks the outputs. From the dispatch layer's view, an\nencapsulating call is just another spec invocation.\n\nThe sub-map's input ports (derived from its marked data boxes)\nare exposed on the encapsulating box's JSON as a normal\n`inputs` array. The user doesn't write that array themselves —\nthe editor generates it from the sub-map on first encapsulation\nand re-syncs it when the sub-map changes."
        },
        "caller":{
          "type":"direct"
        },
        "id":"toolu_012cLbkHyCrqtin4NiGhzgh6"
      }]
  },

A map with no write boxes\nencapsulates to a box with no output (side-effecting only —\nunusual but legal).\n\n### Visual on the canvas\n\nThe encapsulating box renders distinctly — different border,\nmaybe a small \"sub-map\" badge — so the user sees at a glance\nthat this isn't a leaf call. Hovering shows the sub-map's name\nand a small thumbnail of its graph.\n\n## Runtime model\n\nTwo implementation paths exist; pick after prototyping.\n\n**A. Compile-time inlining.** At compile (issue 309), the\nencapsulating box is replaced by its sub-graph: every internal\nbox gets a prefixed id (`<encap_id>__<internal_id>`), every\ninternal wire stays internal, marked-input boxes get their\nexternal bindings hooked to the parent's incoming wires, and\nwrite boxes get their outputs hooked into the packing-into-blob\nmachinery. The runtime never sees encapsulation — one flat\ngraph. Composes cleanly with issue 313's same-language merge.\n\n**B. Runtime sub-graph dispatch.** The graph loader builds the\nsub-map as a child graph, and the encapsulating box's task\nspawns a sub-run that drives the child graph to quiescence,\ncollects its write-box outputs, packs them, and emits. The\nchild runs on the same thread pool — its tasks are just normal\npool tasks distinguished by their box-id namespace.\n\nCompile-time inlining is the cleaner design for performance and\ndebugging (one flat task pool, no recursion in the dispatch\nlayer). Runtime sub-graph dispatch is the more flexible design\nfor hot-reload and dynamic linking (the parent doesn't need to\nrecompile when the sub-map changes). The prototype picks one;\nthe alternative remains an open question until profile data\njustifies the choice.\n\nRecursion (a sub-map encapsulates another sub-map) falls out of\neither path naturally — inlining recurses through; runtime\ndispatch recurses through. Cycles between maps are a compile-time\nerror.\n\n## Relationship to existing issues\n\n- **Issue 207 (source-file-browser)** — the file browser is the\n  entry point for the \"encapsulate\" action.\n- **Issue 239 (literal port shrinks to nodule)** — the\n  external-input slider reuses the same visual idiom on the\n  input-port row."

          "old_string":"## Runtime model\n\nTwo implementation paths exist; pick after prototyping.\n\n**A. Compile-time inlining.** At compile (issue 309), the\nencapsulating box is replaced by its sub-graph: every internal\nbox gets a prefixed id (`<encap_id>__<internal_id>`), every\ninternal wire stays internal, marked-input boxes get their\nexternal bindings hooked to the parent's incoming wires, and\nwrite boxes get their outputs hooked into the packing-into-blob\nmachinery. The runtime never sees encapsulation — one flat\ngraph. Composes cleanly with issue 313's same-language merge.\n\n**B. Runtime sub-graph dispatch.** The graph loader builds the\nsub-map as a child graph, and the encapsulating box's task\nspawns a sub-run that drives the child graph to quiescence,\ncollects its write-box outputs, packs them, and emits. The\nchild runs on the same thread pool — its tasks are just normal\npool tasks distinguished by their box-id namespace.\n\nCompile-time inlining is the cleaner design for performance and\ndebugging (one flat task pool, no recursion in the dispatch\nlayer). Runtime sub-graph dispatch is the more flexible design\nfor hot-reload and dynamic linking (the parent doesn't need to\nrecompile when the sub-map changes). The prototype picks one;\nthe alternative remains an open question until profile data\njustifies the choice.\n\nRecursion (a sub-map encapsulates another sub-map) falls out of\neither path naturally — inlining recurses through; runtime\ndispatch recurses through. Cycles between maps are a compile-time\nerror.",
          "new_string":"## Runtime model — two paths, needs a decision\n\nTwo implementation paths exist. The encapsulating box being a\nnormal `call` box from the editor's perspective doesn't pick\nbetween them; the choice lives in what the map-language spec\ndoes behind the scenes and what (if anything) the compile\npipeline does at build time.\n\n### Path A — Compile-time inlining\n\nThe compile pipeline (issue 309) recognizes encapsulating call\nboxes and **expands them into their sub-graphs at build time**.\nSteps the compile step takes per encapsulating box:\n\n1. Load the sub-map's graph from `ref`.\n2. Rename every internal box with a parent-namespaced id:\n   `stats_pipeline__compute`, `stats_pipeline__filter`, etc.\n3. Copy every internal wire across, with the renamed ids.\n4. For each marked data box inside the sub-map: replace it with\n   a wire that brings the encapsulating box's matching input\n   value directly to wherever the data box's output was wired.\n5. For each write box inside the sub-map: route its emitted\n   value into the packed-blob writer that produces the\n   encapsulating box's output (or, alternatively, expose each\n   write box's value as a separate output wire that downstream\n   consumers can wire to individually — see \"Output unpacking\n   under inlining\" below).\n6. Remove the encapsulating call box from the parent's graph.\n\nAfter expansion, the compiled artifact is **one flat graph**.\nThe runtime never sees `lang: \"map\"`. The map-language spec\nexists only for the editor's sake (validating refs, listing\nthe sub-map's inputs/outputs for the inspector).\n\n**Pros:**\n\n- No new runtime machinery. The dispatch, slot store, and spec\n  registry all operate on flat graphs as today.\n- Best per-call performance — no sub-graph startup cost, no\n  nested dispatch.\n- **Composes cleanly with issue 313** (whole-program same-\n  language merge). The inlined sub-graph's same-language regions\n  merge into the parent's merge as if they were always one map.\n- Debugging stack traces inside the inlined region point to\n  flat box ids — readable once you know the naming convention.\n\n**Cons:**\n\n- The sub-map gets baked into every parent that uses it. Edit\n  the sub-map → every parent must recompile.\n- No hot-reload of sub-maps. The editor would have to\n  re-expand on every parent map edit, or accept that the\n  parent's last-compiled artifact lags the sub-map source.\n- Compile time grows with sub-map size × number of\n  encapsulations.\n- Deep recursion (sub-maps inside sub-maps inside sub-maps)\n  inflates the parent's compiled output proportionally.\n- Output unpacking under inlining is awkward: the packed-blob\n  output format makes sense at a boundary; with no boundary,\n  downstream consumers either wire to individual sub-write-box\n  outputs (more efficient but a different mental model) or get\n  the packer's blob baked in too (the packer is just another\n  inlined function call).\n\n### Path B — Runtime sub-graph dispatch\n\nThe encapsulating box stays as one box in the parent's flat\ngraph. The map-language spec's `invoke` runs the sub-graph at\ncall time:\n\n1. **`map_init(worker_idx)`** — load every sub-map referenced\n   by the running program (or lazily on first invoke). Each\n   worker gets its own copy of the sub-graph state (slot store,\n   dispatch context).\n2. **`map_invoke(handle, sub_map_dir, ..., inputs, ..., out_buf, ...)`** —\n   for each input, write the bytes into the shared-memory chunk\n   that the matching marked data box reads from. Then drive the\n   sub-graph to quiescence using the existing pool's dispatch\n   loop (the sub-graph's tasks are normal pool tasks distinguished\n   by a nested namespace). When quiescent, walk the write boxes,\n   read their emitted values, pack them into the size-index +\n   data-section blob, write the blob to `out_buf`.\n\nThe sub-graph's parallelism uses the same thread pool as the\nparent's. A sub-graph's tasks compete for workers alongside the\nparent's tasks. From the pool's perspective, the difference is\njust box-id prefix.\n\n**Pros:**\n\n- Sub-map loaded once per worker, reused across many parent\n  invocations and across many parent maps.\n- Hot-reload friendly: change the sub-map, parent picks up the\n  new version on next run (no parent recompile).\n- The packed-blob output format is the natural shape — the\n  boundary exists, the spec packs at the boundary, downstream\n  consumers unpack with the helper library.\n- Debugging stack traces preserve the sub-map identity (the\n  task's namespace says \"this came from `stats-pipeline`\").\n- Recursion is natural — the spec's invoke can nest-invoke its\n  own spec for a sub-sub-map.\n\n**Cons:**\n\n- New runtime machinery: the map spec's `invoke` runs a nested\n  dispatch loop. Either the dispatch layer grows a re-entrancy\n  contract, or the map spec replicates enough of the dispatch\n  machinery to drive the sub-graph itself.\n- Each encapsulating-box call pays sub-graph startup cost —\n  seeding inputs, possibly resetting slot state from a previous\n  invocation, collecting outputs at the end. Small but real.\n- Does NOT compose with issue 313's same-language merge — the\n  sub-map's source can't merge with the parent's, because at\n  build time they're separate compilation units. (313 could be\n  extended to merge across encapsulation boundaries, but that's\n  a separate design.)\n- Re-using the sub-graph across invocations requires reset\n  semantics. Either the sub-graph's slots and counters get\n  reset between invocations (cost), or each invocation gets a\n  fresh sub-graph instance (allocation cost).\n\n### What to weigh\n\nThe choice turns on whether encapsulation is **a build-time\nabstraction (like a C macro or a Lua-function-inlined-by-LuaJIT)**\nor **a runtime composition (like calling a function in a shared\nlibrary)**.\n\nPath A treats it as a build-time abstraction. Encapsulation is\nhow the user organizes source; the compiled artifact is one\nflat program. Best for raw performance and integration with\nthe existing machinery. Cost: rebuild propagation.\n\nPath B treats it as a runtime composition. Encapsulation is a\nreal boundary at execution time, with the packed-blob output\nas the wire format across the boundary. Best for modularity,\nhot-reload, and clear semantics. Cost: per-call overhead and\nloss of cross-boundary optimization.\n\nA third option exists — **support both, picked per encapsulating\nbox** via a small flag in the box JSON (`encap_mode: \"inline\" |\n\"runtime\"`). The compile pipeline expands inline-mode boxes;\nruntime-mode boxes stay encapsulated. Each user picks per\nencapsulation based on their needs. Higher implementation cost\nbut maximally flexible. Probably not in the first slice; flag it\nfor later if either A or B alone proves too narrow.\n\nRecursion (a sub-map encapsulates another sub-map) works under\neither path. Cycles between maps are a compile-time (or\nload-time, under B) error."

Runtime sub-graph dispatch.** The graph loader builds the","-sub-map as a child graph, and the encapsulating box's task","-spawns a sub-run that drives the child graph to quiescence,","-collects its write-box outputs, packs them, and emits. The","-child runs on the same thread pool — its tasks are just normal","-pool tasks distinguished by their box-id namespace.","+The compile pipeline (issue 309) recognizes encapsulating call","+boxes and **expands them into their sub-graphs at build time**.","+Steps the compile step takes per encapsulating box:"," ","-Compile-time inlining is the cleaner design for performance and","-debugging (one flat task pool, no recursion in the dispatch","-layer). Runtime sub-graph dispatch is the more flexible design","-for hot-reload and dynamic linking (the parent doesn't need to","-recompile when the sub-map changes). The prototype picks one;","-the alternative remains an open question until profile data","-justifies the choice.","+1. Load the sub-map's graph from `ref`.","+2. Rename every internal box with a parent-namespaced id:","+   `stats_pipeline__compute`, `stats_pipeline__filter`, etc.","+3. Copy every internal wire across, with the renamed ids.","+4. For each marked data box inside the sub-map: replace it with","+   a wire that brings the encapsulating box's matching input","+   value directly to wherever the data box's output was wired.","+5. For each write box inside the sub-map: route its emitted","+   value into the packed-blob writer that produces the","+   encapsulating box's output (or, alternatively, expose each","+   write box's value as a separate output wire that downstream","+   consumers can wire to individually — see \"Output unpacking","+   under inlining\" below).","+6. Remove the encapsulating call box from the parent's graph."," ","-Recursion (a sub-map encapsulates another sub-map) falls out of","-either path naturally — inlining recurses through; runtime","-dispatch recurses through. Cycles between maps are a compile-time","-error.","+After expansion, the compiled artifact is **one flat graph**.","+The runtime never sees `lang: \"map\"`. The map-language spec","+exists only for the editor's sake (validating refs, listing","+the sub-map's inputs/outputs for the inspector)."," ","+**Pros:**","+","+- No new runtime machinery. The dispatch, slot store, and spec","+  registry all operate on flat graphs as today.","+- Best per-call performance — no sub-graph startup cost, no","+  nested dispatch.","+- **Composes cleanly with issue 313** (whole-program same-","+  language merge). The inlined sub-graph's same-language regions","+  merge into the parent's merge as if they were always one map.","+- Debugging stack traces inside the inlined region point to","+  flat box ids — readable once you know the naming convention.","+","+**Cons:**","+","+- The sub-map gets baked into every parent that uses it. Edit","+  the sub-map → every parent must recompile.","+- No hot-reload of sub-maps. The editor would have to","+  re-expand on every parent map edit, or accept that the","+  parent's last-compiled artifact lags the sub-map source.","+- Compile time grows with sub-map size × number of","+  encapsulations.","+- Deep recursion (sub-maps inside sub-maps inside sub-maps)","+  inflates the parent's compiled output proportionally.","+- Output unpacking under inlining is awkward: the packed-blob","+  output format makes sense at a boundary; with no boundary,","+  downstream consumers either wire to individual sub-write-box","+  outputs (more efficient but a different mental model) or get","+  the packer's blob baked in too (the packer is just another","+  inlined function call).","+","+### Path B — Runtime sub-graph dispatch","+","+The encapsulating box stays as one box in the parent's flat","+graph. The map-language spec's `invoke` runs the sub-graph at","+call time:","+","+1. **`map_init(worker_idx)`** — load every sub-map referenced","+   by the running program (or lazily on first invoke). Each","+   worker gets its own copy of the sub-graph state (slot store,","+   dispatch context).","+2. **`map_invoke(handle, sub_map_dir, ..., inputs, ..., out_buf, ...)`** —","+   for each input, write the bytes into the shared-memory chunk","+   that the matching marked data box reads from. Then drive the","+   sub-graph to quiescence using the existing pool's dispatch","+   loop (the sub-graph's tasks are normal pool tasks distinguished","+   by a nested namespace). When quiescent, walk the write boxes,","+   read their emitted values, pack them into the size-index +","+   data-section blob, write the blob to `out_buf`.","+","+The sub-graph's parallelism uses the same thread pool as the","+parent's. A sub-graph's tasks compete for workers alongside the","+parent's tasks. From the pool's perspective, the difference is","+just box-id prefix.","+","+**Pros:**","+","+- Sub-map loaded once per worker, reused across many parent","+  invocations and across many parent maps.","+- Hot-reload friendly: change the sub-map, parent picks up the","+  new version on next run (no parent recompile).","+- The packed-blob output format is the natural shape — the","+  boundary exists, the spec packs at the boundary, downstream","+  consumers unpack with the helper library.","+- Debugging stack traces preserve the sub-map identity (the","+  task's namespace says \"this came from `stats-pipeline`\").","+- Recursion is natural — the spec's invoke can nest-invoke its","+  own spec for a sub-sub-map.","+","+**Cons:**","+","+- New runtime machinery: the map spec's `invoke` runs a nested","+  dispatch loop. Either the dispatch layer grows a re-entrancy","+  contract, or the map spec replicates enough of the dispatch","+  machinery to drive the sub-graph itself.","+- Each encapsulating-box call pays sub-graph startup cost —","+  seeding inputs, possibly resetting slot state from a previous","+  invocation, collecting outputs at the end. Small but real.","+- Does NOT compose with issue 313's same-language merge — the","+  sub-map's source can't merge with the parent's, because at","+  build time they're separate compilation units. Either the sub-graph's slots and counters get","+  reset between invocations (cost), or each invocation gets a","+  fresh sub-graph instance (allocation cost).","+","+### What to weigh","+","+The choice turns on whether encapsulation is **a build-time","+abstraction (like a C macro or a Lua-function-inlined-by-LuaJIT)**","+or **a runtime composition (like calling a function in a shared","+library)**.","+","+Path A treats it as a build-time abstraction. Encapsulation is","+how the user organizes source; the compiled artifact is one","+flat program. Best for raw performance and integration with","+the existing machinery. Cost: rebuild propagation.","+","+Path B treats it as a runtime composition. Encapsulation is a","+real boundary at execution time, with the packed-blob output","+as the wire format across the boundary. Best for modularity,","+hot-reload, and clear semantics. Cost: per-call overhead and","+loss of cross-boundary optimization.","+","+A third option exists — **support both, picked per encapsulating","+box** via a small flag in the box JSON (`encap_mode: \"inline\" |","+\"runtime\"`). The compile pipeline expands inline-mode boxes;","+runtime-mode boxes stay encapsulated. Each user picks per","+encapsulation based on their needs. Higher implementation cost","+but maximally flexible. Probably not in the first slice; flag it","+for later if either A or B alone proves too narrow.","+","+Recursion (a sub-map encapsulates another sub-map) works under","+either path. Cycles between maps are a compile-time (or","+load-time, under B) error.","+"," ## Relationship to existing issues"," "," - **Issue 207 (source-file-browser)** — the file browser is the"]

    "content":"# 249 — Tap input mode: radial-bubble ports and emoji box labels\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Concept\n\nThe editor's wire-connection affordance assumes a mouse — small\nports on the side of each box that the user clicks and drags\nbetween. On a touch screen those ports are awkward: hard to hit\nprecisely, easy to misfire. The full box header eats vertical\nspace that's even more precious on phone-sized canvases.\n\n**Tap input mode** is a parallel interaction model that the user\ntoggles into for touch-first editing:\n\n1. **Wires are formed via a radial-bubble menu.** Tap a box and\n   a ring of larger bubbles fans out around it, one bubble per\n   input port plus one per output port. The bubbles are large\n   enough to hit comfortably with a fingertip. Drag a bubble to\n   another box's bubble to wire them together; tap a bubble to\n   open its inspector menu (same content as the desktop's\n   per-port inspector).\n2. **Box headers shrink to four emoji.** The box's filename +\n   function name (which is long and hard to scan on small\n   screens) is replaced by four emoji glyphs the user picks.\n   Four characters of visual identity. Tap the box itself (not\n   a bubble) to see the full name in a popover.\n\nThe mode is intended to live alongside the current\nmouse-and-port model, not replace it. A user with a desktop and\na mouse keeps the existing affordances; a user with a tablet or\nphone flips to tap mode. The data model (boxes, wires, port\ndeclarations) is unchanged — only the editor's rendering and\ninteraction code branches on the mode.\n\n## Tap-mode wire connection — the radial bubble menu\n\nWhen the user taps a box in tap mode:\n\n```\n              ┌───────┐\n              │ port  │\n              │ bubble│\n              └───────┘\n         ┌───────┐         ┌───────┐\n         │ port  │         │ port  │\n         │ bubble│         │ bubble│\n         └───────┘         └───────┘\n                ┌──────────────┐\n                │  🧮📊✨🔢   │  ← the box (4 emoji)\n                └──────────────┘\n         ┌───────┐         ┌───────┐\n         │ port  │         │ port  │\n         │ bubble│         │ bubble│\n         └───────┘         └───────┘\n              ┌───────┐\n              │ out   │\n              │ bubble│\n              └───────┘\n```\n\n- One bubble per input port, distributed around the top / left /\n  right of the box.\n- One bubble per output port (or output branch, for comparator /\n  iterator boxes), distributed around the bottom.\n- Each bubble is sized for a fingertip — roughly 48×48 px at the\n  default zoom, scaling with the canvas.\n- Bubbles are labeled with the port name, abbreviated if\n  necessary.\n\nTwo gestures on a bubble:\n\n- **Tap** — opens the per-port inspector menu (literal-value\n  field, optional toggle, type selector, etc.). Same content as\n  the desktop inspector's port row, just rendered as a sheet\n  panel that pops up from the bottom of the canvas.\n- **Drag** — initiates a wire connection. As the finger moves,\n  a wire-in-progress follows the touch point. Drag onto another\n  box's bubble (the target box's radial menu pops up\n  automatically once the drag enters its bounding circle) and\n  release on the destination port bubble to complete the wire.\n\nCancellation: tap outside any bubble or box to close the radial\nmenu; release a drag over empty canvas to cancel the wire.\n\n### Multiple boxes selected\n\nIf the user has multiple boxes selected and taps the radial-menu\ntoggle, each selected box shows its own radial bubbles\nsimultaneously. Useful for wiring up a freshly-created cluster\nwithout tap-cycling.\n\n### Discoverability\n\nA small \"tap mode\" icon in the editor toolbar toggles the\nbehavior. The icon's state is persisted per-map (some maps the\nuser edits on a tablet, others on a desktop — the mode follows\nthe device choice for that map).\n\n## Four-emoji box labels\n\nIn tap mode, the box header renders as four emoji glyphs\ninstead of the filename + function name. The four emojis are\nchosen by the user via the box's inspector — a 4-cell editable\nfield, each cell a tap-to-pick emoji selector.\n\n```\n┌──────────────┐\n│  🧮📊✨🔢   │\n└──────────────┘\n```\n\nVisual properties:\n\n- Four cells, each a single emoji glyph at large size.\n- Default ordering reads left-to-right (no semantic meaning to\n  position; the user picks four glyphs that read together).\n- Box footprint shrinks accordingly — emoji-mode boxes are\n  smaller on the canvas, fitting more boxes in view on small\n  screens.\n- Tap the box body (not a bubble) → popover shows the full\n  filename + function name and any other identifying metadata.\n- Hover/long-press → same popover (for tablet stylus users).\n\n### Round-trip with desktop mode\n\nA box has both a textual label and four emoji slots in its JSON.\nDesktop mode shows the textual label; tap mode shows the emoji.\nThe two render independently from one stored shape:\n\n```json\n{\n    \"id\": \"compute_avg\",\n    \"label\": \"compute_avg\",      // textual, shown in desktop mode\n    \"emoji\": [\"🧮\", \"📊\", \"✨\", \"🔢\"],   // shown in tap mode\n    \"...\": \"...\"\n}\n```\n\nA box with no emoji set in tap mode falls back to a default\nglyph (the first letter of the function name framed in a\ncircle, say) so existing maps don't break when opened in tap\nmode.\n\n## Optional: auto-generated emoji labels via word embedding\n\nA more ambitious enhancement: when the user creates a new box\nor hasn't picked their emoji yet, the editor **suggests four\nemoji** by matching the box's textual identity against a pre-\ncomputed embedding space.\n\nSketch:\n\n1. Compute a text embedding of the box's `<filename>__<fn>`\n   string (e.g., `compute_avg__main`).\n2. Compute embeddings of every emoji in a curated list (the\n   emoji's keyword tags + common descriptions concatenated).\n   Embeddings are precomputed at editor build time and shipped\n   as a static lookup table.\n3. For each emoji, compute cosine similarity between the box's\n   embedding and the emoji's embedding.\n4. Pick the top four most-similar emojis.\n5. Present them in the box's emoji slots, with each slot\n   independently swap-able by the user.\n\nThis is a sometimes-works heuristic. A box named `parse_json`\nprobably gets 🗂️📄🔎🧩 or similar; a box named `compute_avg`\ngets something like 🧮📊∑✨. The user corrects when the\nheuristic misses — same affordance as the manual emoji picker.\n\nThe embedding model and the static lookup table are an editor-\nside dependency. Candidate models: a small local model\n(MiniLM, all-MiniLM-L6) bundled with the editor; or an\nembedding lookup precomputed offline and shipped as a JSON.\nThe precomputed-lookup option is heavier on disk but adds no\nruntime model dependency — likely the right tradeoff for an\neditor whose value proposition is \"runs as a Lua HTTP server\n+ static HTML.\"\n\nThis part is explicitly an enhancement, not part of the first\nslice. The base feature (4 emoji slots, user picks each one)\nis what the user actually needs; the auto-suggest is a polish\nfollow-on.\n\n## Relationship to existing issues\n\n- **Issue 207 (source-file-browser)** — tap-mode interactions\n  for browsing files are out of scope here but worth keeping\n  consistent; if tap mode lands, the browser should grow\n  compatible affordances later.\n- **Issue 217 (variadic toggle gates)** — the inspector toggles\n  introduced there have desktop-mouse affordances; the tap-mode\n  inspector panel needs equivalents (probably larger buttons\n  rendered in a sheet).\n- **Issue 235 (literal value replaces port name)** — the\n  desktop-mode visual; tap-mode shows the literal value inside\n  the port bubble itself when set.\n- **Issue 239 (literal port shrinks to nodule)** — same pattern;\n  in tap mode the nodule becomes a smaller-style bubble.\n- **Issue 245 (wire color by classification)** — wires in tap\n  mode use the same color rules.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `assets/index.html` — editor entry; tap-mode toggle in\n  toolbar.\n- `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — box rendering; branches on tap-mode\n  for header (text vs. emoji) and footprint.\n- `assets/js/005-app.js` — interaction state; tap handler;\n  per-map mode persistence.\n- `assets/js/006-wires.js` — wire rendering; touch-drag for\n  bubble-to-bubble wiring.\n- `assets/js/008-radial-bubbles.js` (new) — radial menu logic.\n- `assets/js/009-emoji-picker.js` (new) — emoji selector\n  component.\n- `src/006-server-main.lua` — HTTP backend; reads / writes the\n  `emoji` array on box JSONs.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. **Box JSON schema**: add the `emoji` array field (four\n   strings, each a single grapheme cluster). Persist via the\n   existing HTTP backend.\n2. **Tap-mode toggle**: toolbar button + per-map mode state.\n   In tap mode, the desktop port-and-wire affordances are\n   suppressed.\n3. **Emoji rendering**: in tap mode, box header renders the\n   `emoji` array (or a default if absent). SLOT_FLAG_TAGGED : 0;\n            for (int j = 0; j < b->n_inputs; j++) {\n                /* If any producer feeding this input port declares\n                 * variable-size output (output_capacity == 0), the\n                 * slot needs the large-value heap path so pushes\n                 * larger than default_cell_bytes succeed. Read boxes\n                 * default to output_capacity 0 since they emit\n                 * arbitrary file contents; a call box opts in by\n                 * setting output_capacity to 0 in its JSON.     "oldString":"/* {{{ push_one_connection() — push to a single connection's slot */\n/* The `tag` is the ordering hint for cell-tagged consumer slots\n * (issue 304's iterator-ordering rule). For pushes from\n * non-iterator producers it's 0; for iterator pushes the routing\n * code passes the counter value so parallel iterator tasks\n * preserve invocation order at the consumer. */\nstatic int push_one_connection(dispatch_ctx_t *ctx, const box_t *b,\n                               const connection_t *c,\n                               const void *out_bytes, int out_size,\n                               uint32_t tag)\n{\n    if (c->to_box_idx < 0) return 0;\n    const box_t *dst = graph_box(ctx->graph, c->to_box_idx);\n    if (!dst || !dst->input_slot_ids) return 0;\n    if (c->to_input_idx < 0 || c->to_input_idx >= dst->n_inputs) return 0;\n    if (slot_push(ctx->slots, dst->input_slot_ids[c->to_input_idx],\n                  out_bytes, out_size, tag) != 0) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"dispatch: '%s' → '%s'.%s: push failed\\n\",\n                b->id, dst->id, c->to_input);\n        return -1;\n    }\n    dispatch_spawn_if_ready(ctx, c->to_box_idx, 0);\n    return 0;\n}\n/* }}} */",
    "newString":"/* {{{ push_one_connection() — push to a single connection's slot */\n/* The `tag` is the ordering hint for cell-tagged consumer slots\n * (issue 304's iterator-ordering rule). For pushes from\n * non-iterator producers it's 0; for iterator pushes the routing\n * code passes the counter value so parallel iterator tasks\n * preserve invocation order at the consumer.\n *\n * `conn_idx` is the producer-side connection index (which entry in\n * `b->connections` this is) — used to look up\n * `b->output_edge_native[conn_idx]` when the consumer's slot is\n * dual-ring (issue 312 slice 3). For producers that don't carry\n * per-edge classification (read / write / data boxes — no\n * `output_edge_native` array), the bit defaults to 0 (treated as\n * cross-language; the JSON ring receives the push). */\nstatic int push_one_connection(dispatch_ctx_t *ctx, const box_t *b,\n                               int conn_idx,\n                               const connection_t *c,\n                               const void *out_bytes, int out_size,\n                               uint32_t tag)\n{\n    if (c->to_box_idx < 0) return 0;\n    const box_t *dst = graph_box(ctx->graph, c->to_box_idx);\n    if (!dst || !dst->input_slot_ids) return 0;\n    if (c->to_input_idx < 0 || c->to_input_idx >= dst->n_inputs) return 0;\n\n    int     dst_slot = dst->input_slot_ids[c->to_input_idx];\n    int32_t dst_flags = slot_flags(ctx->slots, dst_slot);\n    int     rc;\n\n    if (dst_flags >= 0 && (dst_flags & SLOT_FLAG_DUAL_RING)) {\n        int native_edge = (b->output_edge_native &&\n                           conn_idx >= 0 && conn_idx < b->n_connections)\n                          ? b->output_edge_native[conn_idx]\n                          : 0;\n        if (native_edge) {\n            rc = slot_push_native(ctx->slots, dst_slot,\n                                  out_bytes, out_size, tag);\n        } else {\n            rc = slot_push_json(ctx->slots, dst_slot,\n                                out_bytes, out_size, tag);\n        }\n    } else {\n        rc = slot_push(ctx->slots, dst_slot, out_bytes, out_size, tag);\n    }\n\n    if (rc != 0) {\n        fprintf(stderr, \"dispatch: '%s' → '%s'.%s: push failed\\n\",\n                b->id, dst->id, c->to_input);\n        return -1;\n    }\n    dispatch_spawn_if_ready(ctx, c->to_box_idx, 0);\n    return 0;\n}\n/* }}} */",

      "content":"                       const char *branch,\n                       const void *out_bytes, int out_size,\n                       uint32_t tag)\n{\n    int fired = 0;\n    for (int i = 0; i < b->n_connections; i++) {\n        const connection_t *c = &b->connections[i];\n        if (!c->from_branch) continue;\n        if (strcmp(c->from_branch, branch) != 0) continue;\n        if (push_one_connection(ctx, b, c, out_bytes, out_size, tag) != 0)\n            return -1;\n        fired++;\n    }\n    return fired;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ push_to_downstream() — fan output to every outgoing connection */\n/* The push triggers spawn_if_ready on the consumer. Tag = 0 for\n * the plain fan-out case; iterator routing uses push_branch with a\n * non-zero tag. */\nstatic int push_to_downstream(dispatch_ctx_t *ctx, const box_t *b,\n                              const void *out_bytes, int out_size)\n{\n    for (int i = 0; i < b->n_connections; i++) {\n        if (push_one_connection(ctx, b, &b->connections[i],\n                                out_bytes, out_size, 0) != 0) return -1;\n    }\n    return 0;\n}"
    }
  },

}

      "numLines":40,

      "totalLines":889,
      "content":"/* {{{ dispatch_push_literals() */\nint dispatch_push_literals(dispatch_ctx_t *ctx, char **err)\n{\n    if (!ctx) {\n        if (err) *err = err_fmt(\"dispatch_push_literals: NULL ctx\");\n        return -1;\n    }\n    for (int i = 0; i < ctx->n_boxes; i++) {\n        const box_t *b = graph_box(ctx->graph, i);\n        if (!b || !b->input_slot_ids) continue;\n        for (int j = 0; j < b->n_inputs; j++) {\n            const input_decl_t *p = &b->inputs[j];\n            if (!p->literal) continue;\n            int sz = (int)strlen(p->literal);\n            if (slot_push(ctx->slots, b->input_slot_ids[j],\n                          p->literal, sz, 0) != 0) {\n                if (err) *err = err_fmt(\"box '%s' input '%s': \"\n                                        \"literal push failed\",\n                                        b->id, p->name);\n                return -1;\n            }\n        }\n    }\n    return 0;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ resolve_path() — join map_dir + relative path */\n/* Caller frees the returned string. */\nstatic char *resolve_path(const dispatch_ctx_t *ctx, const char *p)\n{\n    if (!p) return NULL;\n    if (p[0] == '/') return strdup(p);             /* already absolute */\n    const char *base = graph_map_dir(ctx->graph);\n    if (!base) return strdup(p);\n    size_t blen = strlen(base);\n    size_t plen = strlen(p);\n    char *out = malloc(blen + 1 + plen + 1);\n    if (!out) return NULL;\n    memcpy(out, base, blen);"
    }
  },

          "new_string":"    for (int i = 0; i < ctx->n_boxes; i++) {\n        const box_t *b = graph_box(ctx->graph, i);\n        if (!b || !b->input_slot_ids) continue;\n        for (int j = 0; j < b->n_inputs; j++) {\n            const input_decl_t *p = &b->inputs[j];\n            if (!p->literal) continue;\n            int sz = (int)strlen(p->literal);\n            /* slot_push_native aliases to slot_push for single-ring\n             * slots; for dual-ring slots (issue 312 slice 3), it\n             * writes to the native ring + ordering ring atomically.\n             * Literals are treated as native — they're configured\n             * inline in the consumer's own box JSON, so semantically\n             * they belong to the consumer's language and the spec's\n             * native decoder reads them directly. */\n            if (slot_push_native(ctx->slots, b->input_slot_ids[j],\n                                 p->literal, sz, 0) != 0) {\n                if (err) *err = err_fmt(\"box '%s' input '%s': \"\n                                        \"literal push failed\",\n                                        b->id, p->name);\n                return -1;\n            }\n        }\n    }\n    return 0;\n}"

      "content":"/* {{{ test_end_to_end_calc() — the headline test */\n/* Load the calc fixture (one Lua call box with two literal inputs),\n * push literals, spawn the entry box, wait for quiescence, verify\n * the captured output is \"42\" (17 + 25). */\nstatic int test_end_to_end_calc(void)\n{\n    runtime_t rt;\n    if (runtime_setup(&rt, \"tests/maps/calc\", 2, 1) != 0) {\n        runtime_teardown(&rt); return 0;\n    }\n\n    char *err = NULL;\n    ASSERT(dispatch_push_literals(&rt.ctx, &err) == 0);\n\n    /* The entry box should now have all its inputs ready. */\n    int entry = graph_box_index(rt.graph, \"add\");\n    ASSERT(entry >= 0);\n    dispatch_spawn_if_ready(&rt.ctx, entry, 0);\n\n    pool_wait_quiescent(rt.pool);\n    ASSERT(atomic_load(&rt.ctx.tasks_dispatched) == 1);\n\n    /* Captured output for the add box must be \"42\". */\n    ASSERT(rt.ctx.last_outputs);\n    ASSERT(rt.ctx.last_outputs[entry] != NULL);\n    ASSERT(strcmp(rt.ctx.last_outputs[entry], \"42\") == 0);\n\n    runtime_teardown(&rt);\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ test_calc_mul() — same fixture, different function */\n/* Re-load the calc map, override one input via direct slot_push,\n * and call M.mul instead of M.add to exercise re-use. We just\n * load the calc map, but build a different result by writing\n * different literal values manually (skipping push_literals). */\nstatic int test_calc_mul(void)\n{\n    runtime_t rt;\n    if (runtime_setup(&rt, \"tests/maps/calc\", 2, 1) != 0) {\n        runtime_teardown(&rt); return 0;\n    }\n\n    /* Push our own literal values: 6 and 7, expecting 42. */\n    int entry = graph_box_index(rt.graph, \"add\");\n    const box_t *b = graph_box(rt.graph, entry);\n    ASSERT(b);\n    ASSERT(b->n_inputs == 2);\n\n    const char *six = \"6\", *seven = \"7\";\n    ASSERT(slot_push(rt.slots, b->input_slot_ids[0], six,   1, 0) == 0);\n    ASSERT(slot_push(rt.slots, b->input_slot_ids[1], seven, 1, 0) == 0);\n\n    /* The function name is fixed in the box JSON (\"add\"); we just\n     * verify add(6, 7) = \"13\". */\n    dispatch_spawn_if_ready(&rt.ctx, entry, 0);\n    pool_wait_quiescent(rt.pool);\n    ASSERT(rt.ctx.last_outputs[entry] != NULL);\n    ASSERT(strcmp(rt.ctx.last_outputs[entry], \"13\") == 0);\n\n    runtime_teardown(&rt);\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ test_dispatch_counter_burst() */\nstatic int test_dispatch_counter_burst(void)\n{\n    runtime_t rt;\n    if (runtime_setup(&rt, \"tests/maps/calc\", 4, 1) != 0) {\n        runtime_teardown(&rt); return 0;\n    }\n    int entry = graph_box_index(rt.graph, \"add\");\n    char *err = NULL;\n    ASSERT(dispatch_push_literals(&rt.ctx, &err) == 0);\n\n    /* Force-spawn 8 add-box tasks (bypass the single-spawn guard\n     * via dispatch_spawn).           "old_string":"- **Slice 2 complete (2026-05-21).** `lang_invoke_fn` typedef in\n  `langs/lang-spec.h` gained `const int *input_native` (between\n  `input_sizes` and `n_inputs`) and `int output_native` (after\n  `n_inputs`, before `out_buf`). Because all three callback slots\n  (`invoke`, `invoke_native`, `invoke_json`) share the same\n  typedef, the change propagates automatically. Every spec's\n  invoke function picked up the new params and currently ignores\n  them — the per-input branching is slice 4 (Lua) and 307 / 308\n  (C and Bash). Dispatch's `do_call_box` passes `NULL` /\n  `0` placeholder values; slice 3 wires up the real per-cell\n  flags from the dual-ring's ordering pop. Eleven direct\n  call sites in the spec test files updated to the new signature.\n\nWhat's still ahead:\n\n- **Slice 3** — Dispatch reads from the ordering ring; push\n  selects ring based on `output_edge_native[j]`. Touches\n  `src/012-dispatch.c`. Populates the per-input flags the slice 2\n  signature already accepts.\n- **Slice 4** — Lua spec branches per `input_native[i]`. C and\n  Bash bridges land in 307 / 308 alongside this.\n- **Slice 5** — Remove the per-box `use_native_invoke` field and\n  its computation now that the dispatch consults per-cell.",
          "new_string":"- **Slice 2 complete (2026-05-21).** `lang_invoke_fn` typedef in\n  `langs/lang-spec.h` gained `const int *input_native` (between\n  `input_sizes` and `n_inputs`) and `int output_native` (after\n  `n_inputs`, before `out_buf`). Because all three callback slots\n  (`invoke`, `invoke_native`, `invoke_json`) share the same\n  typedef, the change propagates automatically. Every spec's\n  invoke function picked up the new params and currently ignores\n  them — the per-input branching is slice 4 (Lua) and 307 / 308\n  (C and Bash). Dispatch's `do_call_box` passes `NULL` /\n  `0` placeholder values; slice 3 wires up the real per-cell\n  flags from the dual-ring's ordering pop. Eleven direct\n  call sites in the spec test files updated to the new signature.\n- **Slice 3 complete (2026-05-21).** Call-box input ports become\n  dual-ring slots (in `graph_attach_runtime`) when their shape\n  permits — restrictions inherited from slice 1: not LARGE_VALUE,\n  not TAGGED. Dispatch's `read_inputs` consults\n  `slot_flags(slot_id)` and routes dual-ring slots through\n  `slot_pop_ordered`, populating `input_native[i]` from the\n  per-cell `which_ring` tag returned by the pop; single-ring\n  slots keep the existing `slot_peek` / `slot_pop` path and\n  derive `input_native[i]` from the per-port\n  `input_edge_native[i]` classification. Push side\n  (`push_one_connection`) now takes the producer's connection\n  index, branches on the consumer slot's flags, and picks\n  `slot_push_native` vs `slot_push_json` based on the producer's\n  `output_edge_native[j]`. Literal pushes from\n  `dispatch_push_literals` go through `slot_push_native` (literals\n  are configured in the consumer's own box JSON, so semantically\n  same-language). `do_write_box`'s `read_inputs` call passes\n  `NULL` for the flag array since write boxes aren't spec-invoked.\n  Added `slot_flags(s, id)` accessor to the slot store API so\n  dispatch can branch without storing per-port bookkeeping.\n  Existing tests stay green (22 slot-store, 14 graph-loader,\n  7 dispatch, 11 integration including multi-language `pipeline`\n  and `driver-test`); test fixtures that pushed directly via\n  `slot_push` on what's now a dual-ring slot were migrated to\n  `slot_push_native`.\n\nWhat's still ahead:\n\n- **Slice 4** — Lua spec branches per `input_native[i]`. C and\n  Bash bridges land in 307 / 308 alongside this. With slice 3 in\n  place, every spec receives real per-cell format flags it can\n  act on — slice 4 makes the Lua spec actually act on them.\n- **Slice 5** — Remove the per-box `use_native_invoke` field and\n  its computation now that the dispatch consults per-cell.\n  Optional but cleans up the legacy classification artifact."
        },

Producer/consumer language pair determines per-cell ring at runtime.\n\n**`src/012-dispatch.c`**:\n- `read_inputs` consults each slot's flags. Dual-ring slots use `slot_pop_ordered` and populate `input_native[i]` from the per-cell `which_ring` tag. Single-ring slots use the existing `slot_peek` / `slot_pop` and derive `input_native[i]` from `b->input_edge_native[i]`.\n- `push_one_connection` takes the producer's connection index, branches on consumer slot flags. Dual-ring consumers get `slot_push_native` or `slot_push_json` based on `b->output_edge_native[conn_idx]`. Single-ring consumers keep `slot_push`.\n- `dispatch_push_literals` switches to `slot_push_native` (literals are native to the consumer's own configuration).\n- `do_write_box`'s `read_inputs` call passes `NULL` for the format array since write boxes aren't spec-invoked.\n\n**`tests/012-dispatch-test.c`** — `test_calc_mul`'s direct `slot_push` calls migrated to `slot_push_native` (calc's input ports are now dual-ring).\n\nFull suite green: 22 slot-store, 14 graph-loader, 5 spec-registry, 7 dispatch (was failing 4, now all passing), 13 lua-spec, 11 c-spec, 5 bash-spec, 5 lua-bridge, 11 integration tests including `pipeline` and `driver-test` running mixed-language graphs end-to-end.\n\nThe per-cell format flags now reach every spec's invoke. They're still ignored by every spec (slices 4 onward make them act). The dispatch is correctly wiring native cells through native rings and JSON cells through JSON rings — when slice 4 lands and the Lua spec branches on `input_native[i]`, the existing wire format will already be producing the right per-cell tags.\n\nAlso done in this turn: corrections folded into 248 (encapsulating box is a normal `call` box, `external` flag lives on `data` boxes only, expanded the runtime-vs-compile-time tradeoff with a third option of per-box flagging), and drafted `issues/249-tap-input-mode-radial-ports-emoji-labels.md` for the tap-mode UI.\n\nWant me to keep going to slice 4 (Lua spec's per-input branching), or pause here?"
      }]
  },

M.sum_pair receives\n * the parsed table and indexes into it; if the spec had passed raw\n * bytes instead the indexing would error. */\nstatic int test_invoke_json_input(void)\n{\n    spec_registry_t *r = NULL;\n    const lang_spec_t *lua = load_lua_spec(&r);\n    ASSERT(lua);\n    void *h = lua->init(0);\n\n    const char *json    = \"{\\\"a\\\":17,\\\"b\\\":25}\";\n    const void *args[1] = { json };\n    int         sizes[1] = { (int)strlen(json) };\n    int         native[1] = { 0 };   /* JSON */\n    char buf[32];\n    int  n = 0;\n\n    int rc = lua->invoke(h, \"tests/maps/hello/src/hello.lua\", \"sum_pair\",\n                         args, sizes, native, 1, 0,\n                         buf, sizeof buf, &n);\n    ASSERT(rc == 0);\n    ASSERT(n == 2);\n    buf[n] = '\\0';\n    ASSERT(strcmp(buf, \"42\") == 0);\n\n    lua->teardown(h);\n    spec_registry_destroy(r);\n    return 1;\n}\n/* }}} */\n\n/* {{{ test_invoke_native_input_with_flag() — slice 4 of issue 312 */\n/* When input_native[i] = 1 (NATIVE), the Lua spec keeps the\n * existing raw-bytes-as-string path. greet still receives \"World\"\n * as a string and prepends \"Hello, \". */\nstatic int test_invoke_native_input_with_flag(void)\n{\n    spec_registry_t *r = NULL;\n    const lang_spec_t *lua = load_lua_spec(&r);\n    ASSERT(lua);\n    void *h = lua->init(0);\n\n    const char *name    = \"World\";\n    const void *args[1] = { name };\n    int         sizes[1] = { 5 };\n    int         native[1] = { 1 };           "old_string":"What's still ahead:\n\n- **Slice 4** — Lua spec branches per `input_native[i]`. C and\n  Bash bridges land in 307 / 308 alongside this. With slice 3 in\n  place, every spec receives real per-cell format flags it can\n  act on — slice 4 makes the Lua spec actually act on them.\n- **Slice 5** — Remove the per-box `use_native_invoke` field and\n  its computation now that the dispatch consults per-cell.\n  Optional but cleans up the legacy classification artifact.",
          "new_string":"- **Slice 4 complete (2026-05-21).** Lua spec's `lua_invoke`\n  branches per `input_native[i]`: NATIVE (or NULL slice-2 callers)\n  push via `lua_pushlstring` exactly as before; JSON\n  (`input_native[i] == 0`) calls a new shared `parse_json_to_stack`\n  helper that lifts the bytes into a Lua value via the existing\n  `decode_node`. On JSON parse failure the spec falls back to\n  `lua_pushlstring` silently — that's the bridge to today's\n  cross-language producers (C / Bash) which haven't started\n  emitting real JSON yet; preserves backward compatibility while\n  the input-format contract tightens. `lua_json_to_native` was\n  refactored to use the same helper, just with `verbose=1` so the\n  bridge path remains loud on parse failures (a cross-language\n  wire that ought to carry JSON but doesn't is a real wire\n  error). Output-side branching on `output_native` deferred —\n  that's a coordinated change with the C and Bash specs and the\n  dispatch's per-call output format computation; see \"what's\n  still ahead\" below. Three tests in `tests/306-lua-spec-test.c`\n  cover the new behavior: `invoke_json_input` (JSON table parses\n  and indexes correctly), `invoke_native_input_with_flag`\n  (NATIVE flag keeps the raw-string path), and\n  `invoke_json_input_falls_back_to_raw` (non-JSON bytes with\n  JSON flag fall back gracefully).\n\nWhat's still ahead:\n\n- **Slice 4.5 — output-side coordinated format.** The dispatch\n  passes `output_native = 0` to every invoke today; specs all\n  ignore it. To make cross-language outputs actually emit JSON,\n  three things need to change together: (1) dispatch computes\n  `output_native = (all output_edge_native[j])` so the spec\n  knows whether all its consumers are same-lang; (2) each spec\n  (Lua / C / Bash) writes JSON via its `native_to_json` logic\n  when `output_native == 0`, else its native form; (3) the\n  push path uses one format uniformly (since the spec wrote\n  once) — `output_native == 1` pushes everywhere via\n  `slot_push_native`, `output_native == 0` pushes everywhere via\n  `slot_push_json`. This trades per-edge precision on the output\n  side for spec-write simplicity (write once, push uniformly).\n  Per-edge precision on the *input* side is unaffected — the\n  dual-ring slot still carries per-cell tags from mixed-format\n  producers.\n- **Slice 5** — Remove the per-box `use_native_invoke` field and\n  its computation now that the dispatch consults per-cell.\n  Optional but cleans up the legacy classification artifact."

        "text":"Both slices landed. The combined recap:\n\n**Slice 3 — Dispatch wires per-cell format flags through the dual-ring.**\n\n- `src/009-slot-store.{c,h}` — added `slot_flags(s, id)` accessor so dispatch can query a slot's shape (dual vs. single ring) without per-port bookkeeping.\n- `src/010-graph-loader.c` — call-box input ports gain `SLOT_FLAG_DUAL_RING` when their shape allows (not LARGE_VALUE, not TAGGED). Mixed fan-in now keeps each cell at its right cost.\n- `src/012-dispatch.c`:\n  - `read_inputs` consults each slot's flags. Dual-ring slots route through `slot_pop_ordered` and populate `input_native[i]` from the per-cell `which_ring` tag. Single-ring slots keep the existing `slot_peek` / `slot_pop` and derive `input_native[i]` from the per-port `input_edge_native[i]` classification.\n  - `push_one_connection` takes the producer's connection index, branches on the consumer slot's flags. Dual-ring consumers get `slot_push_native` or `slot_push_json` based on `b->output_edge_native[conn_idx]`. Single-ring consumers keep `slot_push`.\n  - `dispatch_push_literals` switched to `slot_push_native` (literals are configured in the consumer's own JSON, so semantically native).\n  - `do_write_box` passes `NULL` for the format array since write boxes don't invoke a spec.\n- `tests/012-dispatch-test.c` — `test_calc_mul`'s direct `slot_push` migrated to `slot_push_native` (calc's input ports are now dual-ring).\n\n**Slice 4 — Lua spec acts on `input_native[i]`.**\n\n- `langs/lua/spec.c`:\n  - Extracted `parse_json_to_stack(L, src, src_size, verbose)` — shared helper that parses bytes as JSON and pushes the resulting value onto the Lua stack. `lua_json_to_native` reuses it with `verbose=1` (the bridge path is loud on parse failure — a cross-language wire that doesn't parse is a real wire error worth surfacing).\n  - `lua_invoke` branches per input: NATIVE (or NULL slice-2 callers) push raw bytes via `lua_pushlstring`; JSON tries `parse_json_to_stack` with `verbose=0` and falls back to `lua_pushlstring` on parse failure. The silent fallback is what keeps backward compatibility with C / Bash producers that don't yet emit real JSON.\n  - Output-side branching on `output_native` deferred to slice 4.5 — that one's a coordinated change across all specs plus the dispatch's per-call format computation. Documented in the issue's \"what's still ahead.\"\n- `tests/maps/hello/src/hello.lua` — added `M.sum_pair(t)` that returns `tostring(t.a + t.b)`. Used by the slice-4 test to verify that a JSON `{\"a\":17,\"b\":25}` input arrives as a Lua table the function can index into.\n- `tests/306-lua-spec-test.c` — three new tests: `invoke_json_input` (JSON table parses to a usable Lua table, returns \"42\"), `invoke_native_input_with_flag` (NATIVE flag keeps the raw-string path, `greet(\"World\")` still returns \"Hello, World!\"), `invoke_json_input_falls_back_to_raw` (non-JSON bytes with JSON flag fall back to raw bytes — `greet(\"World\")` still works even with `input_native[i]=0`).\n\nFull suite still green: 22 slot-store, 14 graph-loader, 7 dispatch, **8 lua-spec (up from 5)**, 11 c-spec, 5 bash-spec, 5 lua-bridge, 11 integration tests including the multi-language `pipeline` map. Same-language Lua-Lua wires already skip JSON encode/decode (slice 3); cross-language Lua reads now properly parse JSON input when the producer emits it (slice 4); output-side coordinated format is the next coordinated piece.\n\nWant to proceed to slice 4.5 (the output-side coordinated format change across Lua / C / Bash + dispatch), or pause to think about something else first?"

        "text":"Got it, less code-shaped detail, more plain English. The design's done; I'll just walk through what's happening at the human level.\n\n**Slice 4.5: outputs honor the per-call format choice.**\n\nWhat's changing:\n\n1. **The dispatch checks, before each box runs, whether every downstream consumer shares the box's language.** If yes, the box gets a green light to write in its fast native form. If even one consumer is in a different language, the box has to write JSON (slow but readable by anyone).\n2. **The Lua spec now writes JSON when told to.** It already knows how to turn Lua values into JSON (that machinery was built earlier for the cross-language bridges). Slice 4.5 just wires it into the spec's main output path.\n3. **The push side stops second-guessing the producer.** It used to look at each outgoing wire separately and pick a ring per wire. Now: producer wrote in one format, every consumer gets that format. Simpler, and correct because the format was decided based on the whole consumer set."

          "new_string":"    /* Resolve the box's source file relative to map_dir. */\n    char *ref_path = b->ref ? resolve_path(ctx, b->ref) : NULL;\n\n    /* Slice 4.5 of issue 312: pick the box's output format once, at\n     * call time.
